en: (1a) Oṃ, salutations to the gurus beginning with Śiva!
May [the Goddess] protect you— she whose fierce, loud, and boisterous laughter is like the great roar at the end of the destruction of Kāla’s Kāla.
Armed with bone upon bone, she is ablaze with the most terrifying and fierce *Aghora* mantras;
she possesses a flood of streaming rays of light that overflow from the eighty-one paths of the sun,
and she is as fierce as the Night of Doom (*Kālarātri*), rending the ten directions with the bursting of her seals (*mudrā*) and the explosion of her mass of splendor.
May she protect [us]—she who is formidable and terrifying, whose interior is filled with the coils of the serpent-king, whirling, stainless, and quivering;

whose movement is radiant, having subdued the agitation of the Kula through the fierce tongues of the five-faced one; she who roars dreadfully, having seized the soldiers of worldly existence, and possesses the fearsome cries of Bhairavī.

She whose every pore incessantly sheds hundreds of thousands of fires of cosmic destruction, as she shakes her head with the thunderous clashing of her tossing, excellent crest-lock, which delivers piercing blows that shatter the pure, great *hāra* necklace worn by all those subject to the three times.

May she protect you—she who is bold with the radiant light of her head, which is adorned by the circle of the moon; she who, as if oppressed by the weight [of her own splendor], causes her own body to crackle and pop with a *caṭacaṭa* sound;
and whose six-cornered seed-vessel was shattered high above by the impact of her fierce descent.
Rising from that anger, she devours this world with her five mouths during the five nights;
she is Māyā, eternally black-bodied and stainless, who measures out her own time.
With eyes rolling in rage, she is filled with a great, terrifying, and agitated *huṃ* sound.
In the great *vāḍava* fire of the ocean of the exhaustion of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, there is lamentation;
having performed [this], they dance at the junction of the right and left channels where the fire, moon, and sun have arisen in the center.
She joyfully sounds the loud drum of the tree of pure *sattva*.
May that Bhairavī protect you— she whose form is terrifying with her attire consisting of corpses being devoured by ravens,
who wields the sword of consciousness, and who bears the weight of the six thousand masters of the six chakras and their foundations.
May she protect you—she who exists as the essence of semen within the sun, who likewise moves as the moon within the wheel of the wind;
she who is known by the name Parā, adorned by the moonlight upon the head of the one crowned with the crescent;
she whose playful consciousness is curved and fierce, arising from the root of the skeleton of Time.
May she protect you— she whose foot-strike shattered the fierce, throbbing wheel of all the haughty gods, causing them to fall and utter a great roar upon the earth;
and who, like Kālī, has mastered the eighty-one varieties of magical arts as if they were newly acquired.
She is the terrible one, whose form is bone, who delights in the path of the thirty gods, consisting of seven times seventeen syllables;

she is Kādyā, joined with Kaṅkāla, the digit of the lotus of the Kula, Kālikā, whose corner is the root; she is Kaṅkālī, who impels time, the digit of the Kula and Nakula, the wise one, stationed at the bolt.
May she protect you— she whose playful notes are like the warbling of peacocks, who, through her arts, gradually seizes the skull-bowl from the hands of Kāla,
the enemy of Kāma; she who, having heard [the praise] from Maheśvara, the God of gods, once again [bestows grace].
The *Jayadrathatantrarāja* consists of eighteen thousand [verses].
Again, the Goddess asked about the secret of the *Rāviṇīkrama*.
The Śrīdevī said:
O God of gods, I have heard the unsurpassed Triṣaṭka,
which is endowed with the potency of mantra, filled with many secrets,
abounding in various wonders, essential, and most marvelous.
Now I wish to hear the fourth, most excellent hexad:
how did that goddess Rāviṇī proceed through the eighty-one words?
O Lord of Gods, what rites do they accomplish when performed?
The potency of the mudrās, along with its secret, is not understood in this tantra.
How many mudrās are there? What is a mudrā? And how does their potency abide?
"In which [state] is there prosperity? O Lord, how do the mantras of the practitioners succeed?
Which goddess will grant her presence to whom?
Having heard this, the Lord of the Gods appeared in the terrifying form of Bhairavī.
Having entered [the body] through the power of the mudrās, having loosened and bound the sequence [of the channels],
and having churned the multitude of gods and consumed the essence of the five nectars,
the Supreme Lord, resorting to the family of Rāviṇī, spoke.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! That which you have now asked me is for the sake of the victory and welfare of the heroes, O Maheśvarī."

I shall proclaim the tradition of Mudrās, together with its secret teachings, exactly as it exists— the incomparable great secret born from the lotus-mouth of Hara, the matchless and peaceful doctrine which was obtained by me from Śiva in the past.
Listen to that, O highly fortunate lady; today I shall tell you of that Śiva, the supreme cause, who is the ultimate liberation,
who is free from existence and non-existence, and whose form transcends the six paths.
The Supreme Consciousness is of a perfectly tranquil nature, all-pervasive, and free from conceptualization;
it is eternally satisfied, omniscient, and the agent of all. Its potency is a great secret, its true form arising from the principle of inherence.
By him, that entire wondrous universe is sealed;
yet through the piercing [of consciousness], it assumes its own form. This process follows the application of various functions, such as attraction, fierceness, tranquility, and their combinations.
Such would be his energy of sealing; he is undivided, yet slow in his vigor.
O Daughter of the Mountain, that [energy] is to be understood as fivefold according to the distinction of its functions.
Through the distinctions of mind, speech, and body, and through the divisions of painting and clay modeling—
thus indeed is vigor differentiated as it is correctly taught.
And for the first, which is complete, it is simply the radiance of consciousness.
Through the continuous cultivation of that [state], according to the distinctions of the peaceful, the fierce, and so forth— namely, the erotic,
the heroic, the loathsome, the comic, the pathetic, and the furious—
and by means of the abiding within the internal aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) consisting of those [emotions], indeed through the power of that immersion;
First, that has been fully described; now, through its further divisions, it reaches infinity.
O Goddess, this very [speech] proceeds as the second, which is now being told:
Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, which is the fourth.
Their manifestation has been explained according to the divisions of the Mātṛkā;
the second [chapter] has been well-proclaimed, and now the third is being stated:
through abiding under the influence of the immersion into aesthetic flavor (rasa), there is the taking hold of the form of the deity.
In the Karadṛṣṭi [view], the third limb is like consciousness (cit) and consists of density (ghanatva).
Now, O Goddess, hear properly the fourth [limb] as it truly exists:
the form of the deity, beginning with the lotus and so forth, along with the trident, sword, thunderbolt, and the hosts [of attendants].

O Mother of the Gaṇas, that fifth variety of *vīrya* is declared to be the manifestation itself, arising from the fivefold distinctions of color and so forth, and appearing in the forms of a mass, a gem, a sacrificial oblation (*caru*), a substance, and an earthen vessel.
Thus, in every case, that which is called Mudrā is established as manifest within the sacred seat (pīṭha).
That Śāmbhava [state], which possesses great potency, must indeed be followed;
by this very potency of the Sun, Bhairavī becomes all the Mudrās.
Therefore, no distinction whatsoever should be made here within the interior of the vajra.
It is declared that the mudrā known as Prapāna arises from the divisions of the Mudrā-tantra;
O highly fortunate one, it unfolds, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The Mahāmudrā is called Kapālā, and likewise another is Gītimudrā;
the one called Makārā is Mahāghorā, and likewise another is Padmamudrā.
Likewise, there is one named Pañcaśikhā, and another called Karoṭikā;
also the very fierce Muśala and the terrible Mudgara;
likewise another known as Loṣṭhaka, and the mighty Vajramudrā.

The sword-mudrā belongs to Sureśānī; likewise, the bhuśuṇḍī and the tomara. There are the prāsāda-mudrā, the cakra-mudrā, the great matsya, the duṣṭātakī, the one called kacchapa, the boat-mudrā, and another called the vimāna.
By that [means], there are the mudrās known as Patākā, Jvālinī, and Phalā;
likewise Mukula, the one called Kalaśā, and the Chatra-mudrā;
furthermore, Mahāyogeśvarī and another, Mahāvyomā.
The Triśūla-mudrā is difficult to behold, as are the others, such as the Asurabhīti;
likewise the Mṛga-mudrā, another, and the Yoni-mudrā. The mistress of mudrās named Sumanā is proclaimed as the Ekaliṅgā.
And the snake [mudrā] called Ulūka, the corpse-mudrā (śavamudrā) of great power;
likewise the vessel-mudrā (pātramudrā), the horse-mudrā (aśvamudrā), and the boar-mudrā (vārāhikā);
the mudrā named Siṃhavaktrā, and likewise another, Viśālikā.
Siddhirohā, Mahāmudrā, and likewise Yogavajrā;
the Mahāmudrā known as Śamvara, and that which is remembered as Vajrasūcī; the one named Mahāmāyā, and the one called Śāntā, as well as Karttarī.
Likewise, O Dear One, there are Svamaṅgalā, Mudrā, and Praṇatā;
Jyeṣṭhā, Kāmarohā, and another, Śaṃkarā; the one called Samaya, Mahāmudrā, and yet another, Namaskārī.
The mudrā named Prabhakṣaṇī, another called Mahātārkṣī,
as well as Vikaṭhā, Bhīṣaṇā, and Bhairavī,
O Dear One; likewise Kāmarūpā, and another, the Sūcīmudrā, which is most formidable.
(3b) Another great protection, the Vajrapañjara, is likewise [taught].
The Sūrpamudrā, the Karaṭā, and the Kaṃbumudrā are thus remembered.
And Vicitrā is likewise proclaimed, as well as Surohiṇī; O Maheśvarī, the great mudrā called Karaṅkā, Kṣurikā,
the mudrā named Pāśapātra, and likewise Saṃgrāmaneśvarī.
Mudreśvarī is known as Vicitrā, and another is called Cañcalā;
the Mistress of Mudrās named Capalā is proclaimed, and another is celebrated as Kāntā.
Sumudā is to be known as another, as well as Bhṛkuṭī and Paramāmṛtā.
The heroine is Kālakarṇī, and the mudrā is Viśvamukhī, who is supreme.
Rohiṇī is the mistress of mudrās, considered the supreme Citramālā;
she is also proclaimed as Kabaṃdhī, and another is Mokṣaṇī.
The one called *nāda*, another known as *mūrcchanī*, and another remembered as *kaṃpanī*; likewise another called *dhruvā*, another *mudrā*, and another *visarjanī*;
the great *mudrā* called *parikīrṇā*, and another supreme *ānandī*.
O Dear One, there is Vyomacārī Mahāmudrā and likewise Viśvasūcī;
there is the mudrā named Saptaśikhā and another called Cāmarā;
one should know the one named Vitānā, and another is Manoruhā.
Svaśāntā is proclaimed as the foremost; Bhogahastā is another;
Kroṣṭrakī and Śivā are likewise, and Viśālākṣā is another, O Dear One.
Vitānā is to be known, and likewise another, Manoharā.
In the same way, the mudrā named Aṃśumatī is remembered as the attractor;
likewise, Daṃṣṭriṇī, Lelihānā, and another, Phetkārikā;
Karaṅkiṇī, Khecarī, and Bhairavī are remembered as supreme.
Ṣaṇmukhā, Divyamudrā, Bhairavā, Vikṛtānanā,
Mattavikā by name, and another known as Āviddhā.
She who is known as Mahāsaṃrāviṇī is remembered as the leader of them all.
One hundred and twenty-one mudrās have been proclaimed;
they should be understood as being elevenfold each, and that is how they are further remembered.
Furthermore, through their divisions, those [mudrās] are proclaimed to be infinite in the *Mudrāpīṭha*.
Their wondrous power, following the sequence of these [teachings], has been thoroughly investigated in the *Vīryatantra*, the supreme *Śiracchida* among the *Tattvas*.
I shall declare that by which one becomes a hero who speaks the essence of all the Āgamas and is uniquely worshiped in the entire lineage of yogis.
Thus [ends] the fourth hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra (*Mahātantra*) of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraccheda* of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavasrotas*.
The first chapter in the Mudrācandra.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, O Supreme Goddess, I shall fully explain the mudrās.

O Great Goddess, I have told you the ritual procedure along with its secret, as well as the sequence of binding mantras, which has not been declared to anyone else in the compendiums of tantra. By knowing this, O Goddess, even one who is in any state whatsoever attains accomplishment.
O auspicious lady, he who is not born beloved and honored by all the goddesses—
though he be initiated, engaged in austerity and yoga, and devoted to the recitation of mantras—
he shall not attain success if he is separated from these [goddesses].
Therefore, O daughter of the Lord of Mountains, hear this classification of them:
the two hands are joined together with their palms facing upward; by joining the fingers so they are slightly apart, the right thumb is placed on top.
All these, mutually embraced, are this supreme Mahāmudrā;
she should be known as the bestower of great accomplishment and the means for accomplishing the Great Mantra.
She delights the entire triple world when bound; of this there is no doubt.
(4b) At the beginning of all, in the middle of all, at the end of all, and within all,
the Mahāmudrā should be bound for the accomplishment of all desired aims.
O Goddess, when combined with the previously mentioned vigor and employed through the great mantra,
the practitioner indeed flies up within six months to the state of a Khecarī.
Through the application of the binding of this Mistress of Mudrās, his greatness is perfected.
Because it indeed possesses greatness, therefore the mudrā is called Mahāntikī.
Thus ends the Mahāmudrā in the Jayadrathayāmala. Now, the one known as Kapālā, which draws forth nectar, is being described.
Having placed the left hand face upwards with the fingers extended,
and having joined it at the tip of the mouth by beholding the primordial potency,
one should cause the nectar— the wheel adorned with sixteen digits— to melt.
Having contemplated [the deity] melting there, one should satiate the entire universe.
By means of this, one should properly attract [the deity] into one's own body through the continuous flow.
O highly fortunate one, one should draw forth me, who am sealed by the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).

Having given that very vessel to the Goddess, he himself should drink from it. At that moment, O Great Goddess, the practitioner becomes a leader of the circles (cakranāyaka), a sky-farer (khecarī) who floats in the void; of this there is no doubt.
O Gaurī, by binding this [mudrā], the circle of Mothers is pleased;
whatever exceeds the form of Brahmā (the ritual procedure) is all fulfilled in an instant.
Thus ends the Jayadrathakapāla-mudrā.
Then, having made her eyes beautiful with their inner corners slightly closed,
she should cause both creeper-like eyebrows to quiver with a mere hint of joy; indeed,
she should smile faintly, reflecting upon his former prowess.
By joining the little fingers and the middle finger of this hand, one should press those three together; this is known as the Gīti-mudrā.
Having bound this [mudrā], one should chant the Caryāsong or the Samaya;
and I shall explain that correctly—listen, O beautiful one, according to the truth:
"Ho ho Ghoreśvarī" and so forth, followed again by the word "hā ca hā ca."
Having extracted the syllable *haṃ haṃ haṃ*, O Vīrasundarī, one should join it;
having joined the syllable *hāḍa* three times, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and very long [in vowel],
this twenty-four-syllabled Sāman is the Great Melā, which bestows success.
He is the one who is capable of making the great, distant obstacles formidable and terrifying;
he is the one who, like Kālī, Kaṅkālī, Bhairavī, and Kālamātṛ, consumes the flesh and blood of the unborn.
Indeed, he is the devourer of the marrow and fat of those very [beings].
Magañjasu, Akhiṇi, Bhairavī, Kālī, and Pramattī—
having thus [recited] the *Gā* syllable, one should then recite the *Sāman*.
Then, O Dear One, his *melāpa* occurs within a watch (*prahara*).
If one practices this mudrā alone for six months in the house, O Goddess, then one attains the state of moving through the sky; of this there is no doubt.
By binding this [mudrā], O Goddess, one should gratify the circle of Mothers.

Thus ends the *Gītimudrā* in the *Jayadratha*. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the auspicious *Makarākhyamahāmudrā*, which is supreme for destroying obstacles and bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhis*).
O Queen of the Gods, one should firmly press the *jyeṣṭhā* (thumbs) together with both hands;
then, one should press the *tarjanīs* (index fingers) obliquely upon the backs of those [thumbs].
Furthermore, having extended the two *aṅguṣṭhas* (thumbs), which are joined together, toward the navel.
This mudrā, called Makara, is the destroyer of all [obstacles].
It is the supreme mudrā that causes bursting open, strikes terror, and terrifies all who cause harm.
O Great Goddess, by binding this, the mantras of men indeed become accomplished.
O noble lady, the deities indeed protect one who is free from obstacles.
Thus has this mudrā for the protection of the mantra been fully explained to you.
Thus ends the Makāra-mudrā in relation to Jayadratha.
Now, therefore, O fair-eyed one, I shall fully explain the Padma-mudrā,
by which the Vidyā attains proximity to the Lord of the Lords of Mantras.
The wrists of both hands are joined together;
the two thumbs are extended and bent, while the fingers are joined with their joints slightly separated.
O Goddess, this is the Padma-mudrā, as it truly is, which has been described to you.

O Goddess, by binding this [mudrā], one may describe the incomparable enjoyment and fortune established throughout the three worlds; of this there is no doubt. When one practices the mudrā through the power of its primordial vigor (*pūrvavīrya*), [the result follows].
Within three months, that man shall attain the knowledge of yoga;
thus bound, all the Bhairavas always remain present.
All the hosts of Vidyās and Mantras [obey] the lord of practitioners as he desires.
The Procedure for the Lotus Seal (*padmamudrā*) in relation to Jayadratha:
Therefore, O Daughter of the Mountain, hear now of the seal named Pañcaśikhā.
It is that which attracts all things, provides the enjoyment of yoga, and bestows perfect accomplishment.
Make the two hands inverted with the palms facing upward and the fingers bound like braids. The ring fingers should be joined at their tips and pressed crosswise against the middle fingers;
the thumbs should touch them, and the hands should be adorned by being positioned obliquely.
When this is performed, O Goddess, beloved, the five-crested mudrā arises.
O beautiful one, that which is remembered as the most excellent jewel of the world of moving and non-moving beings— good fortune, the continuity of enjoyments, knowledge, and the mind— is attained.
One should draw [the vital energy] by means of the power of the former virility; of this there is no doubt.
Such a mudrā as this, which deludes the three worlds, does not exist at all.
O slender-waisted one, it should be known as the bestower of great fortune and the giver of liberation.
(6a) Thus ends the *Pañcaśikhā* [tantra] concerning Jayadratha.
Now, I shall further explain another [tantra], the *Bhairavī* named *Karoṭī*.

The Sarvasampatkari-mudrā bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. The wise practitioner should interlace the fingers of the two hands with their palms turned inward, then cover the palms and press them together.
This mudrā is named Karoṭī; by pressing the outer thumbs with it,
this mudrā destroys the flood of sins that has been accumulated,
as well as the mass of great transgressions and whatever violation of the *samaya* has occurred.
This [knowledge] destroys all that, just as the rising sun destroys darkness;
when one endowed with the aforementioned heroic power binds [the breath] in the temple of Bhairava,
O Goddess of the lords of gods, then one becomes a partaker of the *melāpa*.
Thus ends the *karoṭībandha* in the case of Jayadratha.
Now listen to the supreme *mudrālākṣā*, which strikes fear into wicked beings;
it utterly crushes whatever infinite host of obstacles there may be.

O Goddess of the Gods, when the wrists are well-joined, with the fingers forming a circle around the palms and the face raised upward, this is the mudrā known as the Musala (Mace). It crushes the peaks of mountains and rends the seven netherworlds.
She is the crusher of all the wicked, the destroyer of calamities; she is the one who tears asunder the *kṛtyā* and the *khākhoda*, the subduer of *bhūtas* and *vetālas*;
she is the crusher of evil lordly serpents and the bringer of destruction to wicked misfortunes.
One shall slay the host of enemies, who are equal to one's foes; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the *muśala-mudrā* in the *Jayadratha*. Listen now to this *mudgara-mudrā*, which is intent on terrifying the three worlds.
And that which subdues everything and crushes even what is like a mountain:
the two hands, with their fingers joined, are brought together and applied;
one should move this mudrā, known as the Hammer (mudgara), again and again.
Endowed with former vigor, he should show his fangs as a living being;
by the mere sight of them, he destroys the heat [of the poison]— of this there is no doubt.
By the mere sight [of this], it destroys the poisons of planets and serpents;
it crushes and dissolves [all] calamities, and even subdues mountains.
It destroys every fear of the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Mudgara-mudrā regarding Jayadratha.
Now, O fair-eyed one, listen as I shall fully describe to you this mudrā called Loṣṭha, which strikes fear into the wicked.
Having raised the right hand and then brought it close together,
one should join the thumbs over the fingers;
O Goddess, all the fingers thus joined are known as the Loṣṭha-mudrā of great power.

He brings under his control the world, including gods, asuras, and humans. O Goddess of the Gods, when the practitioner is endowed with vigor and free from all affliction, then, O Goddess, he shall bind the entire world under his sway.
My word is indeed true, there is no doubt;
there is no other seal like this one, O Goddess, which destroys the wicked and bestows the accomplishment of the Great Melāpa. It has been fully described to you.
Thus ends the *loṣṭhamudrā* in the case of Jayadratha.
Now, I shall describe this supreme mudrā called the *vajra*, by means of which,
when fully mastered, the practitioner of mantra becomes endowed with all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
When the hands are formed in reverse by joining the extended fingers,
one should interlock them with the little finger and the thumb;
joined with the previous vigor, this becomes the Vajra-mudrā.
It should be employed as a treasury-store and likewise for the accomplishment of the *kaṅkāla* [mantra].
This [mantra] burns away mantras employed by others, without a doubt;
it consumes the entire flood of sins and all transgressions of the rules (*samaya*) and so forth.
This mudrā utterly destroys [all obstacles], just as the sun destroys the darkness of night;
it should be known as the bestower of victory in battle and the opener of all the underworlds.
"By means of the great assembly and by the power of former vigor.
Thus ends the Vajra-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-tantra].
Now, O Pārvatī, I shall describe this mudrā known as the Sword (khaḍga).
One should repeatedly move the hand raised upwards.
The three fingers should be directed upward and pressed by the thumb and little finger;
this is declared to be the Sword Mudrā (khaḍgamudrā), which cuts through the multitude of misfortunes.
She is the terrifier of all the wicked, the supreme concealer,
the crusher of the pride of the multitudes of obstacles, and the one who strikes fear into the three worlds.
Within three days, she brings about the gathering at the cremation ground.
O Goddess, this arises for the practitioner alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
As many kinds of fears as there may be, she destroys them all.
O Goddess, when she is bound [in meditation], no flaw in the mantra occurs.
The enemies who have approached to slay him perish.
Thus ends the sword-mudrā for Jayadratha.
Now, therefore, I shall describe the axe [mudrā], which destroys all obstacles.
The destroyer of all wicked ones, it increases the welfare of the three worlds.
Raising one arm upward with the nose, one should extend the other hand horizontally;
O Goddess, shaking it repeatedly, this is the mudrā known as the axe (paraśu).
It shall destroy the multitude of obstacles such as *kṛtyā* and *khārkhoda*, and it shall bring about the binding [of enemies]. It pacifies great delusion, eradicates all misfortune,
destroys the faults of all impurities, and bestows the quality of all-encompassing vigor.
By this, the mantra shall become effective for the practitioners according to their desire.
Thus ends the paraśu-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
O Dear One, I shall now describe this mudrā named Bhuśuṇḍī,
by which obstacles are destroyed and the recitation becomes fruitful.
One should form its fist just as one would with an axe.
O Supreme Goddess, the *ūrddhagā* is proclaimed as *bhusuṇḍī*;
through its excellent union with the power of the east, it is supreme in dispelling obstacles.
Having bound this [mudrā], O Sovereign Lady, one greatly pleases the Supreme Lord.
It should be employed for the accomplishment of the Vetāla and in rites of great attraction;
whatever rite belongs to the cremation ground, one should apply it in each such instance.
Then it succeeds without a doubt—this is the certainty of the scripture.
Thus ends the *bhuśuṇḍī* mudrā in relation to Jayadratha.
Now, O Maheśvarī, hear this mudrā called *tomara*,
by which the practitioner may always become worthy of all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).

Having formed the left hand into a bud-like shape and positioned it obliquely along with the arm, while grasping the right arm—this is the mudrā known as the Tomara. It is supreme for the accomplishment of Vetālas; there is nothing like it anywhere.
Endowed with the primordial seed-syllable, she is the one who grants the fulfillment of all desires.
There is no mudrā in this world that she would not propitiate.
Mahāmudrā is the possessor of enjoyments, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
If she is always accompanied by the mantra, she quickly brings about union;
O Goddess, staying in the cremation ground, she binds [the target]—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the procedure for the *tomara* mudrā in the *Jayadratha[-yāmala]*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Prāsa-mudrā, which possesses great power;
by the mere binding of which the practitioner becomes a possessor of all siddhis.
This shall certainly happen, there is no doubt; my word is not false.
With the two index fingers on the left thumb and the little finger bent,
while the middle fingers are extended and joined— this shall be the *prāsa* mudrā.
Having bound this [mudrā], the Great Hero, relying on his former heroic power,
is beheld by all beings who resemble ten thousand fires of cosmic destruction;
these various classes of spirits and vetālas fall into a state of great delusion.
In the doctrines of mining, the doctrines of sacred fields, the doctrines of mantras, and those concerning the nature of the underworld (*vilātmake*),

as well as in the essences of medicinal herbs and so forth, this mudrā should be employed to bestow the fruit of accomplishment. O Dear One, one should employ this mudrā when all ritual actions have been successfully perfected.
O Goddess, they attain accomplishment at that very moment; there is no falsehood in these words.
Thus ends the *prāsa-mudrā* in the *Jayadratha[-kalpa]*. Now I shall describe the *cakra-mudrā*, accompanied by the entire assembly of Mothers.
By the mere binding of which all obstacles are destroyed:
the two hands, joined firmly at the wrists and crossed over,
are rotated until the release of the clenched fists, and then extended outward once more.
Again and again, this wheel-mudrā is prescribed by its very nature for the purpose of distinguishing all mudrās, for warding off wind and lightning,
for the restraint of clouds, and for the accomplishment of great protection.
The fierce Damanī of the planets destroys all evil-doers;
she pacifies great delusion and bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the Cakramudrā in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
Henceforth I shall describe the Fish Seal (matsyamudrā), which is exceedingly powerful and by which the Lord of Gods is pleased with the high-souled practitioner.
Listen to that, O highly fortunate one; it is another seal beloved of the Mothers.
With the right hand behind and the left hand held horizontally with the fingers joined,
and with both hands turned upward and inverted, by moving both thumbs,
this Matsya-mudrā (Fish-seal) is formed; it is intended for purification.
Among all purifying things, even regarding drinks and foods,
there is nothing more fulfilling than the acquisition of wealth obtained according to the prescribed rule and not in excess.
They satisfy all the deities according to how they have been gratified within the maṇḍala.
She is the mother of all prosperity, the bestower of the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation;
endowed with primordial power, she is remembered as the performer of all rites.
Thus ends the Matsya-mudrā in relation to Jayadratha.
Now, O lady of excellent vows, I shall describe the mudrā known as Kacchapa (the Tortoise),
which fulfills the sacrifice and other rites, and bestows great siddhi upon men.
Having placed the left hand facing downwards and the right hand upon it,
one should draw the index finger (tarjanī) of the right hand down over the downward-facing middle finger (madhyamā) of the left;
one should place the tip of the thumb (jyeṣṭhāgra) against that finger, while the remaining fingers are arranged in the shape of a foot.
One should perform the entry and exit [of breath]; this mudrā is named the Tortoise (Kacchapa).
O Dear One, it is the destroyer of the *ceṭakas* as well as the *kiṅkaras*.
It is beloved by all goddesses and is always dear to the Goddess of the Gods.

O Pārvatī, whatever substance a man offers in sacrifices and other rites, this Goddess fulfills it all; there exists nowhere anyone equal to her. She is the Mistress of the Supreme Mudrā, who bestows the perfection of the union through *haṭha*.
Endowed with former vigor, she is the source of the arising of all prosperity and virtues.
Thus ends the *kacchapa-mudrā* in the *Jayadratha*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra.
O highly fortunate one, this is the *potamudrā*, the support of all, possessed of great power.
The auspicious fingers are extended, resting upon the palm and slightly bent;
the two index fingers are raised, while the thumbs remain positioned below them.
This is declared to be the Potamudrā, by which the deities are seen,
all the Gaṇas dance, and they become honored.
It should be known as the bestower of all good fortune, granting the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
She is the savior from all difficulties and the liberator from all calamities;
she is proclaimed by you as the destroyer of the faults of great sins.
She is declared to be the accomplisher of *japa* and is remembered as the fulfiller of the ritual injunctions.
Thus ends the *pāta-mudrā* in the *Jayadratha*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the *mudrā* that grants the accomplishment of all aims.

The great secret known as Vimāna bestows the power of traveling through the sky. When the thumbs are firmly bent and placed upon the joints of the middle fingers which are turned upward, the Vimāna mudrā is always perfectly formed.
This Mahāmudrā has been proclaimed as the great beloved of the ḍākinīs. When I have performed it even once, the messengers dance with joy.
Endowed with former vigor, she bestows the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation.

The goddess Harṣā dances; she is the delighted mistress of practitioners. O Goddess of gods, when she is always worshipped and gratified, she indeed becomes present. She should be employed in the practice of the sky and in the rite of the great assembly (mahāmelāpaka).
"This is that liberating sequence which has now been made ready for you.
Thus ends the *vimānamudrā* in the case of Jayadratha.
Now I shall fully explain that by which the deities are perceived.

The goddess named Netrā is the mistress of mudrās and the accomplisher of omniscience. When the index fingers of both hands are extended and the remaining fingers are likewise joined with the palms facing inward, that is the [Netrā] mudrā.
This mudrā is called Netrā; it bestows the vision of omniscience. When this is bound, O Gaurī, the Supreme Lord is seen.
If one practices for seven days with the application of the previously mentioned vigor, [the result is attained].
Pierced by the essence of its cultivation, one shall attain the state of omniscience;
this has been fully revealed in you, the supreme tantra, the Jayadratha.
Thus ends the procedure for the Eye-Seal (*netramudrā*) regarding Jayadratha.
O Gaurī, hear now of the mighty Seal for traveling through the sky;
it is the Seal known as the Banner (*patākā*), which accomplishes omniscience.
Having extended the index finger while holding the left hand in a fist,
the right hand is moved sideways with its fingers spread apart;
this is that auspicious mudrā known as the Patākī.
Endowed with the aforementioned vigor, one should always perform the binding in the cremation ground.
O Goddess of the gods, within seven days a man shall attain the *melaka*;
that mortal becomes a *khecarī*, bringing forth a great abundance of enjoyments.
A mudrā equal to this has not been proclaimed in the three worlds;
endowed with former vigor and permeated by rasa and bhāva,
it should be known as the performer of all rites for the high-souled practitioner.
Thus ends the ritual for the banner in the case of Jayadratha.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain another mudrā called Jvālinī,
by which one may set ablaze the entire, endless web of obstacles.
O Goddess, O Beloved, she who effortlessly accomplishes the supernatural powers such as the foot-ointment (pādalepa) and others—
which pacify all obstacles and crush evil poverty—
should form the thumb upon the backs of both [hands].
When [the fingers] are joined and about to be performed, slightly trembling, curved, and extended—
this mudrā is known as the most excellent,
renowned as Jvālinī, which brings all sentient beings under control.
Projected by the previously mentioned seed-syllables and permeated by aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and emotional state (*bhāva*),
the practitioner accomplishes everything in its entirety through mere recollection.
Thus ends the *Jvālinī-mudrā* in the *Jayadratha[-yāmala]*.
I shall now explain the *halamudrā*; listen, O daughter of the Lord of Mountains, by means of which the lord of practitioners may ascend the mountain of great fortune.

O you who bring an end to sin, listen attentively to that which bestows great heroism. O Goddess, this plow held in her hand— specifically in the crooked ring-finger and the right thumb— is now revealed to you.
And through the power of the practitioner’s great fortune,
Hālī, who is situated between the ploughs, the driver of the plough, the mistress of the plough—
she whom he beheld in heaven as she was born— is indeed bound by him.
Upon seeing her, one becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*), endowed with mastery over all *cakras*.
Indeed, this supreme among all *mudrās* has been explained to you according to its true nature.
Thus ends the plow-mudrā (*halamudrā*) in the *Jayadratha*.
O beloved of the Vīrendras, listen to the Mahāmudrā known as Mukula;
by awakening to it, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, even hundreds of millions of mantras all become favorable to the practitioner in this world.
First, one should place the hand itself in the form of a bud at the region of the heart;
O fair-limbed one, by always keeping the elbow level and horizontal,
this [mudrā] called Mukula is accomplished, which grants success in the invocation of mantras.
When an enemy who has come to kill her arrives,
at that very moment this goddess bewilders the enemy with her power;
by the very strength of her former valor, she bestows the accomplishment of the forceful union (*haṭhamelāpa*).
Whatever accomplishment she seeks to achieve, she achieves it by force.
This mudrā is the sovereign mistress, bestowing the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation.
O you who are worshipped by the gods, I have not revealed this to anyone except for you.
The Goddess is beloved, the bestower of portions, the sovereign of all mantras. Thus ends the Mukula-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-tantra].
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Sarvārthakārikā.
The great mudrā called the Vase is another bestower of great good fortune. The fingers of both hands are joined at their tips.
Indeed, this [mudrā] known as Kalaśa, which is elsewhere called Madhyamā, is drenched with the essence of the nectar-stream; it is remembered as the bestower of the accomplishment of all aims.
[It is applied] when [the body] is cut, terrified, burnt, broken, obstructed, or perished.
O Goddess, there is no doubt that this [mantra] is known as the *āpyāyakī* (nourishing) for the mantra;
O Mistress of the God of Gods, one should consecrate oneself with it.
For that mantra, there will undoubtedly be nourishment (*āpyāyana*).
By the mere binding of this [mudrā], all the deities are gratified.
It should be known as the bestower of enjoyment and liberation; it has been correctly revealed to you. Thus ends the *kalaśa-mudrā* in the *Jayadratha[-yāmala]*.
Now I shall further explain another mudrā that accomplishes all aims,
which brings about the presence of all [deities], is known as the "Umbrella," and bestows both enjoyment and liberation:
one should form a fist with the left hand, and then extend the index finger upward.
Having placed it upon its back, either slightly apart or facing downward,
this mudrā is called the *chatrī*; it bestows the accomplishment of all aims,
is endowed with primordial power, and brings about the end of the three worlds.
She should be known as the bestower of great fortune, radiant with the qualities of all prosperity.
Thus ends the *chatramudrā* in the *Jayadrathayāmala*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which is called the *Mahāyogeśvarī*.
The Mudrā Gaurī is highly exalted and the most supreme among all mudrās.
Without her, no accomplishment arises in this tantra;
she draws forth unprecedented power from the great ocean of the Kālikula.
Having understood the *pañcaphalinī* [mudrā], one should perform the binding of the mudrās:
having placed both hands with the eight fingers extended, the [middle fingers] should emerge from the middle joints;
the two thumbs should be joined together, and the hands should be formed like the belly of a jar (*kumbhodara*).
(11a) At that time, O Dear One, the wheel takes on the form of the Goddess; it is the sole devourer that swallows the world,
making a roar as terrible as the sound of Māra, and its mudrā is most fearsome.
The Mistress of Yoga has been described to you as the sovereign of all the mistresses of mudrās;
devoid of her, a practitioner does not achieve success even with great effort.
For she performs all actions and is the destroyer of great sins.
O Goddess, by means of this [mudrā] when it is bound, union with the beloved occurs at that very moment.
As many mantra-tantras as there are, and those arising from the seeds of vidyās—all of them become subject to one's control here; of this there is no doubt.
When this [mudrā] is correctly bound, one blazes intensely and trembles greatly;
one is worshipped by the hosts of deities just like Paramabhairavī herself.
This must never be bound in the midst of the bound souls (paśus).
All fall down, become deluded, and die; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, having worshipped the Supreme Sovereign (Parameśānī) and being delighted by the joy of wine, she must always be bound at night in the cremation ground.
Then the practitioner rises with great speed into the sky along with the *khecarīs*.
What need is there for much speaking here? Nowhere—in the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), the seat of mantra (*mantrapīṭha*), or the seat of mudrā (*mudrāpīṭha*)—is there anything equal to this.
Thus ends the procedure for Jayadratha, the Great Mistress of Yoga.
O lady of beautiful hips, I shall now proclaim to you that which was previously mentioned by me as Mahāvyomā; listen as I speak.
By the mere binding of which the *khecarī* [mudrā] falls;
having made the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*) upward and inverted in the middle,
with the remaining two [little fingers] joined at the back and pressed together, they remain in the form of a pedestal (*pīṭha*).
Having thus brought the wind [into the body] as far as the *saṃjīvanī* channel,
O Goddess, one should send it forth again up to the twelfth station.
Thus one flies through the sky by the grace of Vyomeśvarī.
This [state] called Mahāvyoma has been correctly explained to you;
it is to be applied for traveling through space and is praised by all the *akhacarīs*.
She should be known as the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; what is the use of saying more?
Thus ends the Mahāvyomamudrā in the Jayadrathayāmala.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the mudrā of terrible prowess.
O Great Goddess, she is named the Trident, possessing secret mysteries and great power.
Having gathered the scent of intoxication, as far as the trident extends,
by means of the yoga bound to the three channels, the trident reaches the end of the twelve.
Having visualized [the deity] resembling a blazing fire, crowded with many sparks,
one should properly join the two hands together;
by joining the little fingers and the thumbs, the two index fingers (*viśā*) should be raised upward.
A very great spear, spread forth, which crushes all obstacles—
by the practice of yoga for one month, a man becomes a *khecarī* (a sky-walker),
endowed with all the qualities of supernatural powers and possessed of the eight *guṇas*.

O illustrious lady, by means of this bond, the bull-bannered God himself is seen in all the worlds as that Supreme Lord. O Goddess, by binding this [thread], the Ḍākas and the Ḍāmarikas likewise [are bound].
The sky-walkers (*khecarī*), those who drink from the crocodiles (*nakracūṣyā*), the *lāmās*, and the earth-walkers (*bhūcarī*)—
they remain there with their pride gone, for they become utterly deluded. All of them, such as Mahocchuṣmā and the rest, abide under his control.
This is proclaimed as the supreme of all mudrās, known by the name *triśūla*.
Thus ends the *śūlamudrā* in the *Jayadratha*.

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the auspicious mudrā named Surabhī, which bestows all nourishment and is known as the "Wish-Fulfilling Cow" (Kāmadhenu). The two hands are joined together with the fingers interlaced.
The middle finger of the right hand and the index finger of the left;
likewise, make the middle finger of the left and the index finger of the right extend to the tips.
The little finger and the ring finger [of one hand] should be joined with the ring finger and the little finger [of the other].
Having joined [the hands] and embraced them so that the thumbs are positioned at the base and middle [of the fingers],
and having thus bound [the mudrā] as the "Twelve-End" (dvādaśāntā), one should contemplate the Vidyā as it flows with the nectar-essence of Śiva’s moon,
reaching as far as the interior of the vast sky.
Thus, O fortunate one, this mudrā named Amṛtā has been described to you as "Surabhī. Having bound this, one should gaze upon all substances; indeed, they become filled with floods of pure nectar.
These become inexhaustible and infinite for the deities.
It destroys untimely death and annihilates the evil dreams of the Kali age.
Through the practice of yoga for six months, one becomes equal to Sadāśiva.
The attainment of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation arises for the practitioner.
Thus ends the Surabhi-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-tantra].
Now I shall fully explain the mudrās worshipped by the best of gods.
O illustrious Maheshvari, this is the auspicious mudrā named Mṛgī, which bestows all prosperity. It is formed by joining the tips of the thumbs with the middle and ring fingers;
the index and little fingers are extended and their digits are spread apart.
The Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) named Mṛgī bestows the complete accomplishment of all activities;
endowed with primordial vigor, she brings all sentient beings under her control.
She generates nourishment and good fortune, and is intent upon protecting the three worlds.
Furthermore, for practitioners, there shall be the attainment of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the *mṛgīmudrā* in the *Jayadratha*.
Henceforth, O fawn-eyed one, listen to the description of the mudrā known as Viśvayoni, which destroys great sins.
It is formed by joining the tips of the fingers in a loose, stringed-vīṇā-like binding.
Emerging from the left and passing behind to enter the interior of the right—
this is the Viśvayoni Mudrā, difficult to attain by those of unrefined self.
Endowed with primordial potency, it sets all sacrifices in motion.
It should be known as that which fulfills all rites and removes all misdeeds.
O Goddess, by binding this [mudrā], one becomes equal to Kāmadeva;
all women, afflicted by the fire of passion, become agitated.
He becomes fortunate and accomplished, just like Kāmeśvara himself.
Thus ends the Viśvayonimudrā in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
Hereafter, I shall explain the Liṅgamudrā of great power.

There is no other equal to her; she grants all accomplishments to human beings. She who satisfies the three worlds and even creates and destroys them—this Mahāmudrā is preeminent, the means for attaining the eight [siddhis] beginning with *aṇimā*.
O Pārvatī, this should be known as the mudrā that brings about the presence of the mantra-circle:
with the thumb of the left hand,
one should grasp the thumb of the right hand from within [the fingers].
Below the remainder, O slender-waisted one, a pedestal should be made;
this is called the Single Liṅga, the most excellent of all mudrās. There exists no mudrā equal to it within the interior of the world.
Endowed with former vigor, she is remembered as the attractor of all. There is no such thing here in this world that cannot be accomplished by her.
Thus ends the Ekaliṅga-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
(13a) Hereafter I shall proclaim [the teaching of] the Sovereign of all Sovereigns of Mudrās.
O lady of beautiful hips, listen now with a one-pointed mind as I proclaim it.
Grasping the forefinger of the right hand with the left,
and binding both thumbs together— this is proclaimed as the *paṃnagī* [mudrā].
O Maheśvarī, this should be employed during other planetary afflictions for the purpose of liberation.
She is the supreme provider of all protection, the destroyer of malevolent spirits and epilepsy;
she is remembered as the crusher of the pride of great sins and the attractor of all things.
Indeed, she neutralizes the three types of poison, such as that which is mobile and so forth.
She is proclaimed as the subduer of clouds, winds, and thunderbolts;
she is the subduer of the intoxicated lord of elephants and is intent upon the protection of the three worlds.
Thus ends the Pannagī-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mudrā of terrible prowess.
It is known as Ulūka, a great siddhi manifested through the yoga of the perfected ones.
Listen to it, O highly fortunate one; it is the awakener of all mudrās.
The fingers of the right hand are bent into a bud-like shape on one side,
while the thumb is lowered and bent; by displaying this movement,
it represents a hollow with eyes and a mouth that are exceedingly terrifying.

The mudrā named Ulūkinī is of that same form and is the destroyer [of obstacles]. Endowed with the power described previously, within six months one shall fly up into the expanse of the sky and indeed become omniscient.
O Goddess, by constant remembrance, one shall obtain all desires;
there is nothing that would not be accomplished through the power of this mudrā.
It pacifies great delusion and brings about the attainment of the powers such as *aṇimā*.
Subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, killing, and expulsion;
likewise, paralyzing, stunning, entering the body, and even destruction.

This mudrā, called Ulūka, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has been explained to you; when bound even once, it grants success in paralyzing ships, carts, machines, and the like, and in destroying enemies— it is the crusher of foes.
Thus ends the procedure for the Ulūka-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
Hereafter, I shall explain the Śava-mudrā, which is of great power;
by its complete mastery, the practitioner of mantra conquers Time as if in play.
Having half-closed the eyes and likewise distorted the face,
the pair of arms should be made limp and the neck likewise positioned;
this supreme Śavamudrā pacifies untimely death.
Endowed with the original seed-syllable, through the practice of six months of yoga,
the practitioner becomes a conqueror of death, just like Hari and Hara;
all rites are accomplished by this [mantra], there is no doubt regarding its binding power.
The great assemblies (*mahāmelāpaka*) and so forth will be accomplished; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus has the most excellent corpse-seal (*śavamudrā*) been fully explained to you.
Thus ends the corpse-seal in the *Jayadratha*.
Now, O lady with a vajra-like womb, I shall describe the horse-mudrā exactly as it is;
by binding this, the practitioner of mantra becomes a lord of the melāpaka.
Having assumed the form of a horse through the excellent sound of neighing, [one should perform the mudrā].
One should traverse the ground in a single moment, like a swift horse;
this, O Goddess, is the Aśvamudrā described to you according to its true meaning.
By means of this, every virtuous conduct arises within the practitioner’s self.
Through the attainment of great fortune, he becomes all-pervading like space;
even while staying in a cremation ground as if bound, he then attains the *melāpa*.
Indeed, that practitioner truly becomes one who is worshiped by the circle of *khecarīs*.
(14a) The attainment of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation arises; there is no doubt in this matter.
O Goddess, the horse-seal has thus been explained to you according to its true meaning.

Thus ends the ritual procedure for the horse-seal (*aśvamudrā*) regarding Jayadratha. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain this Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which brings the three worlds under control; listen now with a one-pointed mind.

His left arm is contracted, and his face is positioned between them; the right [arm] is extended wide below, clearly manifesting the shape of the letter *adhā*. The elbows are held high, bent in the *ālīḍha* posture.

This [goddess] is Mahāvarāhī; one should employ her at the beginning of sexual union and so forth. Endowed with the primordial potency (*pūrvavīrya*), she—worshipped by the sky-goers (*khecaras*)—attains union within six months.
"The attainment of higher and lower fruits arises for the souls of practitioners.
Thus ends the Vārāhī Mudrā in the Jayadratha [Yāmala].
Now listen, O Bhairavī, as I shall describe the most terrible Siṃha Mudrā.
By which perfection the practitioner of mantra becomes the lord of the world-protectors:
having filled the mouth with air, having made the eyes fixed on the interior [of the heart],
having drawn up the knees, and having placed both hands facing downward.
One should apply the two hands to the region of the face and move the gaze;
this is the great mudrā called Nṛsiṃha, capable of causing hatred in the world. Beyond this, no more terrible mudrā exists here in this world.
Therein [is] Pātālayatra, the destroyer of bhūtas and vetālas;
the supreme subduer of kṛtyās and khārkhodas, the driver away of nāgas,
the most excellent bestower of all prosperity, endowed with primordial power.
Bestowing enjoyment and liberation, the essence that grants the fruit of mantra-siddhi— thus ends the Siṃhamudrā in the Jayadratha[-yāmala]. (14b)

Henceforth, O Maheśvarī, hear of the mudrā of Viśālākṣī; by the mere knowledge of which, there is nothing in the three worlds that cannot be accomplished. She is eternally beloved by the world-protectors and is the supreme mistress of all mantras.

By means of the mouth that has been properly engaged throughout the day, she who is playful, with disheveled hair and expansive [form], is proclaimed as the protector of consciousness (*cidvipālā*). She destroys even the great sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin, even if they have grown deep within.
When ignited by the expenditure [of breath], she brings great joy to Mahādeva.
She is proclaimed as the bestower of all accomplishments for one who is devoid of all ritual actions and delights in worldly village-dharma; she is the initiator of mantra-yoga.
O ministers, there is nothing in the three worlds that is not [eternal].
This [mudrā] pleases all the gods and fulfills all sacrifices;
it is the essence of all mudrās, as has been declared to you according to its true nature.
Thus ends the procedure for the Viśālā-mudrā in relation to Jayadratha.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mudrā that is the most excellent of all;
it is named Siddhimohā, and it bestows great accomplishment upon human beings.
In a spacious place, one should visualize the circle of goddesses clad in various directions;
one should perform the rite of fire-offering (*homakarma*) with *mahākṣamāja*, *pala*, and other substances.
When one is fully empowered by that potency, it is proclaimed as the "ascent" (*rohā*) of perfect accomplishment.
The yogas of accomplishment (siddhiyoga) are proclaimed as superior, inferior, and middling;
the eightfold powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā) are accomplished through them—of this there is no doubt.
That practitioner of mantra who seeks the practice without knowing this [yoga]...
One afflicted by hunger might strike at the sky with his fist, or one tormented by thirst might try to crush chaff;
he who is parched with thirst will undoubtedly resort to the water of a mirage.
O Goddess, this very essence of the three worlds has indeed been revealed to you.
(15a) Thus ends the Siddhiroha in the Jayadratha[-yāmala]. O Bhairavī, listen now to the true nature of the mudrā called Yogamudrā.
O Bhairavī, hear that [mantra] by which, once perfected, the practitioner becomes the sovereign of the universe;
by which the Goddess enters the body of the lord of adepts—
[hear it], O highly fortunate one, you who are saluted by all the sky-farers.
Having entwined the middle fingers with the ring fingers and thumbs,
and having extended the middle fingers, the practitioner should join the two [thumbs] obliquely and upwards,
and bind it at the region of the bladder with a cloth from the cardinal directions.
The eight-limbed *praṇava* is proclaimed as the yoga-vajra;
there is no mudrā equal to this for the accomplishment of all purposes.
Indeed, by means of the spreading of all colors, they enter into the body of the Goddess.
O Goddess, the perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*) arises, which bestows perfection throughout the three worlds;
it is proclaimed as the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, and the giver of the perfection of the Great Assembly (*mahāmelāpa*). Thus ends the Yoga-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
Now, therefore, O Goddess, I shall explain to you according to the truth:
the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) known as Saṃvara, which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
By the practitioner smeared with all kinds of fragrances and clad in nothing but space...
With the hair on the crown of the head loose, joined with the emission of the *sītkāra* sound,
seated in the *kukkuṭāsana* posture, and reciting the mantra eight hundred times,
one should meditate upon the *padmaka* [mudrā]; this is to be known as the *śaṃvarā* mudrā.
She is proclaimed as the most supreme, bestowing the accomplishment of the great assembly (*mahāmelāpa*).
By means of this, one attains accomplishment within six months; there is no doubt about this.
Indeed, she is the very essence of all things, and thus has been described to you according to the truth.
O Goddess, every day from bondage, the wheel of goddesses undoubtedly attains direct manifestation for the practitioner;
of this there is no doubt.

One obtains all desires as well as the eightfold [siddhis] beginning with *aṇimā*. Thus ends the procedure for the Śaṃvara-mudrā in the *Dvayāratha*. Hereafter, I shall explain the terrifying Vajrasūcī.
O Goddess, one should constantly employ [this mudrā] in rites of great slaying.
Having made the hands interlaced and turned upward, wide and rotated,
and having settled firmly in the svastika posture, one should place [the hands] above that.
This very Vajrasūcī has been proclaimed for the purpose of renunciation;
it should be known as the bestower of yogic accomplishments and the destroyer of great sins.
From this place, one of great splendor is born, [attaining] a single greatness.
The Goddess of the lords of gods, accompanied by her retinue, grants delight;
she is renowned as the bestower of all desires, O Goddess—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the ritual for the Vajrasūcī in the Jayadratha [Kalpa].
O Maheśvarī, listen to this mudrā called Mahāmāyā,
by which the threefold union is perfectly and completely accomplished.
The two hands are interlaced in reverse, with the fingers of the back of the hands extended outward.
Through the practice of circumambulation, one who is composed and naked [in spirit] should move from the east toward the south,
turning with the two shanks;
this is the mudrā named Mahāmāyā, the most excellent of all.
The great accomplishment of the *saṃvara* arises for the practitioners themselves;
it is the most excellent means for bringing about good fortune and for warding off all calamities.
It brings about the perfect attainment of ascending to fortune and the crushing of malevolent beings.
In rites such as exorcism (uccāṭana) and others, there is nothing anywhere equal to this [mantra].
For one who has entered the abode of Hara, there shall be a supreme union;
through constant and excellent service, the threefold accomplishment arises eternally.
"There is nothing here in this world that cannot be accomplished by means of this [mudrā].
Thus ends the *māyāmudrā* in the *Jayadratha[-yāmala]*.

Now, O lady of beautiful hips, I shall describe to you this [mudrā] called Śāntā, which brings the three worlds under control, by means of which the practitioner attains success. Seated in the svastika posture, one should assume the mighty Bandha-mudrā.
When the left hand is extended and placed over it,
with the thumb likewise extended, this mudrā is the most excellent of all;
it constantly bestows sovereignty, grants sons, and increases good fortune.
In the Tantra, Sumaṅgalā is remembered as the one who brings about various forms;
she eternally bestows great peace and grants the fruit of all accomplishments.
[One should practice] in a delightful and pure place, filled with the fragrance of excellent incense.
One should practice this mudrā, which destroys all calamities.
Within six months, O Goddess of the Gods, a man becomes a *khecarī* (sky-walker);
endowed with the qualities of *aṇimā* and the rest, he becomes a creator and destroyer like the Lord himself.
The supreme among men becomes truly endowed with his former seed.
This principal of all mudrās has been explained to you according to its true meaning.
Thus ends the ritual for pacification in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which is known by the name Kartarī;
by means of which, when joined [to the hand], the practitioner of mantra becomes the fulfiller of all desires.
When the fingers are spread apart in the hand, positioned all around like a wheel—
O Goddess, this is proclaimed as the *kartarī* for subduing;
it is the subduer of *bhūtas*, *vetālas*, and *kṛtyās*, and the crusher of the *khārkhoda*.
O Supreme Sovereign, there exists no [mantra] equal to this for the purpose of suppression.
One endowed with former vigor [is required] for the accomplishment of a *kṛtyā* or a *vetāla*,
for piercing the eye and the sky, for the sale of human flesh and the like,
for the practice of sorcery (*indrajāla*), and likewise for the shattering of the three worlds.
(16b) Indeed, it may be employed for all rites; no deliberation is required in this matter.
Thus ends the *kartarī* mudrā in the case of Jayadratha.
I shall describe the *pramāṇamudrā*; listen, O you who are honored by the lords of heroes!
By this, the gods come under one's control and become bestowers of boons.
The hands, with palms turned upward and fingers interlaced, are shaped like a braid.

With the thumb placed between the fingers and the tips of the fingers extended, this mudrā is called *Praṇava*; it effects the summoning of deities. What need is there to mention its power over mantras, yantras, and other such things, as well as over substances and the like?
This [mudrā] has been revealed by you through your former heroic power to bestow all auspiciousness upon men and for the attainment of the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
This is the *pramāṇa-mudrā* in relation to Jayadratha.

Henceforth, O Daughter of the Mountain, hear about the mudrā named Prabhā; O Goddess of the Gods, it accomplishes all rites just as they were previously described. With the middle finger raised upward and reversed, and the index and little fingers [bent] inward—
When it is rubbed against the side of the face and raised to the middle,
with the fingers pressed down from the base, it is known by the name Jyeṣṭhā;
this is called Mahāprabhā, worshipped by all the gods.
At the time of the fire-oblation (homa) and during the offering of food (naivedya), one should bind this [mudrā] for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose.
No mudrā superior to this exists within the tantras;
it should be known as the bestower of all prosperity even through the mere chanting of its name.

Thus ends the *Mahāprabhā* [section] regarding Jayadratha. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mudrā known as Kāmaruhā, which causes the agitation of the three worlds and bestows all auspicious fortune.
Then, having gladdened them, one should cause the *hastiśīrṣa* drum to be played;
the eyes should be made charming, and you should display a slight smile.
This mudrā of yours, named Kāmaruhā, has been revealed.
It pacifies all evils, brings about many sons,
generates great good fortune, and is endowed with primordial vigor.
O Goddess, having gone to the abode of Hara, delighted by the joy of wine,
well-incensed and with a serene countenance, one should perform the binding of mudrās;
one should cause dancing to be performed and play the *vastiśīrṣa* drum for a year.
The *mudrā* known as Kāmaruhā is to be performed with the *kroṃkita* and *recita* gestures; she bestows great good fortune, brings the three worlds under control,
pacifies all sins, and always grants many sons.
By its very name, it brings about the great accomplishment of the assembly (*mahāmelāpa-saṃsiddhi*).
O Goddess, this has been declared to you according to its true nature as the most excellent of all.
Thus ends the procedure for the *kāmarūhā-mudrā* in the *Jayadratha*.
Hereafter I shall explain the Mudrārājñī, the subduer, by the mere binding of which the three worlds fall into servitude.
She performs a charming dance; she is smeared with unguents and her hair is loosened from its braid.
Making a hissing sound (*sasītkāra*), kissing the great beak at the beginning and so forth,
and gliding gracefully with equal ease over the world from the hands and feet onwards—
this is the Mudrā named Vaśaṅkarī, the Mistress who accomplishes all aims.
The *Siddhasaṃrohaṇī* (the Pearl) brings the great world under her control;
she is the accomplisher of servants and the provider of perfected substances.
She is both pacifying and nourishing, and there is nothing anywhere equal to her.
The assembly of the great gathering (*mahāmelāpa*) accomplishes [its purpose] without obstruction.
Thus ends the ritual for Vaśaṅkarī in the *Jayadratha*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which is known as the Great Assembly (*mahāsama*).
It is the accomplisher of commitments and the destroyer of the flood of misdeeds;
it is the remover of the faults of the great commitment. Listen, O Pārvatī, to this according to reality.

With the left hand in the *piṇḍa* [fist] gesture, the little finger is extended; one should hold it reaching toward the navel—this is the mudrā most supreme among all. For if one performs either a sacrifice or recitation without knowing this, [it is fruitless].
O Goddess, when one undertakes [this practice], then she is known as the "one to be accomplished" (sādhinī).
Otherwise, there is no doubt that he will be devoured by the hosts of sky-goers (khecaras).
And once the spiritual son (putraka) has entered, one should test him according to the rule (samaya).
This [mudrā] bestows all accomplishments and fulfills recitation and other rites.
Thus ends the Samayamudrā in the Jayadratha[-tantra].
Now I shall explain another mudrā, named Prabhakṣaṇī.
O Goddess, by means of which [mudrā] a practitioner becomes a consumer of the sacrificial pap (caru) once he has attained perfection:
having formed the *viparītāṅgulī* [mudrā], one should turn it behind; placing the head upon that, one bows—this is the *vimarṣaṇa*.

When the mouth is opened in the shape of a banner (patākā), she is then to be known as Prabhakṣaṇī; by means of her, the consumption [of offerings] occurs. All undertakings are accomplished according to one's heart's desire.
When the complete accomplishment of all types of summoning and other rites is achieved, there is no doubt in this matter.
There is no goddess equal to her, who bestows accomplishments face-to-face;
she is proclaimed everywhere as Bhairavī, the great instrument for the destruction of evil.
The supreme achiever of the three worlds, endowed with the power and vigor of the ancients.
Thus concludes the procedure for the *prabhakṣaṇī* mudrā in the *Jayadratha*.
Next, I shall describe the *mahātārkṣī* mudrā, which is supreme even to that of Vaivasvata.
Bound by which, the heroic practitioner becomes like Garuḍa.
Having made the left hand face downward with its fingers spread and slightly curved, one should meditate upon the middle finger of the right hand being placed above the middle finger of the left.
When the entire thumb is bent crosswise behind the bound index finger, and the [other] fingers are placed upon it,
this is known as the Great Tārkṣī.
In battle, in the midst of enemies, at the king’s gate, and in times of fear; in cases of poison, on all journeys, and likewise in matters of prohibition— there,
one should ward off the enemy in Suvela and Makarālaya.
And in traveling through the sky, there is nothing equal to this on earth.
It brings about all prosperity, is most excellent, capable of uplifting the three worlds,
endowed with former heroic power, and bestows the accomplishment of the Great Melāpa.
She is proclaimed as the most excellent in the *Jayadratha*, the king of tantras;
she should be known as the bestower of success in the netherworld (*pātāla*) and the destroyer of wicked beings.
Thus ends the procedure for the Great Tārkṣī in the *Jayadratha*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe Vikaṭā of terrible prowess,
by whose awakening even the universe trembles;
O Goddess, by the mere utterance of her name, Khecarī comes and goes.
Listen to that [instruction] in brief, which brings about all prosperity and virtue:
the wise man should open his mouth wide and protrude his tongue;
he should make his belly very thin and let his breasts hang down like nipples.
With fists closed and the body naked,
this is the Vikaṭā-ghoramudrā, intended for the rite of universal attraction;
through its application as a means of withdrawal, there is nothing equal to it anywhere.

One attains all desires; there is no need for deliberation on this point. Even one endowed with former vigor, having gone to the forest, should perform the bodily union while his consciousness is intoxicated with the bliss of wine.
O best of men, for as long as it takes even a single watch of the night, the deities will come; bow down to them with your inner self.
Joyful and satisfied, they dance; one should cause the arghya offering to be presented to them. When the arghya has been given, Bhairava truly becomes manifest—of this there is no doubt.
This supreme mudrā is renowned as difficult for men to attain even throughout the three worlds.
Thus ends the *vikaṭavidhi* regarding Jayadratha.
Hereafter, O slender-waisted one, I shall again describe the extremely fierce and terrible *vikaṭabandha*, which is fearsome to all.

The wise one should join both the index fingers of the left hand, held together as a single mass, to the chin; likewise, this is the "emerging tongue" [mudrā]. When the two ears are made wide apart, the wise one should lick the upper lip.
This mudrā is named Vikaṭā; it brings about the destruction of all obstacles.
It never destroys offerings such as bali, flowers, and oblations.
There is no doubt that the practitioner will achieve success through a single meeting [with her].
Endowed with the qualities of former valor, she brings about all forms of prosperity.
Thus ends the ritual for Vikaṭā regarding Jayadratha.
Now, I shall further explain another [rite], namely the Parivartanikā.
For this is the supreme of all mudrās, bestowing great peace and happiness.
In the middle [position], both [hands] are indeed devoid of the thumbs, which are interlocked;
having likewise placed the "peak-path" (koṭimārga) in the mass (piṇḍastha) within the heart.
Through the extensive turning [of the body] by means of three circumambulations, one performs the prostration of the eight limbs; this is turned back by whom?
It is designated as Mahāmudrā, endowed with the primordial vigor.

O Goddess, by tying this [thread], the offerings for the *bali* worship will never be harmed by *yātudhānas* or *vināyakas*. Otherwise, if one performs the worship without knowing this [method], [the offerings will be destroyed].
The fool scratches empty space with his clenched fist;
likewise, he is deprived of all [the fruits of] recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, if he does not know this. (19a)
It should be known as being without beginning, consisting eternally of Śiva and Śakti.
Thus ends the Parivartanī Mudrā in the Jayadratha [Yāmala].
Now I shall explain another, known as the Bhairava Mudrā.
Just as through six months of yoga one will become like Bhairava—
the support of all prosperity and happiness, relying on the power of former vigor, with consciousness blissful with wine, and having shaken off the physical body— so shall he be.
Whether naked, with disheveled hair, or even while staying in the house of one's father,
one should bind the supreme mudrā known as Mahābhairava.
With both hands, one should form fists, with the little fingers extended.
O Goddess, with those [fingers] one should tear apart [the bonds]; having placed the *sṛg* [gesture], the great lineage [is established].
Likewise, when the thumb is extended, one should perform the tossing of the earth once.
In the *avaguṇṭhana* [gesture], the face is made into a distorted Bhairava.
One should protrude the tongue slightly while the eyes are somewhat contracted.
Furthermore, when the task is one of "kaṭara," the nose should be flattened and prominent.
The practitioner, standing in the posture of dance, should have his right knee clearly extended.
Having placed one thumb and turned it back in that same way,
and likewise in reverse on the left, this is the mudrā known as Bhairava.
When properly bound with this, the entire universe trembles violently.
Afflicted by fear, she trembles in all ten directions, seeking refuge in the sky-goer;
the fire of time has moved from its place, and the earth has become like ashes.
There shall quickly arise a great gathering of Yoginīs that draws everything toward itself.
O Goddess, one should not reveal this to a community characterized by destruction.
Through the practice of yoga for six months, Bhairava becomes manifest;
indeed, there exists no mudrā equal to this one in the three worlds.
(19b) Thus ends the Bhairava-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-tantra].
Hereafter, I shall explain that which is named Kāmarūpiṇī.
Within six months, he attains perfection, endowed with all supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
He is served by gods, *gandharvas*, and the foremost among the perfected ones (*siddha*) and those of Varuṇa;
he is constantly sought after as a husband by *apsarases* and celestial maidens.

Listen to that, O highly fortunate one, by relying on the power of the former [practice]. One should perform it daily at the meeting of the thumbs and the bellies of both hands, measured at half of all [the fingers]; otherwise, there would be a transgression.
With both hands, the little fingers are extended upward;
the hands are turned inward, the index fingers are raised and not joined,
and the lower lips are slightly parted— thus is the gentle-faced [mudrā].
With his mouth opened, his tongue withdrawn and then extended again,
he became gentle once more; then, having formed a bud-like gesture with his hands,
his right hand was positioned upon his hip, aligned with the wrist.
One should perform the *vāmanābhimati* with the rotation reversed;
likewise, the *sāmyādisaṃvartā* mudrā is that which takes any form at will (*kāmarūpiṇī*).
With a mind satisfied by what is cherished, one is perfumed by the fragrance of sweet scents.
By means of this binding, the practitioner, being humble, certainly floats after six months;
that best of men becomes endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. O Goddess, through constant practice of this binding, he is joined with all auspicious fortune.
O illustrious Pārvatī, within just a few days,
this rite becomes effective against Jayadratha, who can assume any form at will.
Now I shall describe the *sūcīmudrā*, which performs all ritual actions.
Endowed with former vigor, she bestows the state of Bhairava.
Having placed his hands in the *mukula* gesture,
naked and with a crooked [expression], the wise one, through the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyāga*), [should place them] upon the right knee and elbow.
(20a) Likewise, when the hand has emerged with the palm facing upward and the arm is raised,
one should similarly awaken [the deity] again with the left leg drawn in.
In the same manner, one should simultaneously perform the same with the right hand.
By rotating the shank three times, it is proclaimed as the Ūru-mudrā. For whomsoever this is bound, their fortunes shall be fully consolidated.
Having thoroughly contemplated his form, he will attract good fortune.
Within three months, that man known as Jaya— even if he were a slayer of a Brahmin—
will become a knower of the mantra in the assembly of all yoginīs.
The accomplishment of mantras will certainly arise; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Endowed with all accomplishments through reliance upon former vigor.
Thus ends the procedure for the *sūcīmudrā* in the *Jayadratha*.
Henceforth I shall proclaim that which is known as the Vajrapañjara,
having the form of Mahāpratyamgirā, the impeller against all misfortunes,
the fierce one who provides all protection by means of her former heroic power.
Having formed the shape of the Mahāmudrā, it emerges completely [from the palms].
With the little fingers and thumbs raised and the wrists held apart,
this is indeed the mudrā named Vajrapañjara, which possesses great power.
At the time of the fire-sacrifice for recitation, practitioners should always apply themselves;
then everything becomes complete, and nothing occurs that is devoid of the prescribed rite.
By the power of their former vigor, obstacles shall not pierce them.
This supreme mudrā for you has been taught by me, O beloved.
Thus ends the procedure for the Vajrapañjara in the Jayadratha[-tantra].
Now I shall explain another, which is celebrated as the Śūrpa-mudrā.
She who is intent upon fulfilling the needs of the entire world,
with her fingers joined in the form of a hollowed palm, her thumbs dissolved within her hands.
When the two fingers are wide apart and curved with great luster, it is proclaimed as the *sūrpamudrā*.
O Goddess, when this is bound, nothing becomes deficient in the ritual;
all offerings such as the *bali* and oblations will become complete.
One should offer the *caru* oblation; this Mudrārājñī is highly praised.
O Goddess, there exists no other [mudrā] superior to her, for she possesses great power.
[The procedure for the Sūrpamudrā in the Jayadratha[-tantra].]
I shall describe the Karotikī rite; listen, O Pārvatī, according to the truth.
It fulfills all requirements in the sacrifice through the power of the primordial seed (vīrya).
One should rotate the two hands, which are intertwined and crossed.
By means of the *samāvṛtti* practice, these two are likewise proclaimed.
O lady of beautiful limbs, this [practice] called *karoṭī* is the destroyer of all defects;
however, it must always be performed even when it is deficient or excessive in its ritual rules.
Through the investigation of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, she is endowed with the *kālakūṭa* poison;
she is fully developed in all her vital power (*vīrya*) and is the supreme mother who generates awakening.
Thus ends the procedure for the skull-cup (*karoṭī*) in the *Jayadratha*.
Beyond this, O Goddess Pārvatī, listen to the truth regarding the Śaṅkha-mudrā, which is supreme for dispelling obstacles and bestows victory in battle.
With the fingers interlaced within and the wrists firmly joined together—
One should join the thumbs together and extend the little fingers;
this is declared to be the Śaṅkha-mudrā, supreme for terrifying away obstacles.
A wise person should employ it in battle; it is remembered as bestowing victory in all circumstances.
One attains victory in gambling and other such activities; there is no doubt about this.
This [practice], through the application of the "Bond" (bandha), bestows the Great Conch, Great Peace, and the descent of Great Fortune; after six months, it destroys death.
O Goddess, this supreme and most excellent of all mudrās has been revealed to you. [End] The Procedure for the Conch Mudrā.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the auspicious mudrā named Vicitrā, which performs all rites and is endowed with the power of primordial vigor:
