the middle fingers should be raised, as well as the index and ring fingers.

When the little fingers and thumbs are interlaced at their bases and raised up, this mudrā is named Vicitrā; it accomplishes all desires. One should bind it by means of this method for the purpose of entering another's body.
Endowed with her former power, she invariably unites the lover and the beloved through the play of the swing of passion;
she is declared to bestow all accomplishments, and no further distinction is prescribed.
The Chapter on Various Procedures.
O Pārvatī, O beautiful lady, I shall explain to you in truth the methods for medicinal powders,
collyriums, and other such preparations, by which these are accomplished.
Likewise, when the hand is turned downward with the fingers positioned in a braid-like binding,
and all the fingers are knotted together, it is proclaimed as *surāhā*.
It is used for the sake of perfecting accomplished substances (*siddhadravya*) in all powder-formulations.
One should employ her according to the prescribed rites; she is remembered as the performer of all actions.
Endowed with great power, she has been described to you exactly as she is.
Together with her secret, she accomplishes everything; indeed, there is nothing higher than this.
Thus ends the ritual for Surohā regarding Jayadratha.
Listen now to that seal called Kanakā which was previously described to you;
it is renowned as the remover of all misfortune and is a great bringer of subjugation.
Having placed the two hands with the fingers released and the wrists crossed in reverse order,
endowed with the power of the previous method through the application of this specific rule—
this is known as Kanaka; one should employ it in all types of possession.
In rites for summoning the healthy, in the raising of vetālas,
and in the assembly of all the Mothers— this is proclaimed as the mudrā.

Thus ends the procedure for the Kanakamudrā in relation to Jayadratha. Hereafter, O beloved, I shall explain the Kṣurikā, the great mudrā that instantly severs the vital breaths, together with its secret; listen!
When the little finger, the thumb, and the index finger are joined together while extended,
and the middle and ring fingers are held straight and level, applied beneath the palm—
this is the *kṣurikā* (razor) mudrā of the right hand, which instantly severs the vital breaths.
This mudrā is employed for entering another body, as well as for the rite of immediate departure [from the body],
and for the act of expelling obstacles.
Thus ends the procedure for the Kṣurikā-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].

Henceforth I shall proclaim the Pāśamudrā of great power, which can attract the entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans. By binding it, O Maheśānī, practitioners [attain their goals]; of this there is no doubt.
The ring finger and the thumb are positioned together above;
the little finger of the right hand should be firmly grasped.
This is declared to be the noose mudrā (pāśamudrā); one should employ it in all rites.
O Goddess, by the power of this [mantra], one shall obtain incomparable good fortune.
One should always bind it before the Goddess with the most excellent men.
By the practice of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, one may attract everything in an instant.
Thus ends the procedure for the noose-mudrā in relation to Jayadratha.
Next, I shall describe the wondrous mudrā which grants success in all aims;
it is renowned as the bestower of all prosperity and the yielder of the fruits of many accomplishments.
By means of the practice of circumambulation with the hand in the shape of a sprout, known as the *citrā-nāḍī*, the wise should recognize the *saṃgrāmaṇa* [mudrā].
If this is accomplished through mantra, it may destroy even ten million planetary influences.
He attains great good fortune and is swiftly endowed with wealth.
He who wears garments of the quarters (the sky) and is anointed with pure fragrant unguents—
Within seven days, the practitioner achieves success regardless of his condition;
he beholds all the deities—of this there is no doubt.
He who performs a dance once with his hand turned clockwise [attains the same].
That graha who performs various dances,
making sounds with his mouth accompanied by hissing and the snapping of the palate during his dancing—
he is known as Vicitrā, if he performs such diverse dances.
Within seven days, the practitioner attains success in every situation.
Endowed with its former potency, it is known as the attractor of all.
Thus ends the procedure for the Vicitrā Mudrā in the Jayadratha [Yāmala].
I shall now describe the boat-seal (*potamudrā*), which attracts all men;
by its complete mastery, O illustrious Goddess, the practitioner of mantra floats through the atmosphere within six months— of this there is no doubt.
With the fingers spread apart and the head slightly bowed,
this is declared to be the *pota-mudrā*, employed by the Goddess when engaged in making a request.
Within six months, the practitioner of mantra shall obtain whatever he has requested according to his own desire.

By means of this mantra, the practitioner should invest gold; he shall obtain whatever he desires at will—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. Endowed with its former potency, it bestows the accomplishment of the subterranean realm and the sky.
Thus ends the procedure for the boat-seal (*potamudrā*) of Jayadratha.
Hereafter, I shall explain the one called Mudrākāntā,
by the mastery of which the practitioner of mantras (*mantrī*) becomes capable of performing all rites.
He who performs the dance even once with the right hand,
having ascended the staff-posture (daṇḍakāsana) with his neck and head held straight.
With the left forearm resting upon the right hand, the index fingers of both knees should be extended and held level;
this is the *muṣṭibandha* (fist-binding) posture.
According to the prescribed method, the second [hand] is placed against the chin while contracting [the body].
Then, having joined the ring finger with the thumb, one should contract them;
one should extend the remaining fingers in succession according to the rule for ascending steps.
One should make the face serene and peaceful in form, in accordance with the prescribed method.
The Great Seal (mahāmudrā) is called "the Beloved" (kāntā); when it is bound, ignorance ceases to function.
Through practice, she becomes his plaything, providing the concealment of his own desires.
Gentle goddesses become his companions, and he is seen to possess all objects of desire.
Endowed with former vigor, she is remembered as the performer of all rites.
She brings about the great assembly in the abode of the ancestors for the practitioner.
A mudrā equal to her exists within the interior of the world.
Thus ends the procedure for the beloved regarding Jayadratha.
Hereafter, I shall explain that which is known as *nṛttanī*,
the mudrā endowed with all purposes for high-souled practitioners.
She may become insane and talk incoherently, yet she plays again like a child;
this mudrā is described as one whose speech is refined and who is awakened.
The deities are pleased with her, and the attainment of the sacred sites occurs.
One should perform the movement of a calf accompanied by the sound of "phat.
This mudrā is named Nṛttanī; it brings all the worlds under one's control.
O Dear One, for the accomplishment of the great assembly (melāpa), there is nothing equal to this.
What else, O slender-waisted one, has been fully explained?
There is no accomplishment here that is not accomplished by her;
she is endowed with primordial vigor and is the supreme attractor of all.
(23a) Thus ends the procedure for the dance-mudrās of Jayadratha.
Hereafter, hear the most excellent mudrā of Kālakarṇī.
This is the descent of great fortune for accomplished sages and practitioners.
One should extend both hands with the index fingers directed crosswise in an auspicious manner;
joining them by reversing the wrists, one should withdraw the other [hand].
This is the Kālakarṇī mudrā, which is terrible and the most excellent of all.
O Goddess, it should be employed with one's whole being by a wise practitioner in the accomplishment of Mahākṛtyā and in the accomplishment of the great Vetāla.
Endowed with former vigor, she indeed bestows all prosperity.
Thus ends the ritual for Kālakarṇī in the Jayadratha [Tantra].
Hereafter, listen to Viśvamukhī, the most excellent of mudrās.
Relying upon whose power the world-protectors become her servants—it shall indeed be so, there is no doubt; my word is infallible.
When the back is turned upward, held level, split open, and bent down...
The ring finger and the little finger are held in one's own hand;
the thumb is extended behind [the palm], and it is known as the "face" [mudrā].
As soon as this is bound, the world-protectors together with their attendants [are summoned].
They dance, joyful and well-pleased, bestowing all desired boons.
Moving through the channels (nāḍīs), she is supreme, bestowing all desired boons.
O highly fortunate one, staying in the cremation ground at night for a single month, [one attains this].
He floats through the vast atmosphere, honored by the guardians of the world;
that lord of practitioners is worshipped by Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Yakṣas—
[he who possesses] the former power and is the destroyer of all calamities.
[She is] the one who effects the great assembly and accomplishes the subterranean space.
Thus ends the ritual of Viśvamukhī in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
I shall now fully describe Rohiṇī, who brings about the eightfold realization;
she is the pacifier of great disturbances and the destroyer of fear and poverty.
This Mudrā is endowed with vigor, joined with power, and is the Great Sovereign (Maheśvarī).
Having made the ring finger and little finger extended and knotted,
and having joined the two auspicious middle fingers and forefingers while they are extended,
with the thumbs tucked in and pressed together— this is proclaimed as the Rohiṇī mudrā.
This mudrā is the Mahāmudrā for the rite of touching trees; it is excellent for igniting fire without fuel. One should employ it for paralyzing and causing possession.
By its mere sight, it will destroy yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhūtas.
This supreme Mahāmudrā should be known as Ṛtumālinī;
she bestows accomplishment in all undertakings, nourishing through food, drink, and sustenance. Indeed, she performs all activities and is beloved by the deities.
"Through the union with the blazing crest of vital breath, one will bring about the eight realizations.
Thus ends the Rohiṇī-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
Hereafter, I shall explain that which is known by the name Kabaṃdhī.
The woman who bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhidā*) is endowed with the vigor of the east. O Goddess, she has extended fingers and is encircled by hair upon her fingers;
with her left hand slightly extended, she is proclaimed as Kabaṃdhī.
By means of this bond, the practitioner becomes dear to the goddesses;
for the sake of accomplishing his purpose, he should bind thieves, forest-dwellers, and those on the stake.
It should be employed for traveling through the sky and bestows all supernatural attainments (*siddhis*).
Abiding in the Mahānādakabandha [mudrā], a person may, like one sporting on a playful swing,
attract all the deities within seven days. O Goddess praised by heroes, this mudrā along with its secret has been explained to you.
(24a) The supreme inner great secret, which grants the perfection of the instantaneous assembly.
Thus ends the procedure for the headless torso (*kabandha*) in the *Jayadratha*.
Now listen, O daughter of the mountain, to the *mokṣaṇī* mudrā,
by which an incomparable flood of sins is destroyed merely through its binding.
Having formed fists with both hands, one should release them.

Having joined [the hands] together, it is placed in the hand and is proclaimed as the *mokṣaṇī* (the liberator). By binding this [mudrā], which is endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*, one swiftly destroys even ten thousand instances of the murder of a Brahmin, as well as the entire mass of sins, right here in this world.
It steadies the moving eyes and bestows the fruit of all accomplishments;
it is constantly remembered as the beloved of the Great Heroes, the Lords, and the Sovereigns.
Thus ends the procedure for the Mokṣaṇī Mudrā in the Jayadratha [Yāmala].
Now I shall proclaim another [mantra] called Durgasantāraṇī,
which, when endowed with the previously mentioned vigor, destroys fear throughout the three worlds.
O Goddess of the gods, listen now to its nine names in brief.
When the little fingers are joined crosswise and the thumbs are likewise closely pressed together,
this is the Nāva-mudrā, which accomplishes all aims;
for it carries one across difficult straits and brings about the destruction of great sins.

For this [goddess] removes untimely death; she is the bestower of all fortune, endowed with primordial power, and possessed of great mantras. She swiftly protects one from danger, from the ocean, and from the sea of calamities.
Thus ends the procedure for the Nāvāmudrā in relation to Jayadratha.
Hereafter, O fawn-eyed one, hear of the mudrā called Mūrchana,
by binding which all the deities quickly come into one's presence.
Having thus performed the sacrifice with both hands according to the ritual procedure,
rain falls there mixed with wine and liquor.
O one of great asceticism, by this the goddesses are fully satisfied here;
as long as she does not become satiated with the mandala through this continuous practice,
she— endowed with her former vigor and strength— shall accomplish whatever is desired by the mind.
The Procedure for the Melodic Modes (Mūrcchanā-vidhi).
Now, I shall proclaim the Mudrā, which removes all that is ill-done,
endowed with great power, and the cutter away of the flood of misdeeds.
Having extended the hand and fashioned it into the shape of a sprout, one should likewise visualize the body; this is proclaimed as the *kaṃpanī* [mudrā].
By means of this, all evil deeds arising from the great dissolution [of the world] are destroyed.
There is no doubt that the king of the Citras is pacified by water alone.
Whomever she looks upon while bound should be rendered free from sin.
Having been bound within the mandala, she becomes endowed with former vigor and strength.
"The practitioner shall thus bring about that very state which is free from evil and infinite.
This is the procedure for *kaṃpanī*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme *mudrārājñī*.
She who is called Dhruvā is the well-perfected Yoginī in the Kula.
Grasping the palms of the hands firmly with the fingers crossed,
according to the method of the Piṇḍa-form, she is celebrated by the name Dhruvā.

The mantra that effects the restoration [of power] for the seven rites beginning with *uccāṭana* (driving away) should be employed in the performance of rites such as *śāntika* (pacification), as well as in rites such as *staṃbhana* (paralysis). It is to be used in all undertakings and activities for the pacification of all evil deeds.
Indeed, this [mudrā] is proclaimed as the sign for all accomplishments.
[End of] the procedure for binding the Dhruva-mudrā.
I shall now explain the dismissal; listen to this most excellent mudrā.
By which poison would be destroyed by mere binding, without a doubt:
with the hands extended, the fingers below [the palms], and the fingers interlaced with one another.
Moving with the casting of the other [hand], this mudrā is to be known as Visarjanī.
It should be employed for dismissal as well as for the removal of poison;
O Goddess, no other mudrā has been proclaimed that is equal to this.
Thus ends the procedure for the Visarjanī Mudrā regarding Jayadratha.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the mudrā that is the most excellent of all,
which was previously revealed by me in the *Prakīrṇaka*.
Then, striking the surface of the ground with the fingers of both hands simultaneously, this mudrā is proclaimed as "Prakīrṇā. Indeed,
this highly auspicious mudrā brings about prior success.
The wise one should employ [this] during possession for the warding off of all diseases. It is very auspicious, accomplishing everything, and endowed with the power of the former [mantra].
Thus ends the procedure for the miscellaneous mudrās in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
Henceforth, O beloved, I shall describe that which is named Śamanī;
it is endowed with the power of the previous [mantra] and is the destroyer of the flood of misfortunes.
[It is recited] by one who has rotated his legs and prostrated with his head.
With palms joined in the gesture of reverence (*añjali*), the practitioner is proclaimed as "the Pacifier" (*śamanī*).
By binding this [mudrā], the practitioner attains perfection through great yoga.
O Goddess, they bestow grace; of this there is no doubt.
Thus concludes the procedure for subduing Jayadratha.
Now, O you who are honored by heroes, listen to the Vyomavārī mudrā,
by which, through the practice of yoga for six months, the power of traveling through the sky is born.

O you of excellent vows, when joined with the previous *vīrya* (force) and placed beautifully, this is indeed the *surūpasthā*. When the hands are joined at the wrist with the fingers raised upward and the fingers curved inward, it is the mudrā named *cāriṇī*.
(25b) It should be employed for traveling through the sky as well as in the rite of summoning;
it is excellent for the removal of arrows and for the destruction of great sins.
In the pacification of great delusion, she is the destroyer of calamities.
In the accomplishment of the great assembly (*melāpa*), there exists no one equal to her.
O Goddess of the God of Gods, there is nothing that she does not accomplish by force.
This [mudrā], which is dear to the *khecarīs*, has been explained to you according to its true meaning. Thus ends the procedure for *Vyomavārī* in the *Jayadratha[-yāmala]*.
Now, I shall fully describe another mudrā of terrible prowess.

That which is named Viśvaśūcī brings all accomplishments to men. When the little fingers are bent and wrapped around the thumbs in reverse order, and [the other fingers] are joined and extended, it is proclaimed as the Viśvaśūcī mudrā.
When this [knot] is tied at night and one remains motionless and self-restrained, one perceives the past and the future; there is no doubt in this matter.
Indeed, this should be tied for the protection of children; it is bound by grasping the crown of the head.
And for the beloved wife of the messengers, no deliberation need be made here;
she is endowed with great heroism and grants the accomplishment of the Great Melāpa.
There is no other Mistress of Mudrās like her who knows the [proper] time.
Thus ends the procedure for the Viśvasūcī-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-tantra].
Now, O Goddess Saptaśikhā, hear from me the secret [teaching],
the like of which I do not see anywhere else among all the mudrās on the summit of the seat.
Bound by which the entire universe, with its moving and non-moving beings, trembles;
by the mere sight of which the fruit of my initiation is attained;
and by which one becomes a participant in the great assembly (*melāpa*) in the world of heroes (*vīrabhuvana*).
Listen to that in brief; one should guard it like one's own life, O beloved.
(26a) With the little fingers contracted and the [other] fingers joined to the back [of the hand].
With hair standing erect and well-separated, this mudrā is known as the Seven-Peaked (saptashikhā).
Having entered one's own fire-wheel (vahnicakra) and contracted [the body] through the yoga of upward extension,
by means of the flow along the path ending at the moon, [one proceeds] for a distance of forty-nine yojanas.
Mounted upon seven times seven, like the unfolding of the seventh stage;
O auspicious one, this "seven-crested" [mantra] should be known as endowed with former valor.
By means of this mere binding, one beholds the goddesses at night.
Being pleased, they bestow [powers] through their distribution; of this there is no doubt.
They are proclaimed as those who lead one to travel through the underworld and the sky.
O Goddess, through the practice of yoga for six months, [one becomes] Karangiṇī herself.
Having arrived, the Goddess leads [the practitioner] to the station of the Lord of Sādhakas—a place difficult for all goddesses to attain; she goes there, of this there is no doubt.
O Dear One, she is the supreme of all mudrās, known by the name Saptashikhā.
I have thus explained to you how [these] are accomplished; what else shall I tell you?
Having learned this correctly from the mouth of the Guru, one becomes worthy of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Thus ends the procedure for the seven-crested [mantra] in the *Jayadratha[-yāmala]*.
Henceforth, O Great Lord, hear about the mudrā called Amurā,
by which the preeminent hero may attain peace, happiness, and prosperity.
One should firmly grasp the right arm with the left hand and press it.
With the hand having its fingers extended and likewise arranged with the fingers [in a specific way],
and moved once, it is declared that the mudrā known as the *cāmara* is for the purpose of propitiating the goddesses by those who desire freedom from obstacles at their mouths.
One should bind it for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose and for neutralizing poison.
Endowed with its former potency, it performs all rites for men.
Thus ends the procedure for the Cāmarā-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-tantra].
(26b) I shall now describe the canopy mudrā, which is supreme for the concealment of mantras;
by its complete accomplishment, the practitioner of mantra succeeds in all rites.
For protection, one should also extend the tips of the fingers according to the prescribed rite;
for the accomplishment of one's purpose, one should bind them in the auspicious square (bhadra) formation.
This is declared to be the "Vitāna" [formation], which is supreme for the concealment of mantras.
No fault arises where this mudrā is bound;
endowed with perfect potency, it accomplishes all tasks for men.
O lady of excellent vows, there is indeed nothing equal to it in rites of pacification.
Thus ends the procedure for the Vitānamudrā in relation to Jayadratha.
Hereafter, O blessed lady, listen to the captivating Mudrā,
by which the goddesses steal away and cook the supreme among the supreme.
When the little finger is pressed by the middle finger with the perception of the form of a crocodile (makara),
and the thumb is positioned at the base where the image has emerged,
this is the captivating Mahāmudrā by which this [reality] is grasped.
What need is there to speak of all the deities and others? Even among human beings, there is no one whose mind that best of practitioners cannot captivate.
He brings under his control the entire triple world, including all things mobile and immobile.
Wherever— in a country, a village, or a city—
one may cause all that [place] to tremble by means of a continuous stream [of practice], simply through the single glance of one’s virility.
This most excellent mudrā has been explained to you according to its true meaning.
Thus ends the procedure for Manoharā in the Jayadratha [Tantra].
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for Suśāntā,
by which one attains accomplishment endowed with all perfections.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, the practitioner is bound by this alone; there is no doubt.
With neck and head erect, he should remain seated in the svastika posture with hands upon the chest.
Having formed a fist with both hands and likewise raised the two thumbs,
with the left thumb at the region of the navel and the right thumb joined to it—
this is the mudrā named Śāntā, employed for the attainment of the eight siddhis.
The practitioner of mantra is certainly bound to the rite desired by his mind;
there is no such supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) here that cannot be accomplished for the adept.
Endowed with its former potency, it bestows the enjoyment of yoga from the sixth month onward.
No seal equal to this exists within the three worlds.
Thus concludes the procedure for the Suśāntā seal in the Jayadratha[-tantra].
O Maheśvarī, listen now to the seal known as Bhogahastā.
By means of which the practitioner indeed becomes the Lord of the Five Families:
seated upon an āsana such as the svastika, with the neck, head, and chest held straight,
the hands should be placed on the ground and the eyes should not be closed.
She who has hands of enjoyment is declared to be Abhimukhī, who is both supreme and non-supreme.
By means of this swift-moving [path], the practitioner of mantra attains success; not otherwise.
From the state of Kuṇḍalinī, one perceives the digit (kalā) who is the mistress of enjoyment within the objects of enjoyment.
By binding this mudrā, one performs piercing, falling [of the vital energies], and so forth; of this there is no doubt.
Through the practice of yoga for six months, one becomes manifest like Bhairava himself.
This is the supreme of all mudrās, endowed with primordial potency (*pūrvavīrya*).
Thus has been declared to you, according to its true meaning, that which bestows the fruits of spiritual accomplishment and liberation.
This concludes the ritual procedure for Jayadratha, whose hands hold enjoyment.
Now, I shall fully explain the mudrā known as Kroṣṭraka.
By merely binding this [mudrā], one becomes a participant in the Great Assembly (mahāmelāpa).
Having made the eyes wide, the face is placed upon the left hand;
its half [the right] is on the right hand, while the left is slightly contracted.
Known as Kroṣṭukī, she is the accomplisher of the union of mudrās;
endowed with the power of the past, she should always be bound in the cemetery.
Within twenty-one [days], the great assembly (mahāmelāpaka) occurs;
having obtained the sacrificial pap (caruka) arising from seven births, one becomes a sky-walker (khecara).
This, which grants all desires, has been fully explained to you as a secret.
Thus ends the procedure for the *koṣṭhakī* [seal] regarding Jayadratha.
O fair-eyed one, listen as I describe the seal named Śukā,
by which the wife of the great-souled practitioner is raised up.
The wise one should join the middle finger itself with the tip of the thumb;
O fair-faced one, it should be joined at the tips in the [other] fingers.
The index finger should be bent in form, serving as the single ornament for the body.
It is declared to bring about all prosperity and bestow great energy and strength;
endowed with former valor, one should employ it in all rites.
Thus ends the procedure for the Śukī-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
Now I shall describe the ritual action (*karma*) of the *mudrā* that attracts the three worlds,
by which the mantra-practitioner may attract the supreme circle of deities.
Having formed the *mahāmudrā*, one should contract both index fingers.
When joined with the prāṇa and apāna breaths and engaged in the yoga of the iḍā,
she is declared to be the goddess Ākarṣaṇī, who brings about the presence [of the deity].
Indeed, the wise one draws everything forth by means of this [mudrā] in the ritual procedure of the mudrā-yāga.
O lady of excellent complexion, all the deities are pleased when [this] is bound; O fortunate one, when one is engaged in constant practice for three months,
then one attracts everything in the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving.
Therefore, this is proclaimed as the mudrā named Ākarṣaṇī;
it is secret, O highly fortunate one, and endowed with primordial power.
Thus ends the procedure for the Ākarṣaṇī mudrā in the case of Jayadratha.
(28a) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mudrās, the most supreme among all supreme things,
until the collection of sacrificial requisites becomes complete.
The wise one should turn it over and cause the other hand to be placed face upward;
this is declared as "Entering," which bestows success in the ritual of sacrifice.
Furthermore, the mudrā known as "Supporting the Bond" brings about nourishment for those yet to be.
Everything becomes free of thorns; therefore, it is celebrated as Viśalyā.
Whenever the sacrifice is indeed not complete, one should always perform this [rite];
then everything becomes complete, and no deficiency whatsoever arises.
When properly joined with the previous *vīrya*, it is remembered as the performer of all rites.
Thus ends the procedure for *viśalyā* in the *Jayadratha*.
Now, listen to the most excellent *mudrā*, which brings about good fortune.
Known by the name Bhāṃśumatī, she is secret and increases all prosperity.
Having joined the hands in the form of a bud, one should place them at the level of the face;
the wise practitioner should then form the fingers in the shape of rays of light.
O Aṃśumatī, you are renowned for the act of bestowing fortune;
indeed, by you, even the meager fortunes of the unfortunate are made to flourish here.
Endowed with primordial power, you grant the fruits of all actions.
There exists no mudrā equal to this one in the three worlds. This is the procedure for Aṃśumatī.
Now, O Bhairavī, I shall describe to you that which is called Viśvayoni.
By the mere binding of which the three worlds abide before one;
by the observation of its former power, it brings the world under control.
Having contracted the left hand, [place] the ring finger and the middle finger [upon the thumb].
One should place the thumbs in the middle; this is remembered as the supreme Viśvayoni.
For by binding this, O Goddess, there is the supreme presence of the deity.
O Dear One, this [power] is common to the entire wheel of power (*śakticakra*);
all the deities are pleased as soon as it is bound, there is no doubt.
This applies to both the Left and Right Tantras, as well as the Atimārga, Kula, and Akula.
Indeed, this [mudrā] is proclaimed as the universal one, bestowing the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation.

Endowed with the power of the former [deity], she grants the accomplishment of the Great Melāpa (mahāmelāpa). She should be employed for the purpose of subjugation (vaśya) and especially for the purpose of worship.
One should observe here the mantra-circle of this host of mudrās,
by which practitioners, when joined [to it], attain accomplishment, O best of gods.
Having laid out the letters of the Mātṛkā, one should eliminate twenty-five.
One should cast the thirty-three seed-syllables into the three locations.
O Goddess, one should then pierce them from below with the [divine] light throughout the entire forest;
having joined them with the noose, they become unified as one.
O lady with the thirty-three faces, one should repel [the obstacles] by means of the power of Rudra;
O Pārvatī, having joined the thirty-three [deities] by means of the primordial power (ādi-śakti),
the mantras for these nine have now been fully explained— listen!
The twenty-third [syllable] of Śaktyuṣṭha, situated upon Vajradeha,
pierced by Guhyaśakti, and endowed with the head-bindu—
this is the mantra beginning with Viśvayoni, which possesses the unique liṅga of the King of Mantras.
O Pārvatī, one should bind the Māyā-variṇī at the conclusion of the hundred [recitations] and above;
during the time of sacrifice, one should employ it through the power of the mantra. By binding it in this way, it indeed becomes the bestower of success for the practitioners.
And for the guides, O Mistress of the Gods, she bestows the accomplishment of the great *melāpa*.

According to the conformity of the ninefold aesthetic flavors (*rasas*) and emotional states (*bhāvas*), such as the peaceful and the fierce, each [guide] is to be known as ninefold; furthermore, each one of these is fivefold.
The Śākya [scripture], though divided by distinctions according to its nature as mudrā and vīrya,
is said by me to consist of one hundred; this is declared to be its total enumeration.
It consists of four thousand and eight hundred and sixty;
this has been declared in brief as infinite in its detail, O Dear One.
This was previously taught by me at length regarding the Seat of Mudrās.
Beyond this, their various divisions need not be further explained.
Thus concludes the procedure for the Viśvayonī Mudrā in the Jayadratha [Rāma] [Tantra].
[Now follows] the extraction of the mantras for all [the goddesses].
Henceforth I shall proclaim that which is most wonderful along with its secret;
that which has not been told to anyone, I shall now relate today.
By means of this, a man who studies it correctly shall indeed become like Bhairava himself.
It pierces this entire, whole world, both moving and unmoving.
First among these is the preeminent Daṃṣṭriṇī; listen to her, O Daughter of the Mountain.
Her consciousness is intoxicated with the joy of wine, and she is deluded by the fragrance of incense.
With his teeth beautifully adorned with betel, anointed with sandalwood and aguru,
and assuming the form of the Goddess while endowed with his former virility,
he suddenly rose up, O Queen of the Gods, by means of the yoga of the expansion of breath.
The left knee should be extended and the middle [knee] should be bent.
Having fixed the eyes in the hollow of the chest, one should move the pair of eyebrows.
All the fingers of both hands should be coiled like a serpent.
With his mouth gaped by the tips of his index fingers, he should cast [the offering] into the corners of his mouth;
he should move his tongue with speed while uttering the word *svāhā*.
He should let out a terrible, loud laugh eight times, embodying the nature of Bhairava.
This is that Daṃṣṭriṇī mudrā, whose nature is the arising of the wheel of rays;
it has been explained to you along with its secret, but it must not be told to just anyone.
O Gaurī, when this [mudrā] is bound, the entire universe, from Kālāgni up to Śiva,
trembles at the mere sight of the practitioner;
indeed, just as with the goddess Śrīdaṃṣṭriṇī and the goddess Karaṅkiṇī.
Likewise, it is perceived by all—gods, asuras, and humans alike. For seven days, an incomparable vision proceeds for the practitioner.
After fourteen days, it takes the form of the Goddess; after twenty-one days, one shall fly up.
The accomplishment of the Great Assembly (mahāmelāpasiddhi) is difficult to attain for those who have not disciplined themselves;
O Mistress of the Gods, such a thing is not described anywhere in all the tantras.
Having attained this, the best of practitioners never grieve.
Then, indeed, this final birth should be recognized by the foremost of heroes;
it is to be understood through mantras and yantras, adorned with garlands of a thousand syllables.
Or else, it consists of those very heart-mantras of the Goddess of the gods.
Those [mantras] already mentioned and those yet to be described—when joined with these, one certainly attains success.
She should be known as the performer of all rites, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the Daṃṣṭriṇī-bond in the Jayadratha[-yāmala].
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the terrible and fearsome mudrā known as Lelihānā,
which always causes that which is to be known [to manifest].
By the mere binding of which, the bristling of the hair of the body clearly occurs.
The peerless mass trembles, and jackals will howl;
great laughter, song, dancing, and leaping likewise occur,
as does the expansion of all the wheels, from the mere moment of binding.
Listen to that in brief for the benefit of practitioners:
having risen quickly from one's seat, one should forcibly dry out the limbs.
One should also shake the eyes and their pupils with a wrathful gaze.
One should move the tongue, lick it, and firmly suck the lips.
O Goddess, when the hands are clenched into fists and held at the breasts, [the yoginī] is brought under control.
The best of practitioners should not draw [the tongue] toward the corners of the mouth.
One should discern the great flame, intense with the power of its former vigor;
one should stand in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, shaking it once as if licking.
One should let out a terrifying, loud laugh; this is the Lelihānā mudrā.
Having bound this, the Great Hero can shake the entire assembly of worlds;
he may slay hosts of bhūtas and yakṣas and utterly shatter all obstacles.
He would cause the host of yoginīs, the celestial chariot, and the lineage of the siddhas to fall;
then Sadāśiva and the other gods, terrified by the fear of the fire of time (kālāgni), cried out, "Save us! Save us! and performed rites of pacification out of dread.
When one situated in a cremation ground at midnight, belonging to the lineage of the Great Hero (Mahāvīra),
binds the mudrā while delighted by the joy of wine,
then the powerful Yoginīs residing in the three wheels arrive.
Assuming the form of Mahābhairava, he should cause the sky to overflow together with them.
Whatever action one desires to accomplish, that he achieves by force.
There is no such mistress of mudrās in this world of the moving and the unmoving.
On the seat of the mudrās, the Goddess of gods is proclaimed to be the foremost.
Indeed, whatever rites there may be for the Mistress of the gods,
all of them, if devoid of her, do not bestow the fruit of accomplishment.
Therefore, she is declared to be common [to all], bestowing the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the procedure for the Lelihānā-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-tantra].
Hereafter, I shall explain the mudrā that is the most excellent of all.
She who is called Phetkāriṇī is the source of the arising of the fruit of all accomplishments.
With a soul nourished, satisfied, and full, he dwells in the cremation ground, firm in his vow.
Taking one's stand in the middle of the altar, one should bind the Queen Mudrā.
Now, in a house that has been enlarged or in an empty dwelling, a person may bind it;
otherwise, one should not bind it at all, for from such binding a fault arises.
Having sat down and placed the left foot upon the anus without sloth,
O beloved, one should extend the right leg slightly contracted.
Having doubled both arms with clenched fists at the roots of the ears, [one should hold them there].
With her face turned upward, she should utter a fierce and most dreadful howl like that of a jackal;
with angry eyes and an angry countenance, she should raise a cruel cry.
Her left eye is wine, while her center is the supreme nectar.
"Thus, one should utter 'Vipuladhunvasva Phetkāriṇi.
In this way, one attains the *melāpa* within the interval of two *ghaṭikās*.
The circle of Yoginīs trembles, terrified and greatly agitated."
They remain under his control, just as Bhairavanāyaka does.
This has been fully explained to you: she is the mistress of mudrās named Phetkārī, who performs all actions for men, and she is very difficult to obtain in this world.
O Goddess of the gods, it is proclaimed that [this state] arises from binding the various mudrās;
when this most excellent [teaching] is heard from the mouth of the Guru by the best of practitioners,
then it should be known by the foremost of heroes that this is one's final birth.
When it has entered the path of the ear, then one is joined [to success], without a doubt.
Thus ends the procedure for the Phetkārimudrā regarding Jayadratha.
Hereafter, I shall explain the mudrā named Karaṅkiṇī.
Rare among the lords of the world are those who grant perfect accomplishment merely by being bound.
This is the foremost of all mudrās, causing fear to the three worlds;
I see no other mudrā within the belly of the universe equal to it.
(31a) Listen to that, O highly fortunate lady, which bestows the fruits of spiritual perfection and liberation:
having gone to the formidable abode of Hara, which is gladdened by the joy of wine.
Bearing the great vow of the Hero, adorned with the Great Skeleton (Mahākaṅkāla),
his body smeared with funeral ashes and wearing a corpse as a sacred thread,
he should bind the most terrible mudrā, intent upon devouring the senses.
Established in the *ālīḍha* posture, and then again standing in the *pratyālīḍha*,
one should dry up the strength of the limbs and the arms which are half-bent.
Furthermore, the hands are in a state of wonder and the eyes are fixed in the hollows [of the sockets].
One should rotate the mouth once and emit a most terrifying roar;
by means of the yoga of sequential and reverse order, one should cause the multitude of knots to burst open.
Having ascended to the family of the Great Abode, one is as if swallowing this entire world.
By uttering "Vam," O Dear One, one should lick [the nectar] and swallow everything entirely.
Mounted upon the power of the previous seed-syllable, one should bind the mudrā of great splendor.
By binding this, O Goddess, the three worlds would go to ashes.
One should swallow hundreds of thousands of fires of cosmic destruction and cause the lineage of the sun to fall;
one should agitate all of Māyā through the mere measure of the bond—of this there is no doubt.
Adored by the circle of Yoginīs, one shall float in the sky for half a watch.
And that Bhairavanātha indeed comes into being; it is not at all surprising.
No mudrā equal to this exists within the three worlds;
it should be known as the performer of all rites and the bringer about of universal dissolution.
She should be known as the Great Agitator; she does not bind [the practitioner] without the *samaya*.
This secret of yours has been declared; it must be guarded with great effort.
Thus ends the binding of the Karaṅkiṇī mudrā in the Jayadratha[-tantra].
Now I shall fully explain the auspicious Khecarī mudrā, which performs all rites and is concealed in all tantras. (31b)

O Goddess worshipped by heroes, that [knowledge] by which the practitioner attains the power of moving through the sky (khecaratā) resides eternally in the mouth of the Guru and within the heart of the Yoginī. Having attained it, practitioners who desire spiritual perfection never grieve.

Listen, O fortunate ones, to that [mudrā] which is the eldest of all and beneficial to the world; by the mere binding of which one rejoices together with the sky-goers (khecaras), and whose equal I do not see among the vast array of mudrās and pīṭhas.
Having prepared a delightful place strewn with heaps of flowers,

smeared with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and perfumed with the fragrance of excellent incense; and having performed the sequence of the ritual of worship, one whose consciousness is blissful with wine—

The Goddess should worship her own body just as the goddess Karaṅkiṇī does. Afterwards, established in the form of her true nature, beholding with the light of consciousness and mounted upon the wheel of the trident, she should fashion the maṇḍala.
That [wind] should truly be made to move upward by pressing the thumb with the hand;
likewise, the left foot should be placed in the anal aperture.
With the face turned upward and wide eyes, one should laugh loudly with a smiling countenance.
By means of the practice of swinging on the trident, one situated in the left [nostril] should impel the great sound of the eight elements until it reaches the end of the bolt;
O Goddess, having ascended there, by floating one attains the state of a Khecarī within one watch (prahara).
O Goddess, this mudrā of yours has been declared by the name Khecarī.
It is the sovereign queen of all mudrās, common to all and present everywhere.
Having come down through the lineage of the guru’s mouth, it has not been told by me to anyone.
With eyes rolling and whirling, she quickly enters this [state] called *baddha*;
she utters the howls of jackals (*śivārāva*) and performs the snapping sounds (*sphoṭana*) of leaping.
There is great laughter, great song, and the supreme, excellent assembly (*melāpa*).
The lord of practitioners should perform all [rites], beginning with the binding of mudrās;
he floats through the expanse of the sky, honored by the sky-goers.

For indeed, just as the goddess Karaṅkiṇī exists for seven days and so forth, so too does another [goddess] with a face like that of Haḍḍāhaḍḍa who is fierce; there is no doubt in this matter. O Mistress of the Great Secret Mudrā, you must never disclose [this] to anyone.
Indeed, this most essential of essences has been declared to you according to its true meaning.
Thus ends the Khecarīmudrā.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme among the supreme great tantras.
The mudrā known by the name Mahābhairavā is the accomplisher of all things;
I see no mudrā equal to her among the extensive seats of mudrās.
By the mere binding of her, one becomes the leader Bhairava.
Listen to that, O highly fortunate one, you who are the leader in all streams.
This, O goddess, was formerly hidden in all the tantras, O beautiful lady.
By means of this, a man staying on the ground of heroes for seven nights—
He floats together with the sky-dwellers; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Having gone to the Vīravarodyāna garden, gladdened by the joy of wine, he sits in the *udvāsana* posture, with his body and neck held straight.
With a broad chest, deep-set eyes, and exertion caused by the play of his eyebrows,
he would repeatedly bend his arms as if wearing an elephant hide,
and again and again he would rub [his body].
When the bridge of the nose is flattened and stretched, and one is overcome by fury,
with the mouth slightly agape, one should lick the tongue within;
one should utter a fierce "hā hā" sound, arising in sequence through the eight stages.
With a well-formed body and a radiant self, supported by his former vigor, he repeatedly leaps and bounds; this is the mudrā known as Bhairavā.
O Gaurī, when this [mudrā] is bound, the entire range of worlds trembles;
it agitates the abode of Śakti and causes the mass of knots to fall away.
Filled with joy and free from attachment, one should manifest intoxication through yoga.
Stationed in the center of the altar, the hero shall bind Īśāna; within half a watch, he will become a sky-farer (*khecara*), a lord of practitioners,
endowed with all sovereign powers, just like the leader Bhairava.

O Goddess, that man who, though always violating the rules of conduct, possesses a body as hard as stone, shall— by the mere sight of the Mudrā— attain its true nature instantly and remain established in that very state.

Devoid of this [knowledge], everything is declared to be entirely lifeless, including the extensive details of Bhairava; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. This is common to all tantras, and likewise in the Vidyāpīṭha.
O Maheśānī, this [Mudrārājñāmahāyoga], which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, must not be revealed to a disciple who has not been properly examined.
Thus ends the procedure for the Bhairava-mudrā in the Jayadratha[-tantra].
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mudrā that is supreme among those of the Six-faced One;
together with which the terrible [obscuration] of beings perishes by its very nature.
By the mere binding of which, the God of gods is beheld.
Listen, O highly fortunate one, to this mudrā, the most excellent of all.
In a place abundant with the fragrance of fine incense and strewn with heaps of flowers,
the Lord of Mudrās, delighted by the joy of wine, shall perform the binding of the site.
Neither over-satiated nor excessive, with the lotus of his mouth adorned by betel-leaf,
he should gaze upon the Lord of Rays after establishing the connection of the rays.
Here, one should [stir] from the cavity of the mouth using only the fingers of the hand.
The two eyes are fixed upon the abode of Alakā, and they are rendered motionless;
endowed with former power, one should contemplate the Lord of Rays as consisting of four parts.
By that very Lord of Mantras, Śivā beholds [the deity] situated there.
O Goddess, this mudrā called Ṣaṇmukhā has been revealed to you;
through the practice of six months, it bestows the attainment of the *piṇḍa*.
O auspicious lady, even a brahmin— and how much more so a preeminent hero—
beholds the Lord of Rays at that very moment merely by being bound;
after one month, the Goddess of Gods, having ascended there, shall look upon him.
She would speak of past and future events as if they were present.
For three months, she [revealed] the essential natures of the great mantras.
This Mistress of Secret Mudrās has been explained to you according to its true meaning.
"This most secret rite must not be disclosed by you to anyone at all.
Thus ends the *Ṣaṇmukhabandha* on Jayadratha.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the *Mudrāyogeśvareśvarī*.
By the mere binding of which one attains equality with the [divine] family;
that divine mudrā, the great secret—by binding it, you shall attain yoga.
Listen, O highly fortunate one, to that divine mudrā of great power.
Having reached a place free from distractions, fragrant with the slow-burning smoke of excellent incense,
his consciousness exhilarated by the joy of wine, and adorned with flower garlands and perfumes;
having taken his seat upon a soft cushion, he should cover his eyes and other senses.
Seated there facing east, with the body and neck held straight,
the chest clearly expanded and the neck upright, one should place the left hand palm-upward;
behind it, the right hand should be placed, with the thumb and forefinger [touching].
One should cause [the tongue] to be properly attached and move it back and forth repeatedly;
with a lotus-like face full of joy, one should slightly open the mouth.
One should slightly open the eyes and not allow the teeth to touch one another.
Delighted by the joy of wine, one should gaze upon the primordial vigor (*pūrvavīrya*).
This is declared to be the Divine Mudrā, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Through the practice of yoga for six months, the lord of practitioners undoubtedly floats through the expanse of the sky; he becomes celebrated as a Khecarī. Thus ends the "Binding of the Divine Mudrā" in the Jayadratha.
Henceforth, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the mudrā beloved of Bhairava,
which bestows all accomplishments (siddhis) but is indeed difficult for those of unrefined soul to attain. When this is bound, O Goddess, it becomes the bestower of sovereignty over the three worlds.
Having gone to the abode of Hara at night, delighted by the joy of wine,
and endowed with his former virility, he took his place in the middle of the sacrificial altar;
he should extend his left knee and keep the right one positioned near the anus.
Having doubled the two arms, with the fist formed and the index fingers raised,
one should place them at the sides of the ears; then, O Goddess, with the eyes directed slightly upward, one should join [the hands] facing upwards and raise [the voice] with the face turned up.
Resorting to the power of the *mūlādhāra*, one utters the most terrible cry of the jackal (*śivārāva*).
This is the mudrā named Pheravī, beloved by yoginīs;
when it is bound, one immediately perceives the entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
The Yoginīs residing in various places arrive from all directions.
One should offer them the *argha* oblation by piercing one’s own left side.
O Dear One, when the *argha* has been given, the lord of practitioners becomes Bhairava himself.
Endowed with great sovereignty, [he shall remain so] for half a watch (three hours), without a doubt.
O Goddess, among all mantras, this is remembered as the common one.
O Queen of the God of Gods, this may be given even at the end of one's life, but never otherwise.
(34a) Thus ends the ritual for the seal of the jackal-binding (*pheravābandhamudrā*) regarding Jayadratha.
Now, O slender-waisted one, listen to [the ritual] in the midst of the *Tantrarāja*.
O highly fortunate one, this great, most sublime, and incomparable potency— difficult for all the lords of heroes to attain, secret, and concealed within all the tantras—
I shall now tell you, having been transmitted through the lineage of oral tradition.
O Goddess, having gone to the abode of Hara, gladdened by the joy of wine,
the heroic lord of great being should take refuge in the center of the altar.
There, O Maheśvarī, mounted upon a corpse, he should perform the binding with the mudrā.
She is named Mahāsaṃrāviṇī, the shatterer of ten thousand Bhairavas.
Abiding in the center, having become the one who moves in the middle, she dwells in the central temple;
mounted upon the middle, she is the Great Middle, the Middle of the three middles, and the one who thoroughly pervades the middle.
In the great dissolution at the center, within the trident and the six-cornered [star] shining with the six-footed [mantra],
at the end of the wheel of the abode of the Heart of Power (Śakti), through the yoga of the radiating [light]—
by means of expansion and contraction alone, through the union of light and bliss.
Having meditated upon the Rāviṇī [breaths] eightfold and likewise sixteenfold,
one should forcefully purify the body by directing the eyes toward the hollow of the heart.
In the state of the *ālīḍha* posture during the concentration of the breath, one should float like a frog.
The Goddess Tejovatārcis, who has emerged from eighty-one syllables, is accompanied by her retinue;
when joined with the binding of the mudrā, she is the Resounding One (Rāviṇī).
By merely binding this [mudrā], a man shall agitate the three worlds.
The entire circle of deities will become like servants.
The great Bhairavas and lords of heroes will let out a terrible roar;
a rain of blood will arise, accompanied by a most dreadful cry of "Hā! Hā!"
It would shake the entire universe, from Hūhuka up to Śiva;
all those situated therein—gods, asuras, and humans alike—would cry out.
"The accomplishment of the *piṇḍa*, together with the practitioner, occurs within three days;
of this there is no doubt," so said the Supreme Lord.
"In that regard, as many *mudrās* as are situated in the middle are proclaimed for the King."
O Great Goddess, she alone is proclaimed as the Mistress;
O Mother, everything uttered by Haḍḍācakra is to be accepted.
This is the Treasury of Mantras of Mudreśī—what else shall I tell you?
The Supreme Goddess knows the subtle murmurs;
she is the one who has burst forth, the Savior, the formidable and profound, the supreme art beyond saṃsāra.
Through the power of the Mistress of Mudrās, the entire sky [is pervaded].
This secret, the essence of the Tantra, has been declared, O most beloved one.
Thus ends the binding of the Mahāsaṃrāviṇī Mudrā in the fourth hexad of the Jayadratha.
Now I shall fully describe another mudrā, the most excellent of all.
Accompanied by thirty-six companions,
always endowed with the power of the former [state], and delighted by the joy of wine,
the one who performs the Mantra-Tāṇḍava should perform the binding every day at night in his own abode.
One should proceed according to one's desire, imitating the goddesses.
O beloved of Maheśvara, for a moment one should dance the Brahmāṇi mudrā,
and having bound the Kaumāri mudrā, one should exult for a moment.
For a moment, O Beloved, you appear as the image of Viṣṇu, and again like Varāha;
for a moment, O Maheśvarī, you dance with the continuous performance of the Śākī-mudrā;
and you are like the goddess Cāmuṇḍā, the destroyer of Ruru’s army.
In that same manner, he should either swallow her up entirely or consume her completely;
then, once she has become dry again, he should assume a terrifying form.
Thus, being agitated with rage, he should speak to Sunandā, and likewise, he should strike her while overwhelmed by fury.
And whatever goddesses preside over the quarters, O beloved, they likewise dance for a moment before the Worthy One;
furthermore, Śaurī dances with her own playful grace, just as she did when enraged. (35a)
In the northwest, Vaināyakī, Gāruḍī, Cāndrī, and likewise Kāpālinī dance for a moment;

just as one goddess dances, so too do they all dance for a moment repeatedly. Just as the forest river dances for a moment, so it is. Just as one goddess dances, so too does she dance for a moment again and again. Vaināyakī, Gāruḍī, Cāndrī, and likewise Kāpālinī.
Likewise, he may dance for a moment or as long as he desires, acting according to his own will; or indeed,
he should dance with graceful movements like a peacock,
while the lords among practitioners leap and dance within the deep caverns.
The mudrā named Mattatāṇḍavikā is the most excellent of all.
Having bound this, the lord of practitioners soars through the midst of the sky,
being honored by the Khecarīs just as the moon is by the stars.
Accompanied by her retinue and possessing a beauty according to one's desire, she attains union with him at once as soon as she is bound; of this there is no doubt.
This [mudrā], who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has been described to you exactly as it is.
Endowed with former vigor, one shall accomplish that which is desired by the mind.
Thus ends the ritual for Mattatāṇḍavikā in the Jayadratha [Tantra].
Now, I shall further explain another [ritual], which, together with its secret, bestows great benefit.
The *mudrā* named Āviddhā is the most excellent and supreme of all, which has never been disclosed before;
it is the terrible one, exceedingly dear to Bhairava.
Accompanied by his attendants, the Hero, having established his presence through the mantras of the directions, [performs it].
With consciousness intoxicated by wine, filled with the joy of the *palāli* [wine-vessel],
one should repeatedly perform the placement of the feet like a staff (*daṇḍavat*).
One should strike the sound of the rhythm (*tāla*) again and again, and give it forth according to one's desire.
In this case, there is again the drawing back of the arms and leaping up;
then, having whirled [the weapon] again, one runs forward with the vigor and excitement of a madman.

The Great Power (Mahāśakti), residing within the womb of consciousness (cidgarbha) and situated to the left of the House of Bliss (Ānandagṛha), [is located] in the forehead, the two eyes, and the throat; then, when enraged, she is in the hollow (koṭara).
From the sky (kha), she emits rays that release the life-force of the body.
Seated thus in the cremation ground, one should begin the binding of the mudrās.
All [the goddesses] run, leap, and sing, intoxicated with passion;
they play most sweetly, again filled with the sound of their cries like peacocks.
And repeatedly uttering whistling sounds and even indecent cries—
thus endowed with such vigor, the practitioner shall always effect the binding.
O Goddess of the gods, within seven days, the man shall float in the sky.
Accompanied by his companions, the hero, who is weary of the burden of worldly enjoyments and liberation,
possesses no other seal like this one, which adorns the three worlds,
O Goddess of the lords of gods, and brings about all prosperity and virtue.
This is known as Āviddhā, worshipped by all those who move through the sky. O Great Goddess, O Beloved, by merely binding [this mudrā], one floats in the sky.
There is no such accomplishment here that cannot be achieved through this.
The incomparable Great Assembly (Mahāmelāpa), the great accomplishment of the deity,

and the state of a Great Lord of Yoga (Mahāyogeśvara) along with the eightfold powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā)— these, as well as the ability to travel through the underworld and the sky, are achieved by men effortlessly.

O Maheśānī, by the power of Mudreśvarī, the heroic lord (vīrendra) attains at once liberation itself, the supreme Tantra that transcends all. Thus, O Goddess, has been declared to you this most excellent section on Mudrās.
That which has not been told to anyone, which contains the secret and bestows great purpose—
that today, O Goddess of Gods, all that which transcends the senses has been declared to you.
The mantra and tantra have been fully explained, O Beloved, which had never before been spoken by me.
O Goddess of great fortune, the supreme heart-essence of these [goddesses] has been proclaimed in general;
it is great and common to all.
This is the most excellent group of mudrās, which exalts the families of all goddesses.
Among them, O Maheśvarī, she is declared to be the Heart;
their common support has been described, and these others, O beloved, are nine.
Endowed with former vigor, it brings an abundance of enjoyments;
what else shall I say, O Beloved? There exists nothing superior to this in the collection of seats known as Mudrā, together with its secret teachings.
Thus, your treasury of mudrās, together with its secrets, has been declared in its entirety. Beyond this, O Saṃrāviṇī, that which is to be spoken is the supreme, the very essence of sound.
Thus, in the Bhairava-śrotas, in the Vidyāpīṭha, in the Śiraścheda, in the Jayadrathayāmala Mahātantra, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the fourth Ṣaṭka.
The Mudrā-kośa, the second chapter.
Thus having heard the words of Maheśī, the daughter of the Mountain King became covered with horripilation like the buds of a flower.
Once again, the Goddess spoke further to the Supreme Lord, uttering words endowed with the secret of the ultimate truth.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O Blessed One, by your grace I have now accomplished my purpose.
O God of gods, I have heard this unsurpassed treasury of mudrās.
Now I wish to hear how that [mudrā] is Śabdakālikā.
O illustrious lord of the gods, you have mentioned her to me;

tell me, what is the power of that Great Goddess? How is she, and of what nature is she? She who is the foremost among messengers and the bestower of supreme accomplishment upon heroes—tell me of her.
How can there be a division of her conduct, and how does she grant accomplishment? Tell me:
are there thirty million mantras, or perhaps three million?
For you have taught that they have many faces and yield manifold fruits through various modes of practice.
For the sacrificial worlds are indeed innumerable, characterized by innumerable modes of conduct;
and while there is enumeration through ritual application and the like, the embodied forms themselves are truly beyond number. (36b)
Indeed, when that which arises as the incalculable through the yoga of the incalculable consciousness,
you previously described it as the vast grove of knowledge spread out by various female messengers, door-keepers, assembly members, friends, and servants.
How is Śabdakālī renowned as the bestower of the perfect accomplishment of the Śabdabrahman?
She is the foremost of the tree of knowledge and the unsurpassed messenger of the Cakra.
When she is appointed, she who possesses the vision of the countless [realms] beginning with Śabdabrahman brings about accomplishment.
Therefore, O Lord of the gods, be gracious and grant me a further response according to my desire;
having perceived it with the eye of knowledge, speak to me the secret of words.
Having heard these words from the mouth of the Daughter of the Mountain, the Lord of the gods [replied].
The imperishable Supreme Lord Śiva spoke this with a loud laugh.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Listen, O auspicious one, I shall answer this most excellent question."
O Maheśvarī, just as it was told long ago by Durvāsas on the peak of the Great Himalaya, that [account] which remained incomplete— I shall now relate it to you in detail, exactly as it is.
Unlocked, free from doubt, and filled with the flood of all-encompassing knowledge—O Goddess, let there be no uncertainty for you; I shall explain it to you according to reality.
Just as that Kālikā is formidable, possessing secrets and accompanied by her messenger (dūtī).
In the extreme peril of the final hour, when [the enemy] is concealed by the sound of the Brahman-syllable, by nourishment,
and by the supreme weapon, or even when covered by heroic [demons] or by servants,
he indeed quickly comes under control once the messenger has been dispatched.
Obstructed from the front by the servants and scrutinized by the female gatekeepers,
the reality of the heroic practitioners is accomplished through the circle of messengers (*dūtīcakra*).
That which is deficient by even half a syllable or a quarter-verse, O friend, results in the opposite.
Through the grace of the sound of the fist, the mantra-practitioner attains his desired goal—
he who has abandoned the protector of the field, the noble one, the heroic leader.
O messenger, the man who is the self of the fist (*muṣṭyātman*) attains accomplishment without delay;
he whose self is the yoga of the nourished single part (*puṣṭaikadeśayoga*), through the reversal of the extraction of the wheels (*cakroddhara-viparyaya*),
and moving at night during the practices, partakes for a long time in the nectar of immortality.
By Vīrabhairavanātha, who is devoid of ritual consecrations,
the desired object is obtained from the sixfold reality through the yoga of the Fist, the Suspicion, and the Skeleton; or else,
by means of the union with Śakti, both [are attained] through that half-measure of strength and daring.
The minister indeed attains his desired object; he should worship with sound upon every sound.
O Lord, at the end of the pair of sounds, he who eats in the fire-chamber, practicing the conduct while moving about, attains his cherished fruit.
Furthermore, by means of the external stream of nectar and through the practice of integration (*saṃgraha*),
one who meditates upon Vīrabhairavanātha shall become a leader on the path to liberation.
Then, having practiced this, he should manifest [the deity] within the Supreme Self.
A person whose self consists of the nature of prior cognition floats as something ungraspable;
for thus it was by Sūtā in her own former dwelling.
Having sacrificed in the midst, one obtains the merit of sound, fist, sight, and the unseen.
Now, when a single practice is indeed foremost through repetition,

the ritual procedure at the beginning and the end brings victory and the attainment of one's desired goal; by practicing that which moves along the path of reality, one should worship and always remain united with it, as if proceeding to Puṣkara through two modes of conduct.
Then, having meditated upon it, the righteous-souled one shall obtain the eightfold qualities of the Lord.
Even at the end [of the age], as has been stated, "Today is the beginning of the Age of Strife (Kali-yuga)";
even while reciting [the mantra] amidst fire, the yogi shall become the supreme embodiment of Śiva.
Having joined the first letter with *rā* and so forth, and having recited it eight thousand times,
one should offer oblations of the three sweets and speak of the worldly course of life.
Then, by means of this mantra-yoga, one may display illusions (*indrajāla*) through the application or suppression of various grains from the forest;
by means of the yoga of the beginning, end, and middle, one may cause a previously bound spirit (*graha*) to be seized.
One should recite [the mantra] at night in an empty house; those who consume the *hayatkaula* [offerings] will simultaneously roar with loud cries from their two foremost [mouths].
At that very moment, she shall manifest herself in the battle between the Asuras and the Asuras.

In that very manner, according to the appropriate application, facing south in the sacred field (*kṣetra*), he causes the *yoginīs* to be satisfied with food; the supreme among bound souls (*paśu*) has previously partaken [of the offering]. Having performed the *kaṅkāla* oblation in the constricted space of the field, he fulfills his vow.
A *brahmarākṣasa* with the face of a bull shall bring the solar wheel of Vaivasvata;
likewise, [he brings] the hair of a donkey, field-ash, and the great clarified butter for the crossing.
Furthermore, there is the supreme garland of *piṇḍa* and *āsava*, and the four-footed [offering] for the one with matted hair (*romārī*).
When one has mounted the pestle, with the wheel-marked foot placed upon the face,
and having been gazed upon from the waters as if by the Vaśī in the Saṃvitaṣṭakula fortnight,
one should conquer the courtesan Jayantī, who is borne on her previous vehicle, with a handful of grain.
Remaining in their own abodes, they display a manifold web of powers:
the Pitṛs, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Kiṅkaras, Vīra-guhyakas,
Brahmarakṣasas, Piśācas, royal armies, and great battles.
The Daityas, the sons of Vikādrava, and the Asuras were together with the maidens.
There was a terrible gathering of heroes and sky-faring women of both gods and asuras;
their forms were manifold according to their will, yet they were essentially one with the Supreme Self.
The practitioner, illuminating the worlds and the non-worlds through the ritual application,
[performs] with a loud laugh accompanied by a vessel during the two twilights.
The night, having been enjoyed by its own grasper, is the supreme dispeller of darkness. Indeed, according to the calculation stated in the scripture, there are one hundred guardians of the cattle.
O Goddess, dancing among men, you should bring the wheel of movement under control.

In *ha*, *tha*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ya*, and *na*, as well as in *ka*, *kha*, *va*, *na*, and *nya*, one attains the desired fruit after first worshipping the *āśrayaṇī*. Indeed, the *raudra-vīra-upacakra* should be known; thereafter, the *puṇya* and *laṃpaṭa* [cakras].

The knower of mantras, together with his entire lineage of kulas, proceeds to the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar, reaching Aghora, Bhāskara, Siddheśvara, Pulomaja, Brahmā, Vairāhya, and Vārāha, O Lord of all.
In this way, there are many other thousands of accomplishments;
through the power of these foremost ones, the practitioner may achieve them with ease.
Just as the rays of the sun in the circle of the universe are innumerable, so too are these powers.
In this way, the ministers, as declared by the tradition of the Siddhas,
proceed; O Lord, having covered [the path] with many showers of rain,
so too do abundant obstacles fall upon the practitioner, leaving no gaps.
Just as clouds falling upon a field of ripening rice are dispersed by a skilled leader among mantra-masters,
so too does one whose mind is disciplined dispel obstacles and vulnerabilities.
Therefore, with every effort, one should eliminate obstacles and vulnerabilities.
Having first applied the Fist Mudrā there, the practitioner indeed attains the fruit;
for the Great Goddess Maheśvarī, the deity of deities, is the essence of that Fist Mudrā.
Having heard this from the circle of messengers, Śaṅkara spoke again.
The Goddess said:
Save me, save me, O Great Lord, out of your desire for the welfare of all beings!
Speak to me that supreme knowledge which has not been heard even by the gods and the asuras.
That [mudrā], when all [fingers] are pressed flat like a fist, is the messenger (dūtī) that bestows the supreme accomplishment of the sixfold [group].
In brief and in detail, it is the source of the arising of the fruit of all traditions (āmnāya).
"O Lord, this burden of maintaining the fire-shed is indeed too great for me;
it is difficult even for those equal to Rudra to endure, so what need is there to speak of practitioners here?
Therefore, be gracious, O Great Lord, whose very form is knowledge and realization."
Through the differentiation of perception and form in elephants, horses, and so forth,
as well as the wheel of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the arising of the fruits of one's authority;
and by means of the rules for conduct and practice, there is the concise compendium of accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The fruitfulness of the result of transformation consists of one or two stories, excluding death.
Likewise, the acceptance of the arghya according to one's capacity is characterized by that capacity;
it was spoken by Asiddha so that one may quickly attain happiness.
Having properly performed this extensive ritual procedure exactly as it has been taught,
Rudra, the wise ones do not behold the Goddess of the God of Gods.
Śrī Bhairava said:

Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this knowledge which is very difficult to attain. First, the practitioner [should perform] the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*) through consecration (*saṃskāra*);
thereafter, the experience of karma; and subsequently, the heroic power (*vīravīrya*).

O Lord of those who observe vows, O Indra among heroes, by means of the application of a single instruction and through the power of the yoga of Śakti, you shall likewise attain [the goal] in a solitary,
uninhabited, and formidable place within the interior of a mountain.
At the confluence of rivers, or in an auspicious *mātṛkṣetra*,
one should draw [the diagram] starting from the northeast with thirty-two squares and so forth, knotted at the corners. Indeed,
within all the corners, at the end, is the seat arising from the *puruṣa*.
In accordance with the nature of the *koṣṭha*, one should place the *ātmatattva*— adorned with the *visarga*— as superior, inferior, or middling. (39a)
In the final corners, place the last letters of each group; in the intermediate corners, the remaining first and foremost letters.
Then, together with the others, [place them] from the others on the sides of the lower and upper squares.
Having thus arranged [them] according to the tradition, O knower of all traditions, proceed once more.

Having worshipped the Mātṛkā, one should extract the Fist of Reality (tattvamuṣṭi). Having extracted half of the mantra and the essence (rasa), one should again contemplate it in the ritual of the Piṇḍa:
Akṛti, Anta, Agni, Vāyu, Sāhaṭṭi, Tulā, and Āsana.
The King’s [mantra] consists of the syllables of the first vidyā, the day, and the night, along with fire (*agni*) and a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

With the sixteenth [syllable], and those two at its end, one who has ascended to that [state] removes [all obstacles]. Furthermore, the group of Śiva is indeed endowed with splendor and devoid of fire.

I shall describe another [section] by Agniveśma, together with the *pauruṣa* and the *cañcukas*. Indeed, the fifth alone, preceded by knowledge, belongs to Datya and Atya along with Tribindu. I shall speak of the hymn (*stava*) exclusively in the Uttara[-tantra].
In the house of fire, with the *piṇḍa* and *ikṣu*, one should contemplate the perfection of the sovereign in the scripture.
Indeed, threatening with the *aṅkuśa-mantra*, one should again [offer] oblations to the fires.
One should remember the mantra with a joyful face at the end of the destruction of the jaws of Rāvi.
Indeed, at the end of the *rāva-piṇḍa*, one should present the tip of the weapon (*astrāgra*).
The mantras are: *tayām tagnipiṇḍadīrghīsvarasahaṃ hara*.
In the sacrifice (*niśāyāga*) against the fever of the syllables, one should remember the *duṣṭabharūṭikā*.
Indeed, it arises from the emergence of primordial ignorance, and then again, O twice-born ones, it is without destruction.
In the midst of delusion, there is splendor; that splendor is the *piṇḍa* [of the body], the thunderbolt, and the Rākṣasī.
One should extract the *piṇḍa* from the blue eye with effort, as the guide for the village.
And likewise, O you who bring an end to the seeds of gold,
one should envelop the weapon with the fire of obstruction and then place it within the fire of the weapon.
Furthermore, one should repeatedly recollect the Rākṣasa-pada and the names of the mantras. This messenger named Bharūṭī is renowned for her six hearts.
I shall now describe the division of these hearts individually.
One should worship the Vidyā named Bharūṭī with twenty-four syllables;
one should constantly worship the one called Krūra, which has seven syllables and is of great power;
and one should constantly worship Mahāghorā, which has three syllables and is of great power.
Indeed, he who worships in this manner at the onset of night follows the path of Bharūṭikā;
for one whose self is established in reality will before long attain the state of a sky-walker (khecara).
Having set aside Madana at the beginning of Śānti, one should recollect Saṃjñā at the beginning of Rāva.
One should worship her named Jambhanī with seventeen syllables;
one should worship Bhaṭṭabharūṭikā with twelve syllables;
and likewise, one should worship Rākṣaseśvarī with sixteen syllables.
Indeed, the great consciousness (mahāsaṃjñā) ends with the syllable *namaḥ*, standing at the forefront as if facing directly [the deity].
Carrying the letters, the foremost verses, and the rivers, she whose hair stands erect roars.
Furthermore, she possesses a distorted face and is obstructed by the Night of Time (kālarātri).
And for the sake of union with humans, one should place [the thumb] at the tip of the blood during the meal.
O Bhairava, the two feet of the one whose time has not yet come bestow death.
One should simply raise the index finger twice before the pair of Hānas.
In that same way, one should extract the word "I" (ahaṃ) in two parts;
at the end of "Bhagavatī," the name indeed follows, preceded by the salutation and the foremost face.
With the principal [faces] of Time (Kāla), there is the pair of words "Virūpākṣa" before Dhukeśī.
Tajī, Bhīṣaṇī, Dravinī, and Pratitarjanī; or else, at the appropriate time, the Rākṣasas or the enemies [should be addressed]. Amā, Tṛtīyā, and Agrā; after that, Śāstra and Grāsa.
(40a) With the *vadarogravidā* [mudrā], one should perform the great peaceful supreme placement (*śāntāgranipada*) in two ways;
ending with the *dhāriṇī*, one should apply the threatening gesture (*tarjana*) for the pacification of all fevers.
Rāvaṇa, together with his kinsmen, was indeed encapsulated by the Rāva-weapon.
One should extract the five-syllable mantra of the preceding lore, and then again the final one;
having extracted the syllable from the tip of the "mouth" (grāsa), one should separate it into two distinct parts.
One should apply the word *kāli* before *kalmaṣa*, *vimūḍha*, and *nitya*.
One should indeed remember the scripture by means of two types of final words, according to their previous designations.
Having extracted one from each of the two [groups], the face at the end of the designation is to be measured.
One should meditate on the face of Kāla at the feet of Kālarātri, at the tips of her feet.
One should visualize the wheel, the *bharūṭi*, the beautiful face, the threatening gesture, and the goad.
Having joined the fever (*jvara*) like the *bharūṭi*, one should extract it from the embodied form of the morsel (*grāsa*).
One should indeed join the fever (jvara) with the house of the mass (piṇḍaveśma) together on one side in the midst of the two fires,
according to the distinction of time, which bestows the perfection of non-rebirth.
One should then again remember it as being at the end of the forefinger (agra), having gone to the end of the index finger (tarjanī).
This messenger, named Tryakṣakarṇī, was previously engaged in conflict.
I shall now declare its division; listen to the heart-mantras.
The first is the Vidyā Huṃkāriṇī, consisting of sixty-seven syllables.
The second is Tryakṣakarṇī, consisting of one hundred and two syllables;
the third is Huṃkāriṇī, equal to thirty-three syllables;
and the fourth is Niśūdanī of impurity, consisting of thirty-two syllables.
Kālamukhī consists of five measures and is equal to thirty-one syllables.
Kuleśvarī has seven phonemes, while Vamekhalā has three.
He who worships Cakreśā at the beginning of the night with [the mantra] Tryakṣakarṇī—
Soon, the sage joined with the leader of the fierce ones shall attain the state of a lord of heroes.
At the end of the face, there is a loss of color; one should discern it by means of the mass of colors.
Joined with Dūtī Rājeśvarī, one should apply the three invocations at the beginning of the others;
one should join the twofold Kula in the fire of the Kaulika with the letters of entry.
Thus, one should join the undivided letters, [beginning] with Karaṅka and Mukhi.
