This [mantra] should be set down with separate syllables, including the *visarga*, with the foremost [syllables] being *jvara*.
When the fire is extinguished, the two eyes of Rāvaṇa [should be placed] at the tip of the weapon, well-compacted.
One should place the *praṇava* preceded by obeisance (*namaskāra*) at the beginning and apply it.
Then, having uprooted Keśin, Akṣobhya split Bala in two;
for at his front was the Mistress who destroys other designations,
[accompanied by] the two words that are the seed-syllables of fire.
One should strike down the troop at the outset and restrain it with the weapon-mantra. The Mistress of the Saṃjñā-dūtīs should be joined; one should place the two feet upon the "eater of the tip.
One should join Karaṅkiṇī at the outset, [placing] the two "vāja" syllables above.
One should apply this in the regular and occasional rites, determined according to the directions and in sequence.
Having raised the *ūrdhvakeśī* [mudrā], which is twofold and consists solely of the shaving [gesture],
one should indeed cause it to descend upon the tips of the index fingers with the *astra* [mantra].
The syllables *kaṭṭa* and *nikaṭṭa*, joined as a pair and preceded by the sounds *śānta* and *rāvastra*;
then the face of the fierce mass of fever (*jvarapiṇḍa*), followed again by the mass elongated by fire (*piṇḍognidīrghita*).
Then *rākṣi*, the abode of the house, the foremost of the makers of the mass-peak (*piṇḍāgrakāraka*), and the supreme *rāvaṇa*.

The notion of "Lord" (nātha), the foremost of the firm, and fever (jvara) [are the first three]. Then one should extract the letter *visargiṇ* (ḥ). Next, one should extract the horse-faced one (*aśvavaktrā*) after separately contemplating the letters *akṣara-avi*.
Then, in sequence: *kara*, *kiṇeśva*, *śukle*, *ikṣe*, *āditya*, and *dayite*.
One should meditate on the long *samānāgni* as the wind-piṇḍa syllable.
One should cause it to enter, obstructed by the weapon-mantra, preceded by the *rāva*-piṇḍa and the preceding piṇḍa.
The first piṇḍa is indeed Aṅkuśā, and the ṛkṣa-piṇḍa is Mahābalā;
this is the messenger (dūtī) known as Bhaṭṭānāsī within the heart according to the previous enumeration.
Now listen, for I shall further describe the divisions of its hearts.

The first [mantra] is proclaimed as Bhaṭṭā, known to consist of thirty-seven syllables. They know Dūtīśvarī to be the supreme [mantra] consisting of forty syllables beginning with the letter *va*. That which consists of thirty syllables, containing the three *māyās*, is called Paśunibandhanī.
The fourth is Phetkāraravā, the most excellent with twenty-one syllables;
the fifth is Karaṅkiṇī, beginning with eighteen syllables;
and the sixth is renowned as Viśvabandhā, consisting of three syllables.
And the courtesan-messenger (dūtī-bhaṭṭī) should indeed join the wheel according to the ritual at night.
In the *Kulakaulīśasāhasra*, victory is attained in the Single Wheel (*ekacakra*). From that, there arises the Rāva, the Fire-pellet (*agni-piṇḍa*), Māyā, and further, the Visarginī.
The wheel and goad are in the middle of the *veda*s; again, at the beginning and end, there are the two index fingers (*tarjanī*).
Like the illusory one (*māyāmayī*), moving through the sky, by way of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the foot-step (*pada*).
Indeed, with the separate weapon-mantra, the foot-step is the foot; it is further the fierce one that consumes the foremost.

Having joined the end of the word in five ways, that name at the beginning is "with sound" (*sarāvikā*). At the end of the word, it is "the aggregate with sound" (*rāvapiṇḍa*); one should restrain it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Again, one should remember the name of the leader of the messengers (*dūtī*) as being preceded by the "red sound" (*raktarāva*).
The pair of feet of Kuṃbhadarī is * *; Kārarāvāvaṇa;
Rāvākṣa with the visarga; and then sequentially the word for the weapon of Rāvaṇa.
Sarāvaṇa is the Vaktrotā; the designations are Dūtīśvarī and Graha.
At the end of the *huṇḍa-mukha* [mudrā], there is likewise the *bhaṭṭa-khalūṣikā*;
then one takes up the *rāva-astra*, the *aṅkuśa*, again the *tarjanī-astra*, and finally the *mukha*.
One should utter *nirharaṇi*, *harani*, *jīvaṃhāriṇi*, and the sound *rāva*;
then *haṃkāriṇi*, the internal sound, *rāvarāstra*, and again the face (*mukha*). One should apply the word *ehi* to *harahuṃkāriṇi* and *agrahe*.
One should sequentially place the three syllables *haṭṭa*, *bharūṭi*, and *saṃcintya-kirāna*; then,
having joined *caṇḍālī* and *caṇḍī*, at the end of the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should extract *haṭṭamūlika*, followed by *jagadgrāsa*, and then separately *vaktra* and *tarjana*.
The fever-ball, the goad, the discus, and the bowl bring about the destruction of the world.
This messenger, named Phetkāriṇī, shall first effect the piercing.
Listen likewise as I shall describe how the piercing of the heart is performed by the deity.
The first is Phetkāriṇī, consisting of thirty-five equal syllables;
the second, known as Kumbhodarā, consists of twenty-three syllables;
and the third is Haṭṭakhaluśī, endowed with twenty-seven syllables.
The fourth [mudrā] is Jīvahartṛ, consisting of twenty-one syllables;
the fifth is Harahuṃkā, equal to twenty-eight syllables;
Jagadgrāsā consists of seven syllables; and the last is Dūtināyikā.
He who worships this wheel known as Phetkāriṇī at the onset of night achieves success;
marked by the wheel, he attains the arising of the state of Vīrarudra.
One should quickly join this *piṇḍa* with the radiant rays, ending with the *praṇava*.

O messenger, O Rājeśvarī, indeed, one should first offer salutations to the Bhagavatī; then, according to the Mahāśabdāgama, one should worship her with the name Caṇḍeśvarī. The word "Caṇḍā" is indeed Śākta; thus, one should perform the three invocations in sequence.
One should then extract the great sound "Sarvavīram" and "Bhairavī.
Next, the two words "Phetkāriṇī" and "Nirācāre," followed again by "Māyā," "Ghorā," and "Ve Māyā. Then separately, the "Aṅkuśa" and the "Tarjanī."
(Virāṭavaṇḍā—[entering]) Separately for the two [sides].
(42a) Furthermore, it is twofold as Khaṣolkā... [text missing] ...twofold.
Vīra, Ucchuṣma, Rudreśvarī, and Rāvaphetkāriṇī;
again, there is the threefold sound (rāva) and the devourers (grasa), joined with the syllables ve, ra, ka, and piṇḍa.
Again, the weapon is fourfold, and likewise the forest (vana).
The Śākta [practitioner], engaged in play, should skillfully recollect the three invocations;
in the *Trailokyadīpaka* there is a group of six, and in the *Vaśārudhira* a group of five.
O Dear One, in the *Lambodari* there is a group of four, while the *Bhojana* consists of five.
Likewise, one should extract the name Laṃbikā, the word Bhaṭṭa, and the command "Tarjana. Then one should extract the goad (Aṅkuśa), the roar (Rāva), and the Rāvaṇa-weapon.
At the end of the face [mantra], one should place the two words "Go forth in two ways" (Dvidhā gaccha). Thus ends that Bhūtakapada.
Having extracted [the seed-syllable] with the beloved [mantra], one should employ it in the Blessed One.
Then, separately, there is the "long-breasted" (laṃba-stani), the sound (rāva), and the two-eyed (dvi-dhākṣa).
Having placed the fever (jvara) along with the visarga, the aggregate of sounds (rāva-piṇḍa) is the seat (āsana).
The village-form goddess, with two eyes and long protruding fangs,
brandishes a goad and a threatening gesture; she holds the weapon of Rāvaṇa and, together with Māyā, raises her face toward the eastern sound as Siddheśī.
One should enter *laṃ* and *bo* three times, and again *na* and *ha* three times;
one indicates them with the *huṃ* syllable, ending with the *huṃḍa* sound and the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*).
The word "mouth" (*mukhi*) is expressed by the *visarga*, and at its end, one should contemplate *bhajvara*.
Akṣarāva and Rāvaṇa are the leaders of the weapons within the midst of the splendor;
indeed, one should likewise extract Brahmāṇḍā alone. That messenger named Lambā is enumerated in the heart.
Furthermore, I shall tell you again the division of these heart-mantras.
O Lord of ninety-one syllables, the first is called Laṃbānām;
one should worship the second, Laṃbakā, which consists of thirty-seven syllables.
The third is Laṃbastanī, always consisting of twenty-eight syllables;
the fourth is indeed Laṃbinī, whose form consists of twenty-four syllables.

One should point out that Huṇḍumukhī consists of thirty syllables and is indeed the fifth. Know her to be the one who utters the world; she is the final one, possessing the splendor of the submarine fire (Vāḍava).
He who worships Laṃbāṅka in this sequence, O Night-faced One, [attains success].
Having understood this, one attains the state of a fallen [soul]; through engagement in spiritual practice, one should proceed toward that.
The mass of fever in the form of the wheel, the illusion of fever, reaches its conclusion.
The invocation is the abode of Brahman; the two feet are those of Śiva and Hara.
Bindu, Satya, Agni, Śibi, and likewise the word Śiva;
then Rāvaṇa, Agra, Dayitā, Kāra, Rāviṇī—these five; Saṃjñā, Danī, Īśvarī—these syllables; and Rāva—this should proceed upon the station of Ṛkṣa.
When the universe is being annihilated, one should contemplate the threatening gesture of the goad,
the sound "rāva," the weapon "nirañcana," and place the tip of the mouthful [of breath] therein.
At the end of the fever [of dissolution], one should remember it as condensed like a pill, situated within the vital wind.
*Māryā*, *tavadha*, *māyānte*, *agryastrau*, and *cāntṛrāvaṇe*;
then again, the triad beginning with *huṃkāriṇyā* ending in *navānte*, followed by *rāviṇī*;
and finally, the five beloved ones (*dayitāḥ*) beginning with *siddhi* and ending with *hyavatarā*.
Having extracted the two words "Siddheśvari" and "Śivamukhi," one should contemplate the five [syllables] "Muṇḍadhāriṇi" separately as the two eyes.
From "Rāvo-jvarimatītebhyo," the syllable "rāva" is the body, and "o" is the seat.
At the end of the sound, one should enter with the illusory power (māyā) and contemplate it as twofold;
having meditated upon the one who utters the terrible roar and likewise upon the beloved of Aghora,
one should indeed obstruct the roar at the mouth of Śivā with the Astra-mantra.
One should join the Face (vaktra), Siddheśvarī, and Jvaramāyā again as before; at the end of the four [syllables] of Bhagavati, one should remember the Beloved as previously described.
Within the interval of the name of the Center (madhya), there is the sound "hana daha" along with the threatening gesture (satarjana).
(43a) Another is the four-cornered *huṃkāra*, which is indeed the vessel for the fever of the senses.
One should contemplate Rāvaṇa’s weapon separately; beyond that is the mass of sounds (*rāvapiṇḍa*).
The face, the village, and likewise the weapon; indeed, obstructed by the Vīramāyā-weapon.
The weapon, Rāva, and Saṃjñāta, as well as Tarjana and Aṅkuśa.
Having extracted the Rāvapiṇḍa, [one recites] "astra-saṃsrādva astra-su."
Indeed, the Brahmamūrti spoke: "Oṃ, the blazing power (Tirvvalī) is to be worshipped here with fire.
Know that the Dūtīśvarī is likewise, and the Śiveśvarī is as before.
I shall now declare the distinction of these heart-mantras."
The first is Śivādūtī, whose body consists of sixty-four petals;
the second is the auspicious Śivamukhī, consisting of thirty-eight syllables;
and the third is Ghorarāviṇī, complete with twenty-six syllables.
The fourth is Huṃkāriṇī, equal to thirty-two syllables;
the fifth is Vīraśakti, complete with fifteen syllables.
Mahāghorā consists of a single syllable, while Viśvagrāsā is the final one.

Furthermore, he who worships Śivā’s wheel at the onset of night indeed becomes Vīrabhadreśvara, a practitioner of mantra who is manifestly Paśupati himself. Now, the extraction of the mantra follows in this manner, according to the sequence of the leaders.
The secrets of sound and the secrets of the fist have now been explained by me to you.
Immediately following this, I shall declare the definitive teaching regarding the lords of heroes (vīrendra),
as well as the wheels, mudrās, mounts, and weapons, in brief.

Just as one should extract the fever-piṇḍa and the life-piṇḍa separately, so too, in this case, one should apply the piṇḍas of exertion situated at the end of the [mantra]. With the weapon-mantra, the three vowels, the piṇḍa, and the kalā, one should place the crest.
The third [is] the supreme liberation, equal to satisfaction and the foremost wind;
thus the lords of the Vīras have been distinguished according to their divisions. (43b)
The first is known as Aghora; the second is Mudrāmuṇḍa;
Bhṛṅgirīṭi is indeed the third, and Kuṅkurākṣa is the fourth.
Know that Udbhūta is the fifth, and Mahocchuṣma is the last.
In this way, those lords of heroes should cause the conceptualization to be broken through its own nature. The village-form is known as the heart; the foremost Bhaṭṭa is remembered as the head.
The fever-weapon is the crest-lock (śikhā), and the other is the intoxication of speech.
The face is Śakti, the aperture is the eye; this is the three-syllable [mantra].

The aggregate of sounds (rāvapiṇḍa) is the armor, while the sovereign of the lords of weapons (astraiśvareśvara) is formed by combining the long vowels with the bindu and the rays, [namely] fire and wind.
The root-circles of the female messengers (dūtīs) and the heroic lords (vīrendras) are, in sequence:
Śaktivajradaṃṣṭrā, Vikaṭā, Muśaleśvara,
Atyohu, and the mudrā Svastu among the heroic mistresses (vīreśvarīs).
Having entered [the body] with the fire of Rāva, one should dissolve it through the sequence of the garments;
joined with the Visarga and Bindu, she is the vehicle in the movements of the messenger (dūtī).
In this very manner, all the heroic deities are to be consumed within the hand.
One should employ the ornaments of metal and wood for both purposes.
On the elephant-gate, the seat of Vāyu, and at the end of the *tejas*, one should join them with the vowels;
the messenger (*dūtī*) should be joined among the heroes from the side of fearlessness, according to her arms.
One should employ the "fever-inducing" and "sound-cluster" [mantras], which are like the submarine fire (vāḍava),
for the Kaulikas during the arising of the Kula, amidst terrifying sounds that are the very form of resonance. Thus,
having first meditated with certainty upon the mantras of the Goddess Vaṃ, one should proceed.
Having become one whose intellect is like that of a disciple, he should practice the yoga of the pairs (dvaṃdvayoga).
With the limbs of the mouth [and] the human figures, together with the couple up to the end of the wheel,
having laid down all the outer lines, he should cause the disciple to enter.

Or else, with disciples properly disciplined, one should perform the "fist of sound" sacrifice (*śabdamuṣṭi*) in this manner all around, within the interior of the feet, just like the six deities on every side.
For indeed, the sixfold form of no one whatsoever is taught as being [composed of] seven;
I am the wheel consisting of the six and the essence, which, desiring to pierce, should be joined by both.
Likewise, by means of the nature of the weapon of accomplishment, or again...
I shall explain in due order, in brief, the supreme sacrifice.
At the onset of night, according to the rite of consecration (adhivāsa), one should take a tooth-stick;
indeed, having eaten and obtained permission through the injunction of the Supreme Lord.
At the end of the word *agraṇī*, one should perform the appropriate visualization according to one's capacity.

Having worshipped it, and having offered oblations below it, the leader of heroes (*vīranāyaka*) bestows the command of the messenger (*dūtī*). Having attained accomplishment on both sides, he stands before the power (*śakti*).
Having performed sacrifice and established this station of Vīreśvara—
whether in a solitary, uninhabited, and formidable place at the confluence of rivers known as Nadāna,
or on the beautiful shore of the great ocean, or atop Mount Kuṭaparvata—
On ground that is triangular, quadrangular, or semicircular, or in a well-known cremation ground,
or at a mother’s house, or at a self-manifested shrine, or at a solitary linga, or in a house—
having first purified the ground before it according to the specific requirements of the tradition.
In that same manner, having filled the *sāṇḍūka* vessel and placed it upon the cloth, one should indeed worship it.
Having performed oblations with clarified butter and with equal measures of wine for the mudrās,
according to the prescribed number or as available, one should then draw the mandala.
It is square, with four gates, completed by the elements beginning with earth,
according to the desired dimensions as seen in the tradition of one's own nature.
Within that, indeed, is a twelve-spoked [mandala] possessing the brilliance of the twelve suns.
The circular pestle is radiant, situated in the midst of desire within the salt-ocean;
at its end is indeed the six-cornered fire, which is like the wind.
Upon a couch made of the essence of milk, [he saw] the King of Weapons (Śakti), adorned with garlands of flames. O Lord, at its end was the one possessing the luster of the autumnal sky,
enriched by thousands of blazing tongues of fire, and exceedingly terrifying to behold.
Having thus drawn the gateways and arches at the corners of the doors,
one should arrange canopies equal in number to the banners and mirrors. At each of the doors, one should place jeweled jars individually at the front of the gates.
One should illuminate the limbs of desire with the lamp residing in the three wheels;
likewise, having joined the other mudrās of the weapon along with various ornaments,
one should join the mental deity in the house of the messenger.
The salutation known as the *cakra* is for embodied beings who are lords over their enemies.
One should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) at the base; Locanā is with the Vasu-leader (Kubera).
The twelve-pointed face-mudrā is within the interior of the body, beginning with the *kalā*s.
One should place each of the sounds from *pṛ* to *na* at the end of *lā*, one by one, within the vital breath (*asu*). Having placed them according to the single method of the messengers (*dūtī*),
the hero should worship that which arises from the distinctions of the forms of the principles (*tattva*).
At the end of the long period of wandering in the final age, [the Lord] stands with his flame-like energy in the state of Vāyu;
in the presence of Sadāśiva, at the edge of the forest of faces, the Great Hero, the Sun, and the Primordial Directions appear,
possessing the forms of sages, crocodiles, tortoises, and jewels, with the faces of hundreds of various living beings.
One should write [the syllables] beginning with *lāvaṇya-kṣīra* and adorn the house with the constellations (*ṛkṣa*).
Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Ocean of Mantras at the triple-root (*trimūla*) by means of the branch and sub-branch,
one should then perform the placement of the messenger (*dūtī*), the weapon (*astra*), and the seed-syllables (*vīja*) through a separate placement.
Some have the luster of clouds or gold; others resemble smoky fire.
Some possess the brilliance of a blazing flame, while others have the radiance of a *śirīṣa* flower. They wear various moon-like garments and are draped in hundreds of diverse cloths.
(45a) Abounding in thousands of various foods, radiant with hundreds of various jewels,
laden with various cattle and horses, and covered with hundreds of various flowers.
Adorned with various limbs, blazing with hundreds of diverse wonders,
with hair standing erect, deformed eyes, four fangs, and exceedingly radiant,
she is enraged; she sustains life, her body hairs like flaming fire.
They hold divine vessels, swords, bells, and tridents;
they are formidable, holding firebrands and nooses, with uplifted hands like those of Brahmins;
they carry spears and lotuses, and have maces and skull-topped staffs in their hands.
One should meditate upon the goddesses of the wheel in sequence, each possessing progressively more arms—
the second having two, the third eight, and the others ten and twelve weapons.
Thus, indeed, they are increasingly distinct through their variations in form.

Raktamālā, Vṛkāli, and the others; Kṛṣṇā, with a form like a thorny tree; the third is Aghorā, with a face of bone; the fourth is Aśvavajrā; Lambā has the face of a jackal and fire, while Śivā resembles her own [original] form.
One should worship separately the various qualities of the faces according to the six-cornered [mandala]:
the goat, the horse, and then the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), mixed with the two upper [faces] of the Kaulika.
Then, one should indeed perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mounts of the dūtīs according to the method of the one who can take any form at will (kāmarūpin).
At the beginning, the end, and in the pair of middle [sections], there are indeed the tips of the tridents and the asuras.
By means of the rules of *sādhya*, *adhamaya*, and so forth, they are indeed at the end, the middle, and moving downwards and upwards.
And the form of the vehicle is according to the sequence of the lords of heroes (*vīrendra*).
Those who, in the midst of the prison of enemies, remember the trees of the Vedic tradition—
just as the great hero Rāvaṇa, in his many forms as a tiger,
adorned his eight horses with gold and jewels according to the prescribed rites.

Thus, O messenger, having first performed the ritual placement of the weapons among the heroes, one should then recollect the entire longing for meditation, followed by the offering of oblations and worship. (45b)
Just as the form of the deity exists within the Vīranāthas,
so too do the moving fruits of drink, garments, flowers,
and ornaments for the female messengers (dūtīs) be offered in their proper sequence.

O Chatrasudhvaja, when many sacrificial animals—both various kinds of wild beasts and numerous domestic animals—had been piled upon the funeral pyres by the forest ministers, ||| ... Having first performed the extensive offering of the *bali* and the giving of gifts by the preceptor,
he should then cause the disciple— whose eyes are bound and who is covered with a cloth to be meditated upon— to enter there slowly, having been anointed with the water of the *argha* offering.
One should cause the añjali to be offered with flowers that bear the fruit of precious gems;
furthermore, the eyes should be opened again in detail, one by one.
Excellent offerings of food and flowers should be given to the female and male messengers.
Then, having gone to the fire-sanctuary, according to the traditional injunctions,
the heroes should offer libations with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter into the fires,
reciting the root mantra one hundred times, not less, nor more than eight hundred.
Above that, [is the state] of all attachments; and above that, of the dried-up [impurities].
Again, by means of a specific ritual, the Lord of the Tradition (Āmnāyeśvara) has shown [the following]:
one should sprinkle the messenger (Dūtī) and the Hero (Vīra) upon the mortar, which is the embodiment of the method (Yukti).
Having consecrated [the disciple] with divine substances and the petals of the womb-vessel upon the back of that mortar,
one should then joyfully begin the offering of the first portion;
again, according to the instruction of the tradition, [one should proceed] for the sake of the Lord Kaṅkāla.
The Lord of Heroes (Vīreśa) should accomplish the rite by reciting the mantra of the female messengers (dūtīs); or else,
remaining established in sattva at night in a solitary place, in a cremation ground, or in a house of the Mothers—
whether in a deserted house or a pleasant mother’s dwelling— he should perform the recitation.
(46a) [The self] consists of the power, the mother-of-pearl, the tip, and the garland; it serves as the thread for those two cloths.
Likewise, it is like the Agnihotra fire, the sacrificial ladle, or the eight hundred thousand [recitations].
Then, the mantra-hero, through the constant enumeration of the Kaulika rites, should accomplish numerous divine and terrestrial feats that are skillful in action;
by his touch he burns living beings, and by his speech he causes them to tremble.
Upon seeing the masses of clouds, one should offer oblations with clarified butter, sesame, and sprouts—fifty thousand times for each of the three types of diseases characterized by specific signs.
Having performed the fire sacrifice, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; then the ten-ingredient incense (*daśāṅga*) will manifest intensely before one's sight.
The yogi whose vision is stainless regarding the three times hears sounds from afar;
moreover, by means of the distinction between the heart and other centers, he perceives even that which is concealed.
To the one who has transcended the fourth state (*turyātīta*) amidst the powers of the end of all things, [salutations].

The external [object] is not [attained] through equanimity; rather, while both [the internal and external] are present in the *kumbhaka* (retention), one should accomplish the state of non-dual absorption (*ananya-samādhi*) by means of compassion for both.
By the falling away of all elemental beings, one perceives that which undergoes transformation through the various constituents (*dhātus*).
He destroys fevers, young elephants, and even serpents.
He is to be worshipped at the outer Puṣkara; one should bring the human-Puṣkara [there].
Then, remaining here, he becomes a complete courtesan, as fickle as a courtesan.
They beheld the immensely powerful Kālakūṭa, which was as terrible as the conduct of Caṇḍī, upon the face of the Full Moon, who was charming with his lovely countenance;
just as the twice-born cast away their monkey-like testicles.

As before, by means of oblations of rice mixed in various ways, and by performing oblations numbering one hundred thousand or ten thousand in sequence, one may attract the world. By means of sesame seeds, one attracts a daughter of the Naga race; by means of excellent guggulu resin, a king’s daughter.
With wheat, the yakṣa maidens indeed [dwell], as do the piśācas with horse-gram;
likewise, the celestial maidens indeed dwell together with divine splendor.
The practitioner should honor the Goddess, along with the petals of the lotus;
likewise,
by means of the initial oblation filled with the flames of the ritual manual, he obtains a Yakṣa maiden at the appointed time.
With longing, he gazed at the hero’s distress with his crescent-shaped eyebrows.
Thus addressed by me, as if from the outside, [he spoke] regarding the semen, the body, and the elements;
Śīcī, Kuśī, Bhṛśaṅgā, Bhāradvāja, and Kauśika.

By means of the weapon-mudrā and one’s own mudrās, one should purify the form within the *mārjāra-cilla* (cat-owl). Having observed the characteristics of the crow, the cuckoo, and the *śākhāṇa*, as well as the bull, the elephant, and the bee, one becomes established in their very nature.
Now, with such [an understanding], one whose mind is firm [should perform the rite] with rice mixed with husks or with sesame seeds.
For the protection of the quarters, one facing south [should use] a mixture of *agnihotra* [grains].
In the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣa*), and in cases of negligence, as well as for the pinning down (*kīlana*) by means of the two-fold division [of the directions].
The yogi performs the paralyzing of the jaws, the paralysis of the limbs, and likewise battle, using the seed-syllables of diseases;
and through the mudrās of desire and gold,
he intensely subdues the spirits and the hosts of grahas from a distance of one hundred thousand leagues.

Through *śrīphala* fruits one obtains prosperity (*śrī*); through blue lotuses (*utpala*), Sarasvatī; and through the *sapharī* fish, one becomes Vāgīśvarī, a noble woman with beautiful eyes. (One should accomplish this by means of the fourfold essence in each of the three paths.)
The *mausalī* [mudrā] consists of five bones, two elephants, and five [limbs], possessing the supreme root;
it is distinguished by three mortars and follows the *musala*.
One should rotate the upper wheel and, having grasped the other, cause it to dissolve.
Having settled you both again on the exterior through the whirling of the mixed [breaths],
restrain [the mind] by entering into the fourfold collection at the auspicious [point].
[It is] crowded with the hosts of Skandas, Śukra, and others, as well as Bhūtas and Kumbhāṇḍas.
Protected by eight clay jars, one should pierce the ten-faced Rāvaṇa for a year;
thus, at night, they pierce the three-necked Trishiras with the fourth weapon-wheel.
Having returned according to his desire, he should mount the donkey with the Mothers; thereafter,
having enjoyed the female messengers (*dūtī*),
the yogi then beholds the eight families of the Brahmarakṣasas.
Having worshipped Indra at the tip of consciousness (*cidagra*) with half-moons and crescents within the belly of the root (*mūla*),
one who is equal [to all] should, at the end of the essence of fatigue from the even [recitation], impel the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) equally.
The one whose nature is the crest-vajra (*cūlavajra*) should cause the *yoginīs* to experience [this].
O Blessed One, she, having offered a hundred palas at night with these supreme words of instruction, and having likewise [offered] to Rāvaṇa,
shall roar loudly at the conclusion of the Vidyā; one should then empower the Rāva-piṇḍa with the mantra.
The Paryaṭeśavaras raised a loud clamor;
Rāvaṇa, however, made them roar, [offering] a morsel of food accompanied by a cry.
Then his supreme illusion was that which possessed a whirling wheel.
The lord of practitioners, having indeed offered the supreme cloth-painting with his own power through the application of the self-nature of Śakti, may wander among men according to his will;
[he performs] the heroic vow of sprinkling, worship, incense, and lamps.
In the cremation ground at night, there is a terrible practice involving the sound of "rāvaṇa.
By the power of that sound, one should bring the circle of messengers (*dūtīcakra*) under control.
Having extracted one's own radiance, one should cause it to revolve within the lotus-wheel (*abjacakra*).
By means of the dual roar of Rāvaṇa, one should split the root-Rāvaṇa;
having uprooted him along with his root, and having milked the fourth root,
the hero who chants this on the lunar day of the Dūtī shall, by his own will, become a sky-walker (khecara).
The Great Hero, the peerless hero, who simultaneously causes the two Rāvaṇas to flee;
having entered Mahārāvaṇa, he causes the sound of "rāva-rāvaṇa" to resound.
Indeed, he alone is the one born from the ocean, the white one, the singular source of great prosperity.
(47b) Today my state, along with its arising, goes toward cessation;
by the power of the vow and through the division of the *argha* offering, this great [realization] occurs before Caṭa.
The leader, the hero, offers oblations to the heroes; we shake the hero among heroes.
Indeed, we, being of one mind with the virtuous, shall accomplish what is to be accomplished through the recitation of the mantra.
Having entered all limbs, one should proceed along the path of all the upward breaths.
In the belly of the sky, in the navel, in every navel, do not show valor here;
having wandered through the front of these armies with a perfectly steady gait,
[he spoke thus] with great heat, marrow, and fat.
Through the union with fat, semen, and the rest, one attains the entire *kula*.
The auspicious fruit, beginning with Brahma and Śakti, resides within the great belly of the King of Courtesans (*dūtī*).
Having joined [these] within the belly of the nine *piṇḍas*, it is like a *saṃkalā* in the *Kalo-ttara*.
Having drawn forth the seed-syllables in many ways from the mouths of those who possess equal splendor along with their fathers-in-law,
the one whose self is disciplined may enter his own [body] at will;
at the end of the devouring of Rāvaṇa by Rāvaṇa, within the circle of the aged bull-leather garment.
Having placed the tip [of the tongue] by means of the placement of the placement (*nyāsanyāsa*), like the heat of wood from a branch,
and having drawn the essence (*piṇḍa*) into the essence, the sealing of the tip—
there the yogi drinks the nectar of immortality and may proceed to bliss at will.

Furthermore, at the beginning, middle, and end, one should enter the cave of the Hero (vīrakuhara) by means of the single excellent seed-syllable, which seizes the power along with Brahmā and the others. Having entered the opening of the supreme [cave], [one perceives] the blood and the like, consisting of essence and semen.
In an instant, the yogi may attract [the deity] at will and proceed to his own bliss.
Having offered the *argha* with flowers according to the ritual of the preliminary oblation,
he should worship the excellent cloth and proceed by means of the conduct (*caryā*) in the night.
The ritual procedure for Rāvaṇa consists of the *rāvapiṇḍa* offering accompanied by sound;
it concludes with fruits and grass after six months of practice.
In the place called Karaṅka, the lord of the Kula-indras [performs] the wheel known as Khorvāri.
The practitioner quickly perceives that he becomes equal [to the deity] and resembles the sky;
then, having thus prepared his self, he beholds the expanse of the edge of a sword's blade.
By the application of power and yoga, one should partake of the seven oblations (*caru*) according to one's inclination;
by the application of lamps and incense, there is the arrangement of the ritual procedure for recitation (*japa*) and fire.
Through the supreme resolve, which is foremost and accompanied by its own arising, it is without further arising.
With half of the increasing joy, [I praise] the three-syllabled and the syllable-less;
with the distinction of the hero and through aesthetic union,
I praise the Lord of the best of yogis along with his attendants, joined by the singular hero.

Having seen [this], the hero goes to the sky; one should approach the face of one who is equal to that. At the end of the night, the tree is known to be without thorns, well-endowed with power, possessing beautiful branches, and having very extensive trunks and foliage.
Day and night, whether sleeping or awake,
the hero who is neither agitated nor dull, delighting in the true state of being, should perform the recitation (*japa*) while wearing the *tantrahara* [garland].
Having performed the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) with its own constituent parts, he should shake off the delusions of the lower realm.

Meditating for one month through the union of the breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*), the practitioner— [visualizing] the true Brahman at the opening of the cavity, naturally continuous and devoid of passion, established by the twice-born [sages] in both direct and reverse order— shall obtain the desired goal.
One who causes emaciation should undertake this for seven constellations and one *kāṣṭhā*.
Standing at the fourth [posture], one should indeed desire the practice of a hero (*vīracaryā*) before the cloth.
First, in the *kṛcchra* flag and so forth, or else with heated cow’s urine.
At that entrance of the forest, having kindled a fire with fuel and grass from the east and heated the ground until it was covered entirely by flames,
one should then offer oblations of clarified butter and seven kinds of oils as they are produced.
Having filled its cavity, one should offer oblations into the terrestrial fire;
then the yogi attains the mandala within the flame of the fire.
Then, having taken that very ash and consecrated it with clarified butter through the mouth [of the deity], one should offer a hundred thousand oblations;
thus, kings along with the earth itself come under one's control.
Likewise, for two, seven, or eight [oblations], as well as twelve for one's own wife.
One should add salt with the five [ingredients] and offer it again according to the family tradition (*kulācāra*).
Then, by means of the threefold union (*triyoga*), one should face the center of the two doors.
At the end of the recitation, with the application of *kuśa* grass, [one binds] the head with the noose (*pāśa*) from the throat.
Neither of them could grasp what was to be grasped; thus it was empty and naked.
Having heard this, Śrīdatta’s vision failed; casting off his ornaments and hair, he fell senseless upon the ground, a mere body possessing only consciousness.

Having stepped upon [the victim] with his left foot, he should perform the fire-oblation for a hundred days and nights according to the previous ritual procedure; he should recite the mantra facing all directions and worship before the principal cloth-painting with an inner self absorbed in that.
Then the king will become subject to him, free from pride;

indeed, like the lord of the day (the sun), he shall bring [the king] under his control by means of his body, wealth, and wife. Standing upon a mountain or in a sacred field at night, he should offer oblations of fragrant meat.
Having set fire to the cremation ground with dry wood grown in the forest, one should then bring the corpse according to the traditional instructions over the course of days and moments.
Having bathed it before the sacred cloth (*paṭa*) and offered oblations into the fire, one should ascend the funeral pyre.
With the aforementioned pills mixed with oil, one should offer oblations into the mouth.
Likewise, by the force of the animal of speech, he uttered a loud roar and said:
"O Hero, I am your servant; ascend upon Skanda!"
"Go at will to your own worlds, whether by following behind me or by treading upon my back.
Having heard these words from the mouth of the servant, she then made a firm resolve for her own welfare;
and having seen [the truth], she abandoned her corpse-like state.
Then, having accomplished this sword and emerged from his vehicle,
the yogi becomes a sword-vidyādhara for as long as the earth endures.
Likewise, one should properly prepare Trilocanā in the skull-cup (muṇḍapuṭa) at the beginning;
by this, one becomes a Vidyādhara, marked with a tilaka, and remains invisible for a long time.
By smelling it, Kaṇṭaka should be applied, and likewise to the eyes of men.
When it has matured, the Lord of Beings is said to perform the act of invisibility.
Having thus applied collyrium to your three eyes, one who stands before the eyes can reveal everything; likewise, the beasts shall meet their end.
Cooking food here before the cloth painting (paṭa), having performed the satiation of the fire-hero (agnivīra),
one who abides within the heart-mantra of the Kulanāga should recite it one hundred thousand times according to the ritual rule.
Then, the powerful Kulabhogin will become subject to his control.
Together with your own self, your wealth, your daughters, and those sages,
you shall go to the excellent city of Pañcapārthiva, accompanied by a sword. Thus,
having duly offered oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rites in another *agnihotra* sacrifice, you shall proceed in due order.
Likewise, having offered one hundred thousand oblations of mustard seeds, jaggery, and guggulu in front [of the deity],
the lord of heroes (vīrendra) shall indeed obtain the station of the lord of sky-farers (khecarendra).
By day, he becomes the lord of half a mandala and is eternally liberated from the womb.

By union with that, one should grasp the directions starting from the south; if one desires that face of the directions, one should indeed cause both types of arising to resound with the roar of Rāvaṇa.
In the power of the musical scale (grāma-śakti), there exist gain and the excellence of the recitation of the Vidyā.
One should offer oblations with the mantra "hantu svareti" for the obstruction of sound, and with "aṭṭahāse" for the sounding of a cry.
Then, with "bhūyo bhayaparendrendro rāvaya," one should offer the oblation for the drinker.
Furthermore, having risen in the morning, one should indeed recollect [the deity] throughout both day and night.
Having completed this rite according to the rule through the yoga of animal offerings,
the lord of practitioners beheld, by his own will and in accordance with the tradition, the single visible wheel adorned with the Suvīra [mudrā].
Having seen [the disciple], one should cause him to generate the left-hand [gesture] and grasp it with palms joined;
thus, by means of the messenger (dūtī), he becomes known as a hero (vīra), a performer of sacrifice, and a wanderer in the sky.
One beholds Bharūṭī, who grants all desires, with clarified butter and parched grain;
one beholds Ṛkṣajā and Ṛkṣakarṇī while bearing the huṇḍa discus;
and one beholds the great giver of wealth with bhaṭṭāñjana and nṛgabhoja.
With the gaze of the King of Phetkāra, one sees the servant (kiṅkara) moving upwards;
with the gaze of a dog, one obtains a sword and meat by which one sees;
with the gaze of a jackal, one sees [the truth] through a tortoise; and with the gaze of men, one sees within the circle of crocodiles.
O Heroic Lord, those who are prompt should quickly look back step by step in reverse order at the Vīra-aṃśu-Bhairava. Then,
one should offer the *śakti* before the cloth-painting according to the prescribed rite.
Having extracted the *puṣpendra* [flower], the female messenger (*dūtī*) should recite the mantra of the Hero for half the duration.
Having performed the sacrifice, she should go toward the Śavara [dwelling] in the direction of the excellent field of the *khāna*.
She should avoid all directions except for the east and the west.
Having worshipped the unsurpassed discus with the *nṛgoja* mantra on the forehead,
Vīreśa, the possessor of fortune, shall wander through the quarters of the directions according to their divisions.
Furthermore, those who are like donkeys [should be placed] at the mouth of the *āgneya* [fire-altar] by means of the *bharūḍhī* [mantra].

One beholds the divine Brahmarakṣa family as Lampaṭeśvara; by means of the benefit of the cow-born (Brahmā), one impels the protective Karṇikā. One beholds the face born of Brahmā and Paiśāca, and the eight families.
First, having sprinkled [the offerings] with liquor,
the masters behold the essence of the Yoginīs, the eight families of Brahmā and Yakṣas, in the *nir-iri* [mantra].
With the meat of bull, courtesan, and goat, the *hakāras* face the direction of the wind.
Having sacrificed at the seven families of gatekeepers, one beholds those who are not born from a womb.
Thus, by means of the bull Laṃbāgo, a man enjoys the northern quarter and beholds the divine, wandering family of heroes along with their multitudes.
In the same way, there is Śiveśvarī in the northeast with grains of rice;
and whatever wise ones behold them, they are Bhairavas crowded with heroes.
In this very way, the practitioner surely attains numerous and indeed incalculable accomplishments (*siddhi*) through the power of yoga, as well as the female messengers (*dūtī*).
Indeed, Goṣṭharāja, who is of the nature of a horse, has been worshipped in many ways on the earth.
He experiences even the entire [cycle] in both forward and reverse order;
nevertheless, through the preliminary ritual, whether in brief or in great detail,
the accomplishments (siddhis) of the heroes arise by means of the messenger (dūtī) and the sword (khaḍga), according to the heroic conception.
Having gradually performed the rite according to the traditional injunctions with water that has lost its impurity,
and having abandoned the [old] ashes, one should smear the Linga with fresh earth from a sacred field; then, with a tranquil mind, one should worship the white flower upon it.
In the case of hatred, one should remove [the substance] from the body or strike it outside without doubt;
with flowers at intervals of one [day], it becomes so with seven grains of rice.
Indeed, there is a distinction made by the husks when moving it along with many others.
By means of the full [substance], let there be the piercing, the stupefying, and the pinning;
indeed, the skin should be licked with oil by the heroes and the female messengers in due order.
Thus, in this sequence, through the successive abandonment of the eight enemies of the female messengers.
O Hero, while performing [this], one traverses the edge of the sword by means of the *vraja*;
having bound the *saiṃhinī-mudrā*, which brings about the full emergence of the power of the vow,
the one who gladdens attains the entire *kula* together with Śiva, the Power.
Having heard the sound, the foremost hero, subduing [the enemy],
should follow after her once more and honor her with joined palms. Then, having honored her, he should envelop her by means of the application of the mudrā.
That mind then goes to the sky, and the hero attains the state of a lord of heroes;
the mudrā of the Mistress of the Five Mudrās, making a roar like that of Rāvaṇa, causes [all] to run.
By means of the resonance of both [the vowels] which possess form,
the one who moves through the sequence ending with the grasping of power wanders as the self of the power of the lineage (*vaṃśa-śakti*) toward the lotus of the ritual of his own power.
Having entered the lotus situated on the left, he should recite the *daṭṭahāsa* laughter.
Thus, having completed the ritual procedure, one who has undertaken the vow until the end of the year—
rich in power through the manifestation of power— should enjoy the beautiful state of the conqueror. Indeed,
the branch known as Kula possesses seventy-two faces, just as the Vidyā possesses its own portion.

The practitioner quickly perceives the arising of the *kalās* together with their emergence; having entered that which is the arising of arising, he reaches the state where the yoga has arisen and is beyond cessation—
the initiation that, having attained the directions and so forth, precedes the city that transcends the middle sense-organ.
The hero who has transcended the leap [of worldly existence] sits upon the seat of the great hero Indra;
therefore, through union with that which is equal to Him, the yogi becomes disciplined and attains Him.
In this very way, there are many such [teachings] according to the rules of all the Āgamas.
Although the Siddhis have been correctly described by Indra as being like creepers,
nevertheless, the yogi should perform investigation;
having attained them, he should extract the other [Siddhis] individually, just as they have been explained.
Nevertheless, by carrying the messenger without distinction,
one attains through the purpose of the vow the application of the tip of the flower of power;
and by the application of the power, the application of the yoga of power.

Without [a consort], the excellent hero shall obtain the supreme vow through the heroic messenger (vīradūtī). He shines together with the power of the hero (vīraśakti) in the midst of the night, just as a ray shines when joined with the sun, or as fire blazes when joined with fuel.
Therefore, with every effort, according to the injunctions of the authentic tradition (*āmnāya*),
one should first perform the *punaryāna* (re-initiation) when capable, and thereafter the *vīrasādhana* (heroic practice).
Such is the characteristic of capability, from which the arising of the flower [of realization] follows.
(51a) I shall speak briefly for your benefit regarding the distinctions of the practice of vows and so forth.
She who is dark-complexioned like the petal of a blue lotus is the most excellent among the full [deities] at the gate.
With eyes like full-blown blue lotuses, beautiful with long dark locks of hair,
her braid tied fast, she was radiant with the dust of pearls;
her fresh parting was fashioned with care, and she was perfumed with camphor and aguru incense.
With two crescent-moon-shaped ear-ornaments, gentle, her lips stained with saffron; possessing a beautiful nose and a lovely forehead, she is adorned with jeweled earrings.
The Goddess wears various gems and is resplendent with many kinds of jewels.
With breasts like jars of divine nectar, divine shoulders, and long arms;
with a neck like a conch shell, a level head, serene, and a face like the moon;
adorned with great armlets, with a waist like a diamond and soft skin.
They possessed great hips, were most excellent, and bore large, expansive breasts like water-jars;
they were adorned with beautiful girdles and waistbands,
and their excellent speech was as deep and resonant as the cry of a noble swan.
With hidden joints and hidden body hair, with well-concealed bones, flesh, and sinews;
broad-chested, with a wheel-like pubic region, hidden ankles, and great strength;
with the soles of her toes hidden, she is adorned with flowers and jewels—the most excellent among the goddesses.
Rooted in faith toward the gates of Dharma, devoted to the sacred word,
and possessing great virtues such as devotion to her gurus, heroes, and husband, she was thus intent upon divine rites through the yoga of the hero.
The practice of the vow, which consists of its fruit,
is praised in all rites when it is joined with pure devotional action and that which is to be experienced in the future;
likewise, it should be joined with that body through the yoga of the hero.
As long as there is no power in the *Suvīra* sūtras equal to that [of the hero],
the hero is liberated from all mental afflictions by means of the heroic woman.

Nevertheless, when the application of the wheels is reversed, the qualities of these [deities]—the fierce Vīrendra and Śaktis—result in fruit that is as it were non-existent. There is no gift equal to a hero; there is no wealth equal to a hero.
There is no bond equal to the hero; there is no destiny equal to the hero.
For the hero is Bhairava himself, and the hero’s wife is Subhairavī.
When Bhairavī is united with Bhairava, even poison becomes entirely nectar.
That which is always called Bhairava by Bhairavī is the cause;
I shall tell you all of that state of Bhairava through Bhairavī.
She is the supreme moon among the powers (śaktis) of those intoxicated ones named Bhairavīs.

The preceptor, facing north and wearing a garment dyed with saffron, should worship the feet [of the image] after stepping over them from the south. Standing on three feet, he faces the disciple who stands before him.
Having washed the two thumbs to be grasped with milk-water,
one should fumigate them with clarified butter and parched grain, and then anoint them with the [substance] arising from that.
[One should perform this] by moving the bindu from the position of the head downwards, arising from half [the syllable].
One should worship with the lord of the Rāvaṇas during the utterance of the sound "Rāva" in the auspicious [rite];
and when a disciple has arisen, one should worship again with that disciple or with one born from him.
He, the god of gods, having turned back, entered the head along with the disciple.
One should again worship with a village offering, provided one has the capacity.
When he has crossed over [the obstacles], he desires horses; his arrows are the pure weapons of Brahmā.
Śubhanayanā is at his feet, Candrasūryā is on his face, and Agnijvālā is on his chest.
At the very tip of the messenger (dūtī), one should cause the syllables to arise from the root;
[the elements] fire, water, wind, and earth are located respectively above, to the left, below, and in the other [direction].
One should join them starting from the hand upwards, beginning with the ear and ending with the water.
Viṣṇu himself covers that which is empty; his own rays are like serpents.
That which has grown upon the mouth of the lowest caste is the mortal state of being born from one caste into another.
At the navel, the wise ones are Vikalpa, Bhairavī, and again Bhairava.
Therefore, by means of the *trārkṣa* (the protective constellation), one should join the feet with the feet in the entire *piṇḍa-vij* and bind them together with everything and everyone.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of the *yukti* from oneself or from the disciple,
and having joined it with the *gharṣapuṣpa*, one should worship the heap of flowers.
Having thus worshipped previously, one should perform the meditations for stabilization.
Having obtained flowers, one should enter with the head bowed before the Ācārya of Bhairavī. Then, having been raised up by Bhairavī, one should worship him with the arghya and flowers.
Having worshipped him with the offering of the flower-bond, one should honor him with the presentation of the bali.
One should cause the *avadhūta* to be impelled by means of the wind that has bound the hundred thousand powers (*śakti-lakṣa*).
One should pierce through the directions from the point (*bindu*), thinking "I am Śiva.
Listen to the procedure for the consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the field (*kṣetra*) for the sake of the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
Having distributed [the offerings] during the preliminary and subsequent nights, Śiva himself said:
"O disciple, having thus abandoned all egoism through mental contemplation and having indeed established satisfaction within the mind, one should cause [the ritual] to be performed."
In Bhairava, they are joined with the Bhairava [state] by means of an inner self that is free from hunger;
with a mind undisturbed, O Śākta, O Puṣpa, O Sātvata,
when the disciple perceives the vision of the "desire-path" (kāmaroga).
When at that time the messenger does not become "black-faced" (*kālamukha*) again,
and when the hero proceeds with agitation due to the pride of being white (*vetābhimāna*),
then he attains perfection and the messenger attains the state of a lord of heroes (*vīrendra*).
O Sage Śakti, if one's mother should be present at the foremost of ritual practices, she is to be honored, yet not with food;
likewise for a sister, the wife of a guru, or the wife of a disciple—
provided they are properly engaged and possess the auspicious qualities of the *śālāvāci*.
By means of that [practice], one whose intellect is obscured may attain the unobscured state.
Having worshipped Mahābhairava, Bhairavī, the beloved of Bhairava, [bestows this].
Having placed the beloved upon his lap, the couple should cultivate meditation;
yet that meditation is not truly cultivated unless one meditates by means of their essential nature.
Through this, oneness arises, whereby the very goal of the wise is accomplished.
By drinking the supreme nectar that flows from the union of the three sweets as far as the blood, the couple becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*).
While performing this yoga with a woman, the mantra-practitioner [attains] the *śāśinī* vidyā.
The sky upon the banner is with heroes, and through its splendor, it is the dawning of Bhairava.
Thus, by means of both, he moves as one who has attained immortality through the food of heroes at night.
By the application of the yoga of both traditions, the hero attains the state of heroism.

In reality, the hero named Svasidhāraka is free from all conceptualization; through the yoga of manifestation, he transcends the conceptualization of both the kalpa and the kalpaka. Indeed, that hero, devoted to the supreme power (*varaśakti*), becomes the nectar of immortality.
Delighting in that which has been attained by others, the Hero rises again;
like the moon with its rays upon a flower, he is clothed in the directions of space.
Seated upon the edge of a sword, through the piercing of the *piṇḍa*, there shall be truth.
The placement (*nyāsa*) is performed by attaching the power (*śakti*), arising from the outer hall (*bāhyaśālā*);
afterwards, it is joined with the messenger (*dūtī*) in the cavity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍapuṭa*) of the victim (*paśu*) who possesses the auspicious marks.
The neck (*kaṃdhara*) is one's own hall (*svaśālā*), hidden within the channels of time (*kālanāḍī*).
Having tied the hair of that corpse to the shoulder with the eyes [intact], one should form a skull-casket;
likewise, one should offer the skull-casket with water-offerings (*argha*), incense, and flowers.
While reciting [the mantra], being free from attachment, one should perform this at the three junctions of the day for seven days.
When the incense and lamps are not extinguished, the third twilight arrives;
having awakened, one obtains the lotus that strikes fear into both gods and asuras.
Furthermore, one who is well-refined through their capacity ascends to the supreme state beyond others.
Having given the highest portion and having partaken [of the remainder], the ascetics go to the void, the station of the *yatīs*.
Or, by some other means, one should lead along the sacrificial animals and the lotuses.
Furthermore, by means of the sword-edge yoga (*sidhārāyoga*), one should extract the three worlds;
having bathed oneself, [one should place] that digit (*kalā*) within the enclosure of the *puṇḍra*.
Without establishing it as a bound animal (*paśu*), one should bind it with a rope as before.
With the *Vidyā* preceded by the *Śikhā*, one should worship the *Liṅga* without defiling it. Measured by a period of seven weeks, for each of the seven sets of seven weeks,
one should practice as before, reciting the ritual *Sītkāra* loudly.
Just as a well does not produce [water] through the application of people, so there is no modification of nature;
for one who knows the fire-rites, the mouth is like a mouthful of food.
Again, that Lord of Heroes and Masters remained for a period of seven weeks.
Even if one were a perpetrator of every sin, he obtains a divine lotus;
having experienced seven karmas and transcended the eighth birth,
that hero, having enjoyed himself on the path of the Lord of Heroes (Vīreśvara), goes to a state beyond rebirth.

Or indeed, by the application of power alone, and through the vow itself, O Lord of Immortality, they cause others to cross over and they themselves cross over by means of this tradition. Whether a person be of the nature of *prakṛti* or of *vikṛti*, through transformation, the person who was of *prakṛti* [becomes otherwise].
Even one possessing constant vigor, whose nature is the void, would not proceed by means of successive steps;
nor indeed would one who has attained the three-fold state, [proceed] through the three-fold middle, the measure, and the drink.
Having reached the fourfold state, one attains the lotus that transcends the ladder.
Delighting in the complete state where the arising of the intellect is undiminished, he attains the supreme, ever-rising [state]; and being well-absorbed, he should effect cessation.
Having attained the fourfold goal, he should extinguish the state that arises as the light of the world and the non-world.
With a thousand *kuṣuṇmātras*, there is the transition to the spear [stage] in the wind;
in the path of space, when there is no interval, there is the agitation of successive strides. (53b)
Having abandoned the pentad of sound and the other [objects of the senses], he has proceeded to another arising of the unmanifest.
Through the yoga of sound called *ūrdhvavācā*, characterized by the four *kalās* and consisting of pure being (*bhāva*),
it has been composed in four parts by the Rāmas, who are designated as the "upward-moving" (*ūrdhvaka*).
The forefinger is the seizer; the renunciant is endowed with the power of the seizer. Possessing the practice of the power of swallowing, he assumes forms according to his will.
Thus, in the previous birth, his face was the orb of the moon of the universe.
Since he brings forth many kinds of certificates of success (siddhapatra) according to the doctrine,
and because the bond of the ritual procedure is established in the supreme chest of the rite,
the flawless night enters with the offerings of cooked rice and the hairs [of the victim].
Whatever is desired, by whatever means, and through whichever yoga, one brings about the vision of the Self; just as a servant conveys [an object] from hand to hand, so too,
having performed the sacrifice of the "Good House" (sugṛha-yāga), the performance of the sacrifice becomes easy.
Having worshipped the cloth with *śakti* flowers and caused the best of men to consume it, she—
along with her wheel— goes to the house of the lord of the earth when his hair has fallen out.
Thus, O Goddess, she devours the expanse of the clouds of the gods' skulls.

The sage, who possesses the power of the crow’s wing (*kākapa-kṣākti*), having wrapped [the substance] around his mouth, brings many substances of manifold nature into his own house; then, playing at will, he leads them back wherever he desires. He is one who has conquered the three poisons (*trisāna*).
Having visualized [the deity] as residing within the object of accomplishment and having directed it toward the deity, recite the mantra at the end of the night;
then, from that mouth, behold him in a form of wrath. At the sixty-fourth cycle, whatever you desire, that you shall obtain.
For with its wings, it [the peacock] strikes that very [enemy] which stands face-to-face;
it should swallow the entire body of the *śakti* and strike with its deep [beak].
By means of the owl (*kauśika*), one should shake those who are subject to transformation, such as milk and the like.
He brings together limb with limb, village with village, or equally;
likewise the sacrificial animal, the splendor, the defective [limbs], and among these, the crossroads.
Then, remove the portions of desire, the *bhā*, the *kāṇḍa*, and the *kākiṇī*. Through the manifestation of fierce power (*ugra-śakti*), there is the conceptualization of Rāvaṇa;
indeed, by means of the king of powers, one causes the powerless to roar.
O Lord of Heroes, one who maintains the sacred fire and performs the recitation (*japa*) for six months shall become beloved by all beings, together with the oceans of prosperity.
Through these, I am increasingly pleased during the arising of the previous kalpa.
Having reached the wheel at the half [of the path], as well as the fourth, one should shake it;
through the union of the grasped and the grasper, [one attains] the auspicious Śiva.
Within that, having dissolved the enclosure, one should cause the three Puṣkaras to revolve in the center.
Then, having extracted the subsequent [letters] from both the achievable and the unachievable along with their numerical counts,
they blossom within the confines of one's own abode through the application of going and returning.
Thus, at the arising of the *kalā*s, everything is contained within the body.
On a great path, with offerings accompanied by the fruits that are the abode of Śrī,
the Hero, established in the rite of heroic conduct, should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times;
thus, being disciplined, he shall become Vācaspati himself within six months.
Having worshipped in the void (kha), fully conscious upon the seat of the transcendent fourth (sātītaturyaviṣṭara), he—

whose self is brought under control by the noose and goad— is the leader, for he possesses the supreme authority over the foremost [principles] within the earthly abodes in their true nature and by their own form.
In the interval, the animal has gone to the root of the *sauṣṭha* by means of the *suṣumnā*.

Indeed, by joining the self through the yoga of measurement (*pramāṇa-yoga*), one is liberated among the foremost-born. When all life is drawn forth along with its limbs, where indeed can there be fear?
One should place one's own breath in the mother [vowel], in the middle, at the end of the *kātyā*, similar to an *iṣu* [arrow],
in the navel of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), along with the genitals and the feet, in the heart, the head, and between the eyebrows. (54b)
Recalling them with the *bhayamantra*, those shaped like chariots, jars, and whirlpools were then brought together by Krodha along with the six *ketus* and the sacrificial animals,
amidst all the transformations occurring at the tips of the branches and the edges of the twilight.
Then, while his mother was of the nature of fire, that hero assumed a form resembling water;
all the external elements were drawn toward him,
yet he remained free from the destruction caused by the decay of those transformations.
In the entire group, the seven and so forth are properly applied to the form of Rāvaṇa;
joined upon the upper seat, one should arrange the calculation of the piṇḍas.
And in the field of all objects, there are the four, the transcendent, and the seven.
The deity-essence, together with the bindu, should be rotated from the *tripuṭa* [triangle] by means of the whirling of a chariot. Then, ending with the visarga, it proceeds from there;
and that, at the end of the visarga in the void, is like a fierce fire within the *astra*.
Having turned back [the breath] at the seven *piṇḍas* and having placed the Heroic Leader (*vīranāyaka*) in the lower *agha*,
one should recite that [mantra] while engaged in *kumbhaka*, according to one's capacity, accompanied by the Command (*ājñā*).
One should deposit this at that time upon wood that possesses flowers, juice, and fruit.
Having encircled [the breath] with the bones of the fingers, above the mortar of the index finger,
one should again bind those two moving toward the apāna by means of the goad of the lower power (adhaḥśakti) and the black noose; this is the visualization of the woman of the limbs (dhyāṅgavastrī).
He should strike that sacrificial animal with the flour of the sacrificial cake using the backs of his hands;
then, he should strike it with the thunderbolt-like [mudrā] of the *avasvai* [posture].
Having thus sealed it within the center of the sacrificial circle, he should proceed.
Having meditated thus— on one side the battle-station and on the other side Śiva— and having again, by means of the power (śakti), impelled [the breath] so that it rests at the tip of the nose,
one should, as if causing it to enter the stomach, seize the *piṇḍa* according to the characteristic mark.
In the half [of the path] beyond the fourth state, she is pierced by resonance up to the crest-lock;
having filled it, the wooden beast, through its transformations resembling those of a [living] beast, [is liberated]. (55a)
He enjoyed the sacrificial meat, which was transformed by various flavors,

together with great heroes such as Vīrendra and others who were foremost among those skilled in chariot warfare. Then, from two animals that were like lumps of wood, he extracted the nectar of immortality.
He attains the state of being completely enveloped; the Kalā (Brahmā) shall go to Śiva.
Thus, having seen thousands of Siddhis arising from the heart of all the Āgamas, the leader of heroes taught that one partakes of the plow of the path of enumeration.
— — The messenger (dūtī) is within the cluster of all powers called the Hero (vīra). Having properly scattered the two feet, one should duly perform the ritual arrangement of the Kalpa.
One should thus correctly establish Jyeṣṭhā eternally in the abode of bliss.
The hero who carries knowledge and the other [perfections], even while remaining a householder,
attains thousands of worldly accomplishments (*lokasiddhi*) and hundreds of divine accomplishments (*divyasiddhi*).
Furthermore, by means of the ritual procedure beginning with the three [syllables] *tri-pūrva*, he achieves the fourfold great attraction (*mahākṛṣṭi*).
Thereafter, the hero constantly attains the entry into the divine body;
by his own will, consuming the nectar, he attains the true fruit of his own nature in the Kali age. Jyeṣṭhā is the creditor among the fields (kṣetras), having entered the mouth as it was proclaimed.

But she who is intent on meditative absorption (samādhi) is the Avatārā Vadhūtī; she dwells within the circle of the uneven belly, beyond the ocean of worldly existence. Just as she is to be realized through the meditative absorption of desire, so too is she in the external pavitraka.
One should tie those stakes in their respective directions together with flowers and the limbs [of the deity].
By means of that oil and incense, one should bring forth the seven *piṇḍa-kaulika* mantras while reciting them—
those which exist within the interval between the worlds of *loka* and *aloka*.
Just as one who is protected by his own kinsmen remains established in his home, so too does the lord of the faction (*pakṣeśa*), through his stratagems (*āḍhopa*),
seize the woman who is the source of life and the root of the elements,
just as a snake seizes its prey.
Just as it is in the field of Nandī, so indeed is the conception of the eastern enclosure; the lords of the Kaulikas, urging [this], have observed it in the past.
Through the proper external cultivation of the distinction between the grasper and the grasped,

those who consume mantras, time, and stone according to their desire may enter their own mouths. By means of the yoga of power (*śakti*), both forest-dwellers and householders [attain] the sky-farers (*khecaras*).
Indeed, for those who have mastered the power of their own energy (śakti), there is the attainment of the fruit of the iṣṭi sacrifice even while remaining celibate.

When one is complete with the characteristics as described, one should conceive of energy within the state of energy. Through the practice of devotion, the hero (vīra) goes to the sky by means of the primary energy.
Thus, through the yoga of oral tradition (āmnāya), there is no conceptual construction whatsoever.

A man attains the state of a hero, or power (śakti) is rendered free of qualities (nirguṇīkṛtā). Therefore, the oral tradition is transcendent, devoid of conceptualization, and it is the teacher who reveals the sacred word (hṛpadaiśikā).

Having received permission from the mouth of the guru, one should enter the lifelong stage of asceticism (*naiṣṭhika*), [enduring] the rain of the Great Skeleton (*mahākaṅkāla*) and walking upon the edge of a sword-blade (*asidhārā*). Having constructed a hut of leaves at a mountain site or at the confluence of rivers, one should dwell there.

By this [practice], even a householder attains the fruit corresponding to what has been ascended. Therefore, having worshipped the divine image endowed with a hundred thousand auspicious marks within a hall in the city, one should have it consecrated with clarified butter.

One should indeed collect the *pūrṇareṇu* at the end of the night in a skull-receptacle (*muṇḍasaṃpuṭa*). Upon that, one should place lotuses with pure nectar-water in the east. Then, when the great lamp has been extinguished, [one should offer] incense at the feet of the deities.
In this very way, the food offering (naivedya) is extracted separately from the deceased;
likewise, for the sake of prosperity, the flower-faced servants of the pretas are established in the various directions, bearing the great weapons of the noose and the goad.
Having performed this correctly with the three *puṣkaras* at the beginning of the night of this day and night,
one should go forth making the quarters resound with the roar, the roar, the roar.
Intending for seven generations of his lineage, he should arrange the fire-offerings.
Even while laughing loudly or with a loud burst of laughter (*aṭṭahāsa*),
and even while eating great fruits, they should wear crests made of those flowers.
In that very way, the endless garland of worlds,
which was being torn asunder by the force of his laughter, made the host of beings in the sky laugh with their own laughter;
yet Rāvaṇa, having once again swallowed them up with his power, laughed with a roar of "grāsa" (swallowing).

Again, the high recitation of the mantra is performed separately for the Kaula and Miśra traditions. Then follows the swallowing of the power (Śakti) by Rāvaṇa, accompanied by the laughter of the devouring laugh.
Upon re-entry, one faces south toward the hall of Vaiśravaṇa.
Seated comfortably, having finished other duties, facing the northeast;
that which has passed and that which has not yet passed—each subsequent [topic] is stated thereafter.
Together with time, supported by the full moon, in the middle of the village is the seat of the bindu.

He who is contemplated day and night becomes wise; thus, at the exhaustion of the night’s practice, he becomes utterly void. And as he wanders through the wheel of space, he proclaims the wheel of the Puṣkara.
Thus, one should extract [the essence] from all things through the primordial lotus of transformation.

One who is bound by the divine state does not exist as a self subject to recitation, for he abides in the practice of the fire. Likewise, there is no offering of diverse oblations, nor the conceptualization of performing ritual acts.
Just as the practice at night and the conceptualization of the lineage of devotees are,
so too is the one who is wise and intent on meditation carried away by the night;
that first arm which is the lotus, purified, is his auspicious life.
Then, disregarding the divine [bliss] obtained from heaven,
the second [hero] chose a cave ten times superior; having enjoyed the Mahāpadma [pleasure],
those of great strength, the guardians of the field (*kṣetrapāla*), undergo dissolution at the end of spring.
Having enjoyed the third [state] of non-duality, Padma, the most excellent of lotuses, [attains it];
the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Bhūtas go to dissolution before the Foremost Goddess.
When the fourth lotus has indeed been consumed as prescribed,
all [the powers] belonging to the lord of practitioners pass away through transference by the command.
There is no ritual arrangement for being sustained by the fifth lotus.
The divine [state] attained through the perfected yoga comes under the control of the practitioner. Indeed,
in the sixth lotus, by means of mastery and the sound of the roar,
all the deities go to dissolution within the Lord of Heroes (*vīrendra*).
When the seven Kaulika [elements] have indeed been extracted from the Arthottara, the Indre, and the Indre,
they come before the practitioner within the entire Sevenfold Kaula.
Likewise, the essence is grasped in the Gṛhya, and Bhairava is proclaimed therein.
With a hand that whirls weapons, [the teacher], raised high with the strength of a great hero,
should sequentially bestow even a small portion upon each of all those of his lineage, starting from the eldest, according to their respective order.

Immediately thereafter, in the service of attendance, there were gatekeepers along with their attendants; in the circle of messengers for the protection of the family, there was movement in and out of the family quarters.
When the price had been set, the heroic leader of the circles performed the counting of the various assemblies.
"Having consumed [the offering] from the vessel, one attains sovereignty over the wheel and shall go to Śiva.
Thus, O Goddess of the Gods, has the ritual procedure for the group of six messengers been briefly described;
thereafter, their ritual manual contains the fruit of all fruits."
By merely knowing and studying this, just as before,
the mantra becomes invisible to heroes;
for one who is constantly devoted to the practice of conduct and whose yoga is characterized by solitary discipline.
To him she should be taught in this way; for him, the accomplishments will be fruitful.
Thus has the Goddess Śabdāraṇī been explained to you according to her true nature.
Kālikā Rāviṇī, I shall now explain this correctly.

Thus ends the procedure for the Sound-Kāli and the Wheel of Messengers (dūtīcakra) within the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, a great tantra (*mahātantra*) of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraccheda* division of the Vidyāpīṭha in the Bhairava current.
Having thus heard this wonderful speech from the lotus-like mouth of Hara, the Blessed Goddess spoke again to Śiva words that were gracious and profound.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"I am satisfied, O Blessed One; that supreme state has been correctly understood by me through your grace, O Great Lord of all lords. Now I desire to hear the Kulārṇava known as Kaṅkāla."
Where that goddess Kālikā, whose form is wide-open, manifests;
she who resides beneath the crest-jewel, resplendent with a mass of rays—
within her [is] the sequence, distinguished by its external and internal divisions.
"O Blessed One, honored by the best of gods, I desire to know this.

Having heard this, the Lord of the Gods, having consecrated his lineage with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and having placed the digit of consciousness (cidakāṃśa) upon his crest, spoke these most supreme and great words.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, I shall tell you this supreme secret,
the Great Kaula which has become a closed fist and resides within the sky-farers (khecarīs).
Free from conceptualization, free from doubt, complete, and devoid of both [extremes],
the Sun of Consciousness (cidarka) is her crest-jewel;
and she, Kālikā, is its counter-lamp, the lamp that is ever-illuminating throughout all time.

In that interval, she is always present there in this Tantra; she is the support radiant with the sun, for Kālikā is indeed supported by that. In the six-spoked [wheel], she is the vast support, resembling sixteen flashes of light.
The one who emits the throbbing mind, the devourer through her gaping maw, the creator of emanation—
then the Sun himself, in the form of the deity, performs that very act.

The lamp of the sun has arisen from the midst of the sun in this world; the sun, the radiant one, dwelling within, illumines the entire universe. That which is the solar Kaulinī, the world is filled with her mass.
Therein arise the great mantras, the eight Bhairavas of the sixty-four origins. They are not manifest in space, nor in both [space and time], nor in that which is devoid of fear.
Released from all obscurations, they are the sun beyond all enjoyments.
By which [the world] is covered, enveloped, and fashioned as the lineage of lineages (*kulākula*),
that *Saravi* shines at the end of the fourth solar hour within the fierce and terrifying [state],
having contemplated itself beyond *Rāmā* with its eternally risen rays.
By whomsoever the wheel of existence (bhacakra) is illumined, for him indeed time becomes old age.
Having made the external internal and the mantra internal, and having made the mantra external,
the practitioner who knows the mantra of non-dual continuity shall attain the arising of the mantra.
Having reached mountain caves that are like gardens, delighting in the vibration of secluded objects,
one attains supreme bliss— unmoving and free from both [subject and object].
Behold knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower, all of which are contained within pure awareness.
It dissolves into the supreme abode, which is characterized by the absence of egoism.
Pervaded by the Supreme, who exists in the form of vibration within the womb of the movement of consciousness-bliss, She shines at the end of the veil of the six paths.
In the new [body], having entered between one being and another being for eight finger-breadths,
there arises a conjunction at the root of saṃsāra, capable of churning [the elements].
Having taken space within the self, and the self from within the space—
Through the single-fold union of the void and the self, nothing whatsoever remains.
The inner light and the outer light are all-illuminating and free from affliction.
One should abandon the middle skull, which is the conventional body-grasper,
by which the moonlight of the sky-moon has long been anointed within the wheel of consciousness; thus,
the Self is made to vibrate eternally with the Goddess of Liberation by means of the Self.
