The Lord of the Moon, situated in the abode of the Moon, having abandoned that which pertains to time, expands as the partless (*niḥkala*) one who is empowered by the Kula and whose end is Time.
The two auspicious ones shine, having well departed; through that radiance, he fills the universe.
When the pure fire (the *preta*) becomes the self, then he is the Lord of the Kāli-kula.
When the five radiant rays exist within the fivefold [body],
then, being the self of the five abodes, he has reached the further shore of the five objects.
When the wheel of fortune (*lakṣmicakra*) has blossomed in the abode of the world’s foremost families, then [the yogin] remains in the state of sound (*rāva*).
When situated in the twelfth zodiac sign (*dvādaśarāśi*), he emits a mass of rays.
When the *tālika* [seal] is properly dissolved, then one becomes a *kulapati*.
One indeed becomes liberated from the rays of the various states of existence (*bhava*). When I am free from the agitation of the pale-red [passion], then one becomes a *kulapati*.
Established in the state of the self-sovereignty of consciousness, the sky-like Self remains unbroken as the void of the void;
therein, one who traverses the multitude of rays then becomes a partaker [of that state].
The seer of the vision, the end of the dance of the eyes, shines forth, perceived by the vision of the visible.
Then the Seer is not seen by the seer of the seen; he is the Lord of the Family of Rays.
He is the enjoyer of the non-worldly portion, the one whose fame is intensely attached to the enjoyment of enjoyments.
He is the end-maker of the mass of enjoyments, the Embodiment, and likewise the foremost leader of the Kāla-tradition.
The auspicious hall is your speech; that which is spoken shines forth as it proceeds from you.
He whose speech possesses ninefold radiance is indeed remembered as the Lord of Rays (the Sun). Merged within the temple, he is the temple itself, reaching to the very end of the temple.
The Sun alone unfolds, whose nature consists of movement, abiding place, and expansion;
he is twelvefold, stationed in twelve places, and illuminates that which lies within the limit of the twelve.
Kālikā, the mistress of the wheel, is the one who desires the family of mantra-rays;
through the various distinctions of those rays, they manifest with shimmering splendor.
Within them, the supreme radiance shines forth, bringing all things to their end.
I shall now fully declare that sequence which has come down through oral tradition:
the triad of ten [deities] unfolds, inlaid with emerging rays of light.
The Supreme Goddess, having emanated the Sṛṣṭikālī and the Saṃhārī, [remains] as the one who creates.
Then there is Sthitikālī, followed by Ghorā, and then Saṃhārakālikā;
Raktakālī, who devours [all] according to the divisions of the Raktāgama;
Sukālī, Yamakālī, and the terrifying Mṛtyukālī.
Bhadrakālī, as well as another, Paramādityakālikā;
Mārttaṇḍakālī, Kālāgnirudrakālī, and Maholvaṇā;
Kālī in the lineage of Mahākāla, and Mahābhairavakālikā.
Kālī should be known as thirteenfold according to the distinction of her rays.
Illuminated by the remembrance of the tranquil radiance of the supreme sun,
she is the supreme Kālī whose nature is light, abiding as the one who impels the world.

She is remembered as being of one kind, threefold, and threefold again; she is known as moving in the fourth state, and likewise fivefold, sixfold, and seven-, eight-, and ninefold. O Goddess, O Beloved, she is likewise tenfold, elevenfold, and twelvefold.

Through its thirteenfold division, it devours all that is moving and unmoving. This should be known as Kālikā; hear from me her mantra, which was not previously disclosed by me to you in the *Kūṭeśvarīcakra* in the form of a *piṇḍa*.
Having extracted that with effort, one should then extract the name once more;
at the end of the word, O Supreme Goddess, listen again to another, O Beloved.
The Great Soul (Mahātman) consists of ten thousand Nādas accompanied by the Great Bindu;
it is the Kuṇḍalī pervaded by the Terrible (Dāruṇa), endowed with Bindu and Nāda.
Furthermore, there is the triangle of Bindus, the Kuṇḍalī established in the Abode (Dhāma).

The mantra joined with the names and feet is proclaimed for all [rites]. Having drawn the mandala, O Goddess, which is endowed with the twelve zodiac signs and consists of the twelve great [sections], together with the worshipful Siddhas and the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
In the center, one should draw the thirteenth [mandala], endowed with the colors of the zodiac signs.
O Goddess, one should fill the four lines with red powder.
It is provided with four doors; there, the supreme sequence (kramottama) is to be worshipped.
Mahākālī is the central face, most terrible and exceedingly fierce; indeed,
hundreds of thousands of throbbing fires of cosmic destruction fall into her pores,
while the millions upon millions of points of her crest-flame expand within her womb.
She whose face is radiant, uttering the sound of the syllable *dhak* like a blazing fire,
with the flickering fire of the end of the eon spitting forth from her mouth;
she who terrifies the fierce mandalas with deep-roaring *huṃ* sounds.
Terrifying with her voracious devouring of the lords of serpents, beginning with Ananta; adorned with a hundred thousand severed heads, including that of Aparṇā; resplendent with a garland of skulls;
wearing as a girdle the skeletons of all the lords of the paths; and beautified by her divine abode.
Kālarātrī, who dwells upon the shoulders of Śata-skandha, possessing a terrifying gaze; whose eyes resemble the simultaneous discharge of thousands of flashes of lightning and meteors;
who repeatedly crushes the pavilion of the cosmic egg; and whose face is knit with a frown.
Her dark clouds were like a flock of crows; her eyes were squinting and devoid of expression;

she made a clattering sound with her traveling mat as she struck it with her moving head and hands; and her elbows were rendered prominent by the mass of her hair, which was bound in the seal of the Great Sun (Mahātaraṇi).
Her body is ablaze with the fire from her great, throbbing upward eye;
she is the cavern of the illusory cosmic egg, throbbing with the impact of her staff-like arms and severed heads.
She who has made Sadākhya tremble with fear, who wears a garland of skulls,
who devours the entire circle of deities,
and who is terrifying due to the martial prowess she displays as she strikes down those who create obstacles here.
Her face was illuminated by the violent tossing of her head that causes the destruction of the universe;
she is the Bhairava who, with a thousand skulls, brought about the ruin of the three cities;
and she is adorned with a network of tiny bells formed from hundreds of Yamas and Kālakas.
She is resplendent with a garland made from the severed heads of Mārtaṇḍa placed around her neck;
she is adorned with a girdle-string formed by a multitude of the skulls of Kālāgnirudra;
and she has trampled upon the hips of Nandī, who was himself being crushed under the feet of Rudrarājeśvara.
She whose garland of corpses flashes with the body of Nārāyaṇa;
who finds her sole diversion in playing the fine lute made from the skeleton of Brahmā;
and who devours the entire circle of deities by traversing them in both forward and reverse order.
She who bestows the state of having drunk [the essence] of the Lord of Bhairavas, she who illuminates the Lord of Bhairavas,
she who is the ear-ornament for the bodies of all the Lords of Bhairavas;
she who delights in various dances, manifesting clearly at every moment of destruction.
Having meditated upon her within her own abode, she should then be worshipped in the extended mandala.
Likewise, O Goddess, having thus worshipped her, all [the goddesses] should be meditated upon according to their true nature.
The one goddess of gods, Karaṅkiṇī, has entered into the various manifestations.
O Goddess of gods, one should worship the God of gods with great animal sacrifices and the like, as well as with aquatic, terrestrial, and even aerial offerings.
Having placed a great vessel for the *argha* offering, such as a large conch shell, which has been purified from its great impurity, [one should proceed].
First, one should sprinkle [the disciple] with that [water] while the mind is fixed on the *paśughora* mantra;
thereafter, having resorted to the supreme *bhairava* state of the *ghora* [mantra],
one becomes established in the path of the twelve suns, being of the nature of a Lord of Mantras (*maṃtreśvara*).
O Lord of Beasts, you cause the slaughter of animals by making them fall from the heights of their pride;
yet when one is devoid of this [pride], one becomes a slayer of the animal that is another's [pride].
Having offered it, he should immediately blow upon it again.
Then, O Dear One, having torn it apart with a sword or a sharp weapon,
and having cut off the head and the two feet along with the blood, he should offer them.
O Bhairavī, fashion a lotus and a southern arrow, red in color, with rays of light;
one should smear that place with blood alone.
Having offered various kinds of food, one should perform the bali-offering accompanied by mantras.
O Maheśvarī, one should drink blood or even wine up to the neck;
thereafter, one should worship Kālikā with blossoming flowers from the mouth.
One should display the terrible Karaṅkiṇī mudrā, as well as the Bhairavī and Vāmā mudrās.
Then, O Goddess, one should establish the most terrible Lelihānā.
One should worship the wheel in this manner with extensive offerings according to one's means.
Then, having sprinkled and gazed upon him, one should cause the disciple to enter.
And having set aside those belonging to external sects, inflict beating upon him.
One should offer the sacrificial pap (*caruka*), the wooden staff (*daṇḍakāṣṭha*), and the hero’s drink (*vīrapāna*).
By means of the agitation of the two hands, one should rely upon the swing of power (*śakti*).

Through the application of the natural end (*sabhāvānta-prayoga*) and by means of the yoga of the throbbing upward face (*sphurad-unnāsya*), the penetration of the hands (*karāveśa*) arises; at that time, he becomes a *samayin*.
Afterwards, one should cause the victim (*paśu*) to enter through the Goddess as if his purpose were already accomplished.
One should perform prostration like a staff with a joyful heart. Afterwards, having offered praise, one should enjoy this sequence of worship.
Then, one should purify the disciple according to the previously described application of power.
Having resorted to a meager livelihood, one should thus observe [the mind] as it becomes meager;
then, the practitioner, having once again relied upon the previous mode of livelihood, [should proceed].
Having beheld the full form, one should likewise observe it as emaciated; then,
relying upon that very mode of being,
the practitioner again beholds the full form— Mahākālī, who is both Kula and Akula.

The five [elements] below are likewise fivefold through the division of body, speech, and mind. At that time, the glass has such a form; by means of that conventional designation, they dissolve into that. When the disciple is thus awakened, O beautiful lady, he becomes perfected.
The state of divinity is the fullness of the oneness of consciousness; bliss is its very nature.
At that time, O Beloved, the knower should realize this, for otherwise it is like madness.
Thus should the preceptor, who has reached the further shore of the Krama, perform that gaze.
He whom one thus initiates properly becomes completely liberated from the bonds of existence.
Otherwise, O Goddess of the gods, by means of the application of sesame, clarified butter, and fire,
and by adopting the aforementioned conduct, whomever one should look upon—
That speech of mine is unfailing; it leads each [person] to union (*sāyojya*).
When one is capable [of this], one may perform the conventional usage of words.
Indeed, for whomever that [speech] exists, it leads them to the eternal Brahman.
Whomever one whose mind is full of joy should touch while mounted here, that person is liberated;
of this there is no doubt. This is the truth, the absolute truth, O Mother of the Gaṇas.
Having performed the ritual procedure in this manner, one should thereafter again follow the sequence for the deities.
O Supreme Goddess, one should sacrifice and afterwards offer it to him.
[One should offer] either a *kalaśa* or an *arghapātra* according to the sequence previously described.
O Goddess, he should be consecrated by that [liquid], and then one should reveal this sequence (*krama*) to him.
By the yoga of this practice, one will attain perfection within six months;
wherever the Goddess of the God of Gods resides, there he goes—of this there is no doubt.
O beautiful one, what is the use of speaking much or with elaborate words?
There is nothing higher than this; I tell you this as the truth.
O highly fortunate one, having thus obtained the definitive determination of the Kālika-krama, (61a)

By some auspicious merit, however, in one's final birth, this must indeed be practiced constantly; for through practice, one's own goal is attained. Through speech, one accomplishes the previously established perfection, and not otherwise.

Thus has been declared this secret, well-guarded Kālikākrama. It must not be told here to a disciple who has not been properly tested. For he who would speak it without authorization becomes a perpetrator of a great sin.
He beholds a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings;
he is never liberated from the Raurava hell here.
Having established himself in this state, men should then conduct themselves accordingly.
Thus has this essence of the Tantra been declared to you exactly as it is— entirely noble and the means to all accomplishments.
O you who are honored by true heroes, what more shall I say to you now?
"Speak to me in its entirety, O you who have become the light within my heart.

Thus ends the chapter on the *Kālikrama-vidhi* in the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great *tantra* of twenty-four thousand verses, titled the *Śiraścheda*, belonging to the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) in the stream of Bhairava.
Having heard this, Girijā, her body covered in horripilation,
bowed down to the Supreme Lord of Lords and spoke again and again;
the virtuous lady, free from agitation and filled with her own bliss, recited this hymn of praise.
The Goddess said:
Salutations to you, the Supreme Lord, who is higher than the highest;
salutations to the one whose nature is the supreme *haṃsa*, who is unfailing and imperishable.
To Him who is free from the positions of existence and non-existence, who has transcended the qualities (guṇas), who is the source of all;
whose head is marked by the crescent moon, who bears half the body of His beloved;
who stands upon the feet of twelve suns, and whose splendor is like the fire of the great dissolution (mahākāla).
Salutations to you who abide in the family of Mahākāla, who have transcended time;
to you whose singular form is the eclipse of the sun, who moves within the inner space of consciousness.

Salutations to you, whose womb is the abode of the fire of time, who are the sole devourer that swallows the universe; who abide in the state beyond time, whose radiant foot expands [all things]; who dwell within the inner sanctum of the city [of the body], and who are the whirlpool of the fish.
Salutations to the one whose form is Mahābhairava, who culminates in Nara, Śakti, and Śiva;
to the embodied one who is the destroyer of all, who pervades the ends of all rays;
salutations to the one whose form is the lotus, who rests within the skull.
Salutations to You, whose essential nature is the abode of nectar, the carrier of nectar;
salutations to the splendor of the twelve suns, which is like the fire and the moon;
and with the nectar-like essence of the supreme Lord’s scripture for three weeks.
"O Blessed One, I am filled with supreme bliss by this secret [teaching]. O Mahādeva, I am now fortunate and worthy of the world's veneration.
By means of this King of Tantras, which has been proclaimed today from your own mouth, [I have attained this state]."
This King Jayadratha, now satiated with supreme bliss through your grace, stands right before you. O Maheśāna, this is the secret knowledge of the Kālikākula.
O Śaṅkara, by your grace, [I have received] that which is endowed with the traditional transmission of mantras;
now, O Blessed One, speak of that which was previously indicated by you—
that Goddess Saṃrāviṇī, the sovereign of the eighty-one padas.
How is she called "Supreme" (Paramā), and how does she fight as "Haḍḍā"? Why is she "Ghorā" (the Terrible) and "Karaṅkiṇī" (the One with Skulls)? How can she be "Saptārṇā" (Seven-Syllabled)?
O Lord, why is she named "Mūlā" (the Root), and how is she "Kaṅkālabhairavī" (the Skeleton-Bhairavī)?
Why is she called the Heart of Fifty? Why indeed is she the Mistress of Kaula (Kauleśvarī)? How manyfold is her practice, or what is her mandala and so forth?
What does she accomplish, and for what reason? And what is that unsurpassed yoga?
(62a) Is it not otherwise regarding the pledges (*samaya*) or the secret doctrines (*rahasya*)? Or is it otherwise regarding the vows (*vrata*) and so forth? O Bhairava, tell me the truth!
"O Supreme Lord, out of grace and compassion for all beings!
Having heard this hymn as well as that excellent question, O Great God,
O Supreme Lord, [you] spoke these words at length with a loud laugh."
This great essence of the Tantras is mixed with many secrets.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"O Goddess of the Gods, I am now pleased by this hymn of yours."
"But my heart is pained; how can you ask such a thing, O Bhairavī?
Do not fear, O slender-waisted one, I shall tell you even so.
Yet, O Bhairavī, you have posed a question that is exceedingly terrible."
May there be well-being for all the worlds; may no deficiency whatsoever arise.
May that very Goddess of gods, Karaṅkiṇī, protect the universe.
O Supreme Goddess, this is the churning of the fire-stick from the wood.
Therefore, O Supreme Goddess, being one who relies upon the supreme reality, be well-attentive;
having become so, listen now to that.
On a night during the dark fortnight when it is obscured by clouds, on another day...
In that most terrifying abode of Hara, he was delighted by the joy of wine;
wearing a garland of human hair as his sacred thread, with the head of Śivā as his ornament,
he was accompanied by Svapacī, Puṣkasī, Koṅkī, Mātaṅgī, and Rajasvalā.
Those female messengers should be made joyful with the delight of wine.
Having consumed the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the hero, accompanied by many heroes,
should approach the center of the altar and purify the surface of the earth.
One should rub [the image] with a skeleton and smear it with great blood.
There, upon a stone slab, one should worship the Goddess of the gods, Mātṛkā, the mother of mantras, with the offerings of a hero; thereafter, one should extract the goddess.
(62b) [One should visualize] the fierce Rāviṇī, who holds a club as her weapon, and possesses terrible prowess;
first, that staff, and then again the face situated behind it.
Furthermore, the seed-syllable previously extracted should be made face-downward;
then one should again give the "Single-Tusked" (ekadaṃṣṭra) which resides within all,
having placed it upon the first [vowel] and kissed by three dots (bindus).
O beautiful goddess, a horse marked with that very [seed-syllable] should be given;
then, in the void, one should again place the peaceful pestle endowed with its digits within one's own self.
Having extracted this [seed-syllable] from the womb of these two, one should then extract the other.
O sinless one, having joined the sixteenth part of the great roar and placed it above Rudra,
and having combined it with creation and destruction, this is the seven-syllabled Vidyā;
devoid of Muṇḍapāda, it is the most terrible, causing the manifestation of the Asuras.
The Sole Heroine, omnipresent, all-consuming, and exceedingly fierce—
her name is the Goddess who reaches the limit of the Lord of the Principle of Knowledge (vidyā-tattva).
She perpetually blazes throughout the entire universe like the great dissolution.
Those goddesses, trembling with fear, undoubtedly bring about peace.
By this [goddess], the mistress of the gods of gods, a formidable waist-string was made along with a thousand Sadāśivas, and at its end, a garland of jewels.
Having fashioned garlands from their faces with those mantras, the Bhairavas dance;
when the Goddess is reduced to mere bones, she is then renowned as Haḍḍā.
With a form of profound tranquility, she resides in the center of the Rāviṇīcakra.

O Dear One, having become the six excellent priests within the abode of supreme bliss, and having swallowed the moon, the sun, and the fire, as well as the wind, the wheel is likewise swallowed. Thus, up to the end of the six-spoked sacrificial pit, it bears rows of shimmering flames.
O Sahanoḍḍāmareśvarī, whose cave-dwelling is ablaze with serpents!
The sixfold family is terrible, resounding with the cries of children as they quiver.
When the host of the Saṃrāviṇī [mantra] has raised a most terrifying roar with its foremost sound,
blazing intensely as it devours the world, and when that host is agitated by the arrival of the Mandasamāpatti through the dissolution of the mass of rays;
Then that formidable Maheśvarī indeed vomits forth;
when she is firmly rooted in the vital point (marmā), moving from one vital point to another within the interior of the vital points,
and stationed in the abode of the vision of the vital points, then she is truly Marmeśvarī.
When the state of the sound-syllable (rauti-svara) arises within the wheel of sounds (rāva-cakra), and it is fierce with the great roar of sound, then she is known as Rāviṇī.
She causes the Fire of Time (kālāgni) to resound; she causes Hāṭaka to resound.
She causes the universe to resound; she causes Keśava to resound;
she causes Rudra to resound, O Bhairavī, as she herself utters the cry of the Lord. Again, that wheel causes Sadāśiva to resound.
Then, in the midst of the *rāva* (sound) of the Bhairava-cakra, she is the *rāviṇī* (the one who causes to sound).
She is the *svarāvārāvaravaṇī*, the *rāviṇī* who [utters] "rāve rāva.
Because she cries out (*virauti*) in the *cakra* as the *rāviṇī*, she is known as the *rāviṇī*.
The host of deities resounds through the yoga of the union of rays;
then that Goddess drinks [it] while causing the lineage-tradition (kulakrama) to resound.
Therefore, the Goddess who moves along that path is celebrated as Rāviṇī.

By means of recollection (*smaraṇa*), she is to be known as Memory (*Smṛti*); indeed, by Memory, there is only recollection. Through her, there is the continuous linking of recollections, yet through recollection, she causes that which has been recollected to be recollected; therefore, she is the Sovereign of Recollection (*Smaraṇeśvarī*).

According to her doctrine, that which is known as "mata" (the doctrine) is to be understood; it is the doctrine that reaches the end of the family of doctrines. When she indeed causes that doctrine, doctrine, and doctrine to resound again and again, she is therefore the Goddess Mateśvarī, known by the name "the Destroyer of Doctrines."
Each family is dissolved within the family; the non-family is the Resounding One (Rāviṇī), who is the family.
Abiding in the abode of that Kaula family, the Proud One causes it to resound.
Then she is to be known as Kuleśvarī, situated in the midst of the Dhāma-kuṇḍalinī.
She is to be known as fivefold within the five, and likewise fivefold within the pentad;
when she roars most terrifyingly through the floods of the wheels of the five pentads.
Then that Resounding One (Rāvinī), whose nature consists of the five [breaths], is established.
She is "Beyond the Path" (Atimārga) on her own path, or on each respective path within the paths.
She stands beyond the path, situated in the beyond-path; in every path, she is the Lotus of Dissolution (Virotpala).
Then she herself, standing on the path of the Atimārga, is Rāviṇī, the consumer of the five [objects].
O you who delight in the contemplation of skulls, Kādyaka-Kaṅkālī dwells in the sky;
Keśikā, greedy for the bolt of the door, resides within the lotus of the Kakanda.
Then the goddess Karaṅkiṇī appeared—terrible, supreme, and roaring aloud; moving through the sky, pure as the ether, abiding in the void, devouring both the edible and the unbroken moon;
traversing the firmament with the splendor of a bird, possessing the digits of space, and adorned with earrings of birds.
When that Goddess, whose stainless mind is free from appearances, cries out,
she then becomes established in each of those fourteen places and the five;
then she is the one who utters the cry of the sky-farer, the supreme destroyer.
Ciccitparācit Kuleśī, who resounds there in the center, is called Vidrāraṇī; she expands within the pierced void (viddha-āmni).
She is Haḍḍāyudhā, Haḍḍadharā, Haḍḍeśī, and Haḍḍavigrahā.
With bones for pillars and a face made of bone, she cries out at every bone;
therefore she should be known as Haḍḍasaṃrāviṇī and Haḍḍakaraṅkiṇī. One should contemplate with wonder Carcikā, who is to be worshipped in the pavilion of the Kula.
Even he who would devour all the worlds is himself devoured here;
situated in their midst, she cries out fiercely, and for that reason she is called Carcikarāviṇī.
She cries "bharam," she cries "bharam," and even while crying out, she cries out "bhīmam."
Because she sustains or because she vomits [them], she is Bhairavarāviṇī;
she is Kāmāntakā, Kāmakalā, Kāmagā, and Kāmakāminī.
Desiring each and every desire, she cries out with every kind of longing;
when the goddess utters these cries of desire, she is then to be known as Kāmaraṇī.
Moving within every wheel, she is the one who causes the wheels to resound.
Then she, known as Cakrarāvā, the enchanter who makes the universe resound,
cries out in the abode of the triangle, which has three pillars and is beautifully blossomed with the three times;
she is Puṣpakālī, eternally moist, and the one who utters the divine sound.
Within the inner support at the end of the vital breaths, she who spreads before the eyes and dwells in their midst,
crying out amidst the agitation of projection and dispersion—
that Rāviṇī, established within Kula during that agitation, is Karaṅkiṇī.
She whose form is power (*śakti*), who wields power, who causes the agitation of power within,
who is proclaimed by Śiva and who goes to Śiva— for that reason she is Power, the Mistress of the Kula.
She always devours through devotion, yet not through devotion, nor at all times.
They devour [all] and cry out fiercely; devouring everything, they possess great roars.
Because she devours all, Kālī should be known as Karaṅkiṇī.
Her form is radiant with the mass of rays from the wheel of the Lord of Causes.
Drying up and swallowing [all], the single Karankini acts with force;
O Lord of Mantras, Supreme Lord, she falls upon the entire circle of wheels.
By that, she is neither full nor empty; she blazes and is further agitated.
Then she should be known as Mahārāviṇī, Śuṣkā, Karaṅkiṇī, Brahmāmbucaṃdanā, Jvālī, and one intent on devouring and rubbing;
indeed, she is Akālaravaṇī, who kills the unborn, the immortal, and the self.
And when there is the sound of a female jackal, a great howl, as well as that of a dog or a jackal;
[and when there is the sound] of an elephant, horse, lion, buffalo, donkey, boar, or cock. (64b)
She utters the cries of swans and other birds with a loud, supreme, and excellent sound;
because she resides in the midst of the great cremation ground and makes that sound, she is known as Rāviṇī.
In the abode of the Ādhāra, she is difficult to perceive, yet she is Vīrā, intent upon agitation.
Then the goddess, delighting in devouring, cries out with a roar;
thus, O Goddess, this most terrible one has been revealed to you in this *Ghorasarvasva* tantra,
which bestows the great goal through the severing of the head.
Who is capable of describing you,
whose entire form is such that the lords of the lords of reality (the Rudras) flash forth from the tips of her teeth,
and by whose mere shaking the cosmic eggs are reduced to ashes in an instant?

Emerging from the pores of the skin, tearing one another apart and shrieking with the sound "caṭa-caṭa," they cause a roar upon being seen. O Goddess of gods, who would dare to meditate upon you, who possess tinkling bracelets?

Who indeed would venture to meditate upon that Goddess, whose limbs possess such beauty fashioned by Sadāśivas who were themselves diminished by the flood of destruction at the time of the great dissolution;
she whose anklets are formed from the *ka* and other syllables of hundreds of thousands of fires of cosmic time?
She shines with the terrifying sounds of her moving wheels and cymbals.
O Goddess of gods, who could venture to meditate upon that Supreme Sovereign,
who is difficult to fill even by hundreds of thousands of universes, whose eyes are unfathomable, and who is formidable?
Who would strive to meditate upon that unrestrained [power] whose nature is the destruction of all decay,
extending from the level of Akṣoṇita (or Bhasmita) up to Sādāśiva?
And those Lords of the Tattvas who are there, surrounded by their own messengers—
Having been crushed by the God and Goddess between the tips and the middle of their hands,
they were cast into a terrifying abyss within the great flaming banyan tree;
O Maheśānī, since you are insatiable, who would dare to meditate upon you?
(65a) Those sixty-four who are known as the fierce Bhairaveśvaras,
all together with their own Mothers, uttering cries and bearing a roar.
The Great Goddess Maheśvarī has become stuck between your teeth;
who would dare even to meditate upon you, whose eyes are most terrible and fierce?
You are the one whose form is the universe, whose face is the universe, the sovereign of the universe, and the devourer of the universe.
With a universal belly, universal feet, universal knees, and universal eyes;
with universal hands and universal forms—who could venture to meditate upon Her?
O Beloved, no meditation exists for Her, who is the refuge of all forms.
This goddess Karaṅkiṇī is augmented by all heroic powers.
As many heart-mantras of terrible prowess as are spoken within the essence of reality, so great is the goddess's power; that which is her power has been fully described.
O beloved Queen of the Gods, even if I were equal to Sadāśiva himself, possessing hundreds of millions of mouths and tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of tongues,
I would not be able to describe her prowess, even with hundreds of millions of desires.
Or even a hundredth part of the vigor [of the gods], O Maheśvarī, Goddess of the God of Gods.
Thus has the meditation, accompanied by the mantra, been fully described to you—
this secret, O illustrious one, which is difficult even for Bhairaveśvara to obtain.
O Goddess of the gods, listen now briefly;
I shall duly explain the worship of the Goddess of the gods.
Having reached the altar previously described and having gathered many ritual materials, [one should proceed].
There, having undertaken the sacrifice according to the full extent of the prescribed ritual,

and having marked it out with a measuring cord, one should draw the multitude of wheel-spokes using bone powder and other materials, O Goddess of Gods— making it perfectly level and endowed with the proper characteristics.
In the center is an eight-petaled lotus;
within it is a twelve-spoked wheel, and on the outside is a sixty-four-spoked wheel, as well as another, the king of wheels.
Then, having prepared [the site] with red and black powder, one should worship the Goddess.

One should place the Goddess in the center, and the remaining others according to the sequence of the subsequent rounds. Those who are about to be described, as well as those already mentioned, are to be worshipped, O Supreme Goddess.
Having thus fully worshipped the *cakra* and invoked the Supreme Goddess with a hymn of mantras, O Queen of Gods, O Bhairavī, [one should worship] according to the secret [tradition]. This [hymn],
O Supreme Goddess, is not recited for one who is devoid of the *samaya*.
Adopting a fierce mode of conduct, one should, from the center of the wheel, invoke the Goddess of the gods together with the entire host of Mothers:
"Oṃ! Come, O Sustainer (Dhātrī), who supports the life-force of those established in the supreme path!"
O Goddess, who playfully hides within the forest of the eyes of the three worlds;
O Supreme Raudrī, whose illusory power envelops the cosmic egg and who takes the form of stars;
O Mother, who are the consort of the eleven Rudras—come here and dispel all obstacles!
O Kālāmālinī, who dwells in the hearts of all beings with moon-motes joined by the rays of the sun;
O Mālinī, whose play is the agitation of the submarine fire!
O Bhairavī, wielder of the excellent khaṭvāṅga, bearer of the conch and the discus, possessor of the great bell!
O Śuśilinī, O you who are mounted upon a lotus, come forth!
O Ghorī, O Mahāghoreśvarī, O Jharjara, O Jhaṃkāra, O Hahahahahahaṃsī!
O Tilakā, who has surpassed Kālāgnirudra; O you who are marked by the agitation of fire!
O Kāpālika, O wearer of the *liṅga*, who has destroyed the entire circle of the world with your staff of Rudra; O leader of the untimely hour, O slayer, uttering the syllable *Kṣoṃ*;
O Mother of the Matanga, whose face is adorned with the sound of *vilulihim*; *Hrīṃ*! [Salutations to you.]
Holding a *khaṭvāṅga* and a large human head, with a most terrifying form,
he stands amidst the various vehicles, his three eyes fixed upon the *praṇava* like a blazing fire.
O Māyā of Hara, who bears the form of the Night of Destruction, come hither! You whose hands have the heads of serpents and the crescent moon, who crush with the palms of your hands;
you who, having perceived the howling mouths of the *pretas*, have cast down and restrained your staff-like arms.
O Māri, who brandishes the *ḍamaru* drum with your trembling fangs and makes a tumultuous sound from your forehead;
you whose mouth is bound by a garland of skulls and who faints in the heat of the blood of the gods;
you whose gaping maw has devoured the three worlds through the performance of universal destruction!
O you whose tresses are like a great hall for the dance of swinging bells; O you who shatter the frontal globes of the elephants of the quarters, who are arrogant with the rut of their great ichor;
O you who are as crimson as the fire at the end of an aeon, and who are adorned with dangling Rudrākṣa beads!
O Māhendrī, Vaiṣṇavī, Maitrī, Vināyakī, Gāruḍī, O auspicious Mahādevī!
O Vighneśvarī, Nārāyaṇī, Māruti, O Goddess presiding over Yama, O peaceful Pāvaki!
O Nairṛtī, Pūtanā, Bhairavī, O Goddess presiding over the great Varuṇa! O Brāhmī, O Vārāhī whose body is fire, O Raudrī who wears the skin of the lord of elephants, O Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍacaṇḍinī!

O Caṇḍakāpālinī, of terrifying form, come! O Nārāyaṇī, bearer of strength, you whose form is sleep, great delusion! O Dākṣāyaṇī, Pāramāyanī, Vātāyanī! You who emerge from the womb, supported by the *sambid*s, for the sake of the cause! O you whose form is the *bhaga*, who take away the vital seed! O observer of the vow of Kaumāra, in the state of peace, radiant one, beautiful one! O you who are pierced by men, women, and children; O primordial great meteor with a terrifying mouth! O you whose eyes and the corners of your brows are harsh and red with the intoxication of blood; O you who shook the demon Mahiṣa!

(66b) O you whose glance is like a blazing fire! Alas, alas! O Gīti, you sing with songs; O Gīti, you sing with songs! O you who possess the grace of a swaying creeper, come together with Śiva, Kāla, Kāma, and Māyā, who are infinite!

O Vāmā, O you of left-handed conduct, O Jyeṣṭhā, O Raudrī among beings, O Raudrī of fierce conduct! Because of your creative power (*kalana*), you are Kālī, the supreme emission (*parāsṛṣṭi*), the cause of all beautiful forms (*kala-vikāraṇi*).
O you who bring strength through application!
O you who come as flesh! O destroyer of the opposite of strength!
O you who utter cries that agitate strength! O delighter! O you who are upon the ground with your feet!
Liberated, she is declared by the mind; Manonmanī arrives.
By that God Śambhu, the most sacred path was sung [in the Gītā].
O bearer of the entrails of the Daityas, likewise [is the power] of the supreme net of mantras.

When form assumes various shapes, enter into that [state]. Worship the Śaiva impulse, the supreme Saura sacrifice, and the incomparable Vaiṣṇava splendor; by your own nature, worship the Supreme Power (Paraśakti).
Come, O mistress of the hosts of spirits, together with Tāvilā and Tāli!
O Kāmāyanī, O Great Desire! Hē hē, O Mistress of the World in the realm of Mahendra!
O Śiva, in the peace within the space of the primordial sound arising from universal trust!

The sprout is accumulated as the origin; it is the body that seizes the *vaṣaṭ* of the Vedas. *Svāhā*, *svadhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *gata*, and *vauṣaṭ*—having shaken off these, she licks the edge of the embers produced from the fire of the great dissolution, blazing with the *revatī* stars.

O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods, who have placed the noose of Death—crafted from the very essence of the gods—within the palm of your hand; O you who traverse the three trembling worlds with your sidelong glances!
Bestow all peace upon your disciples and protect every person here.

O Agni, that splendor which has come to you— the Lord who is skillful in swift expansion, who is designated as the vital breaths such as prāṇa and apāna, who is the golden womb (Hiraṇyagarbha), who pervades the radiant expanse of space, and who remains unmoving yet causes all things to move— [I praise] that very [splendor]. (67a)
May she carry you within her heart, in the center of the lotus, along the path of the three abodes, bestowing life; may she bear a heart manifested by grace.

O Goddess of Mantras, whose face is beautiful with the form of blazing flames garlanded by excellent caverns, whose various large mouths are terrifying, mounted upon a donkey, wearing a garland of snakes, and whose limbs are smeared and anointed with oil, fat, and blood!
Obeisance to the one with the great bow, whose wings are like the lord of birds and whose plumage is like the sun;
O Mother, at the time of universal destruction, you are another Great Brahmāṇī.
O you who are intoxicated by the pride of blood from the pair of doors (or temples) crushed by your hands!
You are the universal form whose body extends from the netherworlds (pātāla) up to Śiva;
you reside within the cave-mouth of the mountain where the excellent serpent is bound, where the rudrākṣa beads jingle,
and where the supreme radiance of the three eyes emerges like a stream of breath.

O Mother Dāmbikā, O Lakṣmī, when the world has been consumed by the fire at the end of the aeon, when your body and face are smeared with ashes; when all the worlds have been extinguished and have become a void, and all beings have departed— you alone remain in this most excellent and supreme excrement.
O Maheśvarī, who art bowed down by the fire at the end of the aeon, the ocean with its aquatic creatures, and the terrifying roar;
who art the supreme *tanmātra* of Dharma that has subdued the mouths of the sacrificial fires with the sound "Hā! and "Huṃ!";
you who are the humble recipient of both the offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*), and the protector of the earth—salutations to You!
O Goddess who resides between the sun and the moon, in the sequence of the sun, the moon, and fire; O peaceful one,
O Māyā who destroys delusion, O Mistress of Māyā, O Divinity, O Awakener of all, O Deluder, O Sister of Hari, O Supreme Form of Consciousness!
O Goddess of Secrets, destroyer of the bonds of fear and worldly existence; O Mother, O Perfected One, O Mistress of Speech!
O True Knowledge, moving within the expanse of the sky; O Wisdom, shatterer of the wheel of the heart’s wanderings!
O Transcendent State, O Source of the fire of the vital measure; O Durgā, who draws in through meditation; O Delighter in Fame and Memory, O Embodiment of Forgiveness!
(67b) O Gāyatrī, Mother of the Vedas; O Sāvitrī, you who are established through yoga; O Jñānāmbikā, Sarasvatī; O Durgā, Earth of the Lord of All!

Oṃ jhīṃ jhāpini jaṃbhamohe kṣāṃ hrīṃ mātṛke huṃ haḥ. Jhīṃ Bhairavī, O Goddess of the most terrible ones, Jhāṃkāri, O Lady of the great laugh! O Mother of Rudra, who are adorned with the Tilaka of the fire of the cosmic dissolution; O Sovereign of All, come to me along with Māyā, you whose lotus-like retinue of worlds is agitated and crushed by the fire of the end of time.

KṢAṂ KĀLARĀTRI PARAME SARVAJÑE HUṂ NAMO DIVYE JṚṂBHANI VARAVARADE VARAVĀRE MURU MURU SVĀHĀ । STAMBHANI KINI KINI SARA SARA GHURULI MAHĀGHURILI GAURI GĀNDHĀRI MĀLINI BHĀVĀNI MOṬAYA HULUHU VILAṄGHAYAṂ KṢU KṢAḤ । SIRI SIRI CIRI CIRI SAŚIKHIṂ CICINI MAHĀSICIRI CAṆṬIKI EHYEHI ॥
Carrying [the world] on the path, you are difficult to perceive even by the gods, yet you remain unmanifest.

For the sake of rebirth, O Great Power, with the sound *hūṃ hūṃ*, for the purpose of play, you who are censured by Brahmā, I invoke the dark one; protect the three worlds, which are bowed to by all gods and asuras, while you shine forth.

O Mother Laṃbikā, O Goddess, O Bhagavatī who are worshipped by the hosts of Rudra’s attendants, O White One who are bowed to, O You who rest upon the lotus-garment of the surrounding circle of flames!

Worship Her, the cause of peace for the world; let [the devotee] offer the image, the water of honor (*argha*), as well as the water for the feet (*pādya*), incense, this honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), substances such as wine and meat, the offering, dance, song, and the sixfold power (*ṣaḍaṅga-śakti*).
O Sovereign of All, through devotion to you, or rather, by the protection granted by you, forgive [my transgression], O Supreme Goddess; protect the three worlds, O Ambika who has been bowed to!
O Goddess, deliverer from great fear, protect the sacrificer—[all those] who have taken the vow of this [rite].

Thus has this invocation, which fulfills all things, been proclaimed by me. O Mother of the Gaṇas, it should be known that the invocation of the mantra bestows accomplishment upon one who has fallen from siddhi, is difficult to approach, and violates the great samaya— simply through its recitation.
All mantras and all vidyās are contained within the single eye [of this king of hymns];
none are equal to this King of Hymns—what more need be said?
Having thus invoked the Goddess of the Gods, who brings fear to the three worlds...
One should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with great quantities of blood, water for the arghya and pādya offerings, and various kinds of wine and meat; likewise, with diverse sacrificial animals,
with the sounds of *huḍukka* drums, the howling of jackals, and the clamor of many intoxicating drinks.
One should worship with various flowers, extensive according to one's means.
Accompanied by the previously mentioned messengers and together with those born of that same lineage,
one should sacrifice to the terrible Karaṅkiṇī along with her retinue.
As many heart-mantras as have been declared by me here in this group of six, they are all exactly equal; no distinction is prescribed between them.
O beautiful goddess, they are to be worshipped with the application of all ornaments.
The one Goddess of the gods is thus divided according to her own essential nature;
therefore, she may indeed be worshipped through the eighty-one excellent vital points (marmas) by means of differentiation.
She is to be worshipped according to one's preference, through the union with her lords and her retinues.
O Maheśvarī, there are many different versions of this [text] here,
in which there is no firm adherence to the *Jayadratha*, the king of tantras. Furthermore, the Goddess Karaṅkiṇī, the sole Mistress of the Gods, is to be worshipped.
Having performed worship, one should thereafter display the mudrās Ghorā and Karaṅkiṇī;
then Saṃrāviṇī should be given, and immediately after that, Ābaddhā.
Thereafter, the fire-offering (homa) should be performed in the fire of the funeral pyre's wood. Having gathered a great quantity of meat, one should offer a thousand oblations.
Then, by means of the mudrās, the knower [should proceed] until [the deity] of terrible appearance is fully invoked.
Accompanied by his companions, the hero floats through the midst of the sky;
that Goddess appears before his very eyes in a radiant and gentle form.
Through her alone, the Goddess of all gods, shall the attainment of the *piṇḍa* (the physical body) occur for men.
Thus has been described here this supreme sacrifice of the Goddess,
which bestows all accomplishments, is the very essence, and dispels the darkness of ignorance;
there exists nothing superior to this within the interior of the world.
Thus it has been told in brief; no further detail was given by me from the beginning.
Henceforth, tell me correctly, O beloved, what I shall explain here.
Thus [ends] the fourth hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Bhairavaśrotas* Vidyāpīṭha, the *Śiraścheda*.
The Chapter on the Rāviṇī Sacrifice.
|| || Having thus heard [this] from Hara, the Supreme Cause, the Mistress of the Gods spoke again to Hara, who bears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel. || ||
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, O Destroyer of Tripura, I have heard in its entirety the great sequence of mantras of the Goddess; now, please explain the method of accomplishment (*sādhana*)."
"How is the Goddess accomplished, and how many are the means of accomplishment?
Explain them in detail according to their divisions; the path of yoga is very extensive.
Having heard this, the Blessed One, whose beloved is Umā, spoke as follows:
With the quarters of the sky illuminated by the luster of the swarm of bees upon his crown of the throbbing crescent moon,
the venerable Bhairava said:
"Listen, I shall tell you according to what I have been requested by you."
(69a) This is the means of accomplishment of the Goddess of the God of Gods, presented in brief rather than at length.
It is the extraction of all yogas for one who has exerted great effort in the study of many scriptures.
Abiding within the beautiful lotus of all the channels (nāḍīs) and devoted to the conduct of a hero (vīrācāra),
free from hypocrisy and possessing the quality of sattva— such a person is called a practitioner (sādhaka).
Having gone to the formidable abode of Hara, he himself becomes a supreme and great hero.
O Maheśvarī, whether alone or with a good companion, adorned with ornaments on all his limbs, one should begin the practice of the goddess Karaṅkiṇī.
Standing in the midst of a great cremation ground, one should recite the mantra of the most terrifying goddess.

One should offer ten thousand oblations of the most terrible [substances]— namely, human fat, goat fat, and cow fat— each in a tenth part of that amount, O worshiper of the best of gods. At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the goddess Karaṅkiṇī herself emerges from the midst of the fire.
Assuming a gentle form, she approaches the practitioner as a bestower of boons;
together with her, he goes to where that Supreme Goddess resides.
There dwells the Lord of the Bhairava-circles, the most excellent of the excellent.
Thus, the accomplishment arising from this has not yet been described to you.
O Goddess of the gods, when recited one hundred thousand times, she bestows the siddhi of the great netherworld (mahāpātāla).
Even if unrecited, O Mistress of the God of gods, she will accomplish whatever the practitioner desires to achieve upon merely hearing her.
The accomplishment of the great vetāla, the sādhana of the great kiṃkara, invisibility, the extraction of mercury, the supreme accomplishment of chariots,
the extremely fierce sādhana of bhūtas, and the wonderful sādhana of kṛtyās.
The vision of the Nāgas correctly wards off rain and lightning;
likewise, the foot-vehicle, the sword, the sandals, the sacred thread,
the manaḥśilā ointment and other such items, the staff, and the family water-pot.
The earrings, the deer-skin, the sacred thread, and whatever substances of accomplishment there may be;
the previously mentioned sādhana of Prasena for the Yakṣiṇī;
the dispatching [of messengers], the subduing of the wicked, and the destruction of poisons and malevolent spirits.
(69b) Furthermore, there are the subduing of diseases, as well as the summoning of those under one's control;
killing, expulsion, and so forth, [are employed] in cases of paralysis, immobilization, and the production of magical effects.
The breaking and likewise the paralyzing of ships, carts, and machines; as well as rites for pacification, nourishment, and the production of good fortune—
these and other such [rites] which were previously taught here in the Tantra.
And all those [mantras] which are about to be described shall be accomplished by me through effort and no other means—
the Supreme Goddess Ghoraghaṭṭakarṣiṇī—
[yet] they should be known as common to all in this supreme Tantra.
Accomplishing one’s heart’s desire through the ritual procedure for each kalpa, because she is the goddess supreme over all, she is thus proclaimed.
One should meditate upon her as Yogayogeśvarī, the Terrible One; by so recollecting her, one should cause the wheel to tremble.
Her manifestation is proclaimed to be twofold, by way of both the supreme and the non-supreme forms.
She is the crown-jewel residing within the divisions of the Kula, the primordial source of the Kula, the fire-wood of the Kula.
That goddess, who dwells within the end of the Kula, is Manonmanī.
O auspicious one, by that distinction she is known as the bringer of accomplishment.
Thus has this been fully explained; what else shall I tell you?
Thus ends the chapter on the practice of Rāviṇī in the fourth Ṣaṭka of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, within the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairava-śrotas.
Having thus heard the speech arising from the lotus-like mouth of the Supreme Lord,
that Goddess spoke again these words to the one who has the moon as his crest-jewel.
The Holy Goddess said:
"O Lord, I have heard the unsurpassed *Śiraścheda-tantra*,
which is endowed with mantras and vidyās, replete with mudrās and maṇḍalas,
and contains the doctrines of both the Left and Right [traditions] through their various divisions and sub-divisions."
[He saw] Kravyāda, Nakra, Cūṣa, Apracchusma, and Mahābala;
[and those called] Lehya, Samāhāra, Majjāhāra, and Ghasmara. (70a)
One who is aged in form, one with matted hair, one who terrifies the fierce and the formidable, one who is lustful, one who dwells well, one who plucks out hair while laughing,
and one who feeds on blood— thus, in former times, there were eighteen kinds [of practitioners].
O Lord of Kula, the Kaula tradition has been heard [by you] in its infinite divisions and sub-divisions;
yet that which was proclaimed in the *Kulāvatāra-tantra* concerning the arising of the Transmental (*unmanodaya*) was merely indicated through pervasive union, not fully revealed.
Tell me further how this other form of the Goddess of Gods [is attained] through the potency of mantras,
ritual action, yoga, yantras, tantras, rites, and so forth;
or through the practice of the Krama-Vetāla, or by means of distracted contemplation.
The suffix *samāsānta* has not been understood; please explain it out of your grace.
O Lord, what is called *kula*, and what is said to be *kaula*?
Why, O Īśvara, is that very thing called *kulakaula*?
Thus questioned by the Great Goddess, Mahādeva—the most exalted, whose head was overflowing with bliss due to the arrangement of the great secret—said:
"O beautiful one, why are you so bewildered in mind? Why do you deceive me?"
O sinless one, do you know what that substance is which resides within the belly of the three worlds,
and within which the entire three worlds are always dissolved? It never exists separately from me, my body, and myself.
Through the division of gross and subtle, by means of the supreme, the non-supreme, and the both-supreme-and-non-supreme;
by way of the pervaded and the pervader, through the union of the signified and the signifier;
and through the application of the support and the supported, and the logic of the joined and the joiner.
Likewise, through presiding over it by means of your own form, qualities, and so forth,
and through the penetration of knowledge by both knower and known, you and I have woven together this entire world of the moving and the unmoving by joining cause and effect.
(70b) What is being led forth? Or who is the leader? What is dissolved?
O people, why have you approached me to ask such things?
The Śrī Devī said:
O Destroyer of Existence, O Omniscient One, just as I speak to you with affection, so it is with all things; yet, this is out of compassion for the universe.
I ask you briefly, O Blessed One:
you ought to explain to me the easy means for all afflicted beings through the practices of recitation, fire-offerings, ritual conduct, concentration, meditation, and spiritual accomplishments.
"By which [means] enjoyment and liberation are produced through mere knowledge—
[that] most secret and wonderful [teaching] is in this Saṃrāviṇī-cakra.
Then, having reflected for a moment, Maheśvara spoke.
Bhairava said:
"Out of the bond of great affection, O beloved, this must be told to you. You have already heard its expansion in detail, according to its divisions and subdivisions, within the Kula."
O Goddess, the Vaināyakī [tradition] is beneficial when preceded by ritual action in its entirety;
without the labor of formal procedure, it does not bestow accomplishment.
Furthermore, the Maula and Kaula have been proclaimed, and beyond that is the Siddhakaula.
By the command of Śiva, the efforts of Vaināyaki are ineffable.
Whoever reveals them out of delusion shall suffer the suppression of his karma.
If you must hear this, then you must certainly become a Samayini.
I shall relate to you how this was attained by me as well.
Formerly, there was a lord of the Asuras, a great enemy of the lords of the cities, possessed of immense strength;
blinded by pride, he was named Andhaka and oppressed the three worlds.
Having thus conquered all the gods led by Indra and Upendra,
this Vibhāvasu Vasu, the son of Vivasvat,
has arrived at the field of battle to challenge you alone.
O Queen, together with me, you did not faint at the destruction of the Vidyādharas;
O Rudrāṇī, you waged a fierce battle that shook the world.
Then, having cast aside my *pināka* bow, I shattered it with my sword;
having split into two, it then became fourfold, doubling its expansion of qualities.
Even as it was being cut, it did not cease, but gradually attained infinity.

O lady of excellent vows, that powerful one, having known "he must be conquered," then filled the entire triple world with splashes of blood from his wounds, which rose up in great abundance. At that time, I remained composed.
O Maheśvarī, the supreme power known as Kālikā was remembered by him. Enveloping me from below with his many arms, he stood before me in the form of Mahābhairava, exceedingly enraged.
And he spoke these words quickly: "Let what is to be done be performed immediately! O King of Daityas, let the suppressions (*nigraha*) spoken by me be carried out without delay.
Meanwhile, let those who are near me—possessing the form of Brahmā and bearing the fire-banner (*śikhidhvaja*)—[proceed]."

Just as Viṣṇu, Vaivasvata, Meru, and Sahasrākṣa were [manifested] by me, so too did she remember them; thus he was born again eightfold. With his body cast down by the eight enraged Nābhis, there arose a particular distinction.
Because of their great number, she was struck down by them with their fangs;
then, fully satiated by drinking her blood,
they all assumed terrifying forms and began to dance.
He terrifies all the asuras, the daityas, the dānavas, and the rākṣasas.
Even I, trembling with fear, have praised him by bowing my head;
what else remains to be done for you, O best of asuras? What is the task that must be performed?
Assuming a tranquil form, protect the three worlds forever;
thereafter, assume the forms of Brahmā and the other gods, which bestow color, lifespan, and protection.
Having duly performed the sports of the Goddess, whose mind was absorbed in them,
the female attendants spoke again with humility:
"O Maheśvarī, why do You desire equality with us?"
"Speak thus, my dear son, so that [the Mothers] may grant you heaven.
Otherwise, O Hara, you will become an ordinary member of the Yoginī-cakra.
Therefore, with a gracious mind and out of concern for your beloved, [I say this to you]."
Having embraced her firmly against his chest and covered her with his armor, he said to her, "There is no one else for me; I give you [myself].
The Goddess laughed and said, "He has spoken the truth; there is no fault in this."
"Do you not see whether Kālī remains or not? You do not restrain her. O Maheśvarī, as long as I am looking at you, you do not exist.
Thus addressed, the Pramathas said, "This has been seen by you."
Out of a desire to test you, O Satva, we have shown this son of yours to you.
This does not cause you to lose your composure; rather, O proclaimer of existence, it is ordained for you.
This goddess remains present here, equal among the family of yoginīs.
By you as well, this king of the Daityas was given away as a sacrificial animal through forgetfulness.
Indeed, by this very act, you have become a leader of the lineage in a general sense;
therefore, O fair-faced one, I obtained this [result] through that ritual procedure.
The Śrī Devī said: "O Lord, I indeed remember my entire past history exactly as it was told by you,
including everything concerning the Kulācārya."
Therefore, O Blessed One, I have approached you; let the time for my [initiation] be ordained, by which I may attain the entire true nature of the Kula from the very beginning.
Śrī Bhairava said:
I recall what is appropriate for the sake of others, known as the Ācāra;
that indeed becomes your life, O common Yoginī of the Kula.
Now, therefore, quickly accept my word according to the proper sequence.
The Mothers of the Akula lineage are established according to the division of the four ages;
they are eternally composed of earth, water, fire, air, and space.
And there is no separate designation for the sun and the moon, O beautiful one.
By these [energies], the entire world—both stationary and moving—is pervaded.
Without them, there would be no sound, nor touch, nor likewise taste.
Neither form, nor smell, nor mind, nor even intellect would exist,
O Goddess, nor would there be ego-sense within the fourteenfold universe,
if it were not composed everywhere of atoms whose essential nature is uniform in form.
They move everywhere, in every way, throughout the world of the moving and the unmoving.
These are renowned as the Mothers of the Kula, beginning with Brahmā, who perform their ascetic penance.
O Goddess, this is the Kula that is proclaimed to be the very root.
In this form of Śūla, through its many divisions and subdivisions,
he abides in this world, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
And that supreme splendor of his, though permeated by power, remains free from heat.

O Goddess, that which is free from all conceptual proliferation, characterized by the experience of the Self, descended from the primordial Kula-vīra like a sprout from a seed, and is a secret devoid of constraints— that is called Kaula.

Abiding in all living beings according to the analogy of the seed of the *nyagrodha* tree, it destroys, protects, and ordains the entire world as it desires. O Goddess, this alone is to be constantly propitiated; indeed, this alone is that which is to be worshipped.
Having worshipped this [deity], those desiring the emergence of virtues attained their respective stations:
Brahmā now attained the state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu indeed attained the state of Viṣṇu,
Indra attained the state of Indra, and Prajāpati attained the status of Prajāpati.
O beloved, by whatever state this [reality] is worshipped,
by that very state one always attains identity with it.
[This is] the cultivation of non-existence, which arises from the manifestation of the state of non-existence.
(72b) One should meditate upon that which is to be realized as existence through the state of being; one should realize it by means of being.
Thus [ends] the fourth hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraścheda* section of the Vidyāpīṭha in the stream of Bhairava.
The chapter on the descent of the Kula of the Transmental (unmanā) within the Wheel of the Roaring One (rāviṇīcakra).
Then, having heard these supreme words spoken by Sarveśvara,
the Supreme Goddess spoke to the Supreme Lord without hesitation.
The Śrī Devī said:
"The Mūla-kula as well as the Kaula have been understood through your grace. Everything has been known according to the gross sequence; but how does it exist according to the subtle?"
Thus questioned, the tranquil-souled one spoke of his majesty from the beginning.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, in brief to that which is about to be told, which transcends the senses.
The great power known as Kuṇḍalī is the form of supreme nectar;
from her this manifold world of moving and non-moving beings has emerged,
and into her, O fair-faced one, it gradually dissolves into non-duality.

Thus, I abide either as a subtle form or as the perfected reality itself; I am joined with, or situated within, the speech and the supreme splendor of the Lord. I am the source of the entire world, manifesting in the forms of its creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
She is the Kula-mātṛkā of the Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Siddhānta, and Kaula traditions;

the mother of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman Vedas; the supreme Mistress of Speech (Vāgīśvarī) of all words; and the cause of the destruction of everything, as well as the source of the multitude of mantras and mudrās.
O Dear One, [this is the teaching] of the creator of the collection of principles (tattva) and the womb (yoni),
by means of Mālinī, Lokamālinī, Rāśinī, and Śabdarāśi,
and by the multitude of Vidyās, arranged in groups with their circles formed into mandalas.
And likewise Brahmā and the others, together with the eight ministers, the Bhairavas, the planets, the guardians of the directions, the secondary seats, and the world-protectors; (73a)
[It is] by means of the vital winds—prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna, and so forth;
together with the Vedas and the Upaniṣads, through various subjects and expositions;
and by means of the objects of sight, touch, and so on, which fall within the range of the palate and the lips.
O Great Goddess, by others as well who dwell within the belly of the three worlds—
arising and dissolving day and night—
this very path is traversed by taking steps in accordance with the length of their bodies.
Coiled in the form of a ring, revolving like a swastika,
O beautiful lady, that primordial power, the jewel of the mind, pervades the creation born of the three worlds within all beings and abides in a subtle form.
Bhramaṇī, Bhrāmaṇī, Jambhanī, and likewise Stambhanī;
Gaṃtrī and Gāyatrī, Hasanī and likewise Hāsanī;
Paṭhanī, Pāṭhanī, Nanīkī, and she who also causes dancing.
She is the one who slaps [the world awake], the one who leaps, and likewise the one who draws all things together;
she is the Great Illusion, the Great Abiding, and the destroyer of great delusion;
she is the Great Knowledge, the Great Wisdom, and the one who sets forth the cessation of ignorance.
The subduer of all the wicked, the slayer and attractor of Māra,
the restrainer of tortures and the cutter away of evil deeds—
that meritorious [goddess] is obtained by men through the contemplation of her majestic power.
Neither by drawing [the breath] nor by suppressing it, nor through meditation (*dhyāna*) nor through retention (*dhāraṇā*);
always devoid of horizontal, internal, external, downward, middle, and upward [movements];
neither straight nor crooked, neither long nor circular.
It is neither square nor triangular, nor is it shaped like the moon; it is never fixed by any mark, for it neither goes nor stays.
It is not blue, yellow, or green, nor is it black, white, or red.
Always bearing all colors like the streak of Indra’s bow,
she is as stable as Mount Meru, the golden mountain, like a flash of lightning.
Having the luster of ten thousand suns and the radiance of ten million moons, she cuts through all sins by means of some [mantra] that has been severed [from her].
She is seen by no one, nor is she touched; she is the circle of the sky itself.
It cannot be pierced by anything, yet it pierces the three worlds;
it cannot be obstructed by anything, nor can it be burned even by fire.
It blocks everything, and that single [reality] consumes the entire universe in a single instant.
This subtle reality, which you asked about— the Kula and Akula— has been indicated to you.
That which is its surrounding enclosure, situated at the end of the *khecarī* [state],
is called the supreme Kaula, the bliss that pervades everything.
This [state] transcends the city of eight (the subtle body), is devoid of the support of meditative concentration,
is liberated from breath control, and has passed beyond fixed vows;
it is the object of the knowledge of liberation, characterized by established bliss.

It is indeed the gross, the subtle, and the excellent; it is the supreme, the non-supreme, and that which is both supreme and non-supreme. There is nothing else superior to this, which consists of the three qualities (*trisatva*), is imperishable and unchanging, and is the form of self-realization consisting of the syllable and the word following the nasal resonance (*anusvāra*).
This has been explained in brief; what else do you wish to ask?
That which consists of the nectar of one's own self is divinely tasted in a single way;
nothing else on this earth pleases him by whom that has been tasted.

Then, having heard this description of Śakti given by Parameṣṭhin, the supreme Goddess questioned the Supreme Lord once more: "O Lord, regarding that power called Kaula which has been described by me— "
"How does she attain right knowledge, and whose [is it]? O Great Goddess, what is her experience like? Tell me out of your grace.
The Blessed One said: "I shall tell you everything, O beloved."
Just as Manonmanī transcends manifestation,
so too does Viśveśī— the supreme among letters— transcend both the superior and the inferior, whether she appears as male or female. (74a)
For one endowed with pure devotion, union with Śiva shall be attained—
for one who has turned away from the veil of the worlds, who has taken refuge in that which rests within saṃsāra,
who is joined to the Great Tantra, and whose every karma has been exhausted.
Due to the accumulation of merit performed extensively in previous births,
or through the descent of intense power (*śakti*), he may perceive the divine directly;
whether through desire or lack of desire, this occurs through union with or from the Supreme Lord.
Always, due to the contact with the wind through the application of the sequence of the fingers and thumbs,
or from the excessive application of unguents, or from the performance of rites that are either successful or unsuccessful,
there occurs a constant dissolution (*layana*) through the non-union of speech, mind, body, and sight.
O Goddess of the Gods, these are obtained from the mouth of the Guru through association, observation, non-attachment, meditation, sitting, and entering;
and from the lineage of the Kula deity, the Kula teacher, the Kula tradition, and the Kula transmission.

O beloved, that [attainment] is not achieved otherwise; it is attained by chanting half a *kula* according to the Vedic injunctions. It is not attained even by those who toil through bathing, fasting, fire-offerings (*homa*), and the like, nor by those constantly devoted to meditation, nor by those intent on breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).
It is not attained through sacrifices, worship, fasting, conceptualization, or discursive thoughts;
nor is it attained in any way by means of the instructions of a guru.
For even if it should somehow be encountered by the logic of the "crow and the palm fruit" (i.e., by chance), [it remains unattained].
It inevitably brings about delusion and bestows madness;
it may cause the ruin of one's lineage. Therefore, one should properly practice what has been spoken by the Lord with every effort, according to the prescribed rules.
Inexhaustible, with his self united in yoga, worshipping the Guru, the Deity, and the sacrificial fire;
practicing non-violence toward all beings, meditating upon the lotus feet of Śiva,
and endowed with supreme devotion— especially toward the yogis.
For one who is habituated to sitting during the twilight hours and who always exerts effort in meditation, there arises,
by his own will, a state of noble lineage that is free from conceptual construction.
In the *Jayadratha* and the *Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī*, there is the group [beginning with] *Śakti*.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"The immersion into the Kula, the practice of the Kula, the Kula tradition (*kulāmnāya*), and the Kula transmission (*kulakrama*)."
O Maheśvara, who are those said to be the destroyers of the lineage and the slayers?
O All-pervading Lord, those by whom the great stream of the Great Immortality— which bestows the eightfold qualities of self-luminosity and self-agency— is fully known.
Whether it be from the arrival of a disciple,
or from one who has approached, or even from seeing or not seeing, or from conversation or salutation—
at the very beginning, there may arise an upward thrill or a bristling of the hair of the body based upon that.
In an instant, the rising of all the channels is perceived through its characteristic signs;
or else, a bodiless voice, or one uttered by a perfected being (siddha),
is heard at night by one who is asleep, appearing as a dream-vision directed toward him.

Likewise, the application of the marks (*liṅga*) is unstable; having come together, one who has not yet discerned [the truth] is bound by attachment. Or, through the recognition of the Goddess, as if awakened from sleep, one may hear her words.
One who is always established in yoga perceives only the wind at the outset.
This instruction regarding the directions of the Kula has indeed been accomplished by the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, I shall explain the Kula conduct for both the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya.
O Goddess of the gods, whether he be a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, an outcaste, or even a forest-dweller, if he is endowed with divine knowledge, possesses a steady intellect, is a teacher of the divine,
is free from deceit and hypocrisy, and shows reverence for the divine secret— [he is fit].
He is skilled in mantras, tantras, and secret methods, performing both minor and major rites;
he recites no other mantra, nor does he ever employ any other means.
He was devoted to our worship and did not honor external symbols;
he avoided the company of those who seek only sensory pleasure, was free from hatred and envy, was without worldly desire,
and was never at any time impelled by anger or greed.
One who bows with pride fixed upon the earth, who speaks various forms of excessive flattery, who is unrighteous, sinful, and discontented, who eats and bathes within the herds,
who does not fast, who bathes [only for show], and who is devoid of the rites performed at sacred fords— [such a person is not a true ascetic].

He is pleasant in speech and kind toward his disciples, yet free from the assumption of external emblems; or he may always bear various emblems. He bestows grace upon all, is patient, free from conceptual construction, and devoid of worldly intentionality; he possesses the fourfold virtues beginning with friendliness (maitrī).
By the word *ku*, the supreme state of Mahādevī, which is free from affliction, is indicated;
because the power (*śakti*) dissolves (*laya*) therein, it is therefore remembered as *kula*.
At that time, he who abides by means of the *vāra* [the wheel] regards a clod of earth and gold as equal.
He who has attained the state of non-duality is called a Kulācārya.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Lord of Gods, you previously declared in other scriptures—
"The status of being a teacher belongs, in due order, to the four castes alone.
O Supreme Lord, that which has been stated here regarding those born of other [castes] is contradictory; this is a great wonder to me in this case."
The illustrious Bhairava said: Just as it was previously stated by me regarding all those to be disciplined,
so too [is it] here in this Siddhakaula, which possesses the characteristic of immediate realization.
He whose object of meditation is the manifest primordial power,
*amanonmanī*, who is devoid of inhalation and exhalation— he alone is the Supreme Lord. Because of our liberation from him, there can be no difference whatsoever between us.
"Just as I am, so are you; and just as you are, so indeed is He.
O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods, who pervades all, one should always worship [Him] in this way.
O beautiful lady, he is not tainted by such acts as the killing of a Brahmin or the performance of the horse sacrifice.
To me, one who knows the four Vedas is not more dear, nor is even an outcaste more hateful.
O Goddess, he who possesses that knowledge is always dear to me.
The teacher is the supreme one; he is the Guru, he is Sadāśiva.
Having attained him, who would not be liberated from the bondage born of worldly existence?
He is the cutter of all sins, like Garuḍa is to the serpents.
She sustains the universe even by her mere glance, as if in play.
The consecration (abhiṣeka) of disciples is proclaimed as the "family-bath" (kula-snāna).
I shall describe it in brief; let it be understood exactly as it is.
In a solitary linga, or in a cremation ground, or at the confluence of rivers;
on the shore of the great ocean, or even in a great crossroads;
on the battlefield of a great war, or even in a vast house.
O beloved, in a great and glorious pavilion, or on the roof of a palace,
or in whatever place you prefer, or in a spot made doubly beautiful,
one should draw that pedestal according to the measure of one's wealth.
It is either square with four sides or circular;
it is auspicious, radiant with five colors, and adorned with five lines of *namaḥ*.
In the center is a white lotus with eight petals, possessing a garland-like pericarp.
One should place the nectar, which is the support of the Śakti, within its pericarp. Then, a jar made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay—
known as the Akālamūla jar— and smeared with white sandalwood paste [should be placed there].
Upon that, the yogi should place [the image] wearing a sacred thread and a neck-thread,
adorned with auspicious sprouts of the *aśvattha* and mango trees placed upon its mouth.
With a concentrated mind, [one should worship] the Great Ocean, who holds a conch and a mirror, is immersed in the great nectar,
whose limbs are wrapped in new cloth, who possesses gold,
is mounted upon the Great Power (Mahāśakti), and is of magnificent form.
There, one should worship the goddess Lakṣmī, who pierces the great vital points (mahāmarmavidhāriṇī).
[The sacred sites are] Prayāga, Varuṇā, Kollā, Aṭṭahāsā,
Jayantikā, Caritrā, as well as Ekāmra, and Koṭivarṣa as the eighth.

One should place [the goddesses] beginning with Prāgīrṇā and ending with Antagā upon the petals starting from the southeast; and having worshipped Brāhmī and the others at the tips of the petals in due order,
[one should visualize] the goddesses whose gazes are fixed on the joy arising from drinking the great nectar.
Pavitramātā is in the east, and Keśamātā is in the south;
Meṣamātā is in the west, and likewise Dvijamātā is in the north;
Malamātā is in the southeast, and Kṛṣṇamātā is in the southwest.
The Mother of the Skin is in the northwest, and likewise the Mother of Flowers is in the northeast.

The lamp, incense, and food offerings [should be presented] to the ignorant disciple. Having satisfied [the deities] with the destruction-rite (*vināśa*), one should then recite the mantra and ask for forgiveness.
Then, having placed that lotus upon the seat (pīṭha) preceded by the Sammoha [mantra],
one should place the jar containing milk, curd, river water, and sacred bathing water (tīrtha).
Having placed it, O Lord of the Kula, one should consecrate the disciple through a hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajāpa).

By that [initiation], the disciple who has been consecrated becomes a vessel for spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*). He attains the true state of the *Kaula*, which is described as the fifth, the *Unmanā*. "Who enters into dissolution? Your *kula* was known as Śakti."
The sequence (*krama*), however, is its transition; its domain is the individual self (*ātman*) in its distinctness.
Because it possesses the characteristics acquired through the measures of external and internal bliss, and because it ascends through the *kula*, O Goddess, it is known as the *Kulakrama*.
Through the divisions of *kalā*, *tattva*, and *pada*, as well as by means of syllables (*varṇa*), mantras, and abodes (*bhavana*),
I have explained to you this sixfold manifestation of horses (*aśvaprapañca*).
In this Siddhakaula of the Sage, that which is proclaimed in all the scriptures as the "protection of consciousness" (vijñānagopana) is celebrated as the "Half of Kula" (kulārddha).
Having manifested as Śiva together with Śivā, he stands as the inner self, abiding in the state of division.
O Maheśvarī, that which is called the awakening of that inner self occurs through the division of the royal channel by means of the unfailing power of Śiva.
This is said to be the piercing from Kula; by half of that piercing, one becomes Śiva.
Because they constantly effect a piercing through the process of transference, karmas do not approach them; this is observed to be like [wind] regarding blades of grass.
Through mere contact, there occurs a conjunction with latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) consisting of mere manifestation.
It burns away sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and other worldly transgressions in an instant.
One shall not be overcome by diseases, one becomes beloved by all people,
poison does not enter the body, and indeed, no harm-doers can cause injury.
One shall attain the supreme state, which is beyond the destruction of the aggregate of the elements.
When disciplined in the practice of *saṃdhā*, the moon of the mind becomes absorbed in that;
being satisfied, it bestows the sovereignty of the qualities such as *aṇimā* upon the one who has performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Thus ends the Piercing of the Abhisheka in the *Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī* section of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra.
The Goddess said:
"Previously, you mentioned that which is devoid of sacred seats (*pīṭha*), fields (*kṣetra*), and so forth."
"My practice of the vidyā-worship and so forth is devoid of the cardinal and intermediate directions. Now, this great collection of pīṭhas is mine;
you ought to explain how this indeed exists within the inner self."
Śrī Bhairava said:
