O Goddess, the spiritual procedure is to be accomplished precisely through the external sequence; without the external procedure, one does not know the procedure for the internal.
The realization of the unseen through the seen is what constitutes valid cognition (*pratīti*).
Therefore, the external sequence has been explained; now hear the internal one.
O Goddess, the excellent limb of Ekaliga is known as the cemetery (pitṛvana);
the confluence of rivers is its nose, and the great ocean is said to be its navel. O Goddess, the great crossroads is its heart, and the great battle is its mouth.
The big toe is the house of the earth, while the circle is between the eyebrows;
the knot at the tip of the uvula is the palace, and the upward current is according to one's desire.
O Goddess, the beholding by the power of consciousness (cicchakti) within the seat is called "writing."
The middle [element] is said to be in the middle; the lotus is called Mahāmati.
The birthplace of the nectar of the pericarp is called Kuṇḍakumbhāṇḍa.
O Dear One, its sprouts are Nandana, which are pure due to the destruction of the elements.
The conch should be turned outward; it is the mirror of the space contained within it.
This supreme form, which is profoundly peaceful, is here called the Great Form (Mahārūpa).
One should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī, the Great Māyā, as the support of the Self.
The eight petals are indeed the sacred seats (pīṭhas) such as Prayāga and the rest;
the deities of the gods, Brāhmī and the others, reside established therein.
Likewise, the Guru, the Messenger, the two sides, the arms, and the throat constitute the eighth.

The [initiations] beginning with Avitā and Pradakṣiṇā are to be understood according to the measure of the *kula*. The Vidyā belongs to the *unmanī* family; consecrated by her, one ascends to the shoulder of *unmanas*, where that Śakti, the Sovereign, resides.
By practicing that, one whose self is tranquil shall attain freedom from desire;
secluded, having cast off the body, he goes to the supreme state.
The Goddess said:
The Siddhakaula has been declared by you; now this imperishable [teaching] has been told. O Supreme Lord, how have you also taught its practice?
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, this Siddhakaula which has been spoken is not otherwise;
for it consists of the purification of the path of the principles (*tattvādhva*) and so forth, and is devoid of any cause such as [mere] compassion.
Liberation is presented as resulting from illumination, yet it belongs to one who is still possessed of fear.
O fair-faced one, liberation alone is the supreme accomplishment among all accomplishments;
all other accomplishments arise incidentally, rooted in that very liberation.
Having attained the object of knowledge through knowledge, liberation from objects of knowledge is independent of a lord.
Furthermore, O Dear One, for one who has realized the object of knowledge, the supernatural powers proceed with force and overcome obstacles;
this is the true certainty of the Kaula tradition.
In the *Jayadratha-yāmala*, within the *Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī*:
The Śrī Devī said:
"The *rājanāḍī* has been described; what is said to be its piercing (*vedha*)?"
"O Śaṅkara, by means of which knowledge are enjoyment and liberation equal?
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Those seventy-two thousand [channels] which were previously mentioned by me..."
The channels (nāḍīs) extend horizontally, upwards, and downwards, both in reverse and direct order.
Among them, one is proclaimed as the principal, known by the name Suṣumṇā;
it is called Vicitranāḍī and likewise Amṛtavāhinī.
By that [piercing], the piercing of the inner self is also said to be complete.
That should be known as the Equinox (viṣuva), which, released from power (śakti), effects it.
The Goddess said:
"How is one who has been pierced by the piercing (*vedha*) to be known?
What are the signs of such a person? Tell me [these] through your grace.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Having first examined a disciple who has approached him— having conquered his senses through long-term service, sending on errands, and requests for wealth or women—
and who sits with a body relaxed like the neck of a peacock;
Seated comfortably in the Brahma-posture, with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose,
[the practitioner] should remain in the position of a lamp's flame— neither too high nor too low. (78a)
It is free from gadflies, mosquitoes, and heat, neither too hot nor too cold,
nor too high nor crowded, and it bestows delight to the mind. [One should offer it] to the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī, as well as to one's own guru.
Purely through the measure of a moment, devoid of the activity of consciousness,
by the placement of the sixty-four steps, and through the single reality of the eightfold [path],
the Inner Self, interwoven with the moon, sun, and wind, [is realized] by the Self through itself.
One should cause it to revolve from the navel upward until the characteristic of bliss is attained.
Then, through the piercing of the downward and upward paths, one should unite with Mahālakṣmī.
O Goddess, by failing to protect this, one becomes like a tree whose roots have been severed.
Now, if one desires it to be even swifter, then the stream should be impelled;
having seized that which is skillful within oneself and cast it into the field, one should set it in motion.
Even mountains, by means of piercing, are [moved] in an instant by one whose aim is steady.
Then, either at the end of a specific period of time or until the attainment of the ultimate state,
the state of Manonmanī— eternal bliss— arises for the wise one. This occurs when,
having abandoned other attachments and the impurities of birth and death, one is in a state of supreme union.
O lady of excellent complexion, having pierced the seventy-two thousand channels and the ninefold knot of the vital breaths, the Self,
pervading everything both internal and external, proceeds once more.
Like a great festival at the great whirlpool of the vast ocean,
he experiences the great Lakṣmī with extreme slowness;
he perceives all objects beyond the senses as if they were a dream.
For this is a direct perception, this is the truth, this is the certainty of the Kaula tradition.
However, for the sake of inspiring confidence in the disciple, the ascetic may perform [the rite] out of curiosity.
Then one should agitate a single limb characterized by the *lakṣa* [sign];
only when that very [limb] undergoes paralysis (*stobha*) should one not yet honor the Self.
[One should perform] the paralysis of the arm with the hand of enjoyment, as well as the grasping of the jar.
The shaking of great trees, the trembling of images and lingas—
wherever there is such a desire of the internal state, one should cause that particular spirit to enter.
Here, there is no [fixed] lunar day, no asterism, no fasting, nor likewise any ritual rule.
The sacrificial ladle, the vessel, and the *najarakuṇḍa* are not for those who observe the vow of wandering (*caryāvrata*).

The one worthy of worship desires all these, and he provides them; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, these should not be given to one who is not a devotee nor to one who engages in worldly proliferation (*prapañca*).
It should not be given to one who is always greedy for wealth, nor to one who lives off it;
O Mother of Speech, not to a logician in the world of the gods who possesses little virtue,
nor to one intent on every kind of affliction, nor indeed to one who reviles those who know Yoga.
When there is mutual competition, one should, through the investigation of knowledge and realization,
duly establish the lineage tradition of knowledge by means of the Ācārya.
Having performed the family initiation (kulābhiṣeka), one should reveal the supreme knowledge.
But he who performs the triad [of rites] otherwise, without examination,
at the end of his devotion will undoubtedly be overcome by fierce *śākinīs* and by diseases, even if he is protected by the king’s power.

One who causes obstacles to the destruction of impediments goes to the Raurava hell; likewise, even a disciple, due to not understanding the meaning, shall not partake of the desired fruit. Thus [ends the section] on Jayadratha in the Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Now, O Goddess of gods, listen to the signs of one who possesses the fire of knowledge (upajātavedas), produced by the unfailing power of Śiva, out of a desire for the grace of the teacher.
Trembling, perspiration, horripilation, numbness, as well as throbbing;
the equality of inhalation and exhalation, and the transformation of form;
and movement and the leaving of the ground—this is called the ninefold piercing (navadhā-vedha).
(79a) Their distinct forms are now briefly described in summary:
he has hands, feet, thighs, and shanks; he has a head, and he possesses speech.
Specifically, through the nostrils, ears, eyebrows, and eyes, one should recognize trembling;
this is the domain of divine experience.
This [experience] is fourfold: trembling, horripilation, perspiration, and [the shaking of] the cheeks.
It should be present throughout all the various limbs and the entire body,
such that today all the parts [of the body] are as [insentient] as wood, stone, or a clod of earth.
Then, one should meditate on the paralysis of each individual limb while remaining in one's natural state.

The sound that manifests pride is that of the *ciñciṇī* bird, the *cīravāka*, and so forth; specifically, it is the sound of the *mṛdaṅga* drum, the *kāhala* trumpet, the conch, the great ocean, and the clouds,
as well as the humming of swarms of bees, bells, elephants, and the like.
Due to the manifestation of faint sounds such as blazing fire and wind,
the state of *naiṣpadya* is said to be threefold, and *spandana* occurs in four ways.
This [occurs] through the yoga of the sequential utterance of the placement of the heart-knot (*hṛdgranthi*).
Abandoning its natural state, the movement there proceeds as a flow;
whether characterized by trust or wonder, that sound travels far. This is declared to be "grossness" (*sthūlya*) due to its association with exhalation and inhalation.
One should perceive oneself as supreme and indeed as the Supreme Self;
whether one is situated below the earth, or within the moon, or even at its peak;
whether one is a horse, a lion, a boar, or a divine female yoginī.
The manifestation of the self within the forms of Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Candra, Arka, the sages, Rudra, Anala, Anila, as well as the fish,
tortoise, cow, serpent, locust, owl, and trees—
this is the inversion of form.
Straightforward movement, wandering, vomiting, and convulsions of the limbs;
whirling about, yawning, talking incoherently, agitation, exhilaration, and fainting. (79b)
Turning with the head downward and the feet upward is the *parivarta* (rolling over);

the *rathacārī* (chariot-mover) and *yugāvarta* (yoke-turner) [are performed] with three [steps]; the *gajendralalita* (sport of the lordly elephant) involves the neck, eyes, and trunk; and the *troṭa* (crushing) consists of the twisting of the limbs while standing.
Whirling to the left and right, as well as the antarākuṇḍala;
these are declared to be the four varieties of movement.
Remaining unsupported in the sky and remaining in a state of heat by will [are also included].
With the placement of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), the self-same [body] increases on one side; having firmly bound the posture with both knees, he remains established upon the ground,
and with a playful toss of the *kukunda* [hand], there is the *vimarṣaṇa* [movement].
This fivefold [piercing] of the earth, which brings fear to living beings,
has thus been described, characterized by many various signs;
the extensive variety of piercing is twofold according to the arrangement of its names as they truly are.
And in the region of Aśvakāśya, for one who always practices discipline,
having attained this power of *manonmanī* through the successive stages of awakening,
in what [state] does it bestow the perfection (*siddhi*) upon the yogin?
Śrī Bhairava said:
Therefore, out of affection, I shall explain in brief this secret, which arises from the *kalās* and is known as the *agniccha-vijñāta-saṃkula*.

When practiced with the application of the method of emanation (*sṛṣṭinyāya*), she who is being worshipped effects the destruction of wrinkles and grey hair. By means of the feet, there is the movement of the limbs; by means of the *cyāyāmānyā* [vital energy], the sense organs are purified.
Situated in the wheel of channels at the navel, it pervades all beings in the heart;
at the throat, it is the muttering of prayers; in the ears, it is the hearing of the Goddess;
in the nose, it is the perception of fragrance; and it is the grasping from afar and liberation.
The production of fragrance by means of fragrant substances is characterized by restoration;
likewise, the perception of what is distant, obstructed, or concealed is characterized by the removal of that [obstruction].
On the tongue is the pervasion of the six tastes, which is the all-pervading reality;
at the center of the eyebrows is the sovereignty over the world, and indeed immortality is in the lambaka.
At the place of abiding is the conduct of the deities, and at the end of the khecarī is the supreme-non-supreme (parāpara).
There is nothing higher than the Supreme; this is the true certainty of the Kaula tradition.
The wheel of Jayā, the Mistress of the Sky, transcends all means of valid cognition.
O Goddess, one who is ever mounted upon it shall attain the state of moving through the sky.
Alternatively, O beloved, by practicing out of curiosity, one may bypass the Lord of Birds and perceive, without a doubt, whatever object has been visualized— whether it be a village or a town—
as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.
Then, O Goddess, once firmly established, one shall always attain the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*).
Once established, O Great Goddess, whatever one desires to speak,
one should direct one's attention precisely there and speak it immediately.
Having transcended the atmosphere, he directs [his vision] toward the triple heaven;
and whatever he intends toward the abode of the world-protectors,
he perceives that very thing without doubt, as it is described in the sacred tradition.
It is surrounded by all the planets and constellations;
on Mount Sumeru, it has the same extent as the flow of the celestial river.
That power which is made straight indeed illuminates hundreds of thousands of millions [of worlds].
Having completely rubbed away that pride, which was like sparks arising from a fire of *śivā* wood,
as many sparkling sparks as emerged,
so many cities did he build in front of him, even raising up a city.
The yogi, detached and self-possessed, desires to cast off the body.
Then, having drawn upward from the great splendor of the earth a power that resembles lightning and the moon, he should settle it in the cremation ground.
Therefore, drawing her toward the imperishable one whose arms extend to the four quarters of the earth,
he should pull her together into a single mass and bring her to the roof of the palace.
Having emerged through the gateway of yoga, moving upward through the sky with his feet,
the master of yoga, free from doubt, causes himself to ascend after casting off the body.
Indeed, this present physical body is afflicted by disease and old age.
Desiring to abandon him, she sought to seize him again and again;
then, in the sky, she fashioned a cave according to her wish,
wherein he could not be cast down with his feet upward and his head downward.

Having first placed [the seed-syllables] and then displaced them, one should proceed by means of the "departure" (*utkrāma*) and "transition" (*saṃkrama*) through the gateway of yoga, by applying the method of emanation (*sṛṣṭinyāya*) in due order.
Thus the practitioner, through his desire for conquest, attains everything down to the earth element.
He remains having thus transitioned; no deliberation is required here.
Nevertheless, this sequence of transition has been declared for him.
Now, therefore, I shall speak of the arrangement of the sequence, which is a marvel of knowledge.
Having visualized the desired object to be accomplished as being far away, one should then see it as being near to oneself;
having seen it as a mass of colored and colorless rainbow-hues, one should emit it.
Then, that [mass] becomes a thousandfold within a thousand-petaled lotus.
The realization of the individual soul by the inner self has a stable mark;
therefore, having seized the interior of the lotus like a serpent attacking its prey, may that [Lord], who resembles a flashing self-luminous light, destroy your affliction.
Having taken hold of the empowerment, one should settle in a cremation ground.
Then, having approached there oneself, one should remain at a crossroads.
As it is with oneself, so it is with that; as it is with that, so it is with all things.
O Goddess, one who applies himself to yoga in this manner, remaining untiring for seven nights, may even overcome Śakra; how much more so, then, lesser mortals?
One should cause all desired activities to be performed as being of that very nature.
O you who are fond of devotion, through the power of giving, worship, and other honors,
one may perform the "gate of life" (*jīvanidvāra*) if it pleases [the practitioner].
Through the very process of upward transcendence (*samutkrānti*), that yogi performs various meditative visualizations;
having pervaded the path of the apertures and standing in the state of the celestial realm,
the self-controlled one can, in a mere moment, restrain even the Creator himself.
Then, one should seek the seizing [of the breath] from the bond that brings fear to the bound soul.
Having then transcended that through placement, one should contemplate the individual self (jīvātman) by means of the yoga of union and excellence, wherein the earth is above the wind.
Then one should sustain [the breath] as it has gone into the sky, remaining entirely still.
When the upward power is restrained, for a moment the Lord of the Eyes seizes the bound soul (paśu) with certainty, provided that he does not direct it downward.
Now, O lady of excellent vows, I shall describe to you another true essence of yoga:
the production of stability in the body, the yoginī’s deception of time,
and their conjunction and separation, which should be understood in due order.
O lady of excellent vows, for the yogin who is disciplined in yoga and devoted to his practice, there arises through union a state of concentration that is free from both separation and conjunction.
The Śrī Devī said:
What kind of yoga is this said to be, and what kind is viyoga? And what is that which joins her to him who effects the union?
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Indeed, the conjunction of the self arises from its connection with the subtle body (ativāhika);
conversely, separation from the Supreme Self is said to result from the disjunction from that [subtle body].
For the self is conceived by time as being conjoined with the qualities of the eightfold body;
yet, having abandoned the qualities of the subtle body (*ativāhika*), it is no longer conceived by time.
The Śrī Devī said:
Previously, the subtle body (*tanusūkṣma*), known as the *puryaṣṭaka*, was described by you.
Now, however, how is it to be abandoned, and how can the individual soul (*pudgala*) itself be capable of abandoning it?
Śrī Bhairava said:

By disregarding and abandoning the inhalation and exhalation of breath, as well as the physical body (piṇḍa) of the self, one attains the state of moving through the air; in an instant, one should cast off the subtle body consisting of eight constituents (puryaṣṭaka).
The Goddess said:
If one were to go through the air by abandoning inhalation and exhalation, that would merely be a lapse of time; what else would it accomplish?
Śrī Bhairava said:
Above the *ūrdhvaviddha* [lotus], there is the extraction of yoga (*yogoddhāra*) measuring ten finger-breadths;
it is renowned as *vaihāyasa*, possessing innumerable petals and filaments.

A wheel that has completely overcome all [things], and another [wheel] above it that devours [all things]; one whose self is tranquil, having ascended that [wheel], shall not fall under the power of death.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
This has been declared as wonderful: the self-controlled one, having abandoned the body of both existence and non-existence, does not fall under the power of time when the [proper] time has arrived.
Śrī Bhairava said:
For just as when the lotus stalk is split in two, the subtle part remains known as "nara" (the man),
so too does Śakti remain, O Dear One;
even when liberated for the sake of the self-world, she persists through her pervasiveness both below and above, having abandoned [her former] extension.
Even by subtle time, the extremely subtle Self is not at all affected.
Listen, O large-eyed one, to the means for its worship:
[it is] the coiled serpent residing within the solar orb.

One should contemplate the luminous Kaumudī, who, when the ocean of nectar has been prepared with a downpour of thousands of streams, floods the sun, heaven and earth, and all that is moving and unmoving; she is the beloved of the white water-lily.
In that [mirror], there appeared a mass of rays radiating from the seal of the virtuous,
released from the luster of his eyes, resembling the likeness of the Lord of Fire.
Freedom of will, self-agency, and the possession of the qualities of the finest jewels arise;
the capacity to bestow grace upon all occurs through the deception of time.
Having reached the further shore of the ocean of knowledge, which is as radiant as nectar—
One should contemplate a great rope extending beyond the limit of non-reflection. Then the yogi, assuming the form of the Earth,
will undoubtedly paralyze the receptacles of meditation belonging to those clinging to the mountain-like [obstacles], just as the King of Waters [stills the waves].
One should meditate upon the Great Māyā, who stands at the hub of two wheels, is yellow in color,
and is exceedingly weighty; she remains established in her form through her own arising,
mounted upon the sun even for a moment.
One may even stop a chariot with mere cloth; what need is there to mention heaps of wood?
Furthermore, whatever other things exist here, they should be understood as being included within this [practice], provided one does not rely on mere intellectual knowledge.
Since everything is the object of the consciousness of one whose senses are born of yoga,
how could it be possible to describe that which is always to be known by oneself, O sinless one?
Indeed, Hiraṇyagarbha himself formerly [described it] only in brief.
Then, O beloved, by means of a hundred thousand sublime verses along with their recitation, this [yogin] is like a bird that has reached the end of its journey;
indeed, he does not require lamps or other such aids.
This alone is his greatness: he teaches the yogins.
There is no doubt that for one who applies himself here, future cognitions will arise;
therefore, in this matter, practice alone is the catalyst for omniscience. [From the Jayadrathayāmala, in the section on the *Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī*].
Liberation is said to be the source of the accomplishments (siddhis) achieved through spiritual perfection.
Now, let the attainment of those desiring good fortune and prosperity be described. Śrī Bhairava said:
The yogin who relies on a single liṅga undoubtedly attains success through water-recitation;
he shall obtain great good fortune, which bestows intoxication and exhilaration.
Now listen with a one-pointed mind to its first mode of worship:
it is all-encompassing, resembling Kashmiri saffron and white clouds,
filled with uninterrupted streams, and possessing the nature of flowing saffron.
Having visualized a lotus red as the rising orb of the thousand-rayed sun,
with its circumference of eight petals and beautiful filaments shining forth,
one should perceive oneself seated there, resplendent with many ornaments.

The yogi should meditate every day for a period of six months upon Him who is adorned with fragrant garlands of celestial *aśoka* and *baṃdhūka* flowers, whose face gladdens the world, and who is overflowing with supreme bliss.
All women— whether ordinary or yoginīs— come constantly with minds intoxicated by passion, each vying for precedence in the thought, "I first, I first!
If one desires union with the divine, one should not become agitated upon seeing them.
Then, for a year and more, the Gandharvas and Apsarases always arrive and remain present, granting whatever is desired.
One attains long necks, good fortune, and the application of liquid fragrant ointments.
Clad in garments as red as the juice clinging to a moving, beautiful [bee],
possessing a body as lovely as the honey from the fine flowers of a garden reddened by coral trees,
he is always accompanied by delight and the sound of songs from the lutes of the Apsarases.
With his staff-like spear and bow raised aloft, his banner was the assembly of arrows;
pervading the three worlds with his quivering five great elements,
he performed this vow of the Mind-born God, causing the agitation of the three realms.
Bearing [his staff] according to his desire, the lover of desire may wander the earth at will through lovely gardens, sacred fords, and temples of the deities. (83a)
O beloved, O fair-faced one, he who has formed an association with these [energies] sports upon lofty mountain peaks and other delightful places together with them;
or else, the yogi devoted to yoga remains with me alone.
The Siddhayoginīs bestow that very same supreme Kaulika tradition,
indeed the highest oral transmission (saṃpradāya), or the sacrificial pap (caru) pertaining to seven lifetimes;
in which, from the very beginning, one shall eternally attain the state of moving through the sky (khecaratva).
He always rejoices in the worlds of Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Candra;
he is saluted by Vidyādharas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas.
At the dissolution of the four yugas, he withdraws himself by means of his own self.
She, the sovereign mistress, dissolves there in the supreme void, which is the abode of names.
Now, with a concentrated mind, I shall fully explain the ascent of fortune,
by the service of which one attains the enjoyment of fortune even through non-service.
Seated within the pavilion, she possessed the luster of polished gold;
mingled with the moonlight of Indra, she moved day and night,
her exceedingly brilliant and shimmering radiance like rising droplets of water.
One should contemplate the splendor of rows of shimmering, variegated rubies;
one should practice until the entire universe is pervaded by that radiance.
Such a fortunate yogi becomes wealthy and pleasing to behold.

One who is endowed with yoga for six months becomes glorious, always possessed of the enjoyment of sovereignty, and honored by the world; of this there is no doubt. For one who is disciplined for a year, his youthful splendor is worshipped.
O Goddess, for one who makes the surface of the earth everywhere level with this [mudrā], servants approach like attendants to serve the king; moreover,
various and extraordinary treasures present themselves.
O fair-faced one, even Kubera, accompanied by Padma and Śaṅkha,
having appeared, grants whatever is desired, even if it is improper.
Surrounded on all sides by wealth, grain, gold, cattle, horses, or elephants, as well as by sons, wives, and servants,
one may enjoy pleasures appropriate for such use and then depart from this abode.
The Goddess said:
"By what means does an exaltation arise for a yogi who is joined in yoga, even when his body is afflicted by disease? Please tell me out of your grace."
Śrī Bhairava said:
Although this treatise has been presented with very few measures,
it becomes the Āyurveda through its extensive elaboration and even by means of its concise summary.
Nevertheless, I shall explain in brief the method for pacifying the sensations of various diseases, according to the appropriate strength and lifespan [of the patient].
Diseases are said to be of two kinds: those born of the *doṣas* and those born of karma.
Through the destruction of the defects, those [sufferings] born of karma are surely brought to an end by the cessation of karma; this is certain for one whose body is pervaded by disease,
for the arising of the defect of suffering has indeed been explained previously.
This [treatise], which was formerly taught in its entirety by [Dhanvantari] to his grandfather regarding diseases arising from karma, is a destroyer of karma;
it is like a crystal mirror for the Goddess, who is pleased by the delight of her feet.
Vāta, pitta, and likewise śleṣman are the primary binders of all [the elements];
indeed, this triad is the great source-field for the diseases and so forth.
Vāta is said to be simply vāta itself, while the earth is its playful consort.
Bile is said to be fire, and phlegm is said to be water.
When these [humors] are increased by activities such as the eightfold city [of the body],
they are subdued through the application of their opposites and the employment of one's own power.
It destroys the multitude of diseases within my body in an instant;
it shall always conquer the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta).

Among diseases, the first disease is fever, which causes affliction throughout the entire body. It is produced by the three *doṣas* immediately, as well as other types arising from the combination of all three (*saṃnipāta*). Having correctly identified that [fever] as a storehouse [of ailments], one should treat it through the proper application of sequential methods.
He conquers according to his application, pervading all through the reversal [of opposites].
He is the illuminator of the path to heaven from the sky, the one who flows like a stream of milk, the one whose tide is the Ocean of Milk,
the one who dwells within the Ocean of Milk, and he whose form is raised aloft by his hands.
Residing in the middle of the *dhātus*, situated within the center, and firmly established inside all the limbs—
by worshipping her gradually and day after day for half a month, I have [attained] accomplishment;
she destroys consumption (*rājayakṣmā*), of this there is no doubt.
One should meditate upon her of many forms, situated within the orb of the sun, possessing the pure radiance of the moon;
she blows [the breath] by means of the arrangement of the potter’s wheel through union with her husband,
[manifesting] in the regions of the navel, heart, and head.

Through the practice of the month-long worship (*māsopāsanā-yoga*), there occurs a descent through the sequence of the *anusādhya* stage; it certainly and without doubt eliminates the disease of leprosy.
[One perceives] that which resides within the interior of the lotus of the anus, possessing the luster of split collyrium.
For the ascetic who constantly contemplates the emergence from the logic of creation,
those afflicted by fistula, hemorrhoids, dysentery, and similar ailments,
as well as others of wooden nature, certainly pass away first, according to the Vānikas.
In the hands, feet, thighs, shanks, sides, heart, throat, and head—
through the sequence of counteracting all yogic obstacles,
there is victory for those whose minds are intent on concentration (dhāraṇā) upon the great stream of the supreme nectar.
Whatever diseases constantly arise from the force of agitation,
therefore one should avoid causing disturbance with every possible effort.
Through focused application, one swiftly attains the desired benefit.
In the case of Jayadratha, there was a descent of fortune through the power of Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī.
Then, he became worthy of receiving instruction, having been brought under the sway of prosperity.
Listen further to the abode of one whose body remains in this world according to the prescribed rite, so that the self may not again enter the grasp of rebirth;
having emerged from the celestial realm, it possesses the radiance of the blazing fire of time.

With a one-pointed mind, one should meditate upon her who is like a great net, well-released, whose activity is all-pervasive, who follows the sequential order, who has manifested as the three worlds, who sports in the four aims of life,
and who entirely envelops everything moving and unmoving.

One should contemplate that [wind], which has the form of a *indragopaka* insect, repeatedly swelling up and then entering that body drawn in by the power (*śakti*). Having entered, one should place it in the navel, the heart, the space of the sky, and in the mouth, ears, and eyes.
One should apply [the practice] for as long as it takes until, being drawn up and breathing,
he rises up without doubt, presiding over his own body. Then, at will, one should desire that he be restored to a healthy state, performing the rites for the deceased.

One should apply this through the yoga of power, having extracted the state of moving through the air. As soon as it is joined for even a moment, the individual (pudgala), having ascended with effort, proceeds to the appropriate station; once liberated, there is no doubt in this.
This true essence of yoga has been imparted to you by me;
it must never be disclosed by you to one who lacks the capacity for examination. You shall immediately perceive the characteristic signs of realization within your own body.
One should meditate upon her, rising at will with a splendor as beautiful as vermilion,
wandering through the sky, illuminating the sacrifice with her own radiance,
pervading his entire body, and causing him agitation.
Having stabilized one's own body, one should apply it to the body of the consort;
by applying it for even a moment, the consort will undoubtedly be stirred.
Then, having become identical with that [object], being dear to it and acting in accordance with it,
he approaches and bestows whatever is desired as appropriate.
In this way, O Goddess, some [siddhis] arise from two, three, four, or five [elements].
In the six, seven, eight, and up to nine cities, according to the Sauramata,
a man who is intensely focused through ritual action upon excellent women will undoubtedly cause them to tremble in a mere instant; he is known as Kṣobhinī (the Shaker).
Furthermore, the ancient tradition speaks of the combination of female, male, and neuter [energies]. First, one should visualize the five poisons above the earth, and then the mandala,
because therein the object upon the surface of the earth finds rest within the mind.
The mind is considered to be the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ), its power marked by the reality [of the Absolute].
Having correctly taken hold of it, the primordial Power (*śakti*) is joined;
likewise, it is colored by the union [with that Power] through its own solar radiance.

By employing [this practice] for seven nights, one should agitate [the disciple] and lead him forward. However, due to the consideration of the task at hand, he should not [proceed] otherwise; he is truly one who speaks as the Lord has commanded. O fair-hipped lady, listen now to the truth regarding the arrival at the station on the path.
By means of this, the yogi who moves upon the earth goes wherever he desires in an instant.
One should meditate on the row of palm trees extending from the outer to the inner cheek, which, having emerged from the wheel of wind, increases and fills the circle of space.
Constantly performing the transition, he should gradually bring about the union of the mind;
having perpetually understood the speed [of the breath], he, being established in his station, should lead it to dissolution in the desired [place].
Thus, through the application of practice, even in a single day and night, all three [channels]—
Having wandered about, she returns victorious, O beloved of the world!
Thus, for the sake of creating curiosity among people, she intensely desires food, drink, and ignorance; therefore, one should practice [the yoga] accordingly.
(85b) Having first consumed the light of the universal fire in the conflagration of the [world] system,
one should contemplate [the body] as having its roots severed by the blazing fire of the great cremation ground.
That great serpent, resembling a black cobra, approaches with its great illusion;
it drinks and devours, without hesitation, as much food and drink as has been offered before it.
This, the departure, is declared to be the second transition (*saṃkrama*).
O Goddess, the third is from the ascent (*ākrama*), and the fourth is called the seizing (*graha*).
Discernment (*vicāra*) is indeed the fifth; thus, the fivefold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is complete.
It is declared that [the power] arises upon the emergence of the *ṛṃ* syllable, and is not said to arise in any other;
it is applied to oneself as well as to many others.
There is no doubt here that it effects the fulfillment of one's desired aims according to one's wish.
But [one should worship] the supreme Mahāmūrttivatī, who is embraced by Sadāśiva, who bestows the pacification of all obstacles to that undertaking,
who carries a great skull, who dwells in a skull, and who is the bearer of skulls (Kapālinī).

One should not satisfy the divine nectar with a skull-cup belonging to a Kāpālika; O Goddess, by satisfying this [divine nectar], those residing in the three worlds are satisfied. The Yoginīs, whose selves are united, attain delight when they are thus gratified.
Free from smoke and obstacles, like the clear sky,
it bestows a state of being that is beyond the senses— the Kaula reality—
and grants the accomplishments (siddhis) that arise through the emergence of mental clarity, according to the proper method.
"This supreme secret has been revealed to you out of love; even now, at the three junctions of the day, it remains above [all else]. What more do you wish to ask?
Thus he spoke, having fashioned the wheel and the auspicious mark of the great fish.
(86a) Thus ends the chapter on the agitation caused by the attempt to bring back Jayadratha’s life, titled "The Madness.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the Heart-mantra that grants all desires,
by which the master practitioner shall become an abode of all virtues.
Therefore, O daughter of the mountain, listen to this Lord of the Heart.

I shall now proclaim the extraction of the mantra, which is the essence that performs all rites and brings about great enmity; listen with a one-pointed mind. Having reached the abode of Hara (Śiva) and having purified oneself through diligent effort according to the prescribed rite, [one should proceed].
One should worship Kṛtyāmantra-īśvarī, who is smeared with great blood;
having worshipped her, the practitioner of mantra should extract the Vidyā of terrible prowess:
*mahādhāma*, *mahānāda*, and again that *dhāmarṇa*.

This Piṇḍa-mantra, which is traversed by the movement of the mouth (the breath), adorned with Bindu and Nāda, is exceedingly fierce and the devourer of the entire triple world. It is then joined with the three Bindus, followed by Varuṇa (Va) and Kartaṇa (Ka).
The six-syllable mantra, joined with *bāhu* and *vāruṇī*, marked with three suns, and conjoined with *ajīva* and *kaṭha*,
has been extracted; O highly fortunate Goddess of gods, it is a great producer of enmity.
One should worship Bhairavī within the world of the hexagon— renowned as the Ekavīra, devoid of Muṇḍapāda—
which is streaked with the color of a dove and adorned with four gates.
Having prepared a canopy and donned garments of the quarters, one should commence the sacrifice.
A great conch-shell and an offering vessel filled with blood—
therein one should worship the Goddess of the Gods, who resembles the Destroyer at the end of time.
Terror-inspiring with the force of hundreds of winds at the time of the great dissolution;
fierce, having destroyed her enemies by the mere casting of her veil of great illusion;
resembling a raven, with only fleshless sinews, skin, and bones remaining.
(86b) She whose eight arms are as exceedingly lofty as the revolving pavilion of the universe;
she who is the blackness to the lotus-faces of the wives of the enemies of the gods.
Scaring the entire world as far as the realm of Brahmā,
emitting a wind from a winnowing basket, with a body born of fire,
mounted upon an owl-throne, her eyes momentary and curved with a frown.
Having meditated thus upon the God and Goddess, one should satisfy them according to one's means,
with offerings such as swarms of bees and various excellent essences,
O Goddess, with diverse flowers and various musical instruments.
Having thus worshipped the Goddess of Gods, one should then begin the practice of sādhana.
Free from all distress, one should recite the mantra exactly one hundred thousand times according to the number of its syllables.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one floats in the sky and becomes equal to Bhairava.
O Queen of the Gods, by reciting it one hundred thousand times, the middling accomplishment is achieved;
of this there is no doubt, for my word is infallible.
By reciting it ten thousand times, O Goddess, one shall accomplish the common [attainment].
Now I shall explain this; listen, O beloved of the lords of heroes!
By means of the two [mantras] beginning with *nāya* and *saṃpu*, joined with words of enmity and the application of a great wind, one will cause the entire world to be filled with hatred.
Or else, [one may visualize] two with faces like silk cloth, having the faces of a buffalo and a horse;
they are to be meditated upon as beautiful, auspicious, marked with many weapons,
endowed with yellow eyes, and striking one another.
O highly fortunate one, having ascended into the sky, one should then mutter the mantra of the God of Gods.
In this way, one may cause enmity among all the three worlds, including the mobile and the immobile.
Then, one should have an image fashioned from white clay mixed with *āṣṭaka* [grains].
Having drawn a *vīra* with blood,
provided with the names of those to be targeted and joined with words for inciting enmity, one should place it facing away.
Between their two heads, one should place the wind, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the most formidable knowledge-mantra (*vidyā*).
The master of the rite should offer [the victim] as a gift, causing all that is moving and unmoving to feel hatred;
or else, he should use powder produced from a saw, empowered by the mantra.
O fortunate one, a piece of wood from a funeral pyre should be thrown into the midst of the *ṛc*;
O beautiful lady, those two shall indeed become hated by all the world.
And they shall be at odds with one another, O fair-hipped one; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
O Goddess, one should cause a cloth to be inscribed with the name of the couple to be subjugated, filled with poison and blood, enclosed within the mantra, and buried on a riverbank by a Piśāca.
When two cloth strips are turned away from each other, they cause the world of moving and unmoving things to be filled with hatred.
Having obtained the Vidyā Āvartabhairavī during a lunar eclipse,
one should, at the end of the night, cause a pair of sugar-candies to be seized from the beginning of the eclipse.
O slender-waisted one, at the time of giving it away, the pair should be taken back again.
Having thus received it, the wise man should keep it well-guarded.
And as for the first pair here, by which the name was indeed grasped—
O Mahābhāgā, if the Supreme Goddess should cause these two to be sounded while they are in mutual enmity and on the verge of death, they shall both become Bhairavas at that very moment.
By playing them in the western direction with a pair [of instruments] in direct order, [this occurs].
"O Goddess, the bringing back [of the enemy] shall occur in this way; there is no doubt in this matter.
Indeed, this method for causing hatred, which brings success, has been explained to you according to its true nature.
Now, having taken a *vaibhītaka* creeper, one should place it in one's hand."

O Goddess, having seized that blazing funeral pyre where the mouths of the flames roar with the sound "vak-vak," and having walked away from it a hundred steps while it is still burning, one should then recite the Vidyā and subsequently consecrate it with mantras.
Whomever he might strike with a thousand or even a hundred [strokes],
that person becomes deluded and comes to be hated by all the world.
For whomsoever incense is offered using the two wings of a *dvika-kaushika* [owl], [he likewise meets such a fate].
O fair-faced one, he shall quickly become an enemy for as long as his life lasts.
Having gathered the feathers from those two, he should remain at night in a cemetery.
O Great Goddess, by means of these two names, one shall undoubtedly cause hatred;
thus I have described the immobilization [stambhana] situated within the circle of Indra.
Having visualized the target there as marked with a vajra, that shall come to pass.
For the Supreme Goddess may accomplish other rites as well:
the telling of dreams through inquiry, the excellent possession of a vessel,
the possession of one who is healthy, or anything else through the service of another's manual.
The Goddess of the gods, the bestower of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation, truly accomplishes [all goals].
This goddess Karaṅkiṇī has arisen from the wheel of the feet.
Thus has it been fully explained to you; what else shall I tell you?
Thus ends the chapter on the Kali of Enmity within the Rāviṇīcakra, in the fourth Ṣaṭka of the Jayadratha-yāmala, the twenty-four thousand [verse] scripture.
The Śrī Devī said:
"Everything has been heard by me in its entirety, as you have explained it according to the truth."
Now I wish to hear from you about that which is called *sūtaka*;
O Supreme Goddess, how do these [impurities] flash within the vital points (*marmas*) of the Lord of Gods?
O best of gods, tell me, O Rāviṇī, [how] the eighty-one [parts] exist for me.
"O Lord, tell me: is she one or is she many, divided by various distinctions?
Having heard this, Śambhu—the Blessed One who is saluted by gods and asuras—spoke these words along with their secret meaning to Bhavānī.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, for I shall speak that which was previously indicated by me—
the incomparable great secret that brings about all prosperity and virtues.
Ambikā, whose manifestation is clearly revealed by her body that throbs and blazes intensely, contains the world within her womb; she is most fierce and a voracious devourer of Time alone.
With its own parts and constituent elements, it is like a wound that is both cracked and uncracked;
such is the one of universal form described as the prior meditation.
From the bulb of the womb, the yogin [proceeds] from bulb to bulb, from planet to planet, by means of the vowel.
Not overcome by men, she is most terrible, exceedingly fierce, and garlanded with existence.
Bursting forth with many rays from the supreme abode of her shimmering splendor,
she resounds with a multitude of light-beams and unfolds within every single abode.
From the temple-pavilion of the Kula-fire of the Time of Destruction, which is like a mass of whirling firebrands, Bhairaveśvarī, out of the joy of bearing the peak of the Sphoṭa,
has swiftly caused Mīnā, who is like the submarine fire, to whirl up into another realm of the Kula-fire.
Having bound the appropriate *rāviṇī* seal, which is most terrible and formidable,
that goddess— bound and yet bursting forth— is the bearer of the water-pot (*karaṅkiṇī*) by means of all supports.
This occurs first from the wheel of the fire of time (*kālāgnicakra*) through the application of the well-wheel (*kūpacakra*).
The supreme Kālī has burst forth; she grants [her power] through that very application.
There, in the manner of a well, she is like one who partakes in both gathering and wandering.
Thus, she is Karaṅkeśī for the practitioner—of this there is no doubt.
Then, by means of the practice of vibrating [the breath] within the limit favorable to perception,
one attains the second [state], the *karaṅkiṇī*, which bestows the siddhis of the netherworld (*pātāla*) and the sky;
through the yoga of vibrating the throbbing [energy], one destroys the "tortoise" (the vital breath) like a tortoise.
When worshipped with the syllable *karareṇa*, she becomes the fierce Bhairavī;
she bestows upon the practitioner the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) of the netherworld and the sky.
Beyond this, through the yoga of the movement of the wheel arising from the state of stillness (*sthiti*), [the goal is attained].
Manifest, bearing a skull-topped staff, and fierce, she expands within her own abode.
When she is thus struck by this yoga,
then that third ray, Vīrasundarī, is worshipped.
She should be known as the bestower of all accomplishments and the constant giver of the siddhi of moving through the sky;
she is the Supreme Sovereign (Parameśānī), fashioned from the wheel in the state of contraction. (88b)
Vibrating with a radiance joined by tens of millions upon tens of millions of fierce fires of time,
it effects piercing, casting down, and other rites, and bestows the accomplishment of the Great Assembly (*mahāmelāpa*).
For that very reason, through his eating of that sacrificial pap (*caru*), [the goal is attained].
The goddess Karaṅkiṇī is proclaimed as the bestower of its accomplishment.
Beyond this is the one called Trikoṇā, who is intensely radiant with the circle of circles;
she is the eternal intoxication of the essence of great bliss, and she is indeed the moistener.
Through the yoga of manifestation, throbbing, contraction, movement, and immersion,
and by means of the great churning yoga with that flower-offering as the sacrificial oblation,
the supreme power (kalā), which agitates great bliss, attains liberation.
By that [practice], the entire world, from the realm of Brahmā down to the earth, shall become free from fear.
O beloved, I have declared to you this fifth *dhāman*, which is manifest and bestows all spiritual accomplishments;
it is difficult to attain even among the gods, O highly fortunate one.
Therefore, when that sixth great wheel,
known as the Brahma-knot, is thoroughly agitated by her through the friction of its upper and lower parts,
then, due to the resting of the root of the vital breath (prāṇa), Karaṅkiṇī becomes manifest.
By that very sequence of differentiation, through the consumption of the great water,
she who brings about poetic power becomes manifest there.
Beyond this, in the seventh wheel, the *kanda*, is the supreme digit (*kalā*).
Through the application of the onset of yawning, that Mistress of the quarters throbbed;
then she became manifest as the most terrible Karaṅkiṇī.
Possessing a body equal to ten million times a hundred thousand fires of cosmic destruction, she shone forth resplendent.
She should be known as the bestower of all accomplishments through the yoga of the Great Organ (mahākaraṇa).
The Supreme Goddess arises from the liquid substance of the five jewels and the *kharuka*;
therefore, she is the ever-resounding digit (*kalā*) within the wheel of Kuṇḍalinī.
By means of the practice of unwinding, she was turned back through the application of the *vṛtti*;
then, right there, that most terrible Karaṅkiṇī burst asunder. (89a)

By means of this supreme instrument, O Goddess, she accomplishes the great siddhi of moving through the sky unimpeded; there is no doubt in this matter. As for Karinkiṇī, who was described as having a terrible form among those mentioned in the eighth [chapter]—
Then, when that unbroken Vāmā has entered the heart-lotus,
and when that auspicious Śivā vibrates there through the application of apāna,
then she becomes manifest as the supreme Bhairavī, bestowing all siddhis.
By this sequential yoga, through the experience of a cool touch,
the Great Forest of Bees bestows accomplishment in the ninth wheel.
Therefore, the Supreme Goddess is manifested in the wheel of Saṃrāviṇī.
Then that goddess, the mistress of the immortals, Sphuritā Karaṅkiṇī,
is worshipped among practitioners through the application of the consumption of time (kālāhāra).
O Mistress of the Gods, when she becomes manifest, she bestows the state of being free from old age and death.
Thus, the tenth Mistress of the Wheel bestows all accomplishments upon men.
Therefore, when she flashes forth within that wheel called the Jar (Ghaṭa),
she indeed bursts open through the friction of the contraction known as the vital point (marmākhya).
In this way, one should practice the yoga of application in the eleventh wheel (*cakra*).
For him, that Goddess manifests, bestowing the perfection of being a teacher of the *Kula* tradition.
Furthermore, Rāviṇī vibrates within the wheels beginning with the "well of the throat" (*kaṇṭhakūpa*).
Then the Goddess, resplendent with a hundred rays, becomes manifest there;
when one practices the junction of sound (*nādasaṃdhi*) through the revealed method,
then that terrible [Goddess] is manifested, who destroys hunger and thirst.
That twelfth digit is terrible; it consists of no stalk, clarified butter, or sacrificial porridge.
When thereafter she protects her own throat situated in the wheel of emptiness, below the *laṃba* and upon the back of *lolikā*, then that auspicious goddess has burst forth.
Aṭṭahāsā, Karakeśī, and the one called Mahānādā are bestowers of accomplishment;
thus, through her connection with the Sun, she is the bestower of accomplishment there.
In the thirteenth great wheel, she is solely devoted to feeding on milk;
beyond this, her activity is a great undertaking characterized by hanging flower-garlands. She is to be known as "Ghaṇṭā" (the Bell) when she is vibrating there.
She manifests as the striker at the tip of the thirty-two moving wheels;
through such a yoga, that Supreme Goddess, the bestower of all siddhis, eternally manifests as Karaṅkiṇī.
In the fourteenth great wheel, she brings all prosperity and happiness.
Then, when Karaṅkiṇī reaches the other, the wheel of Īśvara,
the goddess Karaṅkiṇī becomes manifest within that radiant support.
There, by means of unobstructed practice, knowledge arises from the churning of the lotus;
the state of being a Lord of Knowledge (Vidyāpati) comes to these yogins—of this there is no doubt.
This fifteenth wheel has been revealed to you today.
Then, when the Goddess Paramabhairavī, who abides in the state of the Bindu,
vibrates within the five wheels as one characterized by non-conceptualization,
then her omniscience truly vibrates at all times.
She is the unmanifest Ghorakālikā, who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Beyond the Tranquil (śānta) is the Transcendent Tranquil (śāntātīta), and the third is called Knowledge (vidyā). The fourth is known as Establishment (pratiṣṭhā), and the fifth is known as Cessation (nivṛtti).
These are the five great wheels; the sixth is [to be understood] by its own nature.

Through the application of their divisions, according to the sequence of the upward-moving *kāhika*, O Dear One, the attainment of that [sixth wheel] occurs through the state of the opening of the eyes.
Thus, O Bhairavī, the twenty paths have been described to you.
Beyond this, in the Brahma-cakra, that Karaṅkiṇī is vibrantly manifest;
there, the Supreme Goddess is clearly revealed in the form of a half-moon.
(90a) By means of the application of the destruction of intrinsic nature and by the sequence of raising the eyes,
in that very same way, for others, she becomes the one with a sword and a bell, external to herself.
She bestows great peace, a portion of liberation, and the eternal state.
This Mistress of the Lord of the Kings of Marms lasts for twenty-one months;
thereafter, she is the Mistress of the Wheel of Cessation (Nirodhacakra), and likewise when [the breath] resides in the Nāda.
And at the end of the *nāda*, O fair-hipped one, O passionate lady,
within the great wheel called Vyāpinī, as well as in Samana and Unmana,
the Mistress of the Seat of Mantras vibrated; then she burst forth intensely.
Thus, within the seven wheels, Karaṅkiṇī is of terrible form;
through the union with the Great Object of Knowledge (mahāprameya) and ending with the upward emission (proccāra), she is Bhairavī.
She should be known as the bestower of heroic accomplishment (vīrasiddhi) and the purifier through the penetration of possession (vedhāveśa).
It generates the realization of others, is likewise the foremost of all accomplishments,
effects the piercing of the invisible, and is the source of all mantras in due order;
these, in brief, are the twenty-eight vital points (marmas).
I have explained to you the determination of the form of Rāviṇī;
now, O beloved of the lords of heroes, hear about the foreign armies. From that seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), Bhairavī vibrates as the pulsation (spanda).
By means of the movement of power (*śakti*), she clearly [perceives] the tranquil Lord of the Wheel (*cakranāyaka*).
Then the Wheel of the Guru’s mouth, then the equinox (*viṣuva*) called "Contact" (*sparśa*), then the Unborn (*aja*) called the Abode of Emission (*visargadhāman*); mounted upon that is Karaṅkiṇī.
When Bhairavī thus vibrates through the clusters of the six cakras, she then repeatedly emits the Kula born of the six marks.
Therein, the accomplishment is indifferent; the Goddess of the Gods is manifest in six ways.
O fortunate one, through the movement of power,
the practitioner indeed attains the state of the Lord of the Family of Great Pervasion, the supreme universal form. (90b)
And here, the realization of power is the very nature of Śiva-Bhairava.
O Queen of the Gods, the Supreme State is accomplished for the practitioner here.
O Bhairavī, the thirty-four vital points have been declared to you.
Now I shall fully explain how that digit (kalā) vibrates:
the wheel of sound, the wheel of touch, the wheel of form, the wheel consisting of taste,
the great wheel consisting of the Gaṅgā, and likewise the wheel of the sense-organs of the intellect.
Likewise, I fashioned the mind-wheel (manaścakra) as the eightfold fire-drill of the Buddha;
the wheel of darkness (tamaścakra), the one called Aja, and the sattvic wheel—these sixteen [are the components].
When that terrible Karaṅkiṇī has mounted these wheels, [she becomes manifest].
Then the goddesses, the lords of the gods, emerge in the form of rays, possessing great power; they are formidable, like those bearing swords, causing transformation within the multitude of kalās,
and having arisen with powerful currents, they drive the entire world along.
She satisfies her own form, and her forms, adorned with hand-bells,
[satisfy] themselves. Then, O Queen of Men, she who has emerged from my mouth spontaneously grants her own divine family of accomplishments (siddhi) to the abode called Ghora.
Through the yoga of the Lord of Men (*nareśvara*), the visualization of the convergence of rays,
by the power of the recitation of his mantra, and by the assembly of the worship-circle (*pūjācakrakula*);
likewise, *dhukamaṃdhu*, Brahmā, sandalwood, and *vālira*.
The middle, the supreme, the goat, the mixed, and the flower;
likewise, the threefold creation born from the Rudra-kuṇḍa;
the stalk-less, the wine, the clarified butter, and here the sixteen and the nine.
O Goddess of the gods, these must indeed be bestowed by practitioners in due order.
Thus, O illustrious and beautiful one, these fifteen wonderful [mantras] are proclaimed as the Heart and the Weapon; they shall now be described.
And here, through the application of mantra and meditation, the five goddesses of the lords of gods have been described in sequence, by whom Rāviṇī vibrates forth.
Then, fifty [deities] were indeed spoken of as being heart-born and free from division.

Now, those situated in the wheel of passion (rāgacakra), then in that which is known as the wheel of necessity (niyatikālacakra) called the sixteenfold, and in the radiant wheel of the family (kulacakra).
When the Māyācakra and the Puṃścakra have indeed been transcended by means of the three abodes,
then that energy (kalā) which eternally flashes forth at the end of the abode of the six cakras—
then those goddesses, the deities of the sixteen families, manifest clearly.

In this regard, O Sovereign of the Gods, the Lord of Heroes bestows through the application of the practice of others' conduct and through the continuous connection with existence that which is difficult to attain:
the perfect discernment proclaimed within each successive stage of reality (tattva).
O Maheśvarī, that vibration is declared to belong to Karaṅkiṇī;
herein no multiplicity exists, whether through difference or through the differentiation of bodies.
Thus, the form residing in the six [cakras] and so forth has been briefly proclaimed.
Trembling with the form of the waves of the great wind-wheel of birth,
she who possesses bracelets (karaṅkiṇī) vibrates within the breath in four ways: again in the carrier of Citrabhānu (fire), and again in that which consists of both Soma (moon) and Sūrya (sun).
Then the Kula of the Mistress of the Four Wheels (Catuścakreśvarī) becomes manifest;
within one [wheel], the network of twenty-eight Kulas has become manifest,
while in the other, the great hundred of sixteen digits (kalās) has emerged.
Beyond that, in another [center], twelve [channels] are recorded as ten streams;
thus is the manifestation of the Kālakula proclaimed from that very source. Those four, which are of terrible form, bestow the fruits of their respective siddhis.
O best of practitioners, through the yoga of the great friction, all [the goddesses] are present for you in this way;
thus, sixty [pores] are declared as your vital points (marmas) at the moment of the deer.
O Mistress of the Wheel, you are joined with the movements of the left and the right.
O Queen of the Gods, when she vibrates there in five ways,
then she becomes manifest and yet more manifest as the agent of creation and dissolution.
Karaṅkiṇī, the most terrible, is currently the mistress of the South;
she is withered, the seat of the Siddhas, red, and the supreme, great Lord of Rays.
Therein arises Kālanātha over this world of the moving and the unmoving.
To the left is Vīreśvareśāna, along with Jayā and Vijayā;
Aparājitā and Jayantī—these are remembered as the pentad.
Here, the goddess Siddhivatī is proclaimed as the Supreme Sovereign (Parameśvarī).
Kālī, the power of withdrawal, is manifested from the eastern wheel.
Thus, in these two movements, Kālī effects both creation and withdrawal;
for by the persistence of the mass of her radiance, the attainment of that [state] is indeed manifest.
Each and every accomplishment shall arise for the great-souled practitioner.
Thus, O Bhairavī, the sixty-two cakras have been described to you.
Now, [I shall speak] regarding the three eye-cakras through their central rotation.
Then that Karankeśī, throbbing with great manifest power,
was fully capable of destroying the entire multitude of forms of the terrible Karankiṇīs throughout the world through the application of paralyzing and immobilizing spells.
To be contemplated as having the form of a hollow interior, radiant with creation and withdrawal, likewise, in the midst of the foremost practitioners, by way of the path arising from the center;
having become situated in the very middle of the middle, that which stands in the center unfolds intensely.

Thus, the sixty-five other families have been fully described to you. Now, when those two syllables that are uttered by both hands and those two that are at the end of the feet are likewise placed within the six [positions], [it is the next family].
Then the goddesses, manifest and praised, were intensely formidable with the weight of their sounds; they proceeded through the application of *lāsa* by means of the practice of *varttanā*.
Through the practice of the Ugrānana [mantra], that manifestation shall appear to the practitioner;
the complete power of summoning from afar and the ability to travel on foot are accomplished.
The seventy-one vital points (marmans) are [to be known] according to their true nature.
Then, when that goddess Rāviṇī, who makes the worlds resound, vibrated as the unfolding of the sequence of the five great elements (mahābhūtas),
then the five [elements] became manifest within the terrible substrates.
The most terrible Karaṅkiṇīs reside in their respective supports—
located in the half-moon of the fourth state, the śṛṅgāṭa, the hexagon, and the voids of the breath. There,
through the yoga of immersion in the dhāraṇā that contracts the bases and other centers, [one attains realization].
She becomes manifest to the practitioner, bestowing the accomplishment of each respective means of attainment.
O Goddess, these seventy-six vital points (*marmans*) of yours have been revealed;
they reside within the wheel of Sādāśiva, which consists of three aspects.
The Supreme Goddess flashes forth in the forms of will, knowledge, and action;
she is likewise of great power within the circle of Śiva and Bhairava.
When the goddess Saṃrāviṇī appears in her terrible form, bearing a hand-drum.
Then, O beloved, five radiant rays flash forth,
by which this entire universe is pervaded through their own luminous manifestation.
Thus, the five great vital points (*mahāmarmas*) of yours have been correctly proclaimed.
In this one place, eighty-one forms of terrible aspect have been revealed;
she who is the radiant Bhairavī within the abode of Śiva-Bhairava is indeed one,
yet she is proclaimed as many according to the diversity of her functions.
Her form is terrifyingly radiant with a flood of thousands of blazing rays;
that goddess Śivābhairavī shines resplendent in the abode of Kula. By her, the mass of rays and the mass of light are gradually pervaded.
Having concentrated upon each individual morsel through the yoga of the sequence of the three morsels,
[one experiences] that which instantly flashes forth as the essence, beautiful with supreme bliss.
The Mandara mountain of the intense, shimmering, and surging light and bliss [of consciousness],
which produces the multitude of waves of the expansion of omniscience and other [perfections]; [it is] filled with bliss, while all others are but the labor of churning for a mere moment.

Manifesting the terrifying majesty of his expanding power, he is formidable in destroying the intense splendor of the solar race; he is the one who uncoils and rends the crushing weight of the serpent of worldly enjoyment.
Having resorted to that *kulākula* which is pervaded by the reality of the beloved through its state of being thoroughly permeated, she who is the *yāvatkaraṅkiṇī* abides in the supreme station. She,
possessing a beautiful garland of the circle of Rāvaṇīs, uttered a hymn of praise with the joy of blossoming [realization].
She is the family of individual rays (*vyaktiraśmikula*), the shattering of dense delusion and ignorance;
she possesses eighty-one hands, is radiant, and has a distorted face.
She overcomes the host of the very dull-witted and causes the multitude of obstacles to be diminished.
The wise ones, through the Kulakaula, perceive the Great Kāla of the gods as throbbing with the expansion of the undertaking to swallow the entire universe; it is the very marrow,
a circle of terrifying depths arising from the emerging state of being.
The wheels revolve within the interior of the sky of consciousness.
This unmanifest Kula, known as Kālikā, is intensely powerful;
therein, through the differentiation of expanding states of being, there is the expansion of bliss.
They manifest with various forms through their many clearly distinct divisions;
situated within the lotus of the physical body, they are beyond the flickering of the three aggregates.
They are entirely liberated from all bolts [of worldly obstruction], existing in a state free from impediments.
When she pervades and intensely devours the entire world, both the stationary and the moving,
with her waves of power surging through the abundance of her playful and graceful manifestations,
then there is never any end to her within the corner of her power.
In every assembly of wheels, she alone shines forth;
O beloved, I do not see anything whatsoever that is devoid of her.
Herein, the manifestation of the mantra-family has been revealed within the six rays;
it is clearly veiled by secret [teachings], hidden everywhere else.
This infinite variety of the divisions of accomplishment is accompanied by its secrets.
In brief, listen now to the entirety of what is to be said hereafter.
This secret doctrine, which has been obtained in its fullness from the cavity of the mouth of Īśāna, has been declared;
I shall now tell you all the excellent *kalpas* of the Heart in their entirety.
The primary source for the accomplishment of all qualities without exception.

Thus ends the chapter on the description of its essential nature within the Rāviṇīcakra, in the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the Śiraścheda in the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairava stream.

Having heard this, the Goddess of gods, whose lotus-like face was [turned] toward Hara, laughed at those words with her radiant splendor flashing forth, her body bristling with horripilation. She spoke perfectly:
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Lord, I am satisfied, I am satisfied with the nectar of supreme knowledge.
There is nothing further for me to attain here, O Bhairava, O Bhairava.
Nevertheless, O Hara, I wish to hear that which was spoken by you to me."

"Tell me, in brief, the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) for all the heart-mantras (*hṛdaya*), together with their secrets, clearly and according to their true meaning. Having heard this, the Blessed One, whose moment is like a blossomed flower, [spoke].
All the vital points and secrets in their entirety, according to the truth.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O fortunate one; I shall explain properly that which has come at the right time.
The ritual manuals of the Marmeśvarīs have been briefly stated previously.
Now listen, I shall speak of Kālikā, who causes the paralysis of debate.
Karaṅkiṇī, of terrible form, Ghoreśī, of fearsome body—
having gone to the abode of Hara as before, she shall deliver the Goddess of the gods.
Thus has the worship of Saṃdā, which causes enmity, been described by me to you.
Thus, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, one should extract the Lord of Mantras in this sequence;
having extracted what remains after the *muśala*, in reverse order, O Maheśvarī,
it is encased by the Great Wrath (*mahākrodha*) and endowed with *māyā* and the *bindu*.
This supreme and formidable *piṇḍa* causes the destruction of the three worlds.
Once it has been completely fulfilled, one should bestow the sequence once again.
Make the lower fang (*daṃṣṭrā*) the first of all, conjoined with the three dots (*tribindu*).
One should again extract the skull that has grown for five kalpas;
one should worship it after removing the portion below the fangs.
Make its mouth like a well, ascended with wrath, and endowed with both creation and destruction.
O Goddess, this seven-syllabled mantra is remembered as the performer of all vidyās.
It should always be employed for paralyzing debate and also for the subjugation of enemies.
One should meditate upon it as possessing the radiance of ten million times ten million suns of the end of time.
Reddish-black and extremely fierce, she is endowed with eight arms;
she holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, adorned with a hand-drum (ḍamaru);
her hand grasps a black cat, and she is auspiciously bearing a sword and a discus.
Her hands are busily occupied with a bell and a severed head; her hair stands erect and she is terrifying.
Her limbs are entwined with garlands of skulls, and she is adorned with a girdle of serpents.
She is mounted upon the back of Kṛtānta (the Ender) and is a voracious devourer who swallows all things.

One should meditate upon the Sole Heroine (Ekavīrā), who possesses four arms, eyes of lightning, and a splendor like the destruction at the end of a kalpa; she has a great roar, a garland of skulls, and drinks copious blood. Afterwards, one should worship her as she resides within the maṇḍala.
Having drawn a hexagonal city adorned with red and black powders,
one should worship the Goddess situated in its center with all the offerings for heroes.

Having thus worshipped the Goddess of the Gods with divine offerings of liquor, meat, and fermented spirits, with various kinds of food, with various musical instruments and songs, and with beautiful flowers accompanied by incense, one should thereafter commence the fire sacrifice (homa).
Having prepared a large fish or meat from a wild animal, seasoned with salt and well-composed,
and having thus summoned [the deity], one should thereafter begin the ritual practice.
Having reached a mountain peak, one should recite the mantra as many times as there are syllables in it.
O highly fortunate lady, one should then perform the previously mentioned oblation one hundred thousand times.
From that oblation, a most beautiful chariot indeed comes to him;
rising from the midst of the fire, it is equipped with wheels and adorned with gold.
Crowded with throngs of apsarases, honored by various wonders,
resounding with the loud music of diverse songs, and endowed with all auspicious marks—
having mounted that vehicle which is difficult to attain, one goes to whatever world one desires.
Having fulfilled all desires, one shall attain liberation in the end. Furthermore, by reciting [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, the middling body is attained;
for the high-souled practitioner, middling accomplishment arises.
Then, O Goddess of the gods, one will effortlessly accomplish the union of the netherworld and the sky with ten thousand [recitations]; thereafter, one will accomplish the common [siddhis].
I shall explain them all—listen, O you who are honored by the lords of heroes!
One should visualize the tip of the tongue as being drawn toward the palate.
O Goddess of gods, the Mahāghorā [form] described in the previous meditation— by her,
O Queen of gods, even the Lord of Speech himself experiences a complete paralysis of speech.
Alternatively, O Maheśvarī, one should cast a black cat, blazing and licking its lips, into the mouth of the person to be acted upon;
one should visualize it tearing out the tongue and pressing it against the throat.
The eyes of one who has committed a terrible deed should be visualized as being torn out by a cat;
one should then recite the fierce seven-syllable mantra of Bhrukuṭīmukhā.

Meditation and mantras undoubtedly arrest the flow of speech toward its cessation. O fortunate one, taking an unbaked earthen bowl, one should write the name of the person to be influenced with yellow substances mixed with thorns.
O fair-eyed one, fill it with fragments of bone;
having fashioned it according to the mantra, it should be encircled by the syllable *ṭha*.
Thus it shall be filled with excrement; having covered the center, one should conceal it.
And then, by the power of the King of Yantras, one steals away speech;
likewise, all the various accomplishments (*siddhis*) are achieved through the power of the King of Yantras.
In this way, one may accomplish all the common accomplishments as well.

The mantra practitioner may effortlessly accomplish subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, killing, expulsion, and so forth; such is my infallible word. (Thus ends the section) in the Bhairava-śrotas, the Vidyāpīṭha, the Śiraścheda, the Jayadrathayāmala Mahātantra, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the fourth Ṣaṭka.
In the Rāviṇīcakra is the chapter on Vidveśakālī.
Now listen to the description of the single-syllabled, most terrible Kālī Karaṅkiṇī,
the fierce one who accomplishes all rites and bestows the siddhi of Hara’s huṃkāra.
Having reached a solitary place that is well-constructed and delightful,
the Supreme Goddess should draw forth the fierce [mantra] consisting of a single ocean.
It is void, void, and likewise terrible, adorned with the bindu and nāda.
This supreme mantra is formidable, wrathful in form, and possessed of great power;
it is the renowned solitary hero, the most excellent designator of the Goddess.
Radiating from the six-cornered wheel, this is the vital point of great strength.
(95a) Here one should meditate upon Mahākāla, who is the sole voracious devourer of the world,
whose roar is like that of the ocean agitated by the turbulence of the great dissolution.
Her face was illuminated by the radiance of her eyes, which flashed like a million lightning bolts;
she drank the wine of the world with the flickering movements of her dancing eyebrows;
and the fire from the clashing of her teeth, flashing like thousands of meteors, blazed forth.
She possesses the auspicious play of the crow, the cuckoo, the fire of time, and the dark goddess Kālikā; she is formidable and terrifying due to her swallowing of the entire circle of mantras;
she is adorned with all the wheels as ornaments and graced by her arms and eyes.

One should meditate upon her as Viśvarūpā, Vimukhī, Kālāgni, Āstuta, and Bhāsurā; having thus visualized her, one should worship within the hexagonal mandala with various offerings of food and diverse meats, liquors, and so forth.
One should worship all [the deities] with various flowers and great incenses.
One should offer human flesh and the like, or even that which grows on the earth (vegetables) or that of a sheep;
having offered that here while it is still three-fold unrefined (tryakta), one should thereafter begin the sādhana.
O Goddess, O Sovereign of all sovereigns, having gone to the best of mountains, one should perform ten million recitations (*koṭijāpa*) of the Goddess who is devoid of feet and head;
while performing this recitation, the entire universe, with its moving and unmoving beings, shall tremble.
O Goddess worshipped by the best of gods, as soon as one recites [the mantra] up to fifty million times,
the entire reality of the Vidyā-tattva trembles; indeed,
all those [beings] are always terrified before the lord of practitioners.
O illustrious one, they bow down and praise [her] again and again; O fortunate one,
by ten million recitations, indeed until the end of Śiva,
the earth trembles, quivers, and whirls.
Then, as many principles (tattvas) as there may be,
the yogi who has conquered them all enjoys them, pervading everything, just like Paramabhairava.
This supreme accomplishment has indeed been declared to you according to its true nature:
traveling through the netherworld and the sky, the extraction of the six flavors, as well as the subjugation of yakṣas and bhūtas, invisibility, and elixirs.
The successful accomplishment of the Great Assembly has been explained to you according to its true meaning;
likewise, the travel through the netherworld and the sky, as well as the extraction of the six flavors,
and walking on foot, O Maheśvarī.
From that, one accomplishes the Kṣatriya lineage; there is no doubt because of that.
One should accomplish all such things and indeed everything else.
O Goddess, through the common accomplishment, one accomplishes [all this] by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
For him, [there are] the rites of attraction, inciting enmity, killing, and expulsion;
likewise, the raising of a *vetāla* using a wick made of *prasena* and mustard seeds; the accomplishment of a *yakṣiṇī*, and other means for accomplishing a great servant (*mahākiṃkara*).
