O Goddess, one may accomplish all the magical nets (indrajāla) previously mentioned; one may effortlessly achieve paralyzing, stunning, confining, and the wondrous suppression of clouds— whatever one desires in the mind.
For this goddess of gods has been revealed as the performer of all rites.

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the Performer of All Rites (*sarvakarmakarī*) within the *Rāviṇīcakra*, in the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, a great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraścheda* division of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the stream of Bhairava (*bhairavaśrotasi*).
Śrī Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the terrible [mantra] that destroys enemies—
the Great Goddess Mahāghoratarākālī, who resides in the throat.

O Bhairavī, I shall now proclaim the ritual manual (kalpa) of her who slays the three worlds by mere name; listen with a one-pointed mind. Having gone to the abode of Hara at night, one should extract the Great Vidyā.
Having made the earth rubbed with human skeletons, like the ascetic Suvīra,
his consciousness is intoxicated with the bliss of wine, and all his limbs are adorned [with ornaments].
One should extract the Mistress of the Heroic Wheel (Vīracakreśī), situated in fire and struck by a goad,
a mass (piṇḍa) pervaded by the Bindu and Nāda that devours the three worlds.
Thereafter, one should extract Mataṅga, adorned with Indra and a goad.

Furthermore, here one must extract the first of this [syllable], the Lord of the Family (Kuleśvara); the first of the fifth [group], the sign of the abode, intense at its head like a *śṛṅgāṭa* (water-chestnut),
the skull-cup (*kharpara*) established in fire, blazing with the creation of Viṣṇu.
Then, four syllables should be added, obstructed by the *bhīma-śaṅku*.
This supreme eight-syllable Vidyā, extracted as the Supreme Goddess,
can destroy all the worlds, including gods, asuras, and humans.
O fortunate one, though she is merely a name, she is a vast and formidable pit of impurity;
I meditate upon her as resembling a crow from the time of the frost and a cuckoo.
She possesses the brilliance of ten thousand suns and the blazing fire of the end of the eon.
Her body was adorned with the hissing of the fruit of the lord of serpents;
her eyes were like whirlpools, bubbles, and waves of foam upon the flowing waters;
and she terrified the lords of the gods with her incessant and formidable *huṃ* sounds.
She shattered the pavilion of the universe with the violent blow of her soles;
she whirled the surface of the sky with the revolutions of her many terrifying arms;
and she was resplendent with eyes and ears that vomited the terrible fire of the end of the aeon.
One should meditate upon Saṃhārabhairavī— who is mounted on the shoulders of a donkey and a corpse, whose activity is like that of a bear, and who has the form of a sword—
by means of the sequence of the wheel of meditation, she who performs every ritual action without exception.
Within the triangular maṇḍala, one should worship the Supreme Goddess after making the ground intensely heated by means of red and black offerings. (96b)
Having worshipped the Supreme Goddess, the man should offer oblations;
thereafter, he should perform the ritual actions and recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
He should present as an offering to the Goddess one who is of evil conduct and wicked soul.
One should always contemplate [the victim] as having been offered [as a sacrifice], pierced by the trident, and devoured.
O Goddess, within seven days he dies, even if he were Indra himself;
or else, one should contemplate the target as a black corpse among the bodies of the dead.
One should contemplate the goddess as vomiting terrible blood that flows from her nine openings,
her radiant form resembling a flash of lightning;
having thus visualized her, one should reduce even the three worlds to ashes and destroy them.
Within seven days there is no doubt; how much more so for a mere mortal!

Furthermore, by means of the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) yoga, when the object of accomplishment is encased within it, one should constantly recite as if performing the *kumbhaka* breath-retention; thus one may slay even the lords of the gods.
Alternatively, a wise person should have an image fashioned by employing a skilled artisan;
having collected eight *māṣas* of white lead and having made it solid with thorns,
one should have a firm image produced.
Having written the name of the target person on a slip of paper with blood mixed with poison and beeswax,
and having encircled it on both sides with the Vidyā, O Supreme Goddess,
one should place this in the heart and set it down face-down.
Having indeed driven a stake made of human bone into the center of the funeral pyre,
one should pierce it with that stake and then cause the cremation to be performed.
Having struck the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
When this is done, a great burning and terror will be produced therein.
Within seven days, the image is swiftly killed by the fire;
that which cannot be reversed is proclaimed as "killing" (māraṇa).
Whichever name of a curable disease one should lick,
that very disease it produces; this is certain, there is no doubt in this matter.
By that very means one should slay the target; no deliberation is required here.
Alternatively, having worshipped the Supreme Goddess in a hero’s abode with red and black offerings, and having heated the earth itself, [one should proceed].
Thereafter, he should inform the Goddess: "O Goddess, this animal has been offered by me to you. Give me the *nirmālya* (the remains of the offering), so that I may have it slaughtered.
Having been addressed thus, she should then take back everything, including the *sarvaga-caru*.
One should say, "Eat, eat! Go, O friend, to the temple;
bring it with a pure mind to that temple of the Sage.
Having prepared the vehicle of strength by means of the application of the three pungents (kaṭutraya).
One should honor [the deity] here by collecting the great remains of offerings; of this there is no doubt.
Then, O Goddess, when the one to be accomplished is Purandara, ending in the vowel 'e', thus has the rite of killing been explained to you according to the truth.
Indeed, through the application of recitation (japa), the practitioner of mantras may accomplish various other rites:
subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, delusion, and likewise paralysis;
by the power of the Great Vidyā, he may achieve these with ease.
By reciting one hundred thousand syllables according to the previously mentioned method, he shall accomplish the siddhis;
of this there is no doubt, for the Supreme Goddess accomplishes them with ease.
Thus has the Karankaghoravikrama been fully described to you.
This "Throat-Womb" (*galāgarbhā*) is preeminent; it bestows the qualities of perfection.

Thus ends the "Ritual of the Throat-Womb" within the Rāviṇīcakra, in the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraścheda* division of the Vidyāpīṭha in the Bhairava current.
Śrī Bhairava said:
(97b) Now I shall fully describe Kālī, whose prowess is terrible.
Just as Brahmā may cause Keśava or even Hara to be expelled,
hear now, O beloved, the incomparable rite for that [expulsion] in brief:
having gone to the abode of Hara, one should there recite the Karaṅkiṇī [mantra].
Having worshipped the Mātṛkā, the Mother of Mantras, with the services due to a hero,
one should extract the world-delusion and then again extract that which is preceded by *tri*.
One should likewise extract the horse (*aśva*) and the vital point (*marma*) together in one place, and then extract the abode of fire (*vahnidhāma*).
Having again extracted the three [syllables] preceded by *tri*, one should take its clarified butter (*ājya*) fallen from the mark;
this is conjoined with the fire-syllable (*vahni*), the *praṇava*, and the primordial nectar (*amṛta*).
Then there is the horse (*aśva*) with the three vowels on its head, and likewise Vāyu and Agni joined together as one.
This mantra, joined with the *vidvaṃkuśa* and awakened by *bhīmaśaṃkuni*, is declared to be terrifying even to Karaṅkiṇī;
it effects the expulsion of the entire universe.
One should worship this Kuleśvarī, mounted upon the great wind-wheel,
holding a banner in her hand, smoke-colored, devouring ten thousand suns,
garlanded by the entire host of deities, the Mistress of the World.
I bow to Kulabhairavī, who resounds with a torrent of terrible *bhāṃkāra* cries,
who is endowed with eight arms and adorned with severed heads and *khaṭvāṅgas*,
who is intent upon the great *śaṭaka* weapon, and who is formidable, holding a noose and a goad.
Having meditated upon her with emaciated limbs, a terrifying face, three eyes, and a frowning countenance;
with torches for eyes, exceedingly fierce, riding upon the shoulders of the Wind-god,
and satiated by the consumption of the world— she should be worshipped correctly.

Having worshipped in this manner with red and black offerings, such as liquor, meat, and fermented spirits, one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) for the gratification of the Goddess. [The oblation] should consist of human flesh, or that produced from *ulmaga* and *mathana*, or the well-prepared flesh of goats and horses.
After offering the oblation with clarified butter three times, she who eats at the proper time should then proceed to a beautiful,
excellent mountain provided with kindled wood and water. (98a)
There, one should properly accomplish the infinite Bhairavāraṇī.
One should mutter the mantra of the Goddess three hundred thousand times and perform the oblation as previously enjoined.
Then, she shall bring about middling accomplishment for the practitioner's self.
By means of three hundred thousand recitations, one should always accomplish the supreme [attainment];
he is the foremost of practitioners who achieve siddhi—of this there is no doubt. By means of ten thousand recitations, the practitioner should accomplish ordinary rites.
And I shall explain that correctly, O beloved, in brief:
having meditated upon the object to be accomplished as situated upon the wheel of wind, one should recite the vidyā;
by enclosing the name of the object to be accomplished within it, one will cause them to be uprooted in three days.

One should enter directly into the lord of mountains; what need is there to mention this among mere humans? Alternatively, taking a very beautiful piece of birch bark that is free of holes, one should write the name mixed with poison, charcoal, and blood.
O lady of beautiful hips, the name of the one to be accomplished should be interwoven with the mantra. Then, having filled it with husks and charcoal, one should wrap it with hair.
O beloved, [this should be done] on a terrifying tree hanging down in the northwest direction of the sky.
In this way, O Goddess, the practitioner may expel even the immortals from their place by the mere application of recitation; he expels the entire lineage of the Ṛṣis without a doubt—
of this there is no uncertainty.
Through subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, killing, paralyzing, and deluding,
as well as through immobilization and causing hatred, one may intensely and effortlessly accomplish these [rites].
Thus has this mighty Vāyukālī been fully described.

Thus, in the *Bhairavaśrotas*, in the *Vidyāpīṭha*, in the *Śiraścheda* of the *Jayadrathayāmala Mahātantra*, in the twenty-four-thousand-verse [work], in the fourth hexad, in the *Rāviṇīcakra*, this is the *Kālipaṭala*: the Rite of Exorcism.
Now I shall further proclaim the great victory in battle,
which arises effortlessly through the Goddess for the sake of practitioners.
Having reached an auspicious place, strewn with heaps of flowers,
There, one should worship Maṃtreśī with all the offerings for heroes.
Then, one should extract the Vidyā, which displays many wonders;
having extracted Gajendra as the sixth, he is seated upon the throne of Kṛtānta.
Again, one should place it in the fire [the letter *ra*] and adorn it with the bindu of Viṣṇu [the letter *i*].
This is declared to be the *piṇḍa*, which is intent on deluding the world.
Having again extracted the double-tongued [the letter *ja*], the wind [the letter *ya*] should be properly applied.
Ending with the trident (triśūla), situated on the cutter (karttana), marked with three dots (tribindvanka), and consisting of nectar (sudhāmaka);
then the double-tongued (dvijihva) preceded by a dot (bindvādya), restrained by the formidable spike (bhīmaśaṅku)—
this is declared to be the seven-syllable mantra that carries one across great battles.
One should worship her as she resides within the sword with all the offerings for heroes,
using divine offerings of wine, meat, and liquor in manifold ways.
One should meditate upon her as possessing the brilliance of ten million times ten thousand millions of fires at the end of an aeon.
She possesses the roar of the great dissolution and dries up even the ocean of weapons;
she has the thundering sound of an agitated sea, is exceedingly emaciated, and possesses terrifying prowess.
She has fangs, hair standing on end, and wears a garland of severed heads.
One should meditate upon her who delights in terrifying the three worlds, who causes the destruction of the faction of enemies,
and who is seated upon a lion-throne, shining with a crescent moon;
one should remember her as possessing a universal form, pervading the universe, and appearing according to [the needs of] beings.
Having thus first performed the sacrifice, one should afterwards accomplish the rite for Śivā.
Having ascended the peak of the Lord of Mountains, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred thousand times with a concentrated mind.
O lady of excellent hips, after that, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the number of syllables.
In the middle, within the cavity of fire, the human lungs are three-fold;
having gathered ten thousand [breaths], the Supreme Goddess is perceived.
Having seen her, who has emerged from the midst of fire and possesses a gentle form and jingling bracelets,
the preeminent practitioner should offer his own blood as an *arghya* oblation;
by piercing through her left side, she then becomes exceedingly pleased.
And she grants whatever boon is desired to that practitioner;
[she leads him] to the place for bringing the True One (Sadāvāhana), where the Goddess herself resides.
Alternatively, through the heat of yoga, he shall obtain victory in battle.
Having worshipped according to the previously mentioned procedure, the hero among warriors should then advance for battle. Maintaining silence, he should then employ the Vidyā itself;
he should bring the entire enemy army as an offering.
Then the army perishes if [the enemy] has personally performed a sacrifice, provided that one sprinkles with water all the conchs, kettledrums, excellent banners, elephants, horses,
infantry, armor, and all weapons.
One should sprinkle the Goddess of the lords of gods; indeed, they then become invincible.
They will overcome, dwell upon, and conquer the enemy host.
Alternatively, having fashioned a vessel made of bell-metal, one should engrave [the mantra] upon it.

Having worshipped the Goddess of gods, Karaṅkiṇī, who is endowed with her former form, according to the previously mentioned rite, perform it one thousand times. The eminent practitioner should then bring her forth, strike her, and recite the mantra.
Upon hearing that terrible sound, which is tumultuous with elephants, horses, and chariots,
the army will suddenly flee like a dense cloud driven by the wind;
it will be utterly destroyed and fall into delusion, without a doubt.
O Bhairavī, even if that which is protected is conquered with utter disregard— even if Śakra himself were to come in person— it would nevertheless perish.
Thus does the lord of practitioners completely conquer the entire battle.
Alternatively, one should properly fumigate the self consecrated with mantras.
Having first prepared another incense one hundred and eight times,
that which has risen upward should be held here in front of the deity worshipped by the gods.
Having inhaled its fragrance, the enemy soldiers perish;
that supreme hero surely triumphs through the power of the God and Goddess.
Thus has this Vidyā, which crosses over the battle, possessing terrible prowess, been correctly explained by me to you; it brings about all accomplishments and bestows excellent qualities.

Thus [ends] the fourth hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Bhairava-śrotas* (the stream of Bhairava), the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the section on the Severing of the Head (*śiraścheda*).
The chapter on the ritual procedure for Kālī in battle.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme and formidable Heart-mantra.
It is the essence that accomplishes all rites, difficult to attain by those who have not disciplined themselves;
merely by knowing it, one shall succeed in every ritual act. I shall now fully explain it; listen with a single-minded focus.
The Supreme Goddess Caṇḍeśī, consisting of seventeen syllables and the sole devourer who swallows the universe, having reached the abode of heroes,
shall uplift [the practitioner] as the sovereign of the complete wheel of mantras through the service of many heroes.
First one should extract *moha*, and immediately after that the *puruṣa*. One should again extract the *haṃsa* preceded by three [syllables] as it is traversed by *dāraṇā*.
One should extract the *aśva*, the *marman*, and the *vahniveśma* as they are formed into a single cluster (*piṇḍībhūta*).
One should extract the earring (Kuṇḍala) enclosed in fire (Vahni) and the fallen Moon (Candra).

Then, having again placed the pure Nectar (Amṛta) at the end of the trident (Śūla), one should apply the cutting (Kartana). One should then provide the arm (Bāhu) joined with the goad (Aṅkuśa), and further give the horse (Aśva) for the arm.
One should again give [the mantra] with a "well-mouth" (kūpavaktra) provided with three dots on its head;
or, having encased it with fire (vahni), it is endowed with the Great Creation (mahāsṛṣṭi).
Then there is the Wind (vāyu) with the syllable Om (praṇava) upon its head, and Gaṇendra joined with the triangle (trikoṇa).
Having raised the arm ending in the syllable *va* (the seat of Varuṇa), marked with a dot and the triad [of lines],
and holding a bow together with an arrow, encased within the cavity of great radiance.
The supreme *piṇḍa* mantra, endowed with the *bindu* and resembling ten thousand suns,
is the highest knowledge that brings an end to Time (Death).
Merely by its utterance, [the sins] accumulated over tens of thousands of millions of births are destroyed.
Sin is reduced to ashes, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Even after destroying the entire universe, one who is filled with the knowledge of Brahman is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
O Bhairavī,
I am not able to describe his power or his manifestation even in ten thousand years, nor with tens of millions of mouths;
nevertheless, listen as I shall speak something by way of a brief summary.
One should worship this goddess of terrible form, who holds a hand-bell, in the House of Heroes (vīragṛha),
within a six-spoked wheel provided with red and black powders,
having four equal doors, bright, and adorned with musk.
One should install the Goddess in the center according to one's available means:
she who has slender limbs and a terrible countenance, whose face is fashioned from a great corpse,
and who is as terrifying as the roaring clouds at the end of an aeon.
She is endowed with five faces and is terrifying with eighteen arms;
she is adorned with a noose, a goad, a great severed head, and a heart;
her hands hold a khaṭvāṅga, a vessel, a ḍamaru drum, and a banner, and she is formidable.
Her mouth filled with human entrails, emaciated yet radiant of countenance,
possessing the hue of a crow or a kokila bird, brilliantly adorned with a garland of human intestines—
the Supreme Goddess, who is saluted by the lords of gods and asuras, as well as by the siddhas.
Having thus meditated upon Mahākālī, one should thereafter begin the sacrifice. One should worship with divine liquor, meat, and spirits according to one's means.
Having worshipped in this manner, one should offer human flesh combined with the three [substances].
Having thus satisfied the Goddess of the Gods, one should thereafter begin the ritual practice (*sādhana*).
Having gone to a beautiful, excellent mountain provided with sacrificial fuel and wood, [one should proceed].
There, one should recite the mantra ten million times and then perform ten thousand oblations.
Then, having offered human flesh as an equal portion, Bhairavī is accomplished;
she grants her vision to that great-souled practitioner.
It bestows supreme, incomparable perfection upon the practitioner.
Through the application of three hundred thousand recitations, whatever perfections belong to the middle and intermediate levels are attained by him; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
All common accomplishments (*siddhi*) are achieved by one who has performed ten thousand recitations (*jāpa*).
Whatever accomplishments are proclaimed therein—
whether superior, middling, or intermediate— one shall accomplish them with ease.
By this very knowledge, the practitioner shall succeed; there is no doubt in this matter. Whatever rite may please him, that he will accomplish.
This Goddess is the performer of all rites, intent upon the protection of the three worlds.
This great vidyā, Karaṅkiṇī, is everywhere unimpeded.
I do not see anything equal to her within the entire treasury of mantras.
Thus has Kālī, the bestower of all success, been fully described to you.

Thus ends the chapter on the seventeen-syllable Rāviṇīcakra in the fourth Ṣaṭka of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, a great tantra (*mahātantra*) consisting of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraścheda* within the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the *Bhairavaśrotas*.
The venerable Bhairava said:

Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme Mahākālī, known as Mohanā, who performs all rites and is intent on deluding the world. Having reached the abode of heroes, one should extract the Vidyā from there.

One should extract the letter *kāla* (ka) mounted upon *ādyāgni* (ra), marked by the dot (*bindu*) and the fire (*agni*) [the vowel *i*], which causes the destruction of fire; then one should again extract the letter *kāla* (ka) together with *pravahaṃsa* (ha). (101a) One should extract it alone.
One should again extract the Lord of Knots (Ga), marked with three dots (the nasal *m*), and the Lord of Tastes (Ra) alone;
then Gaṇeśa (La) grown upon Varuṇa (Va);
and finally, the Ear-ring (Ra) situated on Fire (Ra) with its head marked by a triangle (the vowel *e*).
Having extracted the moon from the living, this knowledge is delusive in nature;
consisting of seven and a half [syllables], it is incomprehensible and difficult to obtain throughout the three worlds.
O beautiful goddess, it deludes the entire universe.
The goddess is intensely red and radiant, or alternatively, like a parrot’s plumage;
she has two arms and one face,
holds a silken garment in her hand, is mounted upon a great corpse, and is a woman of enjoyment, passionately fond of sensual delights.
One should visualize Mohakālī as having a slender body and a terrifying face;
one should worship her seated upon a lotus, who is everywhere unimpeded and stainless.
She is the terrible bringer of great delusion, [to be propitiated] with wine, meat, fermented liquors, and so forth.
One should offer the human lungs with all the heroic offerings (*sarvavīropacāra*).
Having thus satisfied [the deity] according to the ritual procedure, one should thereafter begin the practice (*sādhana*).
Having gone to an excellent mountain peak that is well-known and renowned in the world...
Having ascended the peak there, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
At the conclusion of the recitation, O Goddess, one should perform a fire sacrifice with the ten ingredients, even if it is a full oblation.
From the midst of that fire, that Goddess of universal form and great majesty [emerges].
She who possesses all forms, who is omnipresent, and the bestower of boons—indeed, she alone arises.
By union with her alone does one attain identity; there is no doubt in this.
Or else, if the practitioner accomplishes it, he shall achieve mental perfection (*mānasī siddhi*).
Then, O Dear One, one shall accomplish all [goals] by reciting three hundred thousand times;
furthermore, one will accomplish ordinary rites by thirty thousand recitations,
such as subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, killing, and expulsion.
She would delude the entire universe through meditation alone; of this there is no doubt.
When properly remembered in the midst of enemies, she is endowed with the power of the mantra.
Then she bewilders the entire enemy host of great power. Whenever the goddess Kālikā, who possesses the prowess of a hero, is remembered,
at that very moment she bewilders this entire world.
Thus she is the cause of delusion, delusion itself, the deluder, adorned with delusion;
she is the nectar of delusion, the splendor of delusion, and enveloped by the essence of great delusion;
she is the sovereign of delusion, marked by the abode of delusion, and possesses the luster of the earrings of delusion.

O Goddess of the gods, out of affection for you, this [teaching] which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation has been explained today according to its true meaning. What else shall I tell you?
Thus ends [the section] in the *Bhairavaśrotas*, within the *Vidyāpīṭha*, in the *Śiraścheda* of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, in the fourth Ṣaṭka.
The Chapter on the Ritual for Delusion.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Now, O Goddess, I shall explain to you according to the truth.
The deception of Time (Kālavañcana) is indeed the foremost means for accomplishing the great siddhis.
Listen, O Maheśvarī, to that Kālī who resides therein. O fortunate one, listen as I describe her, who is anointed with sandalwood and agallochum.
In that place strewn with heaps of flowers, one should extract the Vidyā-mantra:
[the syllable] Bindu (Oṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), situated above the great abode of Mahākāla;
then [the syllable] Kāla (Ka) endowed with all opulence, joined with the arm and the goad.
One should extract the letter situated in the fifth musical note (Ni), preceded by the Yoni (I) and joined with the triangle (E);
then that which is situated in Varuṇa (Va), its end (the Visarga), and the arm (Bha) marked with three signs (the Bindu).
Preceded by the Yoni (I), there shall be the goad (U); one should extract the Veda (Ra) alone.
One should give the *vāruṇa* [syllable] alone, and then extract that which ends with *bhairava*.
O Goddess, the third [syllable] situated at the beginning, marked by three dots (*bindu*) and two *aṅkas*, is the negator.
Joined with the wife of *tejas* and *indu*, this is the Vidyā that destroys Time (*kāla*).
(102a) This terrible [mantra] of fifteen syllables destroys the suffering of the world;
it should be known as the remover of great death, pure as a white jasmine flower or the moon.
Seated upon a white lotus throne, resembling the orb of the moon;
wearing a crest-jewel made of the white moon, her body composed of waves of nectar;
the goddess with long, dangling locks, she who certainly devours Time.
Who here can conquer even the Great Death as easily as play? Now,
when that Supreme Goddess, the state of Kālī’s feet, is meditated upon,
then the lord of practitioners will be liberated from the fear of death.
Then one should recite the Vidya that destroys Time with strict discipline;
then, in just six months, a person deceives Time.
Or else, O slender-waisted one, by reciting it one hundred thousand times with a razor [as the counting tool], [the same result is achieved].
The practitioner here shall undoubtedly become the very embodiment of the Goddess;
he into whose ears this Goddess enters shall live for a hundred autumns.
She is peaceful, nourishing, gentle, and the bestower of success in auspiciousness and good fortune.
Thus has been fully explained to you the Goddess who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
who performs all rites, and who is filled with many supernatural powers (*siddhi*s).
Thus [ends] the fourth hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraścheda* section of the *Bhairavaśrotasi-vidyāpīṭha*.
The Chapter on the Ritual of Amareśvarī.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the wheel that bestows the perfection of the melāpa.
The goddess of gods, most fierce, who bestows many wonderful accomplishments—
by the mere knowledge of whom unsurpassed sovereignty proceeds even after a long time; she is proclaimed to be sevenfold.
I shall describe to you in its entirety her incomparable ritual procedure:
Araṃbhikā, Karṇinī, Lakṣmī, Viśvalakṣmī, and Śivāraṇī.
The Mother of the Gaṇas, who sustains the three abodes, the self of all, and the burden of all souls;
she who is the mass of the three *piṇḍas*, who crushes the various outbursts at the end of karma;
she who is without support, the moonlight of the earth and sky, the Sovereign Goddess of Beauty.

The formidable cave of Śiva’s belly is Kālī, the destroyer of [limited] knowledge; she is the swan sporting gracefully in the sky of radiant consciousness, longing for the swan [of the soul]. She travels the path to the end of the five voids, having transcended the abode of the kalās.
Sarvagrāsā is the mistress of the earrings, formidable with five throbbing hoods;
her body is variegated with great jewels, she is radiant, the devourer of Time,
and she has struck down the host of Vidyādharas with a sound like a flashing lightning bolt.
She whose form is a sword with a cruel, sharp edge that cuts fiercely;
she is Khaṇḍacakreśvarī, the Edge who devours those who have transgressed the path;
she is intent on contraction, situated within, and consists of blood, entrails, and fat.
Delighting in the sixteen supports, she is the illuminator of the three Brahmās;
she is Vāgeśī, mounted upon Kula, Bhairavī with her full face.
She vibrates in the form of phonemes, pervading each of the cakras.
Fierce in her destruction of the eyes of the bears, she dwells in the midst of the circle of bears;
because she is intent upon that seat and glides to the end of Kālacakra,
she is then Ṛkṣakarṇeśī (Kālī), the bestower of fear unto Time.
Resembling a sleeping lord of serpents, she is most fierce and always known as a source of terror;
of her, I shall declare the method that is perfectly effective.
Having first smeared the earth with various fragrances— saffron, camphor, and sandalwood mixed with musk-water— one should [inscribe] the mantra worshipped by all the asuras and siddhas.
Having worshipped Varṇṇābalī above that, with her body divided [into parts], with incense, flowers, offerings, and drinks;
she should then extract [the mantra] arising from the lotus-face in its successive order.
Twice destroying the world— including gods and demons— desiring its destruction,
she is composed of six, five, two, and four syllables, and is wondrous.
Bestowing the fruits of heaven and liberation, bringing joy to the ears on earth—
having first placed another *tāra* (OM) enclosed in the middle of the syllable *saṃ*,
followed by *krū* joined with fire (*ra*), house (*ha*), fire (*ra*), and zero (*bindu*), then the eldest (*ja*) and the double-tongued (*kṣa*).
One should meditate upon the name of the Goddess, adorned with the letter *ī*, the fire (*ra*), and the *visarga*.
Then, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *svāhā* syllable together with the King of Weapons (*astra*) in reverse order.
Indeed, the wise say that this same arrangement of limbs, rays, and powers is both distributed and unified.
One of pure soul should employ only the *sāttvika* weapon for the pacification of obstacles.
Having obtained the permission of the Guru, one should perform the sacrifice in houses, on mountain peaks, at banyan trees,
on sacred seats (*pīṭha*), in temples dedicated to Kali, in the abodes of the Mothers, in deserted shrines, or at crossroads.
Having examined the ground according to the various methods prescribed and having had all obstacles removed by means of astrological calculations and other means,
one should then construct there a [stūpa] measuring one thousand cubits.
This is a silken garment of beautiful gait,
adorned with the dust of heroes— red, black, and white like smiles arising from the abode of Śiva— which is well-smeared and worthy of worship.
The placement (nyāsa) as described by the teachers should be performed with effort upon the body according to the rule and in the proper sequence. Thereafter,
one should invoke [the deity] within the center of the heart-lotus.
By means of one's own mind, through union with the Lord of the Immaculate Intellect,
having placed this [energy] within the center of the heart-piercing pain like the crest of a savior, as if with the sheaths of lotuses...

Having worshipped according to the ritual procedure the Heart, the Topknot, the Armor, and the Weapon-mantra in the four petals located in the southeast and the other [directions], one should worship the Eye-mantra in the center.
With appropriate and special colorful offerings,
one should likewise offer the portion for the oblation at midnight,
using sesame seeds, clarified butter, and the lungs and other organs of the sacrificial animal.
Likewise, on the third day, wise ones should perform a thorough worship in order to sever all obstacles.
One should meditate upon the Goddess Vidyā, who dwells in the sky, whose body is profound with its ornaments,
and who is comparable to a blue lotus, a bee, a serpent, and a lofty mountain peak;
she whose fierce head is crowned by a crest of flames blazing like the fire at the end of an aeon.
She whose tips of the sacrificial ladles were tossed by the winds from the abodes of the sky;
who beheld many worlds with the whirling circles of flames from her eyes;
whose tongue was lightning, who bore a digit of the moon, and whose fangs had tips as sharp as ten million points.
She whose nostrils are like the gills of a fish, whose eyes alone are ever-open for the world, and who possesses a beautiful face;
her entire body is adorned with excellent armlets and other ornaments of serpents;
she holds a full conch, a lotus, a vessel filled with nectar, a thunderbolt, a banner, and a goad.
With the moon and sun held in her hands, and elsewhere a noose and a ray of light;
holding a serpent constantly in her hand,
she stands upon the lofty summit of the highest peak of the most elevated mountain.
She has legs as white and smooth as long stone pillars;
her matted hair is like the blazing fire of the sacrificial altar; her feet are marked with the signs of the bull;
her teeth and palms are like cymbals; and she is terrifying with garlands of blood held in her restless hands.
With the garlands of stars tossed by the wind from the banners of her cloth fluttering at the edges of her skeleton-frame,
she— who dwells in the mountain caves of the gods— bears that exceedingly fierce form with her terrible *huṃ* sounds,
terrifying the sky-dwellers at the onset of the night of Śiva.
In fever caused by wind, she is equal to ten million suns;
in burning sensations, her entire body is filled with nectar.
For subjugation, she is red; for pacification, she is very white.
Even in rites such as *vuccāṭana* (expulsion),
the Great Goddess is inconceivable; she is drunk up by those seeking prosperity,
yet at the time of entering the city, she is merely the measuring-line for the layout.
(104a) The sixfold accomplishment of action, flowing upward from the path of the wheel of arms, is indeed sprinkled by a stream of nectar.
Therefore, one should contemplate the Self with one's whole being as if it were steady and long-enduring within;
through such meditation, all [impurities] then go to their destruction.
The two fluctuations of his consciousness, as restless as the wind,
swiftly attain an exceedingly powerful and perfectly pure speech, like the current of a mountain river.
Or rather, through the power of his perfect realization, he attains the state of omniscience;
she is the sovereign of all, consisting of Śiva, the supreme Mātrā.
He who has come from the void, moving through the sky,
standing in the firmament, established in the infinite and stainless Brahman;
he who moves toward that supreme state of consciousness which abides in the nectar of immortality.
Nourishing the world...
[omitted] ...devoid of form, consisting of sound, with a body of ever-new syllables;
[she whom] Brahmā and the others who partake of the nectar, as well as the hosts of the enemies of the gods (the Asuras), [worship].
Even those whose minds are perfectly purified say that she is not manifold;
though she possesses manifold manifestations, she is one, appearing as if divided in many ways like the crescent moon in various clear bodies of water.
[She] possesses the splendor of the celestial trees with their fruits radiant through the three paths;
she is indeed sought by those desiring liberation who seek an unobstructed path,
[and she is the goal] for those whose minds are fixed upon various vehicles.
It does not destroy cherished or distinguished entities;
for that which is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, distinct from all else, and empty, is indeed the auspicious ornament of itself.
This is indeed a sport regarding objects seen and unseen,
which becomes the means for the happiness of embodied beings;
such devotion as this is to be sought by the supreme seekers.
With various flowers, spirits, perfumes, and incenses;
with many kinds of meat produced from water or from the air, both unprepared and well-prepared.
One should worship the Goddess with an unwavering mind,
having restrained the heart from the web of conceptual constructions.
Having assumed the *badhvāsana*, the *svastika*, the *padmaka*, the *śṛgāṭaka*, or the *arddhanīśākara* posture,
the hero [sits] before the Goddess upon excellent seats.
With a hand marked by a bracelet of human skulls and a conch,
the Lord of Liberated Ones, possessing a portion of the moon, should mutter the mantra of the Goddess on the delightful sandy banks upon this earth.
At Kāliñjara or at the confluence of the Marvuda, likewise in the forest named Amaradāru,
on Śrīparvata, or upon the summit of the great Vindhya mountain;
Whether at Māṃmrātaka or at Prayāga,
in the abode of Caṇḍeśvara, at Gayā,
at the holy sites of Prabhāsa or Puṣkara—
Or in a great cremation ground adorned with bones, take up whatever place you prefer for the sake of serenity;
having performed worship here at the conclusion of the recitation, [proceed].
And in a sacrificial pit well-prepared with consecrations,
[he offered] meat born from human blood, sesame-filled oblations,
and indeed śapharī fish smeared with the nectar of the left.

One should indeed offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with effort, for the sake of fulfillment, using either *amṛta* or clarified butter (*ghṛta*) according to the portion prescribed by the wise; this is the present ritual of oblation (*homakarma*). Or, one may worship [the deity] in the abode of the six-petaled lotus.
Having mentally seated the host of goddesses in the center with various excellent offerings of fragrance, one should worship Maheśa as the desired deity;
however, Sureśvara, Balā, and the others are to be worshipped as subordinate to the Goddess.
Indeed, those goddesses whom I have correctly described here— by performing their individual rites of worship, recitation, and fire-oblation,
one obtains incomparable fruit according to one's wealth.
Therefore, they are to be worshipped according to this entire ritual procedure.
One should write their names at the end of the excellent rite,
surrounded by the syllable *phaṭ* and by others whose limbs are like poisonous blood.
Or else, like a fire in a cremation ground, it carries away the beloved woman who is possessed by a succession of misfortunes, even as far as the interior of a hollow tree.
This composition, which is the jewel of the world produced from the tree of birch bark,
is titled *Rocanā*;
it either protects a proud enemy or [protects] a lord of the earth.
When one brings even accomplished women under complete control,
then one should certainly draw [the diagram] with black mustard oil on birch bark or a peacock feather,
and bury it at a crossroads belonging to oneself.
This supreme rite for inciting hatred,

taught by the Lord of the Thirty-three (Indra) who is the embodiment of the perfection of action, should be performed either on a cloth dyed with saffron or on a cloth dyed with lac, using blood and liquor produced from sugarcane; and that [rite] should be executed upon a cloth from a corpse.
Having placed [the mantra] as before upon wood from the fire of the minor directions (laghudikpāva),
one should destroy the unbearable flood of evils from that place for as long as it revolves there incessantly or for a period of a *yuga*.
Having inscribed [the mantra] with saffron and yellow pigment (*rocanā*) upon birch bark using the *vidyā*,
and having placed it within a beautiful cloth-scroll (*paṭa*) that is adorned with flowers and the name [of the recipient],
one should perform the rite according to the rule and with devotion.
It accomplishes the fulfillment of all desired undertakings when placed on the Vāyu-vega [breath], on the crest-lock (śikhā),
on the throat, on the garment, or likewise on the sacred thread (upavīta).

The divine *vidyā*, which destroys all poisons such as fever and *lūlā*, protects one like a son amidst a host of rising enemies; for him, there is no sudden onset of spirits or other calamities. Even when a multitude of arrows is incessantly scattered by hosts of foes at the front of the battle, [it remains unharmed].
Falling like a flower upon a heap of dust,
this knowledge— which remains written in the Yantra-house— is such that there is no fear of serpents there;
nor is there any fear of thieves, fire, obstacles, or even kings and princes.
The stainless ritual procedure of Bhuvaneśī has been described in brief.
That which was not stated by this method has been explained in the *Parā*.
Thus ends the first [verse].
With joy and wonder, [I worship] the lotus-foot of the Goddess whose name is the Steed of Victory over the Three Worlds, which is constantly sprinkled by the nectar-like speech of the gods.
Upon which [spear] being placed upon the head of every enemy, the entire earth trembles violently;
while the remaining blue-hued serpent, Śeṣa, with his circle of hoods long distressed, is being approached;
[that spear] is the true and fierce [weapon] that generates terror in the entire host of Asuras.
Having bowed with his head for the sake of establishing the second scripture,
he performed the *prastāra* as before upon the surface of the nectar of the gods; from that,
Sāsaddeva extracted the *mālinī* sequence consisting of five and a half syllables.
In the sky, the vehicle of Malaya [is found] within the five waters of the void;
Kubhṛvarata is in the fire, marked by the end of the twelve.
Thereafter, at the end of Dharma, there is the end of the vowels of that color.
Then, on the head of the *vahni* (the letter *ra*), there is the weapon (*astra*) marked with the three vowels;
it should end in *svāhā* and be preceded by the *praṇava*. Now, one should meditate upon this here: having joined the hands and the shanks once, one should place them in the *añjali* gesture.

Having subsequently projected the Vidyā, which pervades the entire body, beginning from the head, and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should then draw [the diagram] on the ground previously smeared and well-concealed,

Because she perfectly draws [all things] toward herself, she is remembered as Saṃkarṣaṇī.
When she draws [the soul] to the supreme station by pressing upon the machine in the void (kha), and because she awakens it, she is remembered as Saṃkarṣaṇī;
and because she moves through the sky (vyoman), she is the one who sets the flow of prāṇa and apāna in motion.
Because she resides at the *dvādaśānta*, Kālī is remembered as supreme (*parā*).
Because she measures time (*kāla*), the deity is indeed Kālī. She is not transparent, yet she is firmly rooted within; she is subtle and all-pervading.
Then Mahākālī is remembered as the pervader of all beings;
she is the power of knowledge, supreme bliss, and one who rejoices in the bliss of her own nature.
By the support of a single utterance, she undergoes a transformation of her essential form.
Having entered the five internal [channels], dry, spreading, and having the nature of vital breath—
formless, shapeless, and subtle— that is remembered as Kālī.
When she has ascended to the state of eternal bliss, transcends the functions of prāṇa and apāna,
and is perfectly absorbed in samādhi, then she is remembered as Kālī.
She is the all-pervading, supreme power, subtle, and having the nature of a thread.
O lady of excellent vows, that supreme power— inactive, devoid of qualities, peaceful, and the awakener— enters into the path of enjoyment in the form of *śakti*.
In its midst is she who has the form of a lizard (*kṛkalā*), whose nature is fragrance, both supreme and non-supreme.
She is the form of the collyrium of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), devoid of activity, and consisting of the nature of power (*śakti*).
Thus ends the first [chapter] in the *Kālikā* [section] of the *Jayadratha*.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, wielder of the trident, three-eyed one! Please tell me by your grace: what is considered the supreme [principle] within the body?
O Lord of the Gods of gods, how is it that this is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*)?
"O Lord of Gods, please tell me today, out of your grace, the distinction between the supports (ādhāra).
Listen; I shall explain it correctly. This is a secret concerning the Kula domain.
Listen as I speak it to you properly, according to the sequence beginning with Ūha."
The *ūha* [vāyu] moves upward; likewise, it reaches the *kālāgni*, *yama*, and *gā*.

That very [vāyu] dissolves into the *sarvādhāra* (the foundation of all), which extends from the ankles, knees, and thighs. Upon contraction, the *sarvādhāra* dissolves into the *saṃkoca*, which resides in the middle of the *turya*.
O beautiful lady, the fourth corner is called "birth" (janma), belonging to the birth-root (janmakanda). That root is within the Kuṇḍalinī, and she is also within the belly of the jar (ghaṭodara).
That indeed is the place of Saṃjīvanī, situated within the enclosure of the elements (bhūtasaṃpuṭa) for all living beings.
O Goddess, O beautiful lady, that thread is the abode of *lolā*;

it is called *laṃbā*, situated in the wheel of the Guru (*gurucakra*), and resides within the mouth of the Unborn (*aja*). The Unborn is situated in the middle of the equinox (*viṣuva*), and the equinox is the point of emission (*visargaka*).

Thus, the sixteen supports have been proclaimed as residing within the *piṇḍa*. O Goddess, listen now to how their essential nature is established, how this correct entry occurs, and what their true form is like.
(113b) O auspicious lady, you have not [revealed] to anyone the secret within the scope of your power—
the supreme reality of the goddesses, which resides from mouth to mouth.
"I shall tell it to you just as it has come down through the lineage of succession and resides in the hearts of the goddesses, so that it may fall within the range of your hearing.
O Goddess, it has been heard by me in great detail, according to the divisions beginning with the *ūha*."
The wheel situated at the base of the feet is renowned by the name Ūhaka;
it is the source of all wheels, possessing a radiance equal to a thousand suns.
O Daughter of the Mountain, enter it with a state of consciousness characterized by bliss.
That wheel is the source of all wheels, granting all desires;
it has sixteen spokes, is very extensive, and is endowed with a pericarp and filaments.
Therein resides that supreme power, the transcendent one whose nature is light.
Above this is the Great Wheel (Mahācakra), the supreme world of the Fire of Time (Kālāgni).
It has thirty-two spokes, is intensely radiant, auspicious, and shines with all colors.
Therein resides the mistress of the wheel (Cakranāyikī) named Viśveśvarī.
Therein, in the center, is the supreme radiance resembling many suns;
in its center is she who is named Śāntā, both transcendent and immanent.
Above that is the supreme wheel, the support of all, possessing great splendor.
Having the form of a blazing fire and joined with sixty-four [deities],
that goddess is the mistress of the wheel, renowned by the name Mahogrā.
Beyond that is the supreme wheel, renowned by the name Saṃkoca.
The vital breath named Apāna is always present there, accompanied by the Maruts;
there resides the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśī), renowned by the name Ambe.
She is merged in the state where existence and non-existence dissolve, having attained the state of equanimity.
At the time situated at the equinox, when both sides have been abandoned,
one should utter the innate sound (*nāda*) which is double-curved and located in the sky of the lotus of space.
By means of that, one should awaken [the energy] there as far as the interior of the aperture of Brahma (*brahmabila*).
The knower of yoga should always practice contraction and expansion until,
through proper practice, [the body] rises up within a month, O beloved. (114a)
He knows the past as well as the present;
he indeed becomes omniscient, for there is no doubt in this regarding the practitioner.
Thus is the supreme scripture of the deity, together with its secret teachings.
This has been taught in this King of Tantras, as well as in the Mādhavaka-kula;
I have not proclaimed this supreme practice elsewhere.
Whoever should become a knower of this will attain accomplishment and partake of its fruit.
Beyond this, hear of the supreme wheel; I shall describe it to you correctly.
It is the great wheel named Turya, the primary abode of the Yogeshīs.
Therein resides that supreme Śakti, who is under the control of Śiva.
Resplendent like a thousand suns, she is the Mother of the Lord of the Universe, Śivā.
Therein, in the center, one should cast the mind upon that which is of the nature of sound, the Great Supreme.
This, O Goddess, has been fully explained; beyond this, I shall tell you another.
The great wheel named Kanda has six spokes and possesses the splendor of the elements;
there resides that supreme goddess Sarasvatī, the Mother of Syllables,
who produces and transforms unstruck sounds.
Therefore, O Goddess, the manifestation of speech is determined to be fourfold.
And the Yoginīs who have ascended therein traverse the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings;
they effect a transformation of form here, of this there is no doubt.
Beyond this is the Great Wheel, renowned as Kuṇḍalinī;
it resembles one who is fast asleep, yet it is ever-risen for the Yoginīs.
There dwells that Śakti, whose form is half of half of the letter *i*.
The sword-blade is of the same form as that [the previous one], awakening through mere touch.
Beyond this, O Great Goddess, O wide-eyed one, listen:
the Ghaṭodara is the great wheel, the most excellent among all wheels.
There, in the center, resides the goddess known by the name Bhāsvatī;
she is the supreme abode of yogins, this ever-arisen deity.
That indeed is named Saṃjīvanī, the supreme abode of all beings;
there he dwells in the midst, consisting of heat and radiance, pure. Having entered there, the Sākinīs become free from fear.
Above that is the throat-cakra where Lolā is established;
there, O Goddess, is she named Śivā, possessing a beautiful form and excellent beauty. Above that is the supreme cakra, renowned by the name Lambā.
There, O Goddess, one should dwell in the center; she is known by the name Vedhikī.
Performing recitation while mounted there, one should bring forth the six flavors of delight.
Above that is the wheel called Gurukta, which illuminates everything.
Therein, in the center, is the Great Radiance, whose form has the appearance of the sun.
Therein dwells that Bindu, whose nature is like an atom.
Through the practice of that, O Great Goddess, the Guru becomes all-knowing.
Above that is the heart-faced wheel, the most excellent of all;
therein resides that supreme power, all-pervasive and sovereign,
whose nature is supreme consciousness and which brings about the realization of mantra.
Therein, in the center, is the supreme power (parāśakti) renowned by the name Dīpikā. Above that is the Viṣuva-cakra, which brings happiness to all sentient beings.
Above that, however, is the cakra called Visarga, the ultimate cause.
She stands situated in the midst of all those wheels,
just as a thread is established in the midst of a multitude of jewels.
Thus ends the division of the Kālikrama within the Kālikula.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Lord of Gods, tell me today indeed the true nature and knowledge of the supports (ādhāras); O Supreme God, describe the meditation on the Goddess exactly as it exists.
"O Lord, tell me the true nature of how they are established— whether with form or without form— and exactly how it is for practitioners. Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O highly fortunate goddess; I shall tell you a secret.
It has never been told by me to anyone; today I shall speak it to you.
The supreme goddess Śuklā Mahāparā is Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī;
she has three eyes and one face, stands upon a white lotus,
is mounted upon a white corpse, and is adorned with white garments.
Four-armed, with a beautiful form, slender-limbed, and adorned with serpents;
wearing a sacred thread of snakes and decorated with snake-bracelets;
endowed with such [divine] attributes and possessed of all auspicious marks.
Listen, I shall explain the *niṣka* in brief according to its true nature:
Mahākālī, whose form is space, who resembles a worm yet is the supreme [reality];
she is the essence of consciousness (*cidrūpā*), a digit of consciousness (*citkalā*), gentle, and adorned with the *anaṅga* [of passion].
One should meditate upon the Great Goddess, whose nature is existence, the goddess who is eternally manifest.
Afterwards, one should contemplate the highly fortunate goddess according to her described form and great splendor.
All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to ask?
Having heard those words then, which had issued from the mouth of the God of Gods,
the Goddess of the Gods again spoke a most excellent question. The Śrī Devī said:
O God, you ought to explain this supreme doubt in its entirety.
O Mahādeva, please graciously tell me the extraction of the mantra (mantroddhāra).
Śrī Bhairava said:
On a level and pure patch of ground, smeared with blood and wine,
one should cause the Mātṛkā to emerge there, accompanied by the eight groups of consonants.
From that, one should then extract the mantra, the solitary hero of great power.
The wise preceptor, facing east and seated upon a throne of wine and spirits, resting his body in the lap of the Śakti and intent on the consumption of the *brahma*,
should thus extract this mantra, the most supreme among all mantras.
First, one should extract the twenty-sixth [letter], situated above the son of Pātu (the letter *pa*),
joined with fire (*ra*) below, and positioned above the sixth [vowel].
This most beautiful syllable is joined with the half-moon and the bindu;
no lamp should be offered to it, for it is illuminated by its own nature.
This syllable is the Great Hero, the shatterer of the seven netherworlds.

By the mere recollection of this, Brahmā and the other deities, as well as all the Śaktis— both those who move upon the earth and those who move through the sky— are satisfied. O Goddess, I have thus declared to you this extraction of the mantra, which possesses auspicious characteristics.
Hear now, therefore, the sacrifice of the Goddess as it truly is:
on a mountain peak, on a riverbank, in a cow-pen, or in haste [at a sacred site],
in a cremation ground, at a solitary linga, or in the house of the Mothers.

In an underground chamber, or in deep sleep, or wherever the mind finds pleasure— O Goddess, one should smear that area of ground with blood, or with the water of Śiva, or with the water of Harṣadeva, or with that produced from a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍaga).
In that very place, Śakti should be worshipped with three, six, or nine [offerings].
One should worship the mantra among mantras which is complete and brings satisfaction to the mind.
O fortunate one, by way of the Bindu, [one should worship] as far as the Sun of great power.
One should worship the supreme sacrifice by bringing the lunar mandala down to the fire mandala through the cessation of the triple union (*trisamghaṭṭa*). Therein,
one should worship those Śaktis joined with vermilion and collyrium.
There, the teacher should sing the verses for those of disciplined soul;
he should burn incense from the lungs, which always goes to the Goddess.
O Goddess, I have thus described this sacrifice to you exactly as it is.
Henceforth, O highly fortunate one, listen; I shall speak further.
Listen as I describe the summary of the binding of the mudrās.
Both of them, namely prāṇa and apāna, are completely restrained and established [in their respective places].
Therein, in the center, is the supreme reality, arising from that which transcends both existence and non-existence.
Therein, in the center, one should effect consciousness; this is the supreme Khecarī mudrā.
And no seal (mudrā) equal to this exists within the three worlds. This, O Goddess of beautiful countenance, has been fully explained as the binding of seals.
Hereafter, O highly fortunate one, I shall tell you something wonderful.

O Goddess of the gods, place the *cit* in the midst of those wheels (*cakras*) which were previously described. O Goddess, one should join the wheels in pairs according to their essential nature (*bhāvarūpataḥ*).
O slender-waisted Goddess, for each pair there are eight groups (*vargas*).
And likewise, O Goddess, the eight planets always abide there;
the King of Mantras always dwells for a muhūrta in every single wheel.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, all mantras dwell at the beginning and at the end.
From midnight onwards for three watches, O illustrious one, [the deities] remain;
then again for another three by means of the Withdrawal [phase] alone;
then again for two, O slender-waisted lady, for those who are situated in the two [final phases].
The principle of the Self (ātmatattva) is established from the feet up to the end of the palate;
the principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva) is proclaimed to extend from the root-center (kanda) up to the throat;
the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) is proclaimed to extend from the throat up to the limit of the cranial aperture (brahmarandhra).
When half the night has passed during the first watch, O lady of excellent complexion,
the lord of the Kaulikas should always practice meditative absorption (samādhi), O beloved;
for that duration of ten muhūrtas, O fair-faced one.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, at the end of that [period] of his own arising of the mantras,
for a duration of ten muhūrtas,
there occurs the arising of the *vidyātattva*; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O Goddess, the supreme arising of the third wheel occurs. This secret Kaulika doctrine has been declared by me, O beloved;
there is no knowledge like this, O Goddess, anywhere at all.
Thus, everything has been revealed by me to you today;
this must not be given to anyone, lest one incur great fault.
The Chapter on the Distinctions of the *Kali* Cycle.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Great God, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge!
O God, O Destroyer of Tripura, dispel this supreme doubt.
O Mahādeva, O Bhairava, tell us the *chummakās* of the deities.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall speak; I will tell you a secret:
she who shows her thumb should show him her face;
she who shows her little finger should show him her crest-lock.
One should display the middle [tongue] and show its own face.
I shall tell you the secret of all the left [tongues] as well; I shall show the state of union (*yugma-pada*) of all the powers (*śakti*).
"Because it dwells within, grasping that which is between the ends of the prāṇa and apāna,
such is the state of the goddesses, a secret hidden by me. Thus, O Goddess, I have declared this secret, the tradition of the deities."
"The secret must be given even to devotees, for he is the deity. Having heard these words, the Goddess of gods then spoke this speech: "I have told you this today; what more do you wish to ask?"
Again he spoke these most excellent words, O Goddess of the Gods.
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord of the God of Gods, O Master, tell me about the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*)."
"By the mere knowledge of which one indeed destroys great sin;
O Blessed One, tell me briefly the supreme characteristic of fire.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, as I tell you everything exactly as it is;
that which has indeed never been told to anyone by me, O you who are honored by heroes,
I shall declare that to you here out of great affection, O fair-faced one.
Having taken up the *tatvakā* and so forth, one should press the *prāṇa* and *apāna*;
one should blow upon the *kaṇḍacakra* until it blazes.
The Supreme Goddess awakens the flow of the prāṇa and apāna;
from their midst, the supreme Śakti, in the form of fire, causes agitation. She burns away the aggregate of the principles (tattvas) and the collection of qualities such as sound.
There, O Goddess of the gods, one offers oblations consisting of Śiva, the Moon, and clarified butter;
having grasped the *śruva* ladle, one offers your own consciousness as the resonance (*nāda*). As soon as it has dawned there, I meditate upon you as being firmly established.
One should unite [the elements] within the supreme abode situated between the sun, moon, and fire.
Thus has the supreme ritual of fire been revealed today;
indeed, he who does not know this is not called an Ācārya.

O auspicious lady, I shall again declare this entire lineage of the Great Mādhava within your family on the summit of Mount Mandara. Why should I tell you anything further in such great haste? Tell me more in detail.

This supreme secret should be given to one's own disciple only after having tested him for a long time; otherwise, one becomes a sinner. Thus [ends the section] on the Rāviṇīcakra in the fourth Ṣaṭka of the Jayadrathayāmala, within the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairava-śrotas.
The Ritual of the Kālikākula.
Having heard this, that Goddess, overflowing with joy and bliss,
prostrated before the Lord of Gods, the Teacher of the World, and spoke again.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Mahādeva, tell me that which has just now been indicated by you—
the true nature of the Mādhava-kula, O Bhairavī, must be explained therein.
"O Blessed One, O Lord, explain briefly in this tantra that which constitutes its thousand [verses], by means of which there shall be the completion of this tantra. Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, I shall speak from the midst of the King of Tantras how that Mādhava family is to be described upon Mount Mandara.
And just as that *Kālā* exists there, so I shall tell you everything:
that which is the peaceful supreme ether (*parākāśa*), completely full and facing in all directions;
eternal, free from both being and non-being, its form transcending all causes.
For he is unborn, infinite, omniscient, all-pervading, the sustainer, auspicious, and immutable.
He is without lineage (akula), facing every direction, and is established everywhere.
This manifest universe is his belly; it is undivided and possesses luminosity.
He who is intensely radiant with his own self-luminosity, overflowing with the essence of eternal bliss,
should be known as Samādheya, the Lord of Kula, the Sun of Kula.
He is unborn, immutable, tranquil in nature, and the agent of creation and dissolution.
He is known as Mahāghoravara, Caṇḍa, and Kulabhairava;
he is proclaimed as being endowed with thirty-eight kalās and possessed of rays.
He exists in one way, in two ways, indeed in three ways, and likewise in four ways.
The Lord of the Kula is to be known as fivefold, sixfold, and sevenfold;
eightfold, ninefold, and possessing ten and eleven forms.
Indeed, he is twelvefold, sixteen-fold, the Bindu, and Nārāyaṇa.
The Lord who possesses the form of the Man-Lion (Nṛsiṃha), terrible, a devourer that swallows the three worlds;
the Master of all wheels, the Protector, who utters a great roar;
the Lord of the wheel, devoted to the wheel, filled with fierce rays.
Attached to the bliss of each individual channel and piercing each respective knot,
that which is proclaimed as the Great Current (mahādhārā) extends from Ūhaka up to Śiva;
within those, the Kula of Mādhava shines forth, intent upon its power.
Shaken by that wheel of rays, delighted by the bliss of the secret,
attached to the essence of the five nectars, and saluted by all yogis;
it is intent upon the sequence of the wheel of winds and is solely devoted to devouring the universe.
Devoted to a terrible, loud laughter, sixfold and of six types,
the Lord of the City, the abode of the immortals, situated within the assembly of the triple union.
The mantra of this Ananta, encapsulated within the cavity of his own great abode,

joined with the four powers and the great bindu, bestows the accomplishment of all aims. It is to be worshipped according to the sequence of the individual cakras, along with its support and its presiding lord.
Therein, she shines, always encircled by rays;
one should worship the goddesses who delight in the ninefold sacrifice and Maheśvara.
In that same manner, the worship should be performed in nine ways, not merely confined to the circle.
"O God, one should fashion the wheel as far as the [circle of] scriptures (yāvacchāstraka), which is ever-newly arisen, infinite, delightful, and possessed of new abysses.
Residing upon this support is the terrible Kālī, the slayer of Time."
She who resides at the end of the seventeenth word should be known as Mādhaveśvarī;
she alone is to be known as Mahāmādhavikā, the one who brings about the lineage (*ākulakaraṅkiṇī*). Therefore, she has been obtained in this supreme tantra named Āvasa.
Abiding therein and moving within that wheel, she is celebrated as Kālī, Kulakālī. O Goddess, in that excellent seat, she whose prowess is both well-concealed and manifest is described—
both what has been said and what is yet to be said— as well-guarded and having a hidden domain.
Mahākālī, the Mistress of Mādhava, is profoundly hidden and arises from the depths;
she repeatedly effects the pervasion of the lineage of the Lord of Mādhava.
Therefore, that power Kālikā, impelling both the *kula* and the *akula*, is so named.
Tearing asunder all objects, shattering the abode of qualities,
and utterly dispersing the entire multitude of dualities,
Kālī moves within speech; therefore, she moves within the discus of Mādhava.

"O Goddess of gods, it has been explained to you; what else do you wish to ask? When Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Gods and benefactor of the world, had spoken thus, the Goddess of gods, having prostrated before the Lord of the Suras, spoke again.
The Śrī Devī said:
I have heard many tantras that are most highly secret;
indeed, they are considered to be devoid of compassion, their functions exhausted by conceptual construction.
In this supreme tantra as well, there are numerous ritual procedures—
both with activity and without activity— which bestow the accomplishment of the goals of liberation and worldly prosperity.
And there is another peerless heroine, devoted to the union of yoga;
others indeed are the various manifestations of Śambarā’s nets in manifold forms. There are others who perform the union of haṭha, known as the piercing of haṭha.
And another [power], by means of the yoga of emanation, pierces the bound souls (paśus) with force;
and yet another, through the potency of mantra, in the Śākta and Śāmbhava yogas;
and indeed another, through the practice of gathering (melāpaka) and through disguised conduct (chadmācāra).
I have heard of the melāpakas and the divine practices of the heroes; I have heard the various rules for the conduct of the Kula and the manifold traditions of the Kaulas;
and I have heard, according to the prescribed ritual, about the confidence shared with the Yoginīs.
But here, having revealed the Kaulika [tradition] continuously in this vehicle,
by which neither hypocrisy nor lack of trust remains, and by which this [system] has truly been internalized—
having thus revealed it continuously as being beyond conventional conduct.
Tell me that supreme sin by which people lose their trust,
through the application of the mouth, from mouth to mouth in succession,
by the power of secret conduct, and by that which is most strictly concealed.
Through conduct they shall proclaim the knowledge of the Siddhakaulikas, which is devoid of the means of bondage. This knowledge shall circulate among those of right and wrong conduct;
it is the secret limb of the divisions of conduct, both hidden and unhidden, belonging to the family of Yoginīs.
Moving through incomparable secret paths and assuming hundreds of diverse forms,
he assumes a physical body in the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) and the seats of yoga (*yogapīṭhas*) where all light has vanished;
by the mere remembrance of him here, all supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are attained.

O Lord, tell me the means by which they may be worshipped so that I may gain their confidence; tell me that by which satisfaction may arise within me— [the worship] of those Kālarāvis in the midst [of the body], who bring about untimely death.
(119a) But regarding the worship of all the pīṭhas, numbering thirty-four in total:
how indeed is their worship performed, and how indeed do they grant accomplishment?
In the *Pūrvatantra*, it was declared by you during the movement of the night-wanderer:
"O Lord, that which is hidden by you is devoid of the middle and does not bestow success;
those twenty-four recitations which are in the middle, and she who is the Mistress of the Pīṭha."
Without her, there would be no accomplishment; the sacrifice would be fruitless.
The wheel, when gazed upon by her, becomes vibrant with life.
Through her, that accomplishment which was previously described by me shall arise.
If, due to negligence, one violates the great commitment (mahāsamaya),
some become great sinners who defile the mantras and tantras;
yet, through the stainless purity of the commitment (samaya) and by being united with the non-duality of the ritual substance (dravya-advaita), [they may be purified].
For those whose swift consciousness is proclaimed at the conclusion of the ritual cycles,
when the transference of the conduct of the pledge has occurred for the purification of transgressions—
O Lord of Heroes, how do they become pure while desiring to go to hell?
Those who are corrupt through negligence and transgressors of the conduct of the covenant,
though they have entered the paths of the *pīṭhas* and the ends of the *pīṭhas*, shall be set in motion [to fall];
attached to nocturnal meetings, their deities will be fruitless due to their violation.
For the benefit of practitioners, there shall be success in all accomplishments.
For the sake of purification through expiation, one becomes a partaker of all successes.
By worshipping [it] even once, a person shall quickly attain the power of moving through the sky.
Tell me that easy means, the power of the mantra of great strength,
the ritual procedure, and the ultimate reality— the sixfold set applied as sixfold.
O Knower of the Nature of Reality, delude me through your grace so that there may be no obstacle.
"Perform the task of great significance, O destroyer of the dissolution of worldly existence!
Śrī Bhairava said:
O beloved, this is most secret, the secret of secrets, and more guarded than the most guarded;
it is the incomparable meaning of the great question, difficult even for the gods to obtain. This speech is not to be told even among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, and the others.
Apart from you, whose capacity for skill in intellect could there be?
O sinless Goddess, I shall proclaim to you the complete Śākta, Śāmbhava, and Āṇava [traditions], as well as the Kula, and the special grace (viśeṣānugraha).
The first is the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama), the second is the descent (avatāra),
the third is withdrawal (saṃhāra), and the fourth is the inexpressible (anākhyeya). Sometimes, from mouth to mouth, the Yoginīs belong to the Puruṣa.
He possesses the oral tradition (āmnāya) and should practice within the secret conduct.
O auspicious lady, he with whom I am pleased—and you especially, O Goddess—he is born of the Kāli-lineage; he clearly cultivates meditative realization (bhāvanā).
His power is great indeed; it does not belong to others who speak falsely.
As long as the practitioner remains established in the station of Kālī and the Kula, how could there be liberation for him? For the second [state] is Nāthabhairavī.
The Krama is devoid of a formal arrangement (prastāra) and is established from mouth to mouth.
Thus, the first is preceded by the Krama; the second is preceded by Siddhi;
the third is the Saṃhāra; and the fourth is from mouth to mouth.
But this, O blessed one, is the fifth; a sixth does not exist here at all.

When their meditation is inferior, being devoid of the ritual expansion (prastāra), it is merely the sequence of the scriptures and the words of the guru meditated upon through the state of self-absorption.

The knower of mantras does not achieve success if he does not find the oral tradition; indeed, such a mortal is of dull intellect. O Goddess, when one becomes wise through non-conceptualization, then I shall explain the sequence of the scriptures to you in brief.
Therefore, I shall fully explain that supreme destroyer of misfortune,
which serves to eliminate the need for expiation and purifies the great commitments.
O Mother of the Gaṇas, one must arrange six [vessels] in each of the four directions.
Without wine, they do not attain success even through hundreds of sacrifices.
They have fallen from the tradition and are deluders of all mantras and tantras.
Those who lack the means of scripture do not find the secret conduct;
deprived of the guru’s oral tradition, delusion always arises for them.
Wandering the earth with such confused knowledge, they do not attain accomplishment.
Then, O beloved, they are overcome by various kinds of obstacles;
however, the cultivation of higher knowledge destroys them, and mantras lead to success.
Indeed, O beloved, such people fall away from both this world and the next.

Therefore, having understood the sequence of the deities with a mind guided by the scriptures, one shall obtain all that fruit which is the result of those [deities] through the authority of the scriptures. From that fruit, one becomes a possessor of siddhi; from liberation (mokṣa), there is indeed no more worldly existence (saṃsāra).

For this reason, O blessed one, O lady of beautiful hips, I have explained to you these three means of proof which accomplish the destruction of darkness. This terrible illusion is difficult to transcend and is hard to comprehend even for the gods and asuras.

All those falling away from knowledge are never uplifted at any time; they are liberated only through her grace, O Dear One, when they recognize that this descent of power (śaktipāta) is itself the one who cuts short their worldly existence.
Thus, having heard the oral tradition (āmnāya) established within the lineages (krama), there can be no accomplishment without them; therefore, I shall tell you that state.
Thus ends [the chapter] titled "The Determination of the Sequence of the Kālī Family" in the Jayadrathayāmala.
Śrī Bhairava said:
First, I shall explain the defects caused by those who are wicked;
one should indeed examine [the candidate] with effort and bring forth the secret disposition.
(120b) Due to the absence of absolute straightforwardness, one's own illusory nature grants the accomplishment of goals;
for those who are devoted to the conduct of the Kula, all things indeed exist in relation to the Self.

Everything becomes existence; when meditation becomes manifest, they grasp the Kaulika [teaching] through your grace, as it is no longer known [otherwise]. Others who are great sinners desire to go to hell.
The great ones enter the Kula teaching by force;
they employ the nectar-like words that are [otherwise] poison and should be concealed.
O Dear One, one should cause them to hear everything and grasp it without remainder.
Afterwards, they will fall into ruin, by which they go to utter destruction.
O Goddess, having entered through deception and great crookedness,
those devoid of the descent of power (śaktipāta) fall forcibly into hell.

The utterance of Bhairava shall be of great significance, born from the vessel of knowledge and realization. One who has personally adopted the conduct and always performs initiation and grace sells his own enjoyments for the sake of the bound souls (paśus) of limited nature.

Indeed, those of evil conduct, thieves of their own souls, and the lowest of men do not realize that they have taken through unjust means a great wealth belonging to the Supreme Lord. Those base individuals who violate the bounds of propriety employ such wealth for their own purposes.
They fall into a most terrible hell filled with darkness,
together with their sons, servants, and friends, and even with seven generations of their lineage; indeed,
they are not able to achieve purification through expiation for that [sin].

In due course, they are filled up one by one in all the hells and other realms; and there can never be any liberation for those who, out of negligence, associate with such people, even if they themselves have attained the state of a Guru.
He indeed attains identity with that [object], yet he sinks into the great ocean;
they seek a place of light where darkness, inhabited by forms of blind gloom, prevails.
One should not eat one's own kind among the fish and tortoises.
Thus do those fools who act with deceit attain their destiny;
therefore, with every effort, one should investigate and reach a firm conclusion.

Those who are devoted to the family path (kulamārga), who have mastered the proper conduct of time (kālācāra), those fortunate ones who follow the conduct of heroes (vīrācāra) and are practitioners in the tantric conduct (tantrācāra),
and those who are intent on the worship of the Krama, being wise with knowledge and realization— [to them belongs this].
Those endowed with devotion, firm in conduct, heroic, and free from miserliness;
those always intent on the food of heroes, greedy for food, drink, and the like;
those whose minds are attached to sense objects, and those who delight in song and instrumental music.
Those who delight in various states of being through laughter, dance, and conversation,
who feel no sorrow at the death of a kinsman nor at the crushing of sesame seeds at a sacred ford,
