The sixth [vowel] preceded by the first [consonant] is conjoined with an elephant-goad (aṅkuśa); likewise, the fifth [vowel] preceded by the first [consonant] is also with an elephant-goad.

Then, having placed a wheel with three dots above it, followed by the syllable *niṣedha* together with the wind (*vāyu*), one should then join it with *sṛṣṭi* and restrain it with the formidable elephant-goad.
This Vidyā of thirty-four syllables, meditated upon, possesses terrible prowess;
O Goddess of the gods, she causes the sun and the moon to fall at the end.
She is the subduer of the seven netherworlds and the crusher of all magical mechanisms.
The churner of the universe, the terrible Kālarātrī,
the bearer of skulls— O fortunate one, by the utterance of her name, the afflicted world trembles;
when she is complete, the entire universe, including all that is mobile and immobile, shakes and quivers.

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, no one who possesses the fortune of a hero shall fail to attain her; she effortlessly draws in all those women who belong to the asuras. One who has taken refuge in supreme non-duality should worship this goddess.
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, you who always grant all desires within the maṇḍala, reside forever upon a lotus or within a jar of wine.
One should worship with a great accumulation of riches the Power who shatters all things—
she who has arisen on the central path by the flow of the *śakti*-mechanism,
who is intensely fierce, active in her functions, complete, and of terrible aspect.
One should meditate on her whose face is adorned with a frown that shatters millions of cosmic eggs,
whose radiance is equal to tens of billions of the terrible fires at the end of an aeon,
and who resembles the throat of Śrīkaṇṭha, dark as a swarm of black bees against the autumn sky.
She is resplendent with all weapons, a great noose, and a goad;
she rests upon the broad shoulders of a black lion, yet possesses a slender form.
Her body is adorned in every limb by the lord of serpents.
She deafened the world with the terrible sound of her bell and the roar of her laughter;
she was supremely terrifying with the mass of flames flickering from her hair;
likewise, she was ever raining down coals and fragments of bone.
Even though she lies within the heart-lotus, she reaches the openings of the underworld (*pātāla*) mechanisms;
thus, meditating upon her as one who agitates the entire world and especially the underworlds, and having worshipped her in the mandala, [one attains] the fulfillment of all desires.
Afterwards, the lord of practitioners should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times on a mountain peak.
Through the offering of excellent substances, she bestows success by way of a tenth part [of the recitation].
Thereafter, O beloved, he should go to the entrance of the cave at night on a Thursday.
While reciting the mantra and meditating upon Kālikā, the goddess of gods who shatters the universe,
all of Pātāla, inhabited by the Daityas, trembles; indeed,
with only fifty repetitions, all the mechanical devices fall down.
By reciting the mantra of Sureśā one hundred times, all those women from whom darkness departs emerge as excellent ladies, taking up the *argha* offering;
they speak "Burnt! Burnt! while trembling and afflicted by fear.
They quickly fall at the feet of the practitioner and pay him homage;
they entreat him with compassion, saying, "Save us, save us, O Lord of Men!"
Having heard this, O Goddess, the supreme practitioner should then enter together with them into that place called Garbhapura, accompanied by his followers and retinue;
it is a station ten million times superior to heaven, difficult to attain for those of unrefined self.
Endowed with those [mantras], O Goddess, he lives for a great kalpa,
possessed of all knowledge and having mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences. Having the very form of Rudra himself, he desires ten million women.
At the conclusion of Mahākālī, however, [the practitioner] merges into the supreme Śiva.
Alternatively, having recited the Amṛta-mantra, the master of practitioners, firm in his vows,
should go to Sugama-Śrīmukha and enter there according to the prescribed rite.
With lamps and foot-ointments, one should crush all the mechanical devices;
O Lord, just as one enters one's own home fearlessly,
so does the knower of mantras enter the interior of Pātāla, which is full of gold, O fortunate one.
Having worshipped it, one should cause this vidyā to revolve up to a hundred times.
Then all those women will arrive, overwhelmed by fear. As before, there shall be success; no distinction is prescribed.
On the new moon day of the month of Ārttika, one should practice the supreme face known as Śrīmukha;
at night, one should revolve the Vidyā through the application of the power of the *randhra*.
Thereupon, maidens emerge from that [aperture] with slender waists, just as before.
The great-souled practitioner shall attain success as before.
Thus has the auspicious Goddess, the agitator of Pātāla, been fully described along with her secret, O highly fortunate one; what else do you wish to ask?

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for the Pātāla-kalpa, within the fourth Ṣaṭka of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraścheda* division of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavaśrotas*.
The Goddess said:
O Maheśvarī, I now wish to hear about that which makes the unfortunate fortunate, by the recitation of which it is brought about.
"O Lord of Gods, tell me by what means one may attain the state of being beloved by all and the favor of women.
Śrī Bhairava said:

Listen, O you who are saluted by the lords of heroes, to this supreme ritual of Karaṅkiṇī, which is most radiant and brings about all excellent qualities. Having reached an auspicious place, one should there extract the Vidyā.
The syllable marked with the sign of the fire-chamber (Ra), situated in fire (Ra) and adorned with a bindu;
joined with the double-tongued one (Sa) mounted on air (Ya) and encircled by a triangle (Ma);
permeated from beginning to end by nectar (Au), it is situated in the moon (U) and bestows all siddhis.
One should extract the sixth [letter] (ṣ) with the first [letter] (a), mounted on fire (ra) and endowed with a head of three dots (m);
then, having extracted the pure wind (ya) situated in the fang (da), one should likewise extract the fire (ra) itself, adorned with three dots at its head (m). Thus: *Ṣma-ya-ra-m*.
The Mistress of the World consists of nine syllables and is joined with the consort Tejendrabhāryā;
she possesses a luster like red and non-red nectar, her eyes gaze into the hollow of the Suṣumṇā,
her hands are busy with the noose and goad, and she deludes all that is moving and unmoving.
Mounted upon a great preta and adorned with all ornaments,
one should meditate [on her] and worship with devotion within the mandala upon a lotus,
using all the offerings for heroes, such as wine, meat, and fermented liquors.
Having consecrated the water-pot with pure mantras and having recited them a thousand times,

the consecration (abhiṣeka) should be bestowed upon one's own body or that of another. Thereby, the dawning of great fortune, the attainment of the heart’s desire, and lordship over the world shall arise.
Having gone to the excellent mountain, one who is most excellent should, without sloth, recite the mantra of the goddess Kālikā one hundred thousand times and perform the fire oblation. (141b)
O illustrious and beloved one, through these ten limbs, it is then fully accomplished. Indeed, when she is perceived as perfected, understand that this is the supreme utterance.
Just as people come to a sacred ford, so indeed do they all come [to her].

And they worship her constantly, O Goddess Maheśvarī, indeed always with various offerings for their own sake, their wives, and great gifts. Through the yoga of six months of practice, one may indeed agitate the entire world.

The inhabitants of the three worlds exist in a state of servitude [to her]. She is renowned as the fulfiller of all actions; she bestows the fruits of worldly existence and liberation, and is the beloved of the entire world. What more do you wish to ask?
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of Priyakālī in the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, within the twenty-four thousand [verse] scripture of the Vidyāpīṭha in the Bhairava current.
The Goddess said:
"Speak once more regarding the purification of the great sins."
That rite which is most fierce, yet bestows the fruit of liberation through mere recitation—
free from the requirement of wooden seats and devoid of the practice of vows—
that indeed is the purification of Mahākālī through recitation alone.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Well asked, O lady of beautiful hips, out of compassion for the souls of practitioners.
I shall explain it to you, O auspicious one—that which destroys even the greatest sins."
The rite of the Goddess of the lords of gods is well-established as bestowing both enjoyment and liberation.
Having worshipped the goddess Mātṛkā, one should thereafter extract the Vidyā.
First extracting the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should then extract the syllable Ḍaṃvara.
One should give Amṛta together with Sṛṣṭi, and Niṣedha alone; then Kāla with Praṇava, and Gaṇeśvara beginning with Kāla.
Varuṇa should be given alone, followed by the five beginning with the first, joined with the three Suns.
The arm [of Gaṇeśa] is endowed with the three feet of Gaṇendra and possessed of the three *bindus*;
Varuṇa is joined with a goad and situated upon Gaṇendra and Varuṇa.
The fifth [syllable] should be made illuminated by three dots (bindus) and ending with Varuṇa (va).
One should place it at the end of the bow (ca), adorned with the abode of fire (ra).
[Then follow] the bow (ca) ending with Varuṇa (va) together with the Praṇava (oṃ), and likewise the wind (ya).
Furthermore, the *kalaśa* (water-pot) should be offered together with the *praṇava*.
One should again extract the first pair of syllables.
Amṛta should be made twofold; mark it with the *bindu*.

Then one should extract the second [syllable], Kāmadeva, who is trampled by a goad. Joined with the wife of Tejas-Indra, adorned with the thirty-sixth letter, this Vidyā has been fully declared to you; it is the destroyer of great sins.
Even if he were to destroy the entire universe filled with Brahmins,
he would not be tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water. Whatever transgression of the rules there may be, even if it be entirely contrary [to dharma], [he remains untainted].

O Goddess, if [the rite] is performed according to one's desire, the seven castes shall perish. O Supreme Goddess, having worshipped Kālī— who assumes the form of Gaurī— just once in a great jar or in the Kādya [vessel], and having performed a hundred circumambulations, [the goal is attained].
O Goddess, he who has been consecrated by this shall become great;
O Bhairavī, among all the principal maṇḍalas and in all the tantras,
that man becomes an enjoyer in the Mahāmoha-kula and attains perfection.

O Goddess of the Gods, by reciting this even once, one shall become a partaker of liberation. By simply chanting it for six months, knowledge itself will arise. Having chanted this over water seven times during the *mṛga* moment, [one should drink it].

O most excellent of practitioners, at the time of death, whomever you sprinkle with this [mantra], him you shall lead to union with Brahman; my word is unfailing. O beautiful one, this [vidyā] which performs all rites has been explained to you.
Or what is the use of saying more? O beloved, as far as this excellent tantra extends, I have described the sādhana to you; for by means of this, that [attainment] is indeed accomplished.
Thus has it been fully explained to you; what more do you wish to ask?

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of Pādyāntakī in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the fourth hexad, in the *Śiraścheda* section of the Vidyāpīṭha belonging to the Bhairava current.
The Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, O Lord, tell me of the divine pillar for the most sinful;
what is that Vidyā, O God, which resides in your heart?
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess saluted by the lords of heroes, to the most excellent Śubhakālī;
by whose practice, O Goddess, one may bring under control all things, both moving and unmoving.

Having worshipped the Goddess Mantrāraṇī, one should thereafter extract the Vidyā. First, having extracted the Wind (Ya), situated upon Fire (Ra) and preceded by Kāla (Ū), one should join it with the sixth vowel (Ū) and the Bindu; this is Piṇḍeśa, the bestower of all siddhis.
One should likewise extract Daṃbara, Mahākāla, Cāpa, and Aya-puruṣa;
joined with the Praṇava, one should extract the Nāda alone.
O Supreme Goddess, it should be made to possess three dots and the fire, and the negation [should be applied].
Having raised only the bow, place it in the position of the fire (vāhna) syllable;
the water (vāruṇa) syllable alone should be given, and again at its end,
only the fanged one mounted on the letter *k* (kartta), marked with three dots (*bindu*).
Furthermore, the two initial syllables should be given again with the *āḍambara*.
This seventeen-syllable Vidyā, when deprived of the "footed" (*muṇḍapāda*) portion,
is the supreme Mahākālī, the devourer of great sins.

At the end of the second hexad, Mahālakṣmī was revealed as before; likewise, Īśā is [revealed], though there is some distinction. In the same manner, her meditation, her *cakra*, and her worship have been proclaimed.
Now I shall explain the application of the extremely powerful yantra of the Mistress of Knowledge (Vidyeśī),
by which one may paralyze even divine beings from as far as a hundred yojanas.
Having collected earth from the bank of a river, fashion a *liṅga* from it.
Within that [liṅga], one should place the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), enclosed in a fold [of leaves],
joined with the word for the divine state (*divyapada*) and accompanied by the word "paralyze" (*stambhaya*).
Having enveloped it sevenfold with *māyā*, with *rocana* and saffron (*kuṅkuma*),
one should worship it with the *vidyeśī* [mantras] and heat it with milk and water.
The practitioner should burn a continuous stream of ghee over the top of the *liṅga*.
One is completely and correctly delivered from [the dangers of] a pot,
rice, hair, fire, and the consumption of poison—
of this there is no doubt— by one who has performed even half a *sūkṣma* [recitation] with her name placed within a folded leaf (*puṭīkṛta*).
O Goddess, this is the truth, the absolute truth, and not otherwise:
this Vidyā of great luster is renowned as the performer of all rites, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, through its application to that which is dependent on another.

Now I shall further explain the most terrible "obstruction of the womb" (*garbhastambha*). One should take the syllable *rū* (the face), joined with the creation-syllable (*sṛṣṭi*), enclosed within a fire-enclosure (*vahni-puṭīkṛta*),
and then likewise form the "double-tongued" (*dvijihva*) syllable along with the visarga.
One should employ Trivarṇā Paramākālī for the immobilization of the womb (garbhastaṃbha). Having drawn the interior of a brick with some yellow pigment,
one should enclose the name of the person to be acted upon within it and cover the second [brick].
"Thus, O Goddess, one should stabilize the womb; this is the truth and not otherwise.
This supreme mantra, O Goddess, is remembered as the performer of all rites.
Thus has the method of stabilization been fully explained to you therein."
One should always cause even wicked kings to perform [this] against those who hate the *tantra*.
What more shall I say? Speak, O you whose belly is like a thunderbolt!
Thus, in the *Bhairava-śrotas*, in the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the *Śiraścheda*, in the *Jayadrathayāmala* Great Tantra, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the fourth hexad.
The Ritual of Stambhakālī.
(143b) The Illustrious Goddess said:
Now I wish to hear about the overthrowing of wicked kings;
likewise, O God, tell me quickly regarding those who are hostile toward you.
Śrī Bhairava said:
O fortunate one, I shall describe to you from the midst of the King of Tantras [the goddess] Ghorā,
who causes the destruction of enemies, who is Time itself, and who bestows the fear of Time;
she who, without a doubt, slays the entire triple world.
Having gone to the abode of Hara, the minister should extract the Tantric lore.
Having prepared the ground rubbed with human bone and having worshipped it in due order,
he should extract Mahākāla, which is devoid of life and movement.
One should give only the *Kuṇḍala* [mantra], which is empowered (*śākta*) and peaceful (*śānta*), and keep it steady.
Then one should give the *Bhīmaśaṅku*, the Vidyā of terrible prowess.
It consists of four syllables, is extremely fierce (*mahāraudra*), and is endowed with two and a half syllables.
O Goddess praised by heroes, one should properly recite the *nairātmā* mantra, which brings about destruction at the appointed time and causes the ruin of the enemy faction,
until that enemy is tormented and no longer causes distress to the king.
One who is exhausted or even struck should perform [the rite] or recite [the mantra].
I shall explain its procedure [and its preeminence]; listen with a one-pointed mind.
O Lord of Men, having gone at night to a solitary linga that is the abode of Hara...
There, having heated the earth with an enraged mind,
one should worship within the triangular world by means of all-black offerings— that [goddess] who resembles a mass of terrible, dark snow.
Having meditated upon her according to the ritual procedure— naked, with hair standing erect, formidable, possessing beautiful shells,
holding a sword in her hand, with blazing hair, mounted upon a donkey, and having squinting eyes—
and having worshipped her with all heroic offerings.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred times there; then it will be accomplished without doubt.
Having thus propitiated her there, one should thereafter begin the rite of slaying.
By employing the practice of *kumbhaka*, the practitioner,
having joined the name [of the victim] with the syllables beginning with *ca* and *gha* placed upon the target, performs one hundred recitations over three days;
having extracted the Lord of the Earth, he shall kill him— of this there is no doubt.
There is no protection for one who would practice this [rite] against him;
O Goddess, he may kill an ordinary man in a single day.
It is not always [the case], due to the splitting of terrible thunderclaps... [and so forth].
Water from the opening of the trident kills the enemy by piercing him.
O Dear One, in whatever manner one recites the mantra while enraged,
in that very manner one may kill even the gods of the three worlds.
Thus, O Goddess, Kālarātrī must not be given to just anyone;
she should be guarded with great effort and must not be bestowed even at the cost of one's life.
If, out of delusion, greed for wealth, or fear, she is given away, O Dear One—
Then the kūṣmāṇḍa fruit will ripen in the forest for an inexhaustible time.
Having thus reflected upon what is beneficial, do now as you wish.
Thus has it been explained to you; what else shall I tell you?
Thus, in the Bhairava-śrotas, within the Vidyāpīṭha, in the Śiraścheda-Jayadrathayāmala Mahātantra, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the fourth Ṣaṭka,
this is the chapter on the ritual procedure of Kālarātri.
The venerable Goddess said:
Tell me how the lord of heroes sometimes obtains the fruit of recitation through the consultation regarding weapons at the time of battle with the king;
or when he performs incomparable sacrifice, or when his enemies have approached.
"O Lord, tell me that means by which those who are wicked toward one who praises [you] as you truly are may be subdued.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"You ask well; may prosperity be yours! These words [of yours] arise from compassion for your devotees."
(144b) Out of affection for you, I shall explain the entire procedure that deludes all.
Having worshipped the goddess Mātṛkā, one should thereafter invoke Kālī.
Then, O highly fortunate one, form the double-tongued [letter *sa*] which is firmly established and joined with emission (*sṛṣṭi*).
Then form the wheel ending in the cutter (*kṛt*), the solitary one situated in the fire of time (*kālāgni*),
joined with the bindu, preceded by the moon, and possessing three bindus.
Extending as far as Tridhāna, it is the supreme state, the intense manifestation of creation. O Ghoravidyeśī, the recitation of these seven syllables bestows accomplishment upon men.
Just as she is called Rāviṇī, so too are the regions proclaimed.
O Goddess, its power, its vigor, its form, and its manifestation— likewise, worship should be performed here without distinction; through such sacrifice,
accomplishment shall arise in this unmoving heart.
For this accomplished heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), there is nothing in the three worlds that cannot be achieved.
When performing sacrifices for the sake of other worlds, those who harbor enmity toward one are instantly and without obstacle destroyed; one should always keep their destruction in mind.
Having sprinkled the various types of weapons, such as swords and others, one hundred and eight times with the *avatyā* mantra,
and having consecrated those weapons, one should seize them and agitate the enemy army.
Indeed, a single person may, in an instant, slay or delude even the army of Indra himself.
The end of the [mantra] syllables is seen directly as resembling Kāla, Antaka, and Yama; it is the subduer of the warriors stationed in the enemy army who possess terrifying forms.
O Goddess, having caused all those beasts to be slain, he flies up into the sky.
Thus has the splendor of the weapons (*astralakṣmī*), which bestows renown, been fully explained to you. (What more? Shall I speak further? Tell me, O Bhairavī, O passionate lady!
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of Kālī in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of the severing of the head (*śiraścheda*) within the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairava current, in the fourth hexad.
The Goddess said:
"Nevertheless, O Lord of the gods of gods, that supreme reality has not been understood by me."
O Lord of the Gods, tell me how the secret union (*rahasyamelaka*), which bestows excellent accomplishment, is to be performed;
by which practitioners and what means it is to be accomplished—
explain this [method] that is free from arduous practices.
Having heard this, the Blessed One, who is saluted by gods and asuras,
spoke the most wonderful secret to the Goddess of the Gods.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, for I shall correctly proclaim that which has never been told before:
the stainless secret, the hidden heart of the Goddess, most excellent.
Having reached the secret place, the supreme Guru, joined by his consort (dūtī), [should proceed].

The sequence of the bali-offering rite is performed with consciousness [induced] by the bliss of wine. Having consumed the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) residing therein, one should then extract the Vidyā.
[It consists of] the double-tongued [letter] mounted on nectar, and again situated in the west (the letter va).
Blazing with the point (bindu) of the fire of time, together with the sound (nāda) and the thunderbolt (śakraka),
with the bindu and the praṇava at the end of its head, the earring (kuṇḍala) situated on the arm,
joined with the fallen moon— this is the Vidyā, the most excellent of all.
The Mistress of the Gods, possessing three and a half colors, the universal form of great splendor,
is to be worshipped in the primordial support through the yoga of my nature and existence.
Having performed the highly delightful libation mantra, it should be perfumed with flowers and incense.
Adorned with cloths such as curtains and beautified by a canopy above,
she— having been brought there, honored, and made to lie on her back,
full of longing, beautifully flowered, provided with excellent betel, and decorated with sandalwood paste from the Malaya mountains and other substances— [was placed there].
Then, having purified its support by churning the water of the wheel,
one should worship the Goddess Kālī, the supreme source of the universe,
who resides there— deep red, auspicious, and adorned with all ornaments.
Having properly [worshipped] her who bears manifold forms and is intensely longing for the five nectars,
the king should thereafter recite the vidyā with all the offerings due to a hero.
Having become absorbed in mind upon the *tallaja*, one should mutter the mudrā of the one afflicted by desire (*kāmāturā*).
In this manner, when exactly three *muhūrtas* have passed,
she shall blossom within the lord of practitioners (*sādhakeśvara*) as the lineage of Vācadrasmī.
He manifests everything, both external and internal; of this there is no doubt.
Herein occurs the most wonderful meeting known as the secret;
thus, in all circumstances, the meeting is never lost.
The union of this [deity] who is already united is "melāpa," yet he is also "milita" through that union.
Due to the union of rays like those of Śiva, it is celebrated here as "melāpa.
It is called "rahasya" (the secret) because it is secret; it is "sarahasya" (possessing the secret) and "rahasyavat" (endowed with the secret).
Through absorption into that secret, one becomes a partaker of the stainless secret.
By virtue of participating in the assembly of the *siddhis*, one becomes a *siddha-aṅganā*, a *siddha-vīra*, established in *siddhi*, and a confluence of *siddhis*.
One is the crown jewel of the family of the wheel of *siddhis*, having attained the assembly of the *siddhis*.

He who is senior in the family, or accompanied by a senior, or through conjunction with a senior brother, or who partakes in the senior *melāpa*—he indeed becomes senior; this is not at all surprising.
When one who has ascended the nine families (*navakula*) performs this sequence, [the result follows].
On the path that carries the nine seats, one who is intent on the nine peaks—
thus, in each and every new [encounter], there shall be a secret assembly (*melaka*).
While they wander together, while he wanders, indeed, as he himself wanders.
For those who do not wander [to the assembly] are indeed wandering, while those who do wander are truly passing their time [in vain].
Thus, the lord of practitioners who engages in the secret *melāpa* becomes fully accomplished. All that was previously stated regarding the detailed ritual procedure for the *melāpa* [applies here].
O beloved, in all ritual procedures,
there is no distinction here between those means and human efforts;
such is the secret union in the *Jayadratha*, the king of tantras.
O fair-browed one, I have told you this; what else shall I tell you?

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of Melāpakālī in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra concerning the Severing of the Head (*śiraścheda*), within the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairava current, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] version, in the fourth hexad.
(146a) The Goddess said:
O Hara, crest-jewel of the moon, I now desire to hear [from you].
She who is the attractor of all, Kālī, the bringer of the end of Time—
by the mere remembrance of whom the world is swiftly attracted— O Goddess worshipped by all the immortals, please tell me of her out of your grace.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O slender-waisted one; I shall tell you of the all-attracting [mantra].
Having gone to the abode of Hara, one should extract the vidyā from there.
The first [syllable] is the Yoni (V) joined with Fire (R), marked by the Bindu and the Praṇava (OṂ).
Again, having extracted the first [syllable] as the Yoni (V), it is well-situated at the end.
This word should be made twofold; the third [syllable] is joined with three Bindus (M).
In the same way, having extracted the *vāhna* (the letter *va*), likewise the solitary *kālādya* (the letter *ka*),
the *bāhu* (the letter *ba*) joined with *kālāgni* (the letter *ra*), and the *musala* (the letter *ma*) joined with three dots (*bindu*);
then, having extracted *mahāmoha* (the letter *ma*), it is capable of attracting the entire world.
This eleven-syllable vidyā is the destroyer of great sins;
she is renowned by the name Bharūḍī, Kālī, the cutter of Time (Kāla).
Holding a noose and a goad, she is fierce and uniquely skilled at swallowing the universe.
She holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, has a great serpent as her girdle, and is mounted upon a massive corpse.
She is exceedingly emaciated, with reddish-brown eyes,
resembling a mass of vermilion, and adorned in all her limbs.
The auspicious Goddess, who has emerged from the single root of the letter *ka* and others within the triangle,
is to be worshipped with all the offerings for heroes, such as wine, meat, and fermented liquors. Thereafter, one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with human beings, goats, sheep, and fish.
Or, O Goddess of the Gods, if [the signs] are unmanifest, one should then begin the practice:
staying within a cave, one should recite the Vidyā three hundred thousand times without weariness.
Then one should perform the previously mentioned fire-offering (*homa*), and it will be accomplished with ease.
From that time forward, the lord of heroes (*vīrendra*) may wander about and forcibly attract women by the power of the God and Goddess.
Within seven days, by means of recitation and fire-offerings on the festival of lamps,
the practitioner can always effortlessly attract Naga maidens from the abode of the Nagas.
By offering black mustard seeds and salt into the fire, he may attract the wives of the gods.
A king or royal consorts may draw [the world] toward them through the yoga of recitation (*japa*).
By means of the power of the vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*), through its mastery and abiding, and by means of the hook (*aṅkuśa*) and the complete withdrawal [of the senses],
one may draw in the afflicted world when it appears in a state of agitation.
By this heroic yoga and through the power of the Great Vidyā,
O auspicious one, there is nothing that she does not attract in an instant.
Thus, Saṃkarṣaṇī Kālī is the supreme attractor of all.
O highly fortunate one, today the secret [of this] has been revealed to you.
This powerful *ākarṣaṇī* (the power of attraction), which draws in this entire world—
this very power that attracts all— has been revealed to you today.
"What should be said? Speak, O you who are worshipped by all the lords of heroes!
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of Sarvākarṣakālī in the fourth Ṣaṭka of the Jayadrathayāmala.
The Śrī Devī said:"
"O Lord, destroyer of Tripura, I now desire to hear about the attraction of living beings (*jīvākarṣa*),
which is extremely fierce and causes complete desiccation;
O God, tell this to me in its entirety."
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, for I shall speak as I have been urged by you today;
it must be guarded with great effort, just as wealth is protected from thieves.
This is the procedure for Hālāhala, intent upon the destruction of the world;
having gone to the terrible charnel ground, one should extract the vidyā there.
One should indeed extract the syllable *jihva* (j) along with the end of the cutter (*k*), joined with creation (*s*) and the heart (*h*).
Likewise, one should extract *śakra* (ś), conjoined with *nāda* (ḥ) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*, i).
Again, one should extract the solitary *nāda* (ḥ), conjoined with *śakra* (ś) and the house of fire (*r*).
One should raise up only the arm joined with the goad of time (*kālamaṅkuśa*).
[The sequence is: *samīraṇa*, *karttana*, and *nāda-karttana*;
then again *nāda-kevalin* and the restrained *bhīmaśaṅku*.
This fourteen-syllable vidyā is intent upon attracting living beings;
by the mere remembrance of it, one may slay even the gods and asuras.
She is cruel, terrible, has Great Death as her vehicle, and possesses a frowning face.
With hair standing erect, with terrifying eyes, and with a winnowing basket in her hand, she is exceedingly fierce;
she bears a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, wielding a formidable sword,
with a great thunderbolt held busy in her hand, resembling a black female crow.

They fashion Śakulā, whose form is terrifying with fleshless bones, who brings about the destruction of the three worlds; her limbs are smeared with the members of corpses, she is adorned with a necklace of serpents,
and she creates a mass of great flames.
Drinking the host of living beings and chewing them here as its cause—
having thus meditated upon the fierce Hālāhala poison, one should worship at night with all-black offerings on a well-heated patch of ground.
Having thus worshipped Ghorēśī with divine surā, meat, and fermented liquors, and with great offerings of incense, one should afterwards present the object to be accomplished.
One should fashion a vessel made of eight *māṣa*-weights of gold, covered with red silk, and fixed with a ritual stake (*kīla*).
"O Goddess, it should be said: 'The sacrificial animal, designated as a person, gives [himself].
Having been addressed thus, she should then cut off his head with a sharp sword.
At that very moment, she became the snatcher of life even for Indra.
By such a rite as this, one may slay gods and asuras;
this method of killing is declared to be irreversible.
O Goddess, I shall now explain the rite of withering according to its true meaning.
One should extract the Vidyā that withers even the three worlds as before:
[the syllable] ending in Varuṇa (va), situated upon Śakra (ra), and marked by the Mohanī (ī) and the Bindu (ṃ).
Kāla joined with Bindu, and again, Amṛta alone;
then having extracted Varuṇa, likewise Amṛta with Aṅkuśa;
and Kālādya, Saṃhāra, and Harṣa marked with three Bindus.
Again, having extracted the first [syllable] of *Kāla*, one should extract the last of all [the syllables] again.
This twelve-syllabled Vidyā consists of *Samīraṇa* and *Bhīmaśaṅku*.
One should meditate upon this *Śoṣaṇī*, which withers all worlds and reaches the end of terrible sounds.
One should meditate upon her who has the appearance of dry smoke, who dwells in a terrible darkness,
who stands upon a wheel of wind, who possesses universal forms, and who wears hand-bells; by this yoga of meditation, one may dry up the wondrous world.
By means of the *jaṃpuṭa* application, one causes the enemy to waste away through recitation;
drying him out completely, one shall kill him who is withering away—of this there is no doubt.
O Dear One, he will be utterly exhausted within seven days at all times.
Thus has the Karaṅkiṇī of terrible form been described in its most secret aspect. Next, I shall explain the "Severing of Sleep," which is intent upon the slaying of the enemy.
Having extracted the letter Ṛ (ṛ) preceded by *u* (u), one places the letter *kuṃ* (k) situated in fire (*ra*).
That [syllable] is joined with the *bindu* of its own house (*veśma*), endowed with the *sṛṣṭi* (the letter *sa*).
Having given the *kartana* (the letter *kṣa*) alone, conjoined with *nāda* and *bindu*;
the *kartana* (the letter *kṣa*) which is the seat of the fifth (*paṃcamāśīna*), and *nāda* conjoined with the destruction of fire (*vahnikṣaya*).
O Dear One, that most terrible knowledge (*vidyā*) suppresses even Bhīmaśaṃ;
there is nothing it does not accomplish, from courtesanship to the end of death.

In whatever manner one should contemplate the universal form, by that very means one performs the rite; this is the truth, there is no doubt about it. Having indeed assumed the very nature of the enemy through the *āmātaka* [mantra], one acts accordingly.
Having written the name encircled by the mantra in vermilion and charcoal,

joined with the [mantra] syllables, and having placed it within a well-prepared belly [of dough], by burying it at the base of the hearth, whatever is desired by the practitioner [shall be accomplished].
Within half a night, the death of the enemy occurs; he lives in terror.
This must not be given to just anyone by one following the irreversible method;
the giver attains the hell called Sāda for eight years.

Thus has been fully explained to you the great and formidable triad of powers (śaktitraya), which is a supreme secret, incomparable, and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Now speak, O fair-hipped Bhairavī; what more shall I tell you?

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of Jīvākarṣikālī in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the fourth hexad of the *Śiraścheda* section of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavaśrotas*.
The Goddess said:
Again my mind desires to hear that which destroys the poison of worldly afflictions.
Who indeed is that goddess Ekavīrā? Tell me how she destroys the limbs of desire.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, I shall fully declare the supreme destroyer of all obstacles, which has not been told to anyone; today I shall tell it to you.
One should extract the nectar-seed situated in Varuṇa and located in Śakra.
O Great Goddess, this *piṇḍa*, marked by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth, consists of the six vowels and the consonants;
it is the nectar itself extracted in person.

Having ignited only the letter *kāla* (*k*), make the tongue (*jihvā*) reside within itself (*ātma-ga*). Then, having raised the arm, take *sāṅkuśa* (*sa*), *gaṇeśa* (*ga*), the first of the five (*pa*), together with the bindu (*m*), and *nāda* (*u*), along with the letter of Varuṇa (*va*) joined with three bindus (*m*).

The Sun and Moon are to be placed; the Sun with a bindu (visarga) at the navel, and the Moon joined with the creation (the vowel 'i'), should be made. This ten-syllabled Vidyā [destroys] thousands of loads of poison and hundreds of loads of semen.
O fortunate one, by her grace, the practitioner may consume [even poison] in abundance.
O Goddess of gods, having propitiated her in the past upon the summit of Mount Mandara,
Garuḍa thereby obtained the power to devour poison.

By the grace of this very [goddess], O fortunate one, the lineage of nāgas was spared from being devoured by Garuḍendra through the favor of Karaṅkiṇī. One should meditate upon her as pure as a crystal from the snowy mountain.
Fleshless, mounted upon Garuḍa, adorned with the limbs of Śiva,
her body variegated by necklaces of serpents, bearing a jar of nectar,
with the moon and sun at the ends of her hands, and holding a noose and a goad— [I meditate on] the auspicious Goddess.

Having worshipped the Goddess in the mandala with all the offerings for heroes— She who possesses manifold forms, who pervades the universe, who brings about the end of time, who is auspicious, who is variegated and adorned, who is wondrous, and who is the means for accomplishing diverse deeds;
One should offer oblations of sesame and rice with various kinds of liquor, meat, and fermented spirits.
Thus she is declared to be the bestower of success and always the warder-off of calamities;
just as the serpents behold the Son of Vinatā as a terrifying being.
Therefore, O Goddess, the Nāgas constantly behold the practitioner with ten-millionfold intensity;
by this, he destroys the three kinds of objects through mere sight.
By administering poison and water, he [destroys] those known as Śaṅka and the people of Yama.
The Dākinī has ear-lobes, and the Bhūta and Rākṣasa have eyes.
Thus, the most terrible goddess has been described to you according to her true nature.
"What else shall I say now? Speak, O you who are worshipped by the lords of heroes!
Having heard this from the three-eyed God of gods, that goddess, with a gracious countenance, spoke again with reverence to the Lord of the worlds:

"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the play (*villāsa*) in the union of yoga (*yogamelaka*), and that incomparable ritual procedure (*vidhāna*); O Lord of Heroes (*vīrendra*), speak of it without delay.
Having heard this, the one who removes the suffering of the world replied once more:
The incomparable Great Assembly (mahāmelāpa), the radiance designated as Yoga.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, I shall fully explain the supreme Great Assembly.
O fortunate one, by the recitation of which one becomes the Lord of the Lords of Heroes:
having gone to the abode of Hara at night, one should extract the Vidyā there;
having placed it within the mouth of Kāla, one stands in the midst of the funeral pyre of the bride.
Then one should extract the Great Vidyā that attracts all yoginīs.
One should place the threefold Śakra at the beginning and end of everything, and again provide the first of everything.
Again, one should apply the mark of Śakra’s delusion, and again make the first of everything.

Again, make Śakra (Ś) marked with three dots (ṃ), followed by that [letter] preceded by the first [vowel]. Likewise, [make] Varuṇa (V) ending [with a dot], and likewise the fifth [consonant] preceded by the first [vowel] together with a goad (anusvāra).
Again, indeed [make] Varuṇa (V) ending [with a dot], and Niṣedha (S) joined with three dots (ṃ).
Having again given the first [letter] from the third [position], and having placed the horse (ha) situated in the mace (sa),
marked by the house of fire (ra), and having placed the earring (ṇa) in the fifth position,
this sixteen-syllable Vidyā should be formed, joined with the Great Creation (mahāsṛṣṭi).
Exceedingly radiant and terrible, she is intent upon attracting the world.
Within the interior of the universe, no one exists who is more intensely luminous than she.
She bears a thousand arms and is formidable with a thousand faces.
Extremely emaciated, possessing all forms, that terrible one with five faces stands there;
having placed the birds in the form of *cillara* upon her outstretched wings. (149b)
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Great Raudrī on the petal; there,
one should offer the fresh supreme goddess with all the offerings for heroes,
and sacrifice the king of men, smeared with oil, as the *cillā* meat.
Thereafter, a small cavity should be made in the mortar, contracted [in shape] like a *cilla* bird.
For the purpose of incense, the Heroic Leader (*vīranāyaka*),
having empowered it one thousand times with the mantra, should then go to the abode of the ancestors (*pitṛgṛha*) together with young *kesara* flowers.
O Supreme Goddess, the preeminent practitioner, his consciousness intoxicated with the bliss of wine and filled with pride,
should take recourse to the altar there, bind the Karaṅkiṇī mudrā,
and burn incense throughout the night.

At that time, millions of Yoginīs— Cillā-rūpā and Mahābalā— arrive, O Goddess of the gods, making the sound "kāla-kalā. One should offer them the arghya water by piercing the left side of one's own body.
Then, choosing them [as consorts], they do not indeed frighten him;
having requested a boon from them, he should always depart.
Having assumed a body through the power of yoga, O Lord of Yoga, he sports wherever he pleases.
Thus has the play of the union of yoga been fully explained to you. What else shall I tell you? Speak, O daughter of the mountain!
Thus [ends] the fourth hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraścheda* of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavaśrotas*.
The chapter on the ritual procedure for Melāpakālī.
The venerable Goddess said:
"Now I wish to hear, O one worshipped by the gods, [the method] for bringing the world under control."
O Lord Mahādeva, by what means do those who are not noble run away from that which abides throughout the three worlds? Please tell me this now through your grace.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Supreme Goddess, to this [mantra] of great power which brings the world under control,
by means of which the women of the three worlds are always brought into a state of agitation.
Listen briefly to that Ghorāpañcaśarakālī.
Having taken recourse to an auspicious spot on the earth, one should indeed extract there the supreme Kālī, the auspicious one who puts the world to flight, from the Mātṛkā.

Having extracted the *cāpādya* (the base of the bow) in two ways and joined it with a *bindu*, there is the "Great Power" (*mahābala*). Likewise, another is joined with a hook (*aṅkuśa*) and enveloped by delusion (*mohana*).
There is the "Kandala" [seed-syllable] upon which Indra has ascended, possessing three *bindus* and adorned with a *bindu*.
Ending with Kuṇḍalā, situated in Śakra, and joined with the great fivefold [set];
joined with five sets of five, it is the nectar conjoined with creation.
This is declared to be the five-syllabled [mantra], intent upon the dissolution of the world.
O Goddess of gods, this is that Kālikā of yours, eternally moist;
she has been declared according to the ultimate truth as the supreme Mahāvidrāvaṇī.
This goddess, the great accomplisher of subjugation (vaśya), has been extracted exactly as she truly is.
I do not see her equal anywhere in the mighty seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha).
She causes the flight of celestial women and the infatuation even of the gods.
One should worship this slender-waisted goddess as residing in the center of the triangular lotus.
O observer of excellent vows, with great abundance of wealth such as wine, meat, and spirits,
and with all red-colored offerings and the conduct of the heroes (vīrācāra),
one should meditate upon her who stands in the center of the triangle, possessing a radiance like that of lac-dyed red.
Extremely emaciated, with a single face and eyes resembling the three sacrificial fires,
she is fierce, holding a noose and a goad, and with her hands raised, bearing a bow and arrows; she is the enchantress,
the witherer, the liquefier, and likewise the moistener.
These five arrows, beginning with Kṣobhaṇa, should be held in the hand;
one should contemplate Jagallakṣmī, Nityā, Kālī, and Maholvaṇā.

Having meditated thus and worshipped in this manner, one shall become equal to Kāmadeva; by the mere sight of her, the practitioner shall agitate the entire universe. A teacher should never recall her in this way.
She who is the agitator of the three worlds, having become the very essence of the embryo;
at whose agitation the lords of the gods, asuras, and pannagas tremble,
their bodies overwhelmed by the fever of passion’s fire and intoxication.
They constantly flow with streams of seminal fluid and blood, and so forth; they all run, tremble, and droop at the mere sight [of the object].

O auspicious lady, by the perfect recollection of her, women [attain their goal]. Therefore, one should always remember that most fierce goddess, the cause of agitation, dwelling within the mountain caves.
He who has not entered even the forest of desire is one whose desire is well-mastered; though situated within the lineage of desire, he is the lord of desires.
He possesses infinite forms of desire, the very essence of the art of desire.
The Lord of Desire is eternally the agitator;
dwelling in the midst of various and wonderful garments,
he expands within the abode of his own bliss.
The Lord of all worlds, abiding as Kulakālikā at the pinnacle of light, shall inundate the entire universe;
he is the solar orb within the interior of the hexagonal wheel.
In her mind,
which is like a forest-fire for the fuel of the mantra-family, she is the fire that consumes desire;
she is the great and fierce one in the form of Kālī, who causes total dissolution.
From the power of the song,
even the intoxicated elephant flees upon seeing her terrifying form;
thus, through the power of the mantra, the Śākta immersion brings about all effects.
Thus, O Supreme Goddess, the rite named Vidrāvaṇī has been described by you in the Jayadratha,
the King of Tantras, together with its great secret. Tell me, what more shall I speak now, O you who are worshipped by all the Vīras?

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of Nityākālī in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra of the Severed Head (*Śiraścheda*) within the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairava Current, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the fourth hexad.
The Śrī Devī said: O Supreme Lord, please describe now Kālī— the fierce one who causes agitation and destroys the evil dreams of the Kali age— for I desire to hear it.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, for I shall tell you that for which you have requested:
Mahākālī, Hanakālī, and likewise Mahākṣobhaharī.

O highly fortunate one, this *piṇḍa* consists of Mahānāda mounted upon Vahni, which in turn rests upon Kālānala; it is joined with the three *padas* and endowed with Bindu and Nāda. This *piṇḍa* is intent upon the protection of the three worlds.
The fire-syllable (RA) joined with the fifth vowel (Ū), followed by the bow (CA) situated in fire (RA),
struck at the head by the goad (A), and marked with three dots (M)—
this five-syllabled supreme goddess is restrained by the formidable spike (KṢA).
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess, who is white as a bright cloud, the moon, snow, or a conch shell; she is seated upon a white lotus throne,
possesses four arms and one face, and is radiant with three eyes.
One should worship the supreme *kalā*, who holds a noose and a goad, who is fierce, adorned by the rays of the moon and sun, who rains down the essence of the nectar of all prosperity,
who resides within the water-pot (*kalaśa*), and who is intent on bestowing grace upon the world.

Having worshipped her who is endowed with all ornaments, the support of all, and possessed of great power, and having consecrated a water-pot filled with milk while reciting the mantra a hundred times,
one should then sprinkle oneself with it, O Supreme Goddess.
For one who has just been consecrated by that [rite], all prosperities arise.
It is the pacifier of great diseases, the destroyer of great delusion,
the crusher of the ill-omened dreams of the Kali age, and the eradicator of royal calamities.
The destruction of diseases such as poison and leprosy,
the warding off of all untimely death, and the eradication of planetary afflictions and insanity—
this sealing and unsealing is proclaimed as the object of meditation known as consecration (abhiṣeka).
O noble lady, it is taught that for others as well, this consecration brings about all prosperity,
removes agitation, and increases all good fortune.

This goddess Sarvasiddhi, who was previously described, will accomplish [all goals] through one hundred thousand recitations, O Mistress of the Gods; there is nothing she cannot achieve. This Supreme Goddess has been declared to you as the bestower of liberation.
"What else shall I tell you? Speak, O fair-eyed one!

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for Śāntikālī in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, a great tantra concerning the severing of the head (*śiraścheda*) within the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairava tradition, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] collection, in the fourth Ṣaṭka.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, tell me now the definitive determination of the supreme syllable (paramākṣara).
How is it the self, and how indeed is it the designator of that Goddess?
Bhairava said:
Listen, I shall tell you the supreme heart of the Goddess—
Kālī, who devours the world within the lineage of the Supreme Sun.
Having worshipped them in the vast abode, the Supreme Goddess should extract them—
adorned with the end of all things, the fire of time (Kālāgni), the bindu, and the nāda.
This is declared to be the supreme heart of the God and Goddess, which bestows excellent accomplishment.
The Āṣacha [mantra], blazing like a mongoose, consuming the brilliance of twelve suns,
is declared to be the Lord of Rays (Raśminātha), the supreme heart of the Goddess.
She is that supreme Kālī, the ultimate digit who devours all.
Karaṅkiṇī, Ghoracaṇḍā, Kālī, the bringer of the destruction of Time;
she is utterly withered, with sunken eyes, blazing with the fire of the three eyes;
she bears a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, adorned with human skulls.
Her hands are busily occupied with a great lotus; she is a voracious devourer who swallows the three worlds.
Mounted upon a great corpse, she is the solitary heroine, intensely fierce.
She pacifies the afflictions of the world and flows as the vital breath in the central channel.
(152a) Beyond conduct, without division, the supreme digit whose nature is consciousness;
the Goddess who grants all accomplishments, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

One should sacrifice to her, remember her, and recite her mantra at all times, O Dear One. O Mistress of the Gods, there is no such thing on the path of the lineage of reality that cannot be accomplished by her through mere recitation, O Maheśvarī.
Subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, killing, and expulsion;
likewise, paralyzing, stunning, agitating, deluding, and pinning down;
as well as the destruction of poison and the great driving away of serpents.
The discovery of treasures and hidden deposits, the supreme rousing of a vetāla,
the attainment of the great kiṃkara-siddhi, and the highest siddhi of the cāraṇa;
the power to travel through the netherworld and the sky, and the accomplishment of the aṇimā and other supernatural powers.
The disappearance of shadows, the accomplishment of *yakṣa*-powers, the practice of *ceṭaka* spirits,
the attainment of messengers, the mastery of *bhūta* spirits, forced summonings (*haṭhamelāpaka*), and so forth—
[all these are achieved] through red and black offerings, such as wine, meat, and fermented liquors.
She who dwells within the lineage of the Kāmāraṇi family, whom living beings there [seek];
or she who, by means of the method of devouring, devours the Great Sun;
the thirteen-fold destroyer, the withered one, the Supreme Bhairavī.
That which exists beyond both consciousness and unconsciousness is the devourer of the sun of the *kalās*.
Having devoured this entire world of moving and non-moving beings by means of her,
she then becomes, through that act of devouring, like a devourer of both the edible and the inedible.

By the very process of eating all things, she will become the devourer of all. Now, O Goddess, listen to how that best of heroes shall accomplish the supreme heart-mantra of the Goddess while subsisting on begged alms.
First, one should extract the syllable ḌAṂBARA, ending with all [the vowels] and situated in fire (VA).
That which is joined with the bindu is likewise proclaimed as MOHANĪ. Having again placed all that which precedes, one should extract the solitary lunar (CA) syllable.

The sixth [letter] with the first [vowel], likewise the moon [letter] with the beginning of time [vowel], and the one with three dots; at the end of all is the letter *ku* stepped upon by *śa*, adorned with the bindu.

This twelve-syllable Vidyā consists of: the bow (ca), fire (ā), the house (pa), the mark (ya), the sound (na) adorned with three vowels (ā-ī-u), preceded by the womb (yo), and joined with creation (sṛ).
One who always dwells on the outskirts of a village should consecrate the vessel with this mantra.
Having consecrated it one hundred times with the mantra, there is nothing that one cannot attract by means of it.
Indeed, for the sake of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one should recite it ten thousand times;
from then on, whatever food one desires shall be obtained.
O Goddess of the gods, if one’s mind is free from impurity through the grace of the Goddess,
one should perform the *piṇḍayātrā* at the beginning of such rites for the accomplishment of the goal.
O Sovereign of the Gods, one should employ those [methods] taught in this Tantra as well as those arising from other Tantras.
By this method, one should accomplish the Supreme Goddess in yoga.
She who accomplishes the universe is the perfectly accomplished, all-pervading Śivā;
she will effortlessly bring to fruition those known as middling, inferior, and superior.
Bhairavī, the destroyer of the flood of great sins, has been realized by me.
The supreme Consciousness, ever-auspicious, unfolds eternally in the highest abode.
Possessing a formidable and steady power, she bestows the accomplishment of all desires and goals.
And in the three eyes, O Goddess of Gods, she is remembered as the one who brings the world under her control. This has been fully explained to you; what else do you wish to ask?
Thus, in the Bhairava-śrotas, in the Vidyāpīṭha, in the Śiraścheda, in the Jayadrathayāmala Mahātantra, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the fourth Ṣaṭka.
The Ritual Manual of the Goddess Paramākṣarā.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
Kālī, marked with three eyes, is uniquely established as the subduer of the world.
I desire to hear that; by the grace of my Lord, please speak it to me.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, I shall tell you as I have been requested by you:
that Netrakālī, who holds the world under her control, resides within my three eyes;
she remains at will, sporting within the interior of the moon, sun, and fire.
Make the nectar (*amṛta*) joined with fire (*vahni*) and conjoined with creation (*sṛṣṭi*) twofold.
Between these two is the supreme one called *ḍaṃbara*, which deludes the world. These three syllables are declared to you as Netrakālī, who holds the world under her control.

The Supreme Goddess, who brings the universe under her control, is said to effect this through mere ritual placement (*nyāsa*) alone— without doubt— by uniting with the ultimate abode of rest, *Cicci*. As she ascends through the three abodes, she is filled with hundreds of shimmering rays of light.
By the projection of the supreme rays, one may subdue the world of the moving and the unmoving.
Through the yoga of the three stations, she is threefold; she is the threefold fire, the threefold beginning, and the threefold attractor.
She is consciousness in the three stations, and thus she brings about the subjugation of the senses from the heart.

Mounted upon a swan, a swan-rider, having ascended the swan like a swan; having likewise joined the *haṃsa* within the two eyes of the *haṃsa*, one who partakes of that *haṃsa* becomes a master of the world. He who enjoys that [state]—in the beginning, end, and middle of his body—[is liberated].
Thus, mounted upon the supreme yoga, one shall bring under control all that is moving and unmoving.
Now, the procedure for even one devoid of yoga is stated:
one should meditate, without weariness, upon the incomparable self in the form of the Goddess.
And that goddess had the luster of molten lac and vermilion;
she was perfectly complete with four faces, surrounded by twelve eyes,
well-endowed with eight arms, and adorned with all ornaments.

One should then meditate upon that goddess of gods, who possesses a universal form, holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, joined with a noose, a goad, and a bow; she is marked with an arrow, a sword, and a sphoṭaka, and is mounted upon a great corpse (mahāpreta). One should contemplate her thus.
Having meditated thus, one should install [the deities] within the body, flowing like the movement of prāṇa and apāna;
thereafter, those residing in the maṇḍala are to be worshipped with wine, meat, fermented liquors, and so forth.
One should indeed offer karavīra flowers for the complete satisfaction of the Goddess.
Afterwards, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times; having performed the oblation, perfection is attained.
Thus perfected, the [mantra] residing in the eyes can bring under control all things, both moving and unmoving.
O auspicious one, by merely beholding her, no further deliberation is required here.
Whomever she meditates upon or gazes at, she will make that person her servant.
Upon seeing an approaching enemy intent on killing her, she shall delude him in an instant.
This supreme goddess, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, agitates the universe;
she protects the three worlds and grants great good fortune. Through the power of her ritual practice, she will swiftly accomplish all attainments and the like.
Just as the goddess Nidhīśvarī is proclaimed, so too is she described.
Thus has Netrakālī, the bestower of perfect accomplishment, been fully explained to you.
What else shall I tell you? Speak, O you who are worshipped by the lords of heroes!

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of Netrakālī in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the fourth hexad of the *Śiraścheda* section of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavaśrotas*.
The venerable Goddess said:

Who is this goddess named Nidhīśvarī Kālī, possessed of terrible prowess? O Lord, how does she, the bestower of all accomplishments, grant the attainment of treasures? Tell me everything along with its secret, O All-pervading One; I have no doubt remaining.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent! I shall speak as I have been urged by you.
Listen, O Kālī of great power, who is known by the name Kubera-jananī.
Having reached an auspicious place, one should worship the Mother of Mantras;
thereafter, one should extract the Vidyā adorned with twenty-four syllables.
Having extracted the three qualities (triguṇa) as the full [syllable], one should extract the bow together with the arrow.
Then the mouth of the well (kūpavaktra), which is the bow adorned with three dots (bindus).
Mohanī is illuminated by the bindu; Ghorā is like the fire of time (kālāgni).
Furthermore, one should cause the crown of the head to be marked with three dots (niṣedha).
Then, the bow joined with the *māyā* (ī) and situated upon Varuṇa (va), adorned with three dots, is the arm; thus, the cutting [mantra] consists of five syllables.
One should extract Varuṇa (va), the body of Vahni (ra), and the solitary arm (bha).
Afterward, one should extract Dvijihva (pha) and perform the negation twice (ṣa ṣa).
Then, one should take Agni (ra) as the first part, conjoined with the vowel of the mantra (e), and struck by the goad (a).
Furthermore, one should extract the arm, the solitary one, and the wind, the solitary one;
indeed, the first of the sixth [letter], established upon fire and conjoined with Dāruṇa. That again, deprived of fire, is in the wind, and then the strength.
O beautiful one, Bhīmaśaṅku should subsequently be given in three parts.
Thus has the goddess Nidhīśvarī been explained according to the ultimate truth;
she is Kālī, the mother of Kubera, the supreme attractor of treasures.
This [goddess] consists of twenty-four syllables; she is of terrible form, difficult to approach, arisen from the wheel of the *kanda*, fearsome, and a voracious devourer of the three worlds.
She possesses the radiance of tens of millions upon tens of millions of the blazing fires at the end of an aeon.
With terrifying fangs from which she spits forth a fearsome fire like that of the end of an aeon;
with eyes like waves, foam, bubbles, and whirlpools of molten gold;
and formidable with hair as fierce as falling thunderbolts and sharp needles.
Resembling the sky at the end of time or the throat of Śrīkaṇṭha,
her form is loathsome with sinews ending in semen;
her face is formidable, and she is terrifying with the sound of her hissing, as she is intent on shattering the pot of the universe.
Resplendent with a noose, a goad, a great begging bowl, and a khaṭvāṅga in her hands,
she holds a mace, a thunderbolt, a great skull, and a human corpse in her palms. (154b)
Seated upon the shoulder of Kubera, situated in the midst of a multitude of treasures,
her body resplendent amidst a cluster of great jewels,
she draws forth even those treasures located in the realm of the Nāgas.
Having meditated thus, O beautiful one, one should perform the oblation with the splendors of worship according to the conduct of a hero (*vīrācāra*),
joined with the mudrā and adorned with the noose and goad.
O Supreme Goddess, the great earth, the recitation, and the others are the three-eyed ones.
If, having gone to the best of mountains, one recites [the mantra] five hundred thousand times,
then by the grace of the God and Goddess, one attains the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratā*).
O fortunate one, by three hundred thousand recitations, all the middling *siddhis* are attained.
They are accomplished; there is no doubt here, for my word is infallible.
O fortunate one, by a hundred thousand recitations, one becomes a lord of treasures.
Having gone to the location where the treasure is situated, one should scatter mustard seeds there.
Having recited the mantra over a hundred gems sprinkled with milk, one should cast them into a vessel;
O slender-waisted lady, just as they remain untouched by the feet,
so too should the oblation mixed with fish be cast there after sleeping.
Then, at the time of dawn, or after seven days,
wherever the mustard seeds gather together, there one should direct the mind.
From a heap of jewels, the *liṅga* [appears] like the full moon within a great treasure.
The *ardhacandra* should be golden, the *padma* a collection of dust-colored [powder],
and that which is circular in shape is known by the name *chidrāvila* located in the center.
Having understood [the mandala] through these characteristics, one should thereafter begin the practice (*sādhana*).
One should perform the binding of the directions with mantras using consecrated ashes and mustard seeds,
or else with stalks, ropes, or auspicious stakes made of khadira wood.
Then, one should worship the Goddess of the Gods with all the offerings appropriate for heroes.
One should offer oblations there of mustard seeds mixed with poison and rock salt;
then, absorbed in meditation, one should further recite the mantra of great power.
By means of a thousand recitations, one may attract a hoard of treasures,
even if it is directly guarded by Vāsuki himself, O Śaṅkarī; indeed,
by the power of the mantra, the earth itself comes before the practitioner.
Through the power of the King of Vidyās, one will undoubtedly attain [success];
it should always be undertaken by the wise with a fearless mind.
Terrifying apparitions, fears of field-protectors (kṣetrapāla), and the like shall perish.
One should not make any accumulation here, for the earth is already filled with treasures.

O Goddess of the lords of gods, having produced [wealth], one intent on enjoyment should distribute it among the gurus, the great adepts (sādhakendra), and even among the spiritual sons (putraka), O Bhairavī.
A great accumulation of wealth should be given to those who know the *samaya*.
One should personally perform the *bhairava-yāgas* day after day.
Temples for the deities should be constructed, as well as ponds, wells, water-stations, and cisterns.
One should always give to the poor, the helpless, and to those who beg;
at all times, the minister must maintain the discourse on the treasury.
He should never remain idle for even a single moment.
Therefore, this cycle of existence is impermanent, terrible in form, and most dreadful;
this life is impermanent, as are youth and prosperity.
For this reason, one should cultivate devotion to Śiva, the remover of all inauspiciousness.
In the paths of Mantra, and especially in those of Bhairavī,
one must recognize that all this transmigratory existence is indeed unstable, consisting of the three phases [of creation, maintenance, and dissolution],
seized by the fear of old age and disease, and afflicted by grief and exhaustion.
O slender-waisted one, having reflected that [the world] is scorched by the fire of the threefold suffering,
one should firmly take refuge in the auspicious path of the Great Maheśvara;
everything else must be abandoned, for life is transient.
One should certainly take recourse in the path, the measure, and the yoga, O Bhairavī.
Thus has this been fully explained to you; what else do you wish to ask?

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for Kuberajanani, within the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, a great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses belonging to the *Śiraścheda* division of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavaśrotas*.
The Goddess said:
Now I wish to hear the Heart-Essence that grants desires,
the essence that bestows all accomplishments, and that which grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Bhairava said:
I shall now explain, as the occasion has arrived, the Heart-mantra known as Mardani,
which is most terrible, unsurpassed, and practiced by all heroes.
O Goddess, having gone to a cemetery, the wise one who delights in the conduct of a hero [should proceed].
Having rubbed the earth with the Kaṅkāla [mantra], one should extract it.
The Dvijiha [mantra] is encased in fire and marked with a Bindu;
thus is the Vīra, the best of syllables, the supreme heart of the Goddess.

One should meditate on her as being without heart, head, crest-lock, skin, eyes, or other limbs; she is fierce, arisen from the *kanda*, and the destroyer who brings about the end of the three worlds.
She has three eyes, is fanged, and is adorned with eight arms.
She wears a garland of human entrails, is adorned with a necklace of ploughs, and sits upon a great corpse. Fierce, she holds a skull-bowl and a khaṭvāṅga staff;
her hands are busy with a vajra and a goad, and she wears an elephant hide. She is auspicious.

One should then meditate upon her who has a mouth filled with human entrails, who resembles a crow or a cuckoo, who is famished by the winds at the end of the aeon, whose splendor is equal to twelve suns,
who possesses the universal form (viśvarūpa), and who assumes whatever form is desired.

Having thus meditated upon her— who is adorned by the eight *kulanāgas* and who is the supreme bestower of all accomplishments— one should worship her within the interior of the hexagonal world with all the offerings of the heroes, such as wine, meat, and fermented liquors.
Having thus performed the worship, one should offer oblations of superior, inferior, and middling [substances].
Then, O Dear One, having gone to an excellent mountain, one should recite the mantra ten million times.

One should indeed offer the previously mentioned substance, smeared with the three [clarified butter, honey, and sugar], for the sake of accomplishment alone. At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, Śivā herself emerges from the midst of the fire;
she becomes the bestower of boons to the lord of practitioners, granting whatever fruits are desired.
If one seeks to establish [the probans] through the distinction of a middle universal (*madhyasāmānya*),
then one should prove what is desired in the mind by means of a corresponding [universal].
Alternatively, if one were to employ it for the purpose of producing a burning sensation in enemies, [it would be appropriate].
Then, one should recollect the Vidyā-mantra while mounted upon the chariot of the Pretas;
having raised the six arms, with the two at the ends accompanied by the Bindu,
O Goddess of the Gods, [holding] goads, and the sixth [syllable] joined with many [others].
That house is overcome by the head; likewise, one should extract the first five [syllables].
However, it should be devoid of fire and restrained by the Bhīma-śaṅku.
This nine-syllabled Great Vidyā is intent upon burning the world.

O Goddess of the gods, if one should indeed recite the name [of the enemy] while enveloping it with the mantra while enraged, he shall surely kill him by means of burning within seven days; there is no doubt in this.
O Beloved, having written down the name of the target (sādhya), one should smear it with poison and charcoal.

Having heated it, one should burn [the substance] placed upon a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*) intensely. Having written the name of the victim to be afflicted, O Śivā, one should place it beneath the hearth.
This causes a terrible burning fever for enemies and causes their bellies to become distorted.
This very great vidyā of immense power is the warrior for the act of slaying;
thus the Supreme Goddess should employ it at the beginning of the final rite.
In this way, [the procedure] from the midst of the Tantra-rāja has been fully explained to you.
The supreme essence is the Heart, accompanied by the Great Sub-Heart;
what else shall I say, O Mistress who moves within the wheel of speech?

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of Hṛdayakālī in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra of the Severed Head (*Śiraścheda*), within the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairava Current, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the fourth Ṣaṭka.
The Goddess said:
"Now I wish to hear about that supreme Manonmanī who is beyond sacrifice—Kālī, who resembles the fire of cosmic destruction. Tell me this today, O Lord.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Now, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme Kālī Nāgāntakī,
who destroys all great sins and liberates one from the bondage of all serpents.
O Parameśvarī, one should extract [this mantra] upon a perfectly purified plot of ground.
One should extract Bhairava conjoined with fire (ra), marked with the bindu of Mohanī (i);
then the triangle (e); then the fifth [vowel] alone (u);
then that [vowel] conjoined with fire and its abode (ra), followed by the negation (ma) struck by the goad (a).
O beautiful goddess, one should first utter Gaṇeśa alone, then Cāpādya alone again, and afterwards the Puruṣa-mantra with the syllable *ko* and *bala*. Then,
one should utter the *niṣedha* (prohibition) syllable as presided over by the three vowels (*ī*, *ū*, *ṛ*), followed by the *kuṇḍala* (the letter *k*) situated in the midst of fire (*r*).
The Great Vidyā joined with creation is proclaimed as the syllable of Rudra;
by name she is Ekatarā Kālī, possessing the splendor of ten thousand suns at the end of an aeon,
causing terror to the three worlds, and crushing spirits and vetālas.
Shining with the brilliance of ten thousand throbbing suns and possessing the splendor of the fire at the end of an aeon,
she has four faces, blazing hair, and terrifying eyes;
she is fearsome and adorned by the hissing of the hoods of great serpents with immense fangs.
She causes affliction to the eight Nāgas of the clans, adorned with a hundred snakes;
likewise, she holds a son in her hand and is resplendent with a vajra and a great goad;
her hands are busy with a noose and a sword, and she is intent upon devouring the Nāgas.
Having meditated upon her as mounted on the seat of a great preta, or as having a universal form, or even in whatever form is desired, one should worship her perfectly. (157a)

In the maṇḍala called Sarvakāmā, having worshipped either the previously mentioned [deity] or one possessing auspicious marks with various offerings of incense, liquor, meat, fermented spirits, and so forth,
one should perform oblations there using clarified butter produced from cow’s milk.
Having thus satisfied [the deities] according to the prescribed rule, one should then commence the practice (*sādhana*).
According to one's desire, it may be superior, inferior, or middling:
through the superior [practice], the superior accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises; through the middling, the middling [accomplishment].
Success is achieved in a lesser degree merely by reciting [the mantra] for a shorter time.
Then, having gone to the abode of the Nāgas, one should perform this rite for neutralizing poison:
taking a staff made of *vainya* wood, twenty-one cubits in length and of excellent quality.
Having gathered these materials— an incomparable thunderbolt of *khadira* wood and mustard seeds as ash— one should then begin the ritual practice (*sādhana*).
One should empower a sharp stake of *khadira* wood one thousand times with mantras.
One should indeed dig those [substances], as well as ashes and mustard seeds, in the various directions. Then, one should offer oblations there of *viṣamāsurika*,
having soaked it in pungent oil, eight hundred times.
Then the water in that lake, which resembled the ocean, would dry up;
for if it did not dry up, why should he not discharge arrows like venomous serpents,
having indeed hurled a hundred of them with a single roar while in a state of fury?
Then, without doubt, the lords of serpents such as Ananta and others blaze up.
Thereupon, one should wrathfully hurl the great vajra, empowered with mantras a thousand times.
Having reached the blazing head of that serpent, it remains there with great power.
Then he arrived, accompanied by his servants, forces, and vehicles, terrified of me.
Crying out, "Save us! Save us! and saying, "We are burnt!
We are burnt!", [they offered] the elixir, the rejuvenative, the sword, the stone, the yellow pigment, and the sandals.
O Goddess, O beloved, one should cause her to accept whatever else she desires— whether it be an upper garment, collyrium, or even a Naga maiden— from that person.
Having written that name in the form of a serpent below [the mantra] within a jar,
one may place it in waterless regions without hesitation;
there he shall remain bound for as long as the moon and sun endure, throughout the earth.
By the power of the Goddess of Gods, my word shall not be in vain.
Indeed, this [mantra] that drives away the *nāgas* becomes a destroyer of obstacles when recited one hundred thousand times; of this there is no doubt.
It shall agitate all who wander about and cause their protective charms to fall into ruin.
She pulverizes heaps of mountains from the accumulation of great sins.
By her mere remembrance, she is known as the Queen of the God of Gods, the performer of all actions.
Through the application of recitation, one may achieve the status of a universal emperor after three hundred thousand repetitions.
Thus, O Girijā, the supreme binding of the *nāgas* has been explained.
Tell me now, what else shall I speak to you in this all-pervading great tantra?
Thus [ends] the fourth hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraścheda* of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the stream of Bhairava.
The Chapter on the Singlefold Ritual.
The Goddess said:
"Now, O Blessed One, speak of the highly powerful ritual of speech."
"Since there is no other accomplishment apart from the accomplishment of speech here with Maheśvara,
therefore, O Lord of the Universe, speak of that now by my grace.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Now, O Omniscient One, I shall speak of the imperishable Kālī, the Mistress of Speech,
by the mere utterance of whom one becomes the Lord of Speech himself.
Having first worshipped Mātrikā, whose body is the mantra, in a pure place—
Then one should extract the Vidyā which effects the purpose of the regulation of speech:
Kāmeśvarī mounted upon Fire, [and] Mohanī adorned with the Bindu.

This first syllable, Vāgbhava, is indeed the source from which all speech proceeds. Furthermore, Varuṇa alone and likewise Āpādya alone—this excellent word should be made twofold; and Varuṇa should be struck by the goad (Aṅkuśa).
The Lord of the Gaṇas, mounted upon Varuṇa, with his head occupied by Vāruṇī;
preceded by the bow (cāpa), occupied by the three vowels (i, u, ṛ), and adorned by that [vowel] as a prohibition (niṣedha);
joined with the wife of the Fire-Lord (tejas) and Indra (i), this single-syllabled [mantra] is of great power.
Vidyā should be known as the most supreme, the dispeller of great darkness.

One should meditate upon her as radiant as a beautiful cloud, a mountain, or the moon, pure as shimmering crystal, her form consisting of the swirling eddies of the light residing within the abode of the root (kanda).
From the banyan tree, she emerged— she whose continuous stream of knowledge was manifested through the fourfold speech,
who illuminated existence with the moonlight arising from the Middle Path,
and who, within her expansive countenance, bestows various and wondrous meanings.
She is the gatherer of the great mass of primordial wisdom, utterly pure;
