she is the digit (kalā) that whirls in the midst of the flashing union of the two hollowed hands (saṃpuṭa),
wearing a necklace formed by a wheel of rays and garlanded with the beautiful light she emits.
She whose body consists of the eight forms of the bow that brings an end to the play of the swing of passion,
who resides within the mountain-forest of consciousness-rest, characterized by the awakening of the mind,
and who dwells in the stream of the syllable *Hā* mounted upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
She is intoxicated by the nectar flowing from the filaments of that [lotus], greedy for the sacrificial offering;
she consists of four digits, yet possesses the form of ten million digits and the nature of the Bindu;
she stands centered upon the uvula within the triangle, like the trunk of an elephant.
From the circle of beautiful sounds pervaded by the sixteen wheels of the arts,
she is a slow-moving river of waves consisting of streams of the nectar-essence of Śiva’s moon;
she is a marvelous and excellent swan resting upon both wings and non-wings.
Her body throbs with fourteen great doors,
and she has the nature of a lotus situated within the terrible end of the breath.
In the great waves of the ocean of existence, which take the form of a whirlpool,

there is the submarine fire (*vāḍava*). From the moon of the delusion of Māyā, seated upon two hunchbacks, arises a mental state (*vṛtti*) that originates from the nature of one's own true self and shines with the power of consciousness (*citkalā*).
She has three eyes and one face, her voice is drenched in the nectar of the heart,
and she is embraced by four arms. She holds a lotus bud and other objects, and her body is resplendent with a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a chowrie (cāmara), and a crown (āpīḍa).
Her face is illuminated by a great crown and excellent jewel-earrings;
she is adorned with the luster of shimmering anklets, armlets, and a girdle;
she is mounted upon a great corpse, possessing a manifest physical form.
Thus, according to this instruction, one should enter into meditation upon her who abides in her own essential nature.
She is Vāgeśī, the incomparable Kālī, who bestows speech and eloquence upon men;
she is to be worshipped within the excellent maṇḍala with great effort.

Having satisfied [the deity] with the supreme oblation (*uttama-homa*), one then attains success; it is not otherwise. Through the power of entering into one's own primordial nature (*svarūpa-samāveśa*) by means of this [offering], one may attain that state of immersion (*āveśa*) wherein the manifestation of the form of speech is no longer perceived.
In that [state], the secondary accomplishments (siddhis) following from great gain are proclaimed;
indeed, O Lord of Heroes, they truly arise for those who have realized their own true nature.
Furthermore, omniscience and agency are held to be its uncreated [intrinsic] qualities.
The beautiful speech of this [author], which brings about the fruit of its connection,
flows with an uninterrupted stream like the Gaṅgā in her current, O Bhairavī; it is slow-paced due to the weight of its sentences, ornaments, virtuous deeds, and authoritative words.

And incomparable good fortune, difficult for all to obtain, arises for him. O beloved, by the fame of that Lord of Speech, the gods, Siddhas, and Pannagas dwelling on the paths of the earth tremble at the mere sight of him as he speaks.
(159a) Indeed,
women run toward him suddenly at the mere sight of him;
the very form of Kāmadeva is seen directly within the sphere [of the heart].

There is nothing, O Goddess, wherein, when one takes hold of the true nature of the Mistress of the Gods, one does not attain perfection; I tell you this truth. This has been told to you today, O beautiful lady of the gods.
In the midst of this preeminent tantra dedicated to the subjugation [of others],
what more may I now grant you, O you who are worshipped by the lords of the gods?
Speak truly from within your noble heart.

Thus ends the chapter on the injunctions for speech in the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the *Bhairavaśrotas*, within the *Śiraścheda* of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, in the twenty-four-thousand-verse [recension], in the fourth hexad.
The venerable Goddess said:
O God of gods, to you who hold the crescent moon upon your crest and the trident in your hand, tell me, O Lord, the procedure for subduing malevolent planets,
which pacifies all spirits; this is my curiosity.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O you who are saluted by the lords of heroes, to the Vidyā of terrible prowess,
named Netrarōṣaṇikā, a Kālī with the radiance of the fire of time.

First, having extracted the *haṃsa*, [one should take] the fire (*ra*), the goad (*va*), and the bindu (*m*). Then the word "Candra" (Moon) should be given, followed by the word "Caṇḍaroṣaśiva. Next, having extracted the word "Bhīma," the word known as "Bhīṣaṇi" should be placed.
Insert the word *grahān āveśaya* and split the word *mama īśabdaṃ* into two.
Then, split the words *hanana āśaya vai vīt sā cūrṇaya* into two parts.
This is the Vidyā known as Bhīma-Śaṅku-niruddhā, possessed of terrible prowess.
This [goddess] is described as having forty forms, she who devours the entire Brahmāṇḍa;
her form is intent on burning the entire multitude of the wicked.
She possesses a body that increases the splendor of the sun at the end of time and the fire of universal destruction.
With eyes set in a terrible hollow, like a fire vomiting forth embers,
she terrifies the hearts of the gods with her fierce frown and the sound of "Hūṃ.
Resounding with the sounds of bells and hand-drums, her matted hair is fashioned into three braids.
With a skull-topped staff, a trident, a mace, a noose, and a sword raised in her hands,
she wears a garland of great skulls and a golden crest upon her head.
With emaciated limbs yet exceedingly majestic, terrifying with her mass of matted locks,
resembling a mountain of black collyrium against the autumn sky;
she possesses wondrous prowess, her body mounted upon a formidable man-lion.
She is resplendent with a garland of cobra-hoods from the most terrible serpent-kings;
she is smeared with the blood of great elephants slaughtered by her; she is the most excellent of goddesses;
and she is the destroyer of hosts of spirits, vetālas, yakṣas, and malevolent grahas.
Having meditated, one should worship the Goddess of the Gods upon a lotus in the mandala;
one should offer oblations with all the services of a hero for the sake of the highest attainment.
From that time forward, that Goddess is remembered as the performer of all actions.
Upon being seen, Bhairavī causes a multitude of spirits and yakṣas to enter [the body];
by wiping [away impurities], she destroys all [afflictions] such as epilepsy.
She would destroy the three kinds of terrible poison merely by her glance.
The goddess Karaṅkiṇī, O Lord, should be known as the destroyer of mechanical engines, the dryer of the waters of the ocean, and the bestower of all perfections;
she is the pacifier of great sins, highly fortunate, and auspicious.
She is the most exalted, the great destroyer, and the terrifying one of universal dissolution;
she should be known as the Supreme Goddess who bestows great enjoyment and grants liberation.
She should be known as the one who bestows success upon recitation, who is established within the cycle of worldly existence.
Thus has it been fully explained to you; what else do you wish to ask?

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for Caṇḍaroṣaṇā in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the fourth hexad of the *Śiraścheda* section of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavaśrotas*.
(160a) The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear this wonderful secret."
Just as that Kālī, who bestows the end of time, agitates the world,
or however she may thoroughly cause agitation— tell me that, O Bhairava.
Śrī Bhairava said:
I shall explain it in brief; listen, O you who are honored by the lords of heroes!
Beyond this supreme tantra, nothing has been taught anywhere.
This ritual procedure is exceedingly fierce and causes the agitation of the world.
First, one should utter the *praṇava* (Oṃ), followed by the word *namaḥ*.
Then, having joined *bhairaveśvara*, after that the word *kāla*. Having joined the word *saṃkarṣaṇī*, [one should join] the word *ḍāmari* at the end.
In the *vikaṭa* [meter], one should place the word "uddhṛtya" twice; "kṣobhaya" should be joined twice;
"cālaya" should be applied twice; and "utpādaya" should be placed twice.
The leader of the *gaṇas* (*gaṇendra*) should be provided three times, ending with a *visarga*.
This Vidyā, consisting of fifty-three syllables, possesses terrible prowess;
it bestows all prosperity, is supreme, and causes agitation in the world.
It deludes the armies of enemies and agitates the interior of the universe.

One should meditate on her whose feet are the Great Power (Mahāśakti), who shatters the crushing machines [of worldly existence] and destroys the enemies of the gods; she whose sound is like the flash of lightning,
who flows through the path of the Suṣumṇā and is crowded with many sparks.
One should meditate upon her who resembles a mass of vermilion, like molten lac juice,
and like a flood of wine, filling the entire world; or,
having recited the mantra for the whole world, one should again [offer it] to one's own heart with "svāhā."
Having contemplated her as having entered [the body], one should remember her as having attained a state of oneness.
Thus, sitting in solitude, O Lord, intent upon the worship of the deity,
one should shake the city and its settlements through the yoga of meditation for seven days.
After three weeks, O Great Goddess, he will cause the maṇḍala to tremble;
within a single month, O Fortunate One, the people dwelling there [will be affected].

They honor that best of men with their own selves, wealth, and wives; even if he does not desire it, they forcibly present these to him alone. Through the practice of yoga for six months, he will cause the earth to tremble.

O lady of virtuous vows, what must one do toward the sovereign lords of the mandala so that they remain subject to this king of accomplished masters? It is just as when [the planets] are present during the conjunction when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu.
People come to that holy ford, O Lord, for the sake of the practitioner;
indeed, by the power of the Great Vidyā, all become givers of themselves, givers of wealth, givers of wives, and performers of service— of this there is no doubt.
That Supreme Goddess should be meditated upon in whatever forms are desired;
she is the remover of terror from the three worlds, the subjugator of the three worlds,
and the destroyer of the suffering of the three worlds— there is nothing that she cannot accomplish.
There is nothing that the Great Goddess Karaṅkiṇī does not accomplish.
She should be known as the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, the destroyer of great delusion.
By reciting her mantra, she is renowned in this Tantra as the leader of Tantras who bestows spiritual perfection.
Thus has this been fully explained to you; what else shall I tell you?

Thus ends the ritual of Jagatkṣobhakālī in the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Bhairavaśrotas* Vidyāpīṭha, in the section on the Severing of the Head (*Śiraścheda*).
The Śrī Devī said: Now, O Destroyer of Tripura, tell me of that *ghaṭṭana* by which the universe is indeed set in motion; explain that sequence of Kālī to me.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now today I shall describe the "striking" (ghaṭṭana), the striking of the universe,
by which one destroys this entire world, both moving and unmoving.
Having gone to the terrible abode of Hara, one should extract the Vidyā after having worshipped it;
first extracting Bhairava, which is mounted upon Fire and characterized by emanation.
Likewise, one should place the syllable *rā* (the great seed), which devours the three worlds as its morsel;
then the trident (*triśūla*) joined with the sixth vowel (*ū*), followed by the arm (*ba*) situated on the horse (*a*).
Then the wind (*samīraṇa*) should be given; this is the three-syllabled word.
Furthermore, Ghoraśūla should be given, and then Candra situated in Agastha;
then Samīraṇa should be given, pierced by Kālāṅkuśa.
Having extracted Vāhna alone, and then Vāyavya alone.
The syllable *ma* (mardana), mounted upon fire (*ra*), with its head pressed down by *a* (akuśa) and joined with the *bindu*,
is the great syllable intent on the shattering of the universe.
Preceded by Gaṇeśa (*ga*), mounted upon fire (*ra*), and adorned with the creation-syllable (*sṛṣṭi*, *au*), it is the *mohanī*.
The *Haṃsa* (the letter *Ha*) mounted on the sixth (*Sa*), joined with the triple-foot (*Tripada*),
endowed with the *Bindu* and the *Nāda*, and restrained by the *Bhīma-śaṅku*—
this is the most terrible *Vidyā*, intent upon the destruction of the world.
Resembling a dark cloud and like the autumnal sky,
she possesses the radiance of tens of millions of blazing fires at the end of an aeon;
with flames in her hands, she is emaciated, fierce, three-eyed, and of terrifying prowess.

One should worship her in a triangular realm with red and black offerings— she who holds a winnowing basket and a vajra in her hands, who is terrible, whose radiance is equal to ten million flashes of lightning, who is mounted upon a great buffalo, and who is greedy for devouring the world.
O slender-waisted one, one should offer oblations with mustard oil or clarified butter;

thereafter, one should recite the fifteen-syllable mantra of the auspicious Goddess of the gods. O highly fortunate lady, one should recite it one hundred thousand times, and then perform the previously mentioned oblation.

Then that goddess Raudrī, of terrifying prowess, becomes accomplished; by her mere remembrance, she can dissolve this entire world of moving and non-moving beings. If the goddess is properly worshipped with the name of the one to be accomplished, she grants success.
One should mutter [the mantra] and strike [the target], whether it be an individual equal to Indra,
or a village crowded with throngs of people, having enclosed it within the *saṃpuṭa* formation.
Through the application of recitation (*japayoga*), one may cause a city or even a town to perish.
By whichever specific application one recites this most powerful Vidyā,
by that very application one may stir up the wondrous world.
Having written [the mantra] by means of the application of yantras and having encircled the Supreme Goddess (vidarbha), she shall agitate the target;
indeed, she may even slay the gods themselves.
Or, having worshipped her according to the previous rite while she resides within the temple of Śiva, [one achieves the desired result].
By means of that yoga of the *nirmālya*, one may slay all things, both moving and unmoving.
Thus has the goddess, the bestower of accomplishment, been described to you according to her true nature;
she is to be known as the performer of past deeds, the granter of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
O Goddess, through this accomplishment, nothing remains unattainable on earth.
This [vidyā], which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has been declared to you according to its true nature.
What else shall I tell you? Speak, O you who are worshipped by the lords of heroes!

Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of Ghaṭṭanakālī in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the fourth hexad, in the section on the Severing of the Head (*śiraścheda*) belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) in the Bhairava Current.
The Goddess said:
Now, O Blessed One, speak of the incomparable ritual of initiation that enables one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra and destroys great delusion—
by means of which, O Dear One, even those who have committed great sins shall attain liberation.
O Supreme Lord, out of your grace, please explain that procedure which is free from painful practices and endowed with great knowledge. Śrī Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! That which has been requested by you, the very essence of the tantra, I shall now explain to you correctly.
By name she is Bhuvanamālā, the Supreme Goddess Kālikā;
he into whose path of hearing she enters is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
How much more so for one who recites her mantra—he is indeed equal to Sadāśiva.
Then, O Vīrasundarī, it should be known that this is one's final birth.
When this Bhuvaneśvarī-vidyā has been written and manifested,
one will become initiated in all the tantras through its mere recollection.
Listen now to its extraction, which destroys great sins: first,
the Great Sound (the letter *ha*) endowed with the sixth vowel (*ī*),
followed by the beginning of the Kalpa (the letter *ka*), then the fifth vowel (*ū*) seated [upon it], and finally Varuṇa (*va*) alone.
Again, there is the mere negation (Niṣedha) joined with the goad (Aṅkuśa);
likewise, Śakra (Ka) with three vowels on its head (Ū), which is also a negator;
then "Śānta Śānta" followed by Vahni (Ra) marked with the Bindu (M).
The eight-syllabled Vidyā known as Bhuvanamālinī destroys even such sins as the uprooting of a linga by mere remembrance.
The Great Goddess burns away the multitude of fetters for the individual soul.
O slender-waisted one, she who has come by the path of hearing is indeed honored;
or else, O Viśvarūpā, she is the bestower of meditation, the giver of liberation, and the destroyer of death.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
To whom are the bonds said to belong, and what kind of person is considered [bound]?
How do they become his binders? O All-pervading Lord, sever my doubt.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, that person who is this very self matures;
its fetters, O Beloved, are said to be like copper-colored stains,
indeed covered by innate impurity and by longing.
That is declared to be the *āṇava* [impurity], which consists of beginningless engagement in action (*karma*).
That which is known as *unmohanī* is *māyā*, whose nature is both being and non-being. (162b)
Through the agitation of that [state], this individual (pudgala) remembers [his true nature] precisely by means of his condition as a bound soul (paśu).
Thus, the threefold bond (pāśatraya) is declared to be the cause of the sprout of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra).
By this very [bond], one is bound; when liberated from it, one is said to be liberated.
The Goddess said: O Lord, regarding this Self which is spoken of as being either embodied or unembodied— if it were embodied,
it would be subject to destruction, and its eternity would be contradicted by its having a beginning.

If it were corporeal, it could not be eternal; rather, it would be merely a form. Because it is produced, its beginninglessness is contradicted by its perishability. Therefore, the corporeality of this *pudgala* is not established.
If you say that the Self is indeed the formless Mahādeva, then how could the bonds be concealed from that which is formless? O Lord, you ought to explain this doubt of mine exactly as it is.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Due to the influence of the bond of power (śakti-pāśa), this Māyā, through agitation, assumes a bodily form;
it is declared to belong to the individual soul (aṇu) alone, yet it is metaphorically attributed to the Goddess."

The embodied nature of the Self is correctly inferred from its embodiment, just as the existence of fire is inferred from smoke; for that [Self] is bound by the fetters (pāśas). O Goddess, the fetters are the cause, while the Supreme Lord is the agitator.
The body is designated as the effect; let that be investigated by you.
Always existing through the distinction of cause and effect, the Self alone is indeed always to be grasped within the body by means of valid cognitions.
O Goddess, through sound, touch, form, taste, smell, and those things pertaining to the mind—
designated as smell and so forth— that which is of the nature of consciousness is indeed embodied.
For if one were not the self who is the grasper, how could one cause sound and the other objects to be grasped?
O beloved, who then produces the determination regarding objects? If the self does not perform even this mere volition here, then who does? (163a)
Alternatively, if you think that the self is not distinct from the body of a fair-browed woman,
that is certainly not established, because we observe corpses and such.
While this body is still present, a corpse does not smell anything at all.
Having attained the state of wood, he would not perceive sound and the other objects of sense;
therefore, he is established as formless, consisting of consciousness, and devoid of body and the like.
O Goddess of Gods, his eternity is proven by this very absence of material form.
Thus has the determination of the formed and the formless been explained to you. The Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, how are the fetters established for that which is formless?
"By which virtuous ones has this been heard as 'bound like a skinless beast'?
Śrī Bhairava said:
"The Self is traditionally remembered as beginningless, consisting of consciousness, and white in nature."

You alone are its nature as consciousness, its indivisible pervasiveness; that [pervasiveness] is said to be his innate state, though it is perpetually obstructed by fetters. And just as his capacity for sentience is perfectly established and free from delusion, so too is this [nature].

O Supreme Goddess, those [states] associated with intentional desire are indeed impure, while those free from it are pure; they should be understood as having the nature of the pure and the pierced, like the coolness of that which is formless when it has entered into consciousness.
Therefore, impurity resides within consciousness.

These great bonds are formless and are established as belonging to the bound soul (paśu) alone. While these exist, his entire state of worldly existence is designated as "experience" (bhoga). Because of that, his condition of being a transmigrating being (saṃsāritā) is metaphorically described as having form.
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Supreme Lord, if it is thus established that the self is bound, why is it not likewise logical for Śiva? Please explain this to me."
The illustrious Bhairava said:
He is unborn, stainless, pure, all-pervading, and untainted.
The Supreme Lord is of the nature of Śiva, of the nature of consciousness, and higher than consciousness. The Supreme Lord is the essential nature, the pure agent, and the knower.
Formless like time, he is the perfected one who effects the slaughter of bound souls (paśus).
That which is his supreme consciousness is his power, which is his own capacity.
By means of that, the Lord is designated as "the Possessor of Power" (Śaktimān), and she is designated as "Power" (Śakti).
The descent of that [power] is to be known as the female; indeed, Aghora is of terrible form.
Likewise, the most terrible Śivīs are divided according to their specific functions.
Furthermore, O Goddess, they attain infinity due to the diversity of their tasks;
for that reason, their mouth is proclaimed to be "bhūṣṭhamāna."
The manifold nature of their concealment by the fetters has been proclaimed;
the multiplicity of the God of gods is said to arise from His power.
Maheśvara bestows upon the individual souls a state of equality with Himself.

Having understood that agency belongs to him, as well as the strength and weakness of the fetters, he is therefore both the agent and the knower; he is perfected through the observation of his effects. The Goddess said:
"It is so, O Mahādeva; it has been spoken by you exactly as it is.
For if that [reality] is established only through duality, how can it grant the realization of non-duality?
Śrī Bhairava said:
Consciousness is established as the true nature of the self from the perspective of ultimate reality. That which is called its state of bondage is indeed the identification with the body;
when liberated from that, its very nature is Śiva-hood, the supremacy of consciousness.

The nature of consciousness (*cit*) is that which is here intended as "supreme" (*para*); it is non-dual. Those liberated souls (*aṇu*) who have become supreme consciousness are one with Śiva’s path along with them;
for they know that what is called "Śiva-hood" consists precisely in that supreme consciousness.
Devoid of activity, beyond dissolution, and free from causes and examples—
all those belonging to the individual soul (*āṇava*) are indeed of that same nature, established in unity through identity with consciousness.
Therefore, O Goddess, how is it that this very duality arises?
O beloved, having reflected thus by means of your own consciousness, become free from doubt.
I am the powerful Bindu, the Great Lord who is the creator of all.
And having known this, O Supreme Goddess, the eternal Śiva was addressed:
"The Supreme Self is then the Haṃsa, possessed of power, the cause of all;
this [world] is his own essential nature, manifest from his very form."
The Lord of Causes, the all-pervasive Giver, has been concealed by someone or other. Thus, O Supreme Goddess, the innate stainlessness of Śiva remains as it is, like that of a crystal,
whereas that of the bound soul is adventitious, like the blackness of copper.
The state of being a bound soul (paśutva) is eternally established; why then are you thus deluded?
To sever that [bondage], the power of action and that called the power of knowledge unfold.
Indeed, mantra-yoga, ritual action, and initiation are always of the very nature of Śiva.
For this purpose, initiation is correctly proclaimed in the Great Tantra.
When one is unable to perform it, or even due to the ignorance of the Guru—
for that reason, know this Vidyā by the name Bhuvanamālinī.
By the grace of this [Vidyā], the bonds previously impelled are completely destroyed;
they do not arise again, nor do they ever sprout forth.
For this reason, this Vidyā has indeed been described for the purpose of the sequence of initiation (dīkṣākrama).
She who moves with auspicious grace in every direction should be worshipped with offerings according to one's power and devotion.
One should meditate upon the Goddess as omnipresent, possessing whatever form is desired—
she who is the universal form, highly blessed, and the cutter of the bonds of both being and non-being.
I bow to the auspicious Goddess, the bearer of the six paths and the source of all mantras.

The path of reality (tattvādhvan), the path of planes (padādhvan), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), the path of mantras (mantrādhvan), and the path of kalpas (kalpādhvan)— these are proclaimed as the sixfold path.
(164b) The complete purification of all this is achieved through knowledge by means of the application of fire-oblations (*homa*).
The teacher, having encapsulated [the mantra] with the names of the Goddess of the God of Gods, [should perform it] with sesame seeds and other materials.
O Supreme Goddess, one may offer a thousand or ten thousand oblations;
by means of the rite of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), even immobile beings may be initiated.
Once initiated, they attain the state of Śiva—what need is there for further elaboration?

By reciting this [mantra] for six months, the supreme knowledge of the Lord will arise spontaneously within the great-souled practitioner. One should recite it just once for one who has been initiated into all mandalas.
O illustrious lady, my word shall indeed be unfailing:
for whomever this [mantra] has properly entered within by means of time, and who recites it here,
his bonds shall perish and shall certainly never sprout again.
One attains liberation through the power of the Goddess of gods; of this there is no doubt.
She should be known as the performer of all actions, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
There is nothing that the Supreme Goddess cannot accomplish for them.
Thus has the burning of the fetters been fully explained to you, O Maheśvarī. What else shall I tell you? Speak, O Daughter of the Mountain!
Thus ends [the section] in the *Bhairavaśrotas*, within the *Vidyāpīṭha*, in the *Śiraścheda* of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, in the fourth hexad.
The chapter on the ritual of Bhuvanamālinī.
Having thus heard it from the mouth of Hara, the Great Goddess, her face like a blooming white lotus, filled with the nectar of contentment, spoke again.
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord of Bhairava, I am satisfied; you have been worshipped as the true essence of the Mothers. Now, O All-pervading One, I desire to hear the incomparable secret."
There is another [teaching] which is not a prescription for material substances, but which resides in the heart of the Lord;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes an Arhat who has attained all perfections.
O Supreme Lord, crush the cosmic egg like a clod of earth in an instant!
Tell me that supreme rite which is the heart of the Goddess,
than which no other more terrible knowledge exists within the belly of the world.
Having heard this, the Lord of Heroes, whose crest is the shimmering crescent moon,
spoke these most wonderful secrets with a loud laugh.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, who desires the welfare of Jayadratha!
I shall tell you that which you have asked, even though it is unspeakable, O beloved. Having gone to the abode of Hara, O fair-browed one, you should extract this lore."

Having worshipped her with the requisite materials for the ritual like a great hero, Mahākālī should draw forth the bow together with the arrow, pressed between the fire (Ra) and the upward-pointing vowel (Ī). Likewise, she should extract the earring (Kuṇḍala), which is accompanied by Mohanī (Ū) and Sṛṣṭi (E).
In the same way, O Goddess, the supreme heart of the Goddess is double-tongued,
the highest, consisting of three syllables, the supreme abode, the one hero of great power.
Transmitted from ear to ear, O Goddess, it is not to be written in books or similar media.
Situated within the temple of karma, that which is both Śākta and Bhairava—
by means of the recitation of the [mantra] from the mouth, through the throbbing, striking, contraction, and expansion [of the breath],
the lord of practitioners may enter [it] by the power of the Great Vidyā.

By the power of possession, one may declare everything—past, future, and so forth; there is no doubt in this matter. All mudrās proceed [spontaneously], and he utters the roar of Śiva and likewise sings with great intensity.
The physical body trembles and leaps high into the air.
By the power of a single recollection, the destruction of great sins and the shattering of all obscurations arise for the practitioner.
In the secret triangle, she should be worshipped with all the services for heroes (vīra),
as well as with divine liquor, meat, spirits, and various kinds of food offerings. (165b)
Through great oil lamps and through oblations of great flesh and other substances,
that Mahākālī— three-eyed and of terrifying appearance— is accomplished;
her form is as unbearable as ten million fires at the time of the terrible end of the aeon.
Fleshless, resembling a black frost-cloud or a water-jar in her neck;
like a diamond-needle, harsh to the touch, with a face of raised eyebrows and a gaping mouth;
sounding like the roar of clouds at the meeting of the oceans during the dissolution of the world.
Indeed, she is infinite, radiant with the bodies of the gods strung upon her virtues;
she is adorned by the mass of the bodies of Brahmā and Viṣṇu as her girdle,
and she shines brilliantly with the great skull-armlets of Rudreśvara.
Her face has a frown, with half-closed eyes that touch the tips of her vajra-needles,
and she is adorned with a garland of severed heads strung together with the qualities of the Naga-kulas.
She is surrounded by hundreds of various terrible great attendants and jewel-palm trees.
O Dear One, she is mounted upon the Great Nṛsiṃha and seated upon the Great Preta;
she is resplendent with a trident, a discus, a khaṭvāṅga, and a vajra-goad,
and her bannered hands are adorned with a skull, a noose, and a severed head.
Having intentionally meditated upon the Supreme Sovereign Goddess, who dwells between the states of consciousness and unconsciousness,
one should accomplish various desires, O Goddess, whatever is intended by the mind. Afterwards, one should always recite [the mantra] eight hundred thousand times on an excellent mountain.
The practitioner should indeed offer oblations into the fire ten times the number of recitations, beginning with the *mahākṣmā* mantra.
At the conclusion of the *homa*, that Sovereign of the Gods (*sureśvarī*) shall arise from the center of the sacrificial pit.
Having granted the practitioner his desired boon, she shall depart.
That lord of practitioners attains union with the God and Goddess. Alternatively, one who knows the *melāpa* should unite with a woman of great power;
having gone to a terrifying cemetery, she should adopt a fierce mode of conduct.
Having bound the Karaṅkiṇī mudrā, the practitioner of mantra should extract the heart-mantra of the goddess;
as many as a hundred times as desired, the deities will arrive.
Indeed, practitioners worship the great mistresses in various forms;
having become the lord of their circle, he floats through the midst of the sky.
Endowed with all supernatural powers, he becomes Bhairava himself.
Or one may accomplish subjugation and other rites by means of a hundred thousand recitations;
Bhairavī, the slender-waisted goddess of gods, should be known as the bestower of all siddhis.
There is nothing that the Mistress of the Gods does not forcibly accomplish.
Thus has the heart that grants all desires been fully explained to you.
What else shall I speak? Tell me, O Bhairavī, without delay.
Thus [ends] the fourth hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraścheda* [section] of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavaśrotas*.
The Ritual of Hṛdayakālī.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I am fully satisfied by listening to this flood of scriptures."
O Mahādeva, by your grace, I now desire to hear another great *hṛdaya*, which is filled with the nectar of secrets;
by the study of which, O Blessed One, one becomes a possessor of the attainments of worldly enjoyment, liberation, and the like.
"O Bhairava, tell me that, for it truly exists, O Lord of Heroes.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Lord of Heroes; when the heart is bowed, it becomes supremely auspicious."
Merely by attaining which, a person becomes like Bhairava in this world; she who,
when not supported by the supreme abode, is the imperishable Kālī in her sevenfold form—
she has arisen in her supreme aspect as the seven-syllabled Bhairaveśvarī.
The supreme [state] remains as long as it has not fallen away from its own root, which is the immortal bulb;
she is the treasury of the abodes of all luminaries—listen now to her exalted [nature].
Having smeared the region of the earth with the substances of the heroes, Maheśvarī [is present].
Having worshipped there the Mistress of Mantras, one should then extract the Vidyā:
the Supreme Nectar (Ha), Varuṇa (Va), endowed with Śakti (Ī) and the Bindu (M). (166b)
The second syllable is Varuṇa (va) joined with three dots (bindus),
the most excellent Vāruṇa (va) marked by that [same] and having its head struck by a triangle;
having extracted that very same [syllable] again, however, it is devoid of the mark.
One should utter the arm [letter] *ba*, which is well-composed in three ways and possesses great power;
then one should extract the arm [letter] *va* of Varuṇa, joined with the *māyā* (the letter *i*) and the *bindu*.
This is the Vidyā of the two-tongued [serpent], conjoined with creation, and it is the leader of all.
Neither a lamp nor an awakener should be given to her;
she is known as self-luminous, the terrible Kālakaraṅkiṇī,
the Supreme Goddess who rains down a shower of the essence of supreme nectar.
The Sovereign of All, possessing universal form, situated between the states of consciousness and unconsciousness;
manifest, most terrible, and fierce, she is the sole devourer who swallows the world.
She possesses the radiance of tens of millions of tens of millions of tens of billions of fires at the end of a dreadful aeon.
She resembles the autumn sky with the neck of Śrīkaṇṭha and the throat of Kāla;
her internal fire is agitated by the disturbance caused by the devouring of the terrible suns,
and she tastes the fat and flesh with the flood of her thousand flickering tongues.
She who resounds with the utterance of the devouring of the entire wheel of the night; she who is the great illusion of impurity and karma, the sole purifier that washes away the bonds;
she who rests upon a beautiful lotus and a corpse, garlanded with Bhairavas.
One should contemplate Kālakarṣaṇī, who is the ornament of all things,
everywhere. Having meditated thus, one should worship the Supreme Goddess within the hexagon with all the offerings of heroes, such as wine, meat, and fermented liquors.
One should always offer a *mahāpala* oblation for the complete satisfaction of the Vidyā.
Thereafter, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) should accomplish the rite through the recitation (*japa*) of one hundred thousand syllables and so forth.
O auspicious lady, at the very conclusion of the recitation, Bhairavamālinī herself [manifests].
She belongs to that great-souled practitioner who goes to the cremation ground;
she swiftly leads away the lord of practitioners who is firm in his vows. (167a)
In that regard, there would be equality with that; what is the use of saying more?
This very Goddess of the God of Gods, as enjoined in the *Pūrvatantra*, shall accomplish everything in its entirety through the application of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
O fortunate one, by mere remembrance, the practitioner becomes perfected;
from the moment that [deity] dwells within the heart of the great-souled practitioner,
from that moment on, the practitioner becomes equal to Śakra.
One who desires long life should write this down in a book.
Neither the goddesses nor the lords of men will ever find a flaw in him;
by the mere recitation of this for three nights, he becomes supreme among both the high and the low.
The power becomes manifest through its manifestation, immediately producing conviction.
Having attained such conviction, the practitioner shall become satisfied.
Thus everything has been told to you; what more do you ask?

Thus ends the procedure for Bhairavamālinī in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra of the Severed Head (*Śiraścheda*) within the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairava Current, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the fourth Ṣaṭka.
The Śrī Devī said:
"Now, O Destroyer of Tripura, proclaim the heart-essence,
by the mere knowledge of which I may wander according to my will.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, I shall declare that essence which was concealed in the *Brahmayāmala*,
but which today has been revealed to you in this *Jayadratha-tantra*.
It is the heart-essence of Kālī, characterized by the collection of all [teachings].
By means of that one [reality], the treasury of mantras of great power clearly arises;
having dissolved the entire universe, it expands forth—
that great Lord of the sequence of the most terrible dissolution.
Because that which was not remembered has been extracted and withdrawn for the sake of its retention,
it is therefore celebrated as the "Heart" (*hṛdaya*), the cause of reabsorption.
I shall proclaim its extraction, which is the most essential of the essential.
Having gone to the formidable abode of Hara and taken my place in the center of the sacrificial altar,
I beheld there the earth, strewn with skeletons and smeared with blood.
Having smeared the Mistress of Mantras with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should worship her.
Then, one should extract the Vidyā that bestows many wonderful siddhis:
the Lord of the Great Dissolution (Mahāsaṃhāranātheśa), who is the Haṃsa with the sixth vowel and the bindu.
Having raised up the Great Power (Mahāśakti) once again as Saṃhārabhairava,
Kālī, the bestower of the fruit of Time, thus becomes fourfold in color;
she is the destroyer of the faults of the great covenant and the annihilator of great sins.
She is the pacifier of great delusion and the destroyer of great confusion;
she brings about the rise of great fortune and increases great wisdom;
she slays the time of great dissolution and strikes down fear and poverty.
Delighting in great diversion, terrifying in her great withdrawal,
liberated by the feet of Muṇḍa, she is the sovereign of all lords of mantras.
She is the solitary heroine with a face like a *huṃ* sound, possessing the splendor of ten thousand *yoṅgaḍās*.
One should meditate upon her who has the luster of crushed collyrium, resembling a shimmering sapphire;
whose form is like the autumnal sky at the throat of Śrīkaṇṭha;
and whose formidable body is similar to the fierce seat of Bhavānī.
In the ground of dissolution, they dance, intoxicated by the abundance of fat and flesh;
she is the devourer of all forms that have emerged from the sequence of semen and blood.
She is the supreme one who dissolves terrible conceptualizations regarding existence and non-existence.
She who has entered her own true nature through the dissolution of the great mind that is free from obstruction;
she who is mounted upon the lion that destroys the elephant of duality; she who is endowed with non-duality;
she whose form is the throbbing radiance expanding within the midst of all phenomena.
By means of the beautiful perfection of the manifestation of the abode of uncontracted consciousness,
she shines forth, having conquered the inner space between the suggested meaning and its suggester.
She who sports in the great lotus of my mind like a restless crane,
whose warbling is the humming of bees in the form of diverse sounds, who is intent upon the water of the world,
and who takes the form of the moon that fulfills the rest of the touch between consciousness and the unconscious.
She whose consciousness is refined by resting in the true form of the unmanifested three abodes;
she who is intent on savoring the essence of the true form obtained through hearing;
she who is greedy for the great taste within the darkness; she who causes the universe to resound.
Victorious is the great drum of the Indīvarī, which arises from the supreme devouring of the wheel of the four-fold great bindu;
she possesses the skill of striking the fierce wheel that begins with the letter Ū and ends with Śiva;
she is the spreading wave of her own radiant nature.
[One should worship] Kālikā, who is the manifestation of the resonance of the laughter "hā hā ha," who is known as Sādākhya,
who flashes forth in eight ways, whose essential nature is the potency of the mudrās,
and who is the formidable abode that makes manifest the vast potency of both movement and non-movement.
One should always meditate upon Kālī, who is adorned with a crown of black fire, whose splendor is victorious, who possesses a universal form, and who assumes whatever form is desired;
one should worship her within the interior of a hexagonal world with heroic offerings.
One should offer a thousand or ten thousand oblations of human flesh;
thereafter, one should propitiate the Goddess Śivā, the crusher of the three worlds.
Having gone to the abode of Hara at night and having formed the Karaṅkiṇī mudrā, [one should proceed].
One who is firm in his vows should recite [the mantra] for as long as he remains seated until a hundred [recitations are complete].
Then the goddesses of great power, appearing in various forms, will arrive.
O Mistress of the Gods, they repeatedly entice the body of the lordly practitioner.
O best of practitioners, even if you were to grant them the state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, or Sadāśiva,
one who is superior to them would have no desire for these, nor would he speak a word with them.
One should describe the binding of the mudrās and recollect this vidyā;
within half a watch, the goddess Karaṅkiṇī arrives.
Accompanied by her retinue, the formidable one grants boons to the practitioner.
She chooses the Lord together with his consort by means of the very boon desired.
Therefore, O Dear One, the practitioners thus attain union (sāyojyatā).
This supreme accomplishment has indeed been declared as the most excellent.
Alternatively, through the practice of recitation (*japa*), there is nothing that it cannot achieve.
O fortunate one, by a hundred thousand recitations, all common accomplishments (*siddhis*) are attained.
The goals of the foremost practitioners are accomplished; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
By doubling [the practice], one attains middling success, but by tripling it, one attains the highest success.
There is no doubt in this; my word is infallible.
Thus has the auspicious Naṭṭeśvarī been described to you by name.
At the time of the wheel of withdrawal, the Supreme Goddess dances;
she is that supreme goddess Karaṅkiṇī proclaimed in the Tantra.
What else shall I speak? Tell me what has entered your mind.

Thus ends the chapter on the Arising of the Naṭṭeśvarī-Saṃhāra-Cakra, in the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra (*Mahātantra*) of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraścheda* division of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the stream of Bhairava.
Having heard this from Maheśvara, the God of gods, the Goddess,
her body bristling with horripilation, spoke again to Maheśvara.
The Goddess said:
Now I wish to hear, O beloved of Mahābhairava,
about that fierce Mudrā Phekkāriṇī, who is the leader of the Maṃdrās. O God, how is her pervasion, and what are her means of accomplishment?
Tell this in brief, O Great Destroyer of Tripura.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, for I shall tell you the most secret and wonderful [teaching].
I have not revealed this secret *Rāviṇī-krama* to anyone.
This is the fierce *Phetkāriṇī*, who utters a terrible and resonant roar.
Let them agree: "One shall not think of her who causes terror to the spirits.
Having gone to the abode of Hara, the hero, delighted by the joy of wine, having consumed the sacrificial pap of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta-caru*), took his place in the middle of the altar.
Having then rubbed the earth with a skull-bone and sprinkled it five times,
one should worship the mantra-mother there with the liquors offered by heroes.
Having bound the Rāviṇī mudrā, one should then extract the vidyā.
One should extract the Supreme Lord by means of the eight-spoked wheel:
first, the seed-syllable situated in the fire-wheel (RA), adorned with the Bindu and its abode (the vowel U);
second, that which is inscribed in the womb (the vowel I); and four are remembered as being alone (the vowels E, AI, O, AU).
The seventh is Sānicitra, and the eighth is remembered as being as before.
Thus is the eight-syllabled Ghorā Rāviṇī, worshipped by Rāvaṇa;
she is the destroyer of all sins and the one who effects instantaneous possession.
It causes horripilation through its power and effects the piercing of the *mudrās*; it is the great [mantra].
Among the previously mentioned varieties of *Rāviṇī*, this is the supreme heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
O Goddess, there exists nothing equal to this within the belly of the universe.

The pervasiveness, majesty, power, and perfection of valor of this Goddess cannot be described even by those who have attained the state beyond the named (*sādākhyai*) through the paths of the transcendent;
she is the supreme digit (*kalā*), waveless, incomparable, and nameless.

O fair-hipped one, she consists of the nectar flowing forth from the vast expanse between Śiva and Śakti; manifesting through the sequence of the *vyakta* [manifest] state, she extends from the beginning up to the syllable *HŪM*. By her, the entire multitude of causal principles previously impelled reaches its end.

This [world], which was formerly swallowed and then vomited forth by Rāvinī as she was impelled by it, possesses the capacity to manifest its own heroism; it is languid with the joy of its sovereign power through its connection with the lineage of Krūma and by means of the application of the Great Sound (mahārāva).
Having thus performed the expansion and contraction, she who is garlanded with the *bhaga*,
who delights in the supreme state beyond both vibration and non-vibration, is the eternal Supreme Bhairavī.
One should meditate upon her through sequential pervasion, possessing a smile like a white cloud or the moon,
shining with the luster of frost, a conch, or a *kunda* flower, with a body of shimmering crystal,
and radiating a brilliance equal to hundreds, full nights, crores, ten-millions, and hundreds of millions of moons.
Then, one should always remember her as she is desired— possessing a beautiful form, seated upon the full moon, the moonlight that shatters the darkness of great delusion,
adorned with a garland of moons, variegated by the moon, and ever smiling.
One should remember her alone, who is untiring at all times, resembling mist,
comparable to the throat of a bee in the autumn season,
seated upon the shoulders of a great corpse, and remembered as the fiercely terrifying Bhairavī.
One should remember her who makes the sound "rāva," who is the roaring one (rāvinī), who devours the great abode (mahāśayā),
who rests in both sequential and reverse order, and whose form is the supreme consciousness (citpāra).
Having thus meditated upon her, who possesses three forms at the end, she brings about immediate realization.
O Lord of Men, if one should worship her who effects purification within the triangle, the sovereign performs the binding of the mudrā, shaking his entire body and tossing aside the net of fetters.
One should worship the gentle Goddess, the Great Goddess in the form of emanation, who resides upon a sixteen-petaled lotus and bestows manifold wonderful accomplishments;
one should worship her, who is free from waves and delights in consciousness, at the beginning of the mandala and elsewhere.
In this manner, one should worship the Supreme Goddess with the substances of the most excellent heroes;
and one should offer oblations of great earth, recitations, and the like, as well as wine, meat, fermented liquors, and so forth.
One should also offer the previously mentioned substances, which are suitable for the great oil-offering.

Having thus performed the worship according to the ritual rules, one should then cause the disciple to enter— his eyes bound, his hands joined in *añjali*, holding flowers, and being irreproachable. (170a)
Then, once the flowers have been struck and sprinkled, he should cause them to be cast; thereafter,
by means of the yoga of upward-transference,
he should pierce the disciple himself with the resonance of the five hoods through the application of the eight *pheṭkāra*s.
Thus, as soon as he has attained perfection, he trembles and shakes violently;
like a tree whose roots have been severed, that disciple— once pierced by the practice— falls to the surface of the earth without a doubt, just as Kāśyapa did.
Thereafter, one becomes a knower of the nature of Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
Thus is the initiation described, which effects the cutting of the cycle of transmigration. Now, the ritual action (kriyā) should be performed as previously enjoined.
Thus, having always established this deity as his presiding authority through the Guru,
from that time forward he shall succeed in all [practices].
Then the Goddess Sādhanī, having gone to the great abode of Hara...
One should recite the mantra of the auspicious Śivā, the sovereign of all mantras, one hundred thousand times;
then one should offer oblations of human flesh, purified with the three [substances], in the tenth part [of the recitation].
The lord of practitioners, firm in his vows, should offer pellets (*guḍikā*) weighing one *karṣa*.
Then the earth trembled and whirled repeatedly like a wheel;
all the quarters blazed, crowded with meteors and thunderclaps;
jackals howled in many ways, and most terrifying winds blew violently.
At that very moment, the yoginīs stationed upon all the wheels assemble:
those with faces like vultures, those with faces like owls, and others with faces like dogs;
those with faces like horses, cats, cows, donkeys, and birds.
With faces like lions and boars, and various other faces, they are intoxicated with passion.
Then that goddess of terrible form, carrying a hand-drum, arrives;
she herself leads the foremost practitioner to the state of moving through the sky (khecara).
There is no need for deliberation regarding this [mantra] when accompanied by its retinue;
or else, through one hundred thousand recitations, all ordinary accomplishments are attained. (170b)
The Goddess of the Gods accomplishes [her purpose] effortlessly for those whose souls are practitioners.
By three hundred thousand recitations, the Goddess of the Gods will accomplish the middling [siddhi].
Alternatively, even for one devoid of formal practice, her means of accomplishment is now declared.
Possessed of courage, endowed with vigor, generous, and free from greed, the eminent practitioner,
having taken a corpse with uninjured limbs, should go to the abode of Hara while remaining naked,
until he reaches the center of the sacrificial altar.

There, the lord of heroes (vīrendra) should worship the goddess of gods, the slender-waisted one, with various offerings of food, liquor, meat, wine, and the like. He should properly adorn the corpse with saffron, garlands, and ointments.
Then, after covering [the corpse] with a pair of garments, one should subsequently bind the mudrā.
One should extract that Rāviṇī, who causes the terrible cycle of existence to resound.
At that moment, that corpse, with its distorted face, rises up with great force.
Making a most terrifying sound, she dances and leaps about violently;
she says to the lord of practitioners, "I am your servant," or "Command me, O Noble One.
Whatever is desired should be told to her by the wise lord of practitioners.
She bestows elixirs, swords, sandals, collyrium, and gorocana;
she grants all treasures and everything else without a doubt.
This goddess Kṛśodarī brings about all prosperity and virtue.
O beloved, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by this perfected [vidyā] in matters such as subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, killing, and expulsion. By means of it,
the practitioner of mantra may effortlessly achieve even the casting down of a royal canopy.
The supreme possession by Svasthā occurs through the entry of a *khārikā* measure of mustard seeds;
there is nothing that the Bhairavī of the Supreme Bindu does not accomplish.
He shall accomplish the siddhis, beginning with the Great Assembly (mahāmelāpaka).
Thus has been fully declared to you the supreme essence of the Heart,
having attained which, O fair-complexioned one, the practitioner does not grieve.
"What else shall I speak? Tell me, O you who are worshipped by the lords of heroes!
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of the *Upahṛdaya* (Heart-mantra) of Rāviṇī, within the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the twenty-four thousand [verse] scripture.
The Goddess said:

O Śambhu, the conduct of practitioners throughout the three periods of time cannot be understood without knowledge of that [reality]; thus practitioners have fallen into a state of ruin. How can practitioners devoted to the mantra come to know it?
"I desire to know this, O Blessed One; tell it to me, O Auspicious One, by the mere knowledge of which one shall become a partaker of the goal of all accomplishments. Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent, O illustrious one, that I have been urged by you!
Therefore, I shall explain everything; listen, O daughter of the mountain.
Kālī is the knower of the three periods of time and the bestower of the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should extract Bhuvaneśāna, which is encased within the two jaws of Krodha;
having formed the enclosure of Vāta and Aṅkuśa, it is adorned with the Bindu.
Indeed, the five [vowels] are firmly established at the beginning, struck by the head consisting of three Bindus.
One should again give the seed-syllable of Śakra (L), which is stepped upon by the goad (A) and the womb (I);
then the Great Moon (M) joined with a bindu (M̐); then the syllable of Varuṇa (V) marked by the womb (I);
and finally, the mere bow (D) preceded by the knot (A) and struck by the three vowels (Ā, Ī, Ū).
Furthermore, having first recited the great mantra honored by the gods,
the nine-syllabled Mahākālī, who offers oblations at the three times of day—
when properly recited even once, she is the dispeller of all sins.
She who pacifies all worlds, who crushes wickedness and poverty,
she who is renowned as the bestower of all accomplishments, Mahālakṣmī, the initiator.
This auspicious Kālikā should be meditated upon in whatever form is desired.
On an excellent mountain, the preeminent practitioner of firm vows should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
O Maheśvarī, he should offer oblations of pure guggulu resin with *śatāṅga* wood.
Having set aside sesame seeds at the tenth part [of the offering], and ghee at the hundredth part, it is said to be the most excellent;
thus she is declared to be the bestower of success, announcing the three times [past, present, and future] in the lamp,
in water, in the sky, in the sword and so forth, and within the surface of a mirror.
O Great Ascetic, on the thumb or even on the eyes of young maidens,
this slender-waisted Goddess of gods should be invoked by the practitioner.
When she is visible of her own accord, the auspicious one clearly reveals the three periods of time.

Whether for oneself or for another, this is seen here; of this there is no doubt. Whatever has passed, whatever is yet to come, and whatever exists in the present—all that one sees for oneself by means of a twofold recitation.

By performing the recitation three times, that excellent practitioner indeed hears everything himself; there is no doubt about this. O Goddess, once it is well-accomplished among humans, he will achieve what is known as the "dream" state.
By worshipping in the region of the head, the practitioner [attains success]; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus understood the three times, perform your ritual action as you desire.
Having known this Goddess Kālī, who bestows fear upon Time itself, [one is liberated].
Performing the acts of restraint and grace, one is not obstructed.
Thus has this been fully explained to you; what more do you wish to ask?
Thus ends [the section] in the *Bhairavaśrotas*, within the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] version, in the fourth Ṣaṭka.
The Chapter on the Means for Accomplishing the Perception of Time.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
Now I wish to hear how one should perform the act of suppression.
How can the supreme practitioner, with a mind full of wrath and a malicious intent toward enemies, effect the subjugation of those who seek to harm,
or achieve such rites as the power of bringing others under control?
"Tell me how the rite should be performed with substances conjoined with mantras.
Having heard this, the Blessed One [spoke] the *Prayogamañjarī* concerning the one whose crest-jewel is the shimmering moon, exactly as it truly is.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Great Goddess; I shall describe the yoga that is most difficult to attain, by the knowledge of which one may perform all actions.
First, extract the *mohanī* (the letter *ma*), marked with the *nāda* (the vowel *u*) and the *agnikṣaya* (the bindu).
Then, having extracted the *sabindu* (the letter *ha*), take the *kūpacakra* (the letter *ra*) alone.
Next, take the *cāpa* (the letter *dha*) preceded by the *yoni* (the letter *e*). Form two syllables in this dual manner.
One should extract only the tongue (jihvī), mounted upon Varuṇa (v), and Śakra (ś) alone.
This [mantra] should be made into two parts, consisting of two syllables that torment the enemy.
One should extract only the vital point (marman), which is conjoined with the lower portion of Śakra (ś).
This word should be split into two parts, and then the *kuṇḍala* (the letter *m*) should be extracted again;
its body is variegated by fire (*ra*), illusion (*ī*), and wonder (*ca*), and it is adorned with the *bindu*.
This is the *vidyā* known as Bhīmakuviruddhā, possessing terrible prowess.
This Caṇḍā, consisting of seventeen syllables, brings about the destruction of enemies;
it grants success merely by being recited—this word of mine is not false.
Regarding the Ṛkṣakarṇī, whatever matter was previously declared concerning its ritual application [applies here as well].
All that is to be accomplished by means of this [mantra] through the yoga of its recitation and meditation;
or else, O Dear One, one should fashion a figure (*prakṛti*) out of flour mixed with poison,
blood, and charcoal, and covered with the dust of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*).
Having thus made it the size of a span, place it upon his heart;
joined with the name of the person to be acted upon and accompanied by the disease,
one should then write the mantra with poison mixed with *kṛtaja* on a reed.
Having thus prepared [the ritual site], one should heat [the substance] situated in the center of the altar for the rite of fever; specifically,
in whichever parts of the body one desires the manifestation of disease to occur.
O lady with a vajra-like womb, one must perform the ritual placement of the stakes (kīlaka-saṃnyāsa) among them;
there, the terrible [deity] Ghorā will intensely produce a great disease that lasts for seven births.
That cannot be warded off even by the gods and asuras, including Indra himself.
O Goddess of the gods, O beautiful celestial lady, as long as that [act] was performed by him whose mind was drawn by compassion—
preceded by a bath with molasses and milk— and as long as he caused your [penis] to fall away, how could there be purity for this [man], O goddess?
O Śakra, when one desires to kill the sādhya from all sides,
one should burn him in the fire of consciousness with eyes bloodshot with anger;
he will certainly be killed perfectly within half a watch, without a doubt.
Thus, O slender-waisted one, the rites of subjugation and so forth have been proclaimed.
Now, listen to the applications that are devoid of mantras:
having taken equal parts of honey and ghee, and having extracted the seed-syllable ending with the letter *la*.
One should have the collyrium prepared at night when there are no people, on a day presided over by a *bhūta* [the fourth lunar day], for the practitioner;
by the application of this collyrium with milk, it remains effective for as long as one lives.
It undoubtedly destroys even a terrible and formidable lineage for as long as one lives.
Or else, by means of the gift of drink, he performs that rite intensely.
O Lord, kill him without doubt—he for whom food equal to honey and ghee is given; no deliberation is required in this matter.
One should perform that rite intensely so that it does not yield half the result as given;
having gathered the "scanty gain" (kṛkalābha), one should once take up its ashes.
Having cast them there within, one should smear [the site] with it from the wheel.
O Supreme Goddess, if one lets the betel roll hang with its face downward, he will suffer from a severe disease of the mouth; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
When it is extracted, one attains liberation from even the most terrible diseases of the mouth.
Likewise, having taken betel leaf or even a tooth-stick,
if it is thrown into the mouth of a black cobra, it will cause the disease of the mouth to subside completely.
O woman of excellent complexion, having brought Dakṣa under his own control,
he would strike him with that [authority], and thus offense arises against him;
for servants are considered to be like drops of water from a full jar.
Then, one should take the fat produced from a frog mixed with food;
for whomever it is extremely fierce and brings about the end of his body,
a stake smeared with that [fat] should be driven into the vagina of a dead woman.
At the time of cremation, one should take that which has become like charcoal;
having taken that *sūryagupta*, one should rub it with spittle.
O highly fortunate lady, on whatever skull [it is applied], a tilaka mark of that very form shall appear.
Whether it be a dog, a donkey, a sheep, a goat,
a horse, or a mule; or a man, a cow, a snake, a buffalo, a lion, a tiger, or any other beast—
a man can assume the form of whichever creature he desires.
That very form desired by the practitioner quickly comes to be;
thus occurs the transformation of the form of men with wicked minds,
as long as they have not been liberated while still alive.
Then, having taken a rat's skull and smeared it with *viśva* [poison],
wrap it with the hair of a corpse and bury it in the house of whomever you wish;
that person will be swiftly driven away, along with their servants, forces, and vehicles.

By this very procedure, O Goddess of the Gods, a great stake made of human bone, when driven into the ground with the utterance of the syllable *cī*, causes that house to be utterly destroyed. Thus has the ritual for the eight *cikāra*s been proclaimed.
"Even for a crow, my word shall likewise be unfailing:
he shall be snatched away from the sky by a clod of earth, or from the wind, or even from fire.
If one causes [this] to be buried in the house of someone who is joined with Viśvākeśa,
it is effective for expulsion (uccāṭana); it brings about witchcraft and quarrels,
produces terrible other diseases, and causes intense burning fever.
O lady of excellent complexion, from the recitation of that [mantra], peace shall arise for the one to be accomplished.
Chicken eggs, skull-cups, *citraka*, and likewise *padmaka*,
combined with *mātula* in the cavity, constitute an incense that causes the three worlds to tremble.
By means of this king of incenses, one may delude the entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
Bees, *mātulānī*, *mātula*, and poison,
along with the shells of hen’s eggs— this incense is a deluder of the mind.
By means of which incense, once its scent is inhaled by anyone, it causes men to suffer.
O deer-eyed one, one's own two nostrils should be smeared with ghee. Taking a full-blown flower, it should be ground with the powder of *viṣayatūra*.
When smelled, that [mercury] pierces, deludes, and causes one to fall to the earth.
O Goddess, having taken the mercury born from the eight [substances],
one should place it in a copper vessel and strike it with a diamond-paste seal.
The chief practitioner must place that [substance] upon the house and ignite a fire above it until it reaches such heat that the entire mansion trembles; of this there is no doubt.
Having covered pure sulfur, dried it, and hidden it within a triangle, one should place it in a vessel containing heated ghee, without the application of fire. Then,
having taken *śrotoñjana* from a woman’s womb during her menstrual period—
One should cause it to remain there in this manner until it becomes pure; one should do so for seven [days].
Once it has been taken up within a red cloth and well-concealed, one should not examine it. Having brought that which has entered the fire, one should show it to Puruṣottama.
Arising from fire, blazing with its own brilliance, and causing great wonder— this is proclaimed as the ritual application. (174a)

Then, having gathered wood from a tree struck by lightning, one should fashion a *kāra* with it—whatever one desires in one's mind. That very object will remain in the sky without support; of this there is no doubt.

Having obtained the herb called *bhaṅgā* on a Saturday coinciding with the lunar day (*tithi*), one should extract its root at night during the *kaupina* period. When administered, it removes dancing and laughter from children and, when well-concealed, induces delusion.
In that manner,
one should thoroughly apply that [substance] to her in such a way that the *cille* tree itself acts as the *cille*.
At that very time, one should take the upward-pointing inner bark from that tree.
One should cause it to descend and crush it by means of the "pillar-function" (stambhavṛtti); thus separate it.
O Maheśvarī, whomever the target is, once he is dusted with that [substance] upon the head, he shall remain under the power of the downward-moving wind for as long as he lives.
Through the application of upward powder (*ūrdhvacūrṇa*), there is liberation for her...

Or else, at the end, one should grasp the essential [elements] as the binding support. Whatever has not yet arisen, in that same way one should properly extract the mountain of the lineage (*kulliga*).
Having dried it in the shade, one should grind it finely on a smooth grinding stone.
When that powder is applied over the genitals during sexual intercourse,
a firm union of the female organ and the male organ indeed occurs for those [who use it].
O auspicious one, for seven days alone, without taking food,
she who always desires a man should properly smear her genitals with this king of powders mixed with ghee and honey.
She will surely come under his control if she is Trilottama herself;
she shall desire no other husband, for my word is infallible.
Upon her, the power of the upward and downward breaths vibrates, being held back by the flood of her vital energy.
Having reached the tip with those two, separate the leaf from the powder.
One should apply the powder that has gone downward to the vulva of the woman.
That woman quickly attains the state of a maiden; of this there is no doubt.
Through the immersion in the upward powder, she returns once more to her natural state.
In this manner, the two sections should be prepared for Gopāla and Kīṭanāyaka.
That which is joined with the portion of vision (dṛgbhāga) is known as the "hand" (kara) from its base;
it attains an upward nature—of this there is no need for doubt.
Now, the powder produced from the *markaṭaliṅga* [plant], combined with honey and ghee, [is used].
By that, one becomes equal to Kāmeśvara, a hero whose banner is unstained.
This king of ointments is proclaimed by the name Kāmāṅkuśa.
Now, on a black day, black rock salt is cast into a cobra's hood.

O Goddess, one should burn [the effigy] with wood from the *kṛṣṇamātula* tree; this is the fourth [rite]. Having taken salt together with the products of the sense organs (*indriyakṣaja*), for whomsoever such a drink is given, he shall become like a slave along with his wealth.
Alternatively, having taken two bowls and making a hole in them,
one should draw a serpent in one with charcoal from a cremation ground,
and in the other, this [mantra] of Aitareya, placed upright within the bowl.
O beloved Maheśvarī, having well-anointed a *mallikā* flower with the *adhyāmudagara*— so named for the sake of the goal to be accomplished— and having prepared it to the proper measure,
one should subsequently place fire within the interior of a jar and cast it therein.
One should cause the incense of cat-vomit, mouse-vomit, rain-water, *tallolā*, and *saindhava* salt to be placed in that crucible situated above the *kuṃbha*.
O beloved, as soon as it is applied, even the "desire-destroyer" (*kāmadhūti*) is subdued.
The supreme yantra known as Dharmaja is the Lord of the Universe.
Now, both the Piśāca and Vyakṣa nails,
which are split at their tips, should be used to inscribe the name interspersed with the neuter syllable (na).
Know that this [rite], filled with poison, blood, and gnats, with its face turned away and sounded by a river, causes enmity in this world of the moving and the unmoving.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe another great yantra known by the name Śatrapura, which is a powerful means for paralyzing all [enemies].
One should first write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), and afterwards, one should write that same name separately.
The first of the counts, situated in Śakra (the letter *śa*), is endowed with three feet (*m*, *r*, and *u*);
having then applied the bindu (*ṃ*) above it, one should encircle it from below with that [vowel].
Afterwards, the one situated in the middle (*h*) should be made, and again the end of the Vajra-city (*kṣ*).
Having decorated it with the essential parts of the *kalās*, and having triple-encircled it with the *māyā* [syllable],
one should draw it on a wall, a wooden board, or on birch bark (*bhūrja*) of moderate thickness.
Written with yellow pigments in the form of a pillar, one should cover the surface with *aruka*.
A structure covered with bricks should be used to paralyze one who is intent on killing;

this chief mantra, as it truly is, shall effect the paralysis of speech, the paralysis of an army, and the paralysis of the womb in a single application. It has been explained to you according to its true purpose.
Having seized a chameleon, one should place it upon that [image] and cause it to enter. Make a needle-threaded red thread and fashion it from copper.
When that thread emerges through the lower and upper openings, one should cross over it with fear.
She discharges blood in abundance, mixed with semen, thick and copious.
By means of emesis and fasting, she returns to her natural state; of this there is no doubt.
One should indeed apply this same procedure to that "red-throated" [patient].
One should cast it into the middle of the jar and leave it there for three days.
Then the mountain (the master) should give it to a person with a severed nose or one who is foolish to eat as food.
Having taken that which is disliked by him, one should smear it upon the nose of the person [against whom one intends to work].
His [condition] is seen to be severed; his liberation comes through molasses and milk.
O beautiful goddess, talaka should be given to him in his food.
With hands smeared with that [substance], one should remove the eye;
or, by clenching a fist, one may extract a painting situated on a wall.
Then, having taken the placenta produced from a woman, mixed with palmyra [sap]...
When that smoke is applied to a painted wall, it causes the painting to weep profusely.
Taking one's own peg, measuring four finger-breadths in length,
and having smeared it with great blood, one should cast it into the mouth of everyone.
In the case of an enemy's fever, it should be buried under a constellation presided over by the Fire deity (Kṛttikā).
Within seven nights, O Goddess, that *kṛtyā* (sorcery) arises there;
the entire house is destroyed and becomes like a cremation ground.
One should smear the hair from a Brahmin, a Caṇḍāla, a cat, a rat, and a snake, as well as cow-bone and human bone, and cause them to enter [the image].
One should offer one's own teeth as incense upon a tooth-stick that has four protruding points.
The mantra for causing enmity between two people is *animantra-śire-dantam*.
Regarding this, I shall declare the great mantra that bestows accomplishment; listen!
Having first extracted the *praṇava*, it is indeed the supreme severer of affection.

This is the *vidyā* declared for recitation; it has been explained to you according to its true meaning.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the terrible and marvelous rite of killing.
One should first utter the *praṇava* (OM), then the syllable *ḍambara* twice;

Having given the two excellent seed-syllables, one should then give Sadāśiva;
thereafter Bhīma, then Śaṅku, and after that Devadatta again.
Having given the words "grasa grasa," this is the fifteen-syllable Vidyā.
Taking a fragment of bone measuring one *kiṣku* in size,
the wise practitioner should write the name in its center with this mantra:

Having turned toward the southern direction, one should wrap [the object] with the hair of a dead person; then, smeared with the previously mentioned substances mixed with dust from the feet, poison, and charcoal,
one should bury it in the center of the funeral pyre.
One should perform worship there for seven days; by that, even an enemy equal to Indra himself will perish, and there is no doubt about this.
O Bhairavabhāminī, there is no bringing him back at all in this case.
Now I shall describe the most terrible rite of killing, which brings about evil.

Having first extracted the three syllables, they are joined with the *ḍambara* (the letter *ḍa*). It is preceded by the bow (*ca*), marked with the womb (*yonimudrā*), situated in the west (*vāruṇa*), and established in the northwest (*vāyusaṃsthita*).

One should extract the syllable of withdrawal preceded by the *yoni* (the letter *e*) and accompanied by the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*), wherein the end of the bow (*ca*) is stepped upon by the goad (*aṃ*) and adorned by the *yoni*. One likewise extracts the child (*ba*) together with the three dots (*u*) and endowed with the dot (*m*).

Then, having extracted the *nara* from the path, there is the *naivedya*; then again, the *pada*. Having extracted Sadāśiva, who is tranquil with the portions of the *grasa*, that which is known as *māla* is the *niruddha*; it is proclaimed as *kālarātri*.
The terrifying Vidyā of Kālabhayaṅkarī consists of nineteen syllables.
Taking funeral ashes mixed with black gram flour and combined with the dust from the feet [of the target],
one should fashion an image of such a nature.
With the *arikṣa* mantra dedicated to the deity Vahni, one should draw the head and neck of the unconscious victim,
measuring a span (*prādeśa*), using the tips of the fingers smeared with poison and blood;
then, one should project the unmixed mantras of knowledge (*vidyā*) into its heart.
The *saṃhāramudrā* should be formed, striking the head with the forearm;
again and again, one should utter the most terrible sound accompanied by the syllables of the *hikkā-saṃhāra*.
One should worship that form with *vīra*-flowers and offer that *bali* to it.
One should not smear this image at night during the period of the *niśigocara*;
after seven nights, it leads [the practitioner] to the abode of the Endowed with Siddhi (*ṛddhimanta*).
When that which has been heated on an equal [fire] is consumed and kept secret by the lord of practitioners,
a fever with burning sensations arises, as well as eruptions the color of fire. Then, when it is cast into the midst of water and drunk, phlegm is produced.
If it goes upward from the house, it causes emaciation; of this there is no doubt.
If it is situated within a conch-shell, it causes a burning sensation and produces worms.
And if it is situated within alkaline matter, it generates intense pain in the head and the body.
In this manner, one should perform the rite that effects both withdrawal and emergence.
On Saturdays or Tuesdays, during the three *pūrvā* constellations,
or under *Bharaṇī* or *Āśleṣā*, or always starting from the month of Māgha, one should carry it out.
In the event of the ruin of one's country, great suffering, fear, or grief regarding a beloved, the terrible act of killing must certainly and invariably be performed.
By uprooting [the source of harm], peace is attained through this "milk-bath"; of this there is no doubt.
O Lord of Men, having raised the right hand of the person,
