In whichever house he should whirl that [hand], in that house there shall be the destruction of all.
This indeed occurs, there is no doubt, through the power of the King of Yogas (Yogarāja).
One who falls into the snare will likewise burn the dry grass on the ground;
now, these flowers smeared with its ashes have been cast into the sky.
These [mantras], which produce great wonders, attain invisibility.
O fortunate one, by placing the name-mantra at the mouth of a well and using that very mantra with the *visarga*, one may remove poison from the hand.

One should indeed consume it like a meal, O Goddess; there is no doubt in this matter. That herb of the Lord, known as Praharaṇā, combined with milk and jaggery, and joined with Niba, [should be taken].
And whatever woman should drink this, her fetus will undoubtedly fall away;
O highly fortunate one, my word is indeed infallible.
Having taken the embryo of a pigeon and *śaṅkhapuṣpikā*,
one should thus fashion a pill; having placed it inside a small vessel filled with ashes,

One should write down the mantra known as Pucchadeva, which is proclaimed as Gāruḍa, and cover [the area] with it; by this one would reveal hidden treasures.
Indeed, O lady of excellent vows, by this very mantra and medicinal herb, [this is accomplished].
And mustard seeds, when properly smeared with it, certainly fulfill one's purpose through their application.
One should extract oil from the seeds of the *mātuliṅga* (citron);
that oil, placed within a piece of copper while the sun is at its zenith, [is effective].
There, the sun is seen together with its chariot and its retinue, possessing form and a divine body; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
First, ghee should be given for the purpose of drinking, and then it should be given again.
With that [mixture], one sees [the truth] when followed by very cold water mixed with *viśva* (dried ginger).
One should administer the flesh of a pigeon cooked on *airandra* wood; it is declared to be the supreme remedy for abdominal tumors (*gulma*). I tell you this as the truth.
O auspicious one, peacock meat fried in mustard oil quickly kills fever; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
O Goddess of gods, [the same] with black sesame oil causes great burning fever.
O Supreme Goddess, one kills the krakaca [a type of fish] when it has been roasted with impurity;
there is no doubt that by merely eating an offering of saffron-colored food, [the same occurs].
Likewise, O lady of excellent vows, by eating the meat of a grey partridge or a partridge, [one incurs the same sin].
By frying [the seeds] in buffalo ghee or in mustard oil,
and by eating them, premature graying of the hair is produced.
Raw meat cooked in *āsali* oil, when eaten,
is known to produce many diseases and cause great afflictions.
Likewise, when the flesh of a swan or a goat is fried in ghee, [it is similarly harmful].
Then, O Goddess, by consuming that, one will produce fire at will;
this should be known as a rite of great power.
Likewise, the meat of a monitor lizard, cooked with pungent ingredients and the juice of *vīra* plants, [achieves the same].
By this, Romakṛt has declared, O Goddess, that there is no doubt in this matter:
likewise, the meat of a cock, equal to [the size of] a myrobalan fruit and devoid of oil,
is said to cause the disease of urinary disorder (prameha) for enemies of wicked intent.
Likewise, that which is given with the food of a chameleon causes disease;
and that which is called "the barber" (nāpita), together with the food of a worm, O Goddess, will kill [the person] violently from indigestion— of this there is no doubt.

By means of a disease, one should kill the *bhramara* [scorpion]; by means of consumption (*yakṣman*), the *kṛṣkasarpa*; by means of abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and dropsy (*udari*), the *maṇḍūka*—of this there is no doubt.
One should kill the one associated with the blue fly (*nīlamakṣika*) and the one associated with the wood-carrier (*kāṣṭhabhārika*).
The *bhojanādagdhakṛt* is said to cause distinct abdominal distension (*ānāha*) and a pale complexion; the *kṣārakīṭa*, *pānadanta*, and *citrīkaraṇa* are likewise mentioned.
The *kauṇḍinya* is declared to cause insanity and death—of this there is no doubt.

The *pratīkīṭa* is known as the cause of epilepsy (*apasmāra*) through its consumption; the flesh of the *chuchundarī* indeed brings about death by consumption (*anāha*). The insect called *paśupāla* causes death by pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*).
The *uccaṭāṅga* and the *kīṭa* likewise cause fever and aggravate poison;
the *gomārikā* causes difficulty in urination, and the *druṃdruta* produces *raktapitta*.
That [leech] belonging to the *jalaukas* species properly kills one afflicted by abdominal disease.
It should be known that the *abhīṣṭa* [plant] destroys consumption; there is no doubt regarding its action on the limbs of the body.
(178a) One should kill the excellent insect *indragopa* with dysuria.
O Goddess, if an ant is given for food by someone, that person will surely be killed by boils; this is the truth and not otherwise.
One who gives a *nāgikā* ant will be killed by pain in the side; of this there is no doubt.
These and many other such deceptive practices have been proclaimed; for the purpose of counteracting them, I shall describe this supreme remedy:
abhayā, citraka, and likewise another, trivṛt.
Śatāvarā, guḍūcī, and likewise dagdharuhā; somarājā, indrahastā, and mahākarkaṭikā;
bandhyā, cāṇḍālikā, and another, as well as gandhanākulī.
Mahāgandhā, vīrabhayā, and likewise karkaṭakā; triphalā, atyūṣaṇa, pātā, aśvamana, and agnikā— these,

Poison is destroyed by consuming this; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Whether it be artificial poison, or that which is natural, whether stationary or mobile, this king of medicines, possessing the form of the Great Nectar, shall destroy it all.

Then the best of practitioners should recite the mantra of the goddess Pratyaṅgirā, who destroys deceivers and other obstacles and pacifies all misfortunes. O lotus-eyed one, listen as I declare its extraction.
One should extract the nectar preceded by the womb (yonipūrva) as joined with emanation (sṛṣṭi); likewise,
one should again extract that which is preceded by the three (tripūrva), given alone, situated in the vital point of the horse (hayamarman),
marked with three dots (tribindulāñchita), and followed by the negation (niṣedha).
Furthermore, one should extract Soma conjoined with Sṛṣṭi, as well as Yoni and the others;
this is declared to be the seven-syllable Caṇḍakālī of great power,
which pacifies all sins and crushes all misfortunes.
She destroys all faults of confusion, crushes wickedness and poverty,
pacifies all diseases, and removes all mechanical obstacles and bolts.
It shatters all obstacles, brings about every excellence and virtue,
causes the destruction of all misfortune, and bestows great fortune. It will effortlessly destroy the sins arising from [the improper handling of] the Linga or from recitation and other such acts.
From the moment this knowledge of terrible appearance was placed upon the ear,
from that time forward it has been worshipped everywhere like Bhairava himself. In its recitation, there is no obstacle whatsoever, such as wicked mantras or bolts.
O God and Goddess, for that man who practices this,
every obstacle is completely countered a hundred thousand times ten million times over.
He in whose heart this [mantra] resides shall attain the perfection of mantra.
No science equal to this is seen here upon earth.
This [knowledge] is most radiant, terrible, fiercely wrathful, and exceedingly powerful;
there is nothing it does not burn, and there is nothing it cannot accomplish.
O Bhuvaneśvarī, for practitioners who remember Pratyaṅgirā Mahākālī, there is no restriction regarding time or occasion, nor is there any need for meditation, recitation, vows,
or austerity.

O lady with a vajra-like womb, she accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings by mere remembrance; she can never be thwarted by anyone at any time. O fair-hipped one, by mere remembrance, all women melt away.
O highly fortunate one, those practitioners who are agitated by passion, exhausted by desire, and eager for union,
always become struck down by pride;
yet this auspicious Vidyā, known as Kāmaraṇī, is the destroyer of all mantras.
She shines eternally within the hollow center of the heart-cakra;
likewise, Caṇḍeśvarī is remembered as she who constantly makes her meal of the vital breath.
That consciousness, the bearer of the supreme light, is steadfast and unfolds for the noble ones;
by its mere remembrance, it certainly [destroys] the great delusion of the net of bonds.
It is from her body that the seventy million mantras have arisen.
O Goddess, likewise Prativarṇṇāntarā and Saptakoṭeśvarī; O Goddess,
their power, heroism, pervasiveness, manifestation,
and prowess cannot be described even in ten thousand years by those known as the Sādākhya.

O Goddess of gods, by the mere remembrance of the four seats (*catuḥpīṭha*), one becomes initiated; and by this, O fortunate one, one will become consecrated as Bhairava. One shall become worthy of worship and honor, bringing forth all prosperity and virtues.
When that best of men recites it, then [the goddess] abides as the granter of success.
Thus has this Vidyā of terrible prowess been fully described to you;
by the mere remembrance of which one may indeed traverse the earth without fear.
Wherever one may go swiftly, there one shall become like Bhairava.
What else shall I say? Speak, O Sovereign of all Sovereigns!

O Goddess of the gods, I shall now fully explain the method of immobilizing even the wind:
the name [of the person] should be placed in the middle of the syllable *hrīṃ* and joined with the sixteen vowels;
it should then be encircled three times with the syllable *kṣī*, using a writing pen made of turmeric.
Having wrapped it with yellow thread, one should bury it beneath a stone.
O beautiful one, this indeed causes the supreme paralysis of movement even for the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa).
The name, placed in the middle of the syllable *la* and encircled by the enclosed vowels, [should be used].
O Dear One, one should place [the object] beneath a tree outside a square city;
having worshipped with yellow flowers, one may paralyze even the gods.
One should write all the letters of the name above the letter *la*.
One should encircle with Māyā those [syllables] whose beginning and end are blocked by the letter *i*.

Having worshipped them with yellow flowers beneath the stone, O lady of excellent complexion, this indeed brings about the supreme immobilization of movement, even of the wind, O beautiful one. (11.3)
One should accomplish the rite named Hodara, joined with the letters beginning and ending with *la*.
O Maheśvarī, outside the mandala, Indra’s circle should be marked by a vajra.
One should have a beautiful image fashioned from the clay of a potter.

One should place a mechanical device upon its mouth using a peg made of bone. O lady of excellent hips, the tongue should be pierced; one should smear it with powdered black gram (*māṣa*), enclose it within a pair of earthen saucers, and bury it in the abode of the ancestors.
It even seizes the speech of the Creator; what need is there to mention [the power over] human beings? 12. 4.
The Ritual for Paralysis.
I shall now declare the method for causing enmity among enemies, as it is performed.
In the center of that [lotus], the name preceded by Hara is indeed placed;
situated within the fiery mandala, outside of which is the city of Varuṇa.

Having drawn [the figure] with the blood of a buffalo, one should have it written upon the hide of a camel. With the blood of a cat, O beautiful one, one should write the name on the hide of a dog for the purpose of causing enmity or for the sake of love. (13)

One should take [the syllable] joined with the beginning and end of the "excellent color" (the letter *ya*), conjoined above and below with the letter *vaṃ*, and having wrapped it with a blue thread, bury it; this will bring [the person] under control.
The creature becomes hostile and departs toward that direction. 18.3.

Having mixed [the substances] with the blood of an owl and a crow, one should perform the consecration (*bhāvayet*). With that [mixture], one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), preceded by their lineage (*gotra*), enclosed within the letter *ra*. Outside of this is a four-cornered city (*caturasra-pura*), and outside of that is a circle of fire (*vahnimaṇḍala*).
Having wound it with yellow thread, one should place it upon a royal road;
the enemy will then incur hatred from all people. 18.2.
One should write the name of the person against whom the rite is directed using the blood of a cat.
On the skin of a mouse, one should draw a diagram joined with the *hetu* and other signs;
having taken two potsherds from a street, one should worship [the deity] between them.
When this is cast beneath a solitary tree, it causes enmity among all living beings. (1)
The Ritual for Causing Enmity. Now I shall proclaim the rite of eradication for enemies of evil intent:
[one should write] the name of the conch-shell with the feathers of a crow and red ochre pigment.

Joined with the letter *ya* at the beginning and end, and encapsulated by the two *pa*s, one should wrap it with blue thread and bind it around the throat of a crow. O beautiful one, this is declared to be effective for the eradication of even mountains. (71) (700)
O beautiful one, one should write the name upon a camel skin with the blood of a crow.
One should write the letters of the name evenly, ascending with the seed-syllable of Vāyu (Ya). That very syllable, accompanied by the *visarga*, should be placed at both its beginning and its end.
One should bind the hide [of the victim] with the hide of a camel for the purpose of eradication, even in the case of immobile objects.
Having drawn [the figure] with the blood of a camel at the [vital] points (*saṃjñā*), one remains steadfast through ascetic heat (*tapas*).
Restrained by the syllable *ya* at its beginning and joined with the sacrificial oblation (*ājya*) of the syllable *phaṭ*,
one should worship it with black flowers for the sake of expulsion, killing, or binding. One should write the name located within the belly of the syllable *ya* using a crow’s wing feather.
With the essence of the madman itself, situated on both sides of the *phaṭ* syllable, one should bind it within the wind mandala at the throat of a camel;
this is declared to be the eradication of enemies who are arrogant in spirit. (20.8)
Exorcism.
Now I shall fully explain the suppression of enemies as it is performed:
with poison mixed with blood, [one writes] the name upon a splinter of bone.
Having written it on birch bark, obstructed at the beginning and end by the letter *repha* (ṛ),
and by this very same procedure, having taken the head of a snake placed within the belly of the letter *ṣa* (ṣa), one should have it ground into a fine powder.
One should cast a large machine mixed with powder into the enemy's arsenal;
thus, a terrible bloody dysentery will certainly be inflicted upon the foes.
One should write [the mantra] on birch bark using the juice of a poison-intoxicated [plant].

Constrained by the letter *pha*, joined with the upper part of the letter *ra*, situated within the fiery mandala, and placed in the midst of cow’s urine—thereby the head of the enemies suffers from pain; of this there is no doubt. (23.3)
By this very procedure, O excellent lady, one should encircle the name joined with the beginning and the end with seed-syllables consisting of the moon and the sun;
situated within a triangular mandala, one should heat it beneath a stove.
There is no doubt that the loss of sight occurs for the sages;
[this is] the subjugation.
I shall now fully explain the rite of killing, which strikes terror into formidable enemies.
But for those who cause harm, the practitioners act as follows:
taking a skull-fragment, they should write their names upon it with those two [substances].
With poison mixed with blood and combined with funeral charcoal,
one should cast each letter— from the beginning to the end— into the outer triangular mandala, positioned above the syllable *rāṃ* and in the center of the funeral pyre.
When seven nights have passed, staying at night in a cemetery for the dead,
the practitioner, naked, mad, with his hair disheveled, and possessed by wrath, should take up a pair of skulls and rub them against each other.
One should rub those two together until they have become whole;
then, taking them both as complete, one should offer them as an oblation in the center of the fire-pile.
When the conclusion of the oblation has been reached, one should offer an oblation filled with blood.
One should wrap it with black thread using the previously mentioned collection of materials.
From a jar containing fermented grain (*śukta*) and the month of Āṣāḍha, one should fashion an auspicious effigy.
Into its heart, one should insert a yantra by means of a peg made of bone.
Having pinned the heart, one should place it in the center of the funeral pyre.
When seven nights have passed, one may slay even the immortals.
With these substances, the practitioner should write the name of the enemy in the midst of the charnel ground.
One should cast that bone, enclosed at the beginning and end by the syllable *phaṭ* and joined with the letter *ra* above and below, situated within the fiery mandala, into the entire [ground]; then,
having kindled a fire in the middle of the funeral pyre, one should bury it upon that.
When seven nights have passed, one may slay even the gods who possess the three eyes.
[This concludes] the procedure for killing.
Now I shall proclaim the supreme rite of nourishment, the great Mṛtyuñjaya.
One should write the name in the center of the *jīva* with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and saffron (*kuṅkuma*).
Having surrounded it with sixteen vowels from the middle of the letter *pa*,
one should again place the letters beginning with *ṭha* on the outside, ending with the letter *ṭha*.
(183a) One should draw the yantra that destroys great death in the midst of milk. O Dear One, one should write the name as before, situated within the belly of the letter *sa*.

One should place the seed-syllable consisting of all the letters (*sarvavarṇamaya*) in the four cardinal directions. One should draw the seed-syllable of *māyā*, the great seed-syllable, situated in the intermediate directions. Having placed the syllable *ṭha* in the center, it should be surrounded by sixteen digits (*kalā*).
O Maheśvarī, having placed within that which is called the *kūṭamantra* of Ananta,
it should be encircled thrice with *māyā*.
Having wrapped it in three metals, one should bind the amulet around the neck.
Alternatively, O lady of excellent complexion, one should place it in the midst of milk;
this is indeed the Mahāmṛtyuñjayā, which has been well-guardedly explained by me.
O beautiful goddess, one should write the name in the center of the *jīva* as before.
One should encircle the two [deities] with the seed-syllables consisting of the Moon and the Sun.
Having placed [the mantra] within the belly of the letter *kṣa*, one should encircle it three times with *māyā*.
Then, having encircled it with *jaṃtu*, one should worship it with white flowers.
One should wear this destroyer of death on the neck, the arm, and the crest-lock;
one should likewise inscribe the name on the belly,
and having inscribed it again on the belly, one should inscribe it once more on the belly.
One should cast everything situated within the triangular mandala into the belly;
then, once again, all [the substances] into the small belly with kusha grass in the four directions. Having encircled it repeatedly with the Māyā mantra, one forms a square.
Having written it thus, one should place it within the prescribed vessel;
then, one should worship it with white flowers in the midst of ghee and milk.
For this is Mahāpratyāṅgirā, the destroyer of great death.
O Goddess, this supreme yantra, which is well-guarded, has been declared by me in the *Mahāsaṃmohana Tantra*, which extends over a hundred crores [of verses]. (183b)

This supreme *yantrasaṃgraha*, previously proclaimed in the *Jayadratha*, the king of tantras, has been extracted here today. It must not be given to one who is not a disciple, nor likewise to one who hates their guru.

To a disciple who is devoted to the Guru, the gods, and the sacrificial fire; who delights in the Śakti-tantras; who is endowed with goodness and courage; and who possesses an expansive mind—[for such a one] is the procedure for the transmission [of the teaching]. // 28 // Procedure for the Transmission. // //
Indeed, O Beloved, this supreme Cintāmaṇi should be given.
Thus ends the Compendium of Yantras.
I shall now proclaim the divine and incomparable compendium of the purpose of all yantras.
It is auspicious, joined with sacrifices, fire-oblations, and the like, and brings about good fortune;
it is manifold, incomparable, and performs auspicious divine rites.
It encompasses everything from rites of subjugation to those of killing, as well as rites of pacification and so forth.

I shall explain in brief for the benefit of practitioners those rites which are unfailing, indestructible, and accomplished through recitation; those joined with mantras and conjoined with the yoga of the lunar mansions.
These, when correctly applied, are accomplished; there is no doubt in this.
First, the Veda [the letter *a*], then its end [the letter *m*], struck again by the goad [the letter *r*];
then the double-tongued one [the letter *j*] with the moon [the bindu] as its companion, pierced by the creeper-like brow [the letter *i*].
The end of Yamānta, and Yamānta itself, and then its end again;
that which has three divisions, and the first of that, joined with the head by means of its end;
together with the sixteenth part, and the upward stroke of the creeper-like brow, and then again the end of Yamānta.
That [mudrā] is threefold, ending with the goad (aṅkuśa) and extending both downward and upward;
furthermore, it is joined above by the creeper-like eyebrows, then the *saudaṃsa*, and then the *bedhaka*;
and then, O God, the *bedhaka* is endowed with the creeper-like eyebrows.
The first is the ceased [letter], followed by the empowered [letter];
then the final [letter] of that [group], having extracted the one ending in *aśva* (the letter *v*), and that [same letter] joined with its eighth [consonant].
Having extracted its first [syllable], one should join it again in sequence.
Having extracted the excellent deity [from] *kveda*, preceded by *soma*, one should be divided by the circle of deities;
there is no end to that which arises from it.
Having pierced the *ṭeṭibha* with the hook (*aṅkuśa*) at its end and its final part,
in this manner the mantras are placed within the intervals of the wheels, preceded by the ritual assignment (*nyāsa*).
Now, upon the back of the wheel, by means of the knowledge-mantra (*vidyā*) in the form of a coil (*kuṇḍalākāra*).
Having extracted Vyāpinī, one should extract his mother Visaṇī;
having first extracted Soma, which is joined with Ṭīṭibha in the belly,
one should thereafter extract Soma conjoined with Asvara.
One should join together in one place these three: *sthirāntam* preceded by *śakti*, then *chedakam*, and then again *ṭeṭibham* preceded by *śakti*.
Furthermore, one should join *aśvāntam* marked by *aṅkuśa* with *rāvadyām* in two ways.
One should fear Yamāntaka; and Yamāntaka from the end of Yama.
With the goad, the head is split; the end of Yamānta has three dots.
It is devoid of qualities, the primordial sound, and devoid of qualities yet endowed with resonance.
Then, having formed Yamāntaka, endowed with the curved *kaṃdalī* [flower],
having fully aroused wrath itself, joined with the quality of the end of existence (*sattvānta*),
one should place the initial [syllable] with the third [syllable] by means of the step of double repetition.
In the group of six, having extracted that [syllable] and differentiated it with its final [part],
there is that which resides in the heart preceded by Śakti, and immediately after that, that which resides in the heart;
then the space ending with Krodhamantra, and after that, the plantain tree (kadala).
Having first extracted the Lord of Mantras, the Leader of Mantras, preceded by the syllable *ra*,
one may bring the worlds *bhūr* and *bhuvaḥ* under control by means of this King of Mantras;
one may slay all the asuras and delude all that is moving and unmoving.
Enraged, he could dry up the mountains and grind even the Himalayas to powder;
he could arrest the wind and hold back all that is moving and unmoving.

For this very king of mantras, there is no need for initiation nor for libations into the fire; one need not wait for a conjunction with a favorable lunar mansion. Seated within the wheel, one should practice intensely;
by reciting it one hundred thousand times, one brings about manifold forms—of this there is no doubt.
One should draw a twelve-spoked wheel, likewise marked with the footprints of a hungry ghost (preta) left over from a meal,
rubbed with charcoal from a cremation ground, and smeared with the juice of a madman;
having drawn it with a crow’s wing feather under the lunar mansion presided over by Rudra.
Standing facing the northwest, one should properly bury [the object] in a cremation ground;
it will be swiftly expelled from its place, there is no doubt about this.
As for the rites of killing and so forth, as well as those of pacification and so forth—

O practitioner, all the *prase* [planets] and so forth, as well as all the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) and days, are like moments [in time] due to the power of the goal to be accomplished. I shall now explain in brief that which grants success in the accomplishment of the *yantra*.

For killing, the wise man should draw [the deity] residing in the body within the constellation presided over by Yama; for inciting enmity, he should draw it within the constellation Āśleṣā, which has Mahiṣa and Aśvattha as its lords.
For sending forth [a messenger], he should draw it residing in the hand, using the constellation Hasta.
In the *rohiṇī* nakṣatra, for the purpose of pacification (*śāntika*), one should draw [the deity] seated upon the moon; of this there is no doubt.
For the subjugation (*vaśya*) of women, one should draw it in the heart [of the mandala]; and in the *puṣya* nakṣatra, one should likewise draw it.
For nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), one should draw it mounted upon the back of a horse, using the *mūla* nakṣatra.
For inducing muteness, one should draw [the diagram] while Pūrvāṣāḍhā is situated in Aries;
for immobilization, it should be drawn in Śravaṇa in the center of Meru—of this there is no doubt.
For subduing, O Saunaka, the wise man should draw it while Kṛttikā is situated in the body of Agni.
Likewise, having inscribed [the mantra] upon a *jvala* (flame), it undoubtedly remains within this very body.
For the purpose of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), one should inscribe it while situated upon a *śarabha*, from the constellation Jyeṣṭhā to Uttaraphalgunī.
For the paralyzing (*stambhana*) of divine beings, one should inscribe it; of this there is no doubt.
All rites performed while established in the *liṅga* accomplish their goal by force.
One should likewise draw [the deity] established in the *liṅga* for the destruction of scorpions, fever, and other ailments.

One should perform such rites as these in accordance with the left channel (vāmā-nāḍī). Now, I shall briefly proclaim the extensive treasury of mantras for the King of Yantras and so forth, in their entirety, including those for Prasena and the rest.
With that [cloth] by which one goes directly to Bhūrloka and Bhuvarloka when placed in the hand—
[a cloth] mixed with the ashes of the three sacrificial fires (tretāgni) from a deceased person—
the practitioner of mantras (mantrī) should worship according to the rules and serve it with great affection.
Then, having performed one hundred recitations, the knower of mantras should burn that [substance] by means of *haṭhapāka* (forced cooking).
Having caused it to be empowered by the King of Mantras through one hundred recitations,
he should wipe the mirror with this ash according to the prescribed rite.
With water for the guest-offering (argha), flowers, incense, lamps, and likewise with sacrificial porridge (caru),
the wise one should perform one hundred and eight recitations (japa) before it.
Then, it should be consecrated by the King of Mantras, the God of Gods.
By the power of the mantra, the entire earth and the atmospheric realm (bhūr-bhuvaḥ) are perceived;
indeed, all that exists in the worlds is perceived, for it is from this that the world of speech proceeds.
This is the descent of the entire earth, known as Prasena; of this there is no doubt.
I shall now fully explain the rite of killing, which is unfailing in destroying the enemy.
Having drawn the auspicious wheel that moves within a circle upon a cloth from a corpse,
one should mix it with charcoal from a cremation ground and powdered bone.

Those [remedies] which are purgative and emetic should be administered; one should then inscribe the unsurpassed mantra located in the heart of the previously mentioned [deity], as well as the name [of the patient], with a peacock feather. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship [the deity] with black flowers.
One should worship the King of Wheels with various mantras for a month.
Alternatively, the mantra-practitioner may bury it in a cremation ground or within a circle of corpses.
Standing at night, inflamed by wrath, he can slay even the gods.
(185b) There is no talk of men for one whose self is cultivated; however,
with the juice of red nimba and the fruit of arakhūra and ahakī, [one should perform the rite].
The wise practitioner should also draw buffaloes positioned within the mouth of the [central] figure,
with the name of the target joined to words of incantation for causing enmity. Having performed this, the mantra-master should bury it in a cremation ground when midday has arrived.
It creates enmity even with Indra; what need is there to mention humans here?
Having inscribed it with the juice of *jātī* flowers upon a piece of birch bark held in the hand, there is no doubt that one obtains a divine, most excellent wheel, beautiful with twelve spokes.
One should duly place [the object] inside a sealed container upon a red cloth;
one should worship the King of Mantras and establish it within a water-pot (*mallaka*).
By the power of the King of Mantras, this should be done for either three days or seven.
Even an enemy becomes a friend if it should be a matter of life and death.
Having drawn [the design] with milk on the back [of the palm], the knower of mantras should, using sandalwood paste,
inscribe the divine and supreme wheel at the distance of a cubit from the body.
By placing [the object] within milk, peace indeed comes to him.
One should draw the woman on birch bark using the juice of the *caṃpaka* tree;
on that [bark], one should draw a very beautiful twelve-spoked [wheel] upon a cloth.
Having worshipped with red flowers, one should offer [the oblation] in honey.
Thus, even Urvaśī or Tilottamā will quickly be brought under control.
Furthermore, one should write [the mantra] on birch bark with saffron, and then [place it] behind the person to be subdued.
One should draw the wheel in the midst of clarified butter; that is auspicious and brings nourishment.
One should draw the wheel on birch bark with the juice of the *unmattaka* plant.
It should be joined with words for the paralysis of speech (*vākstambha*), and previously placed above a *huḍa* [clay vessel].
One should wrap it in cow dung while it is still fresh and allow it to dry in the shade.
Having placed it inside a mouse hole and worshipped it continuously,
the entire world of moving and non-moving beings becomes mute in an instant.
The wheel situated in the center of Meru is marked by two turmeric squares;
it is surrounded on all sides, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, by the lattice of the vajra-fence.
The knower of mantras, having written the name and the *gata* on a stone,
and having covered it with a second [stone] above it in a secluded house,
brings about the paralysis of the movement of the Lord of Birds; of this there is no doubt.
One should prepare it with the dust from the feet of a person who is neither poisoned nor impassioned.
One should draw the king of wheels (cakrarāja) using the wing of an owl, inscribed with the words "dry up!
(śoṣaya), and place it over fire.
The practitioner of mantra should heat it at the three junctions of the day for twenty-one days;
thereafter, even if it were equal in weight to the oceans placed beneath him, he would dry them up—
how much more so a human being in this world who is constantly beset by suffering?
This very procedure is prescribed for cruel acts when setting out against an enemy.
If one knows that [the omen] is fierce and terrible, it is known that there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus, the knower of mantras, during a single season, should wrap [the object] with the hair of a corpse.

One should smear the ground with a mixture of two kinds of poison for the *rājasa* [rite]. Having drawn the wheel alone, it should be provided with the name of the [target] together with the word "Sākhya," mixed with yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and one's own blood.
Having taken clay from both the near and far shores and kneaded it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*),
one should fashion an image of the God of gods and place it in the center;
then, having covered it with a second [layer], a person should worship it according to the prescribed rite.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, as well as with *kṛśara* and milk-rice,
one should place [the image] into a full pitcher and cover it from above.
One should fill a shallow dish (*śarāva*) equally with its divine, boon-granting, and protective [symbol].
Then, one should place a lamp above it, using clarified butter as oil, without a doubt.
One should worship again according to the rules and offer guggulu incense,
for as long as that most beautiful lamp remains standing there.
By this means, one shall paralyze all divine powers; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should draw this wheel according to the previously described procedure.
One should draw a wheel joined with *rocanā* and saffron;
one should then place that very wheel in water mixed with milk.
This is the destroyer of all fevers; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having drawn a most beautiful wheel with yellow orpiment,
with the auspicious name of the person to be protected placed above this figure of Śarabha,
a man should place it within wine in the center and worship it according to the prescribed rite.
Taking the southern form, one should cause it to be established in a single liṅga.
By the power of the mantra and the ritual substances, it effects the attraction of clouds.
This is done by means of this king of mantras, which pacifies the aforementioned floods.

He shall accomplish all the thirty gods; what need is there to mention mortals on earth? I shall now fully explain the supreme method for the severance of mantras—be they Śākta, Śāmbhava, or Āṇava—as enjoined by the scriptures.
All [obstacles] are cut away as soon as it is merely written; of this there is no doubt.
One should draw the divine, supreme wheel upon pieces of the *vaibhītaka* fruit.
According to the prescribed rite, one should write it with poison and blood upon the site of a funeral pyre.
One should have Yamarāja perform the mantra interspersed with syllables.
In all eight directions, it should be marked above with a vajra;
having encircled it with a great cord, one should place it in a jar or a potsherd.
The practitioner of mantra should place [the seed-syllable] in the mother’s house at the beginning of the ritual; of this there is no doubt.
By means of this, he will forcibly become established in the night for the cutting of all mantras.
Furthermore, regarding this sovereign king of mantras, [there is the mantra] of Yamarāja.
The name of the object to be accomplished should be joined with non-living things such as bracelets and so forth, or with the minister [of the rite] such as anger and so forth;
furthermore, it should indeed be applied according to the specific nature of the ritual action. (187a)
One should encircle the King of Mantras with three times twenty mantras;
this King of Yantras is common to all and forcibly accomplishes even the impossible.
One should accomplish it in every way and always worship Gaṇeśa.
Thus, this *Prayogamañjarī* has been described by me to you today.
What more shall I say beyond this? Speak, O you who are praised by heroes!
Thus [ends] the fourth hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, a great tantra (*mahātantra*) of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraścheda* section of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavasrotas*.
The Chapter on the Ritual of the *Siddhaprayogamañjarī*.
Having thus heard this, the goddess who destroys sin, saluted by the lords of heroes (*vīrendras*),
bowed again to the Lord of Gods, who is worshipped by the deities, and spoke once more.
The Śrī Devī said:
I have heard in its entirety this most excellent of tantras,
the essence that bestows all siddhis, from the feet up to the head.
Now I wish to hear that which is the most excellent essence, the supreme:
how is she the Supreme Kālī, the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
the Mistress of the Wheel, the most formidable, the giver of victory and the increaser of victory?
"How is she whose face is Bhairava? How does she grant marvelous accomplishments?
Tell me that in brief, along with its secret, for it yields great fruit.
Having heard these words arising from the lotus-face of the Goddess, [he spoke].
The Lord spoke with profound words regarding the supreme ritual of Cakreśvarī.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Excellent! I shall tell you the unsurpassed ritual of the Goddess."

Having attained that which is free from waves, resembling curdled milk, which is called the Supreme Consciousness— pervasive, eternal, auspicious, full, and free from ailment— the practitioners who desire spiritual perfection do not grieve.
That power, whose nature is that [reality], is like the luster of gold;
having flowed forth through its expansions, it is the primary agent that brings about the threefold creation. (187b)
The emission of power (śakti-sarga) is declared to be the pure mantra;
everything born of the two types [of causes]—the personal (pauruṣa) and the primal (prākṛta)—is impure.
In the primal [emission], Māyā is the cause; when agitated, she gives birth through agitation.
Everything here is of that very nature; it is the form of power (*śakti*).
Through the agitation of the fetters (*pāśa*) of the individual soul (*aṇu*), it attains the manifestation of particularity.
Therefore, there is no reality here whatsoever that has not been unfolded from power.
The Goddess, whose nature is the flow of the Command, is fivefold and fivefold;
she is Action, Will, Strength, Subtlety, and the eternally expanding Power.
Therefore, Bhairavī should be known as twenty-five years of age.
She who yields the milk of the six Vedas from the bundle of all the branches of knowledge,
and who pours forth a downpour of the essence of nectar— the five jewels—
emitting the perfectly pure lunar nectar adorned with a multitude of digits.
Having meditated upon that which produces great bliss, the fulfiller named Candana,
the manifest semen of those possessing splendor through their power, having the form of nectar,
and possessing a most wonderful essence situated within the Kuṇḍalinī;
The all-pervading, filling, pure [consciousness], which is the essence of both Śiva and the non-Śiva;
beyond that is the Bindu, the most excellent clarified butter (ājya) that has been strained.
That which flows from the bell and the wheel is the Śākta, the supreme wheel.
The fourth [syllable] arises from reabsorption; it is gross, all-hearing, and great.
It is born from the mass of power (*śaktipiṇḍa*), consisting of the unborn and immortal state.
It is known as the supreme salt, red in color, and arisen from the state of Śiva.
The Great Illusion, which is the destroyer [of ignorance], is all-pervasive and consists of all things.
Thus that Goddess, having dissolved, exists in the form of five substances;
again, she is of five kinds, fivefold, and possesses five bodies.
By means of the differentiation of the five jewels, she is the Mistress of the Five Jewels;
here, she is the cause of Brahmā, having the nature of the great elements.
Thus, she whose nature is Time should be known as fivefold, likewise by means of her colors;
O Goddess, I shall now declare her extraction by means of twenty-five [syllables]. Having reached a pure place smeared with the five jewels, [one should proceed].
Covered with a profusion of flowers and filled with the thick fragrance of excellent incense,
he summoned there a female messenger who was endowed with all auspicious marks,
beautiful, lovely in every limb, and whose face resembled the autumnal moon.
Her eyes were long and beautiful, her eyebrows curved like a bow and exquisitely adorned; her lovely forehead was graced by the crescent of the eighth-day moon.
Her hair, beautifully arranged, shone like a swarm of blue bees.
She had a neck like a conch shell, was beautiful to behold, possessed a prominent nose and a sweet fragrance;
her speech ended with a voice as soft as a swan’s, and her breasts were like the frontal lobes of an elephant.
Her waist was slender, she was highly fortunate, and her abdomen was marked by three folds.
She possessed high and beautiful hips, moving slowly under the weight of her loins;
her thighs were like plantain trunks and her ankles were hidden by fleshy calves.
Her feet were red, her limbs were most lovely, and she was graced with long toes.
She has well-rounded, muscular arms, is adorned, and possesses a beautiful smile;
she is truthful, her hands resemble serpent-hoods, and she flows with loveliness.
Adorned with all ornaments, she is full of passion for the practitioner.

One should always indeed appoint as a messenger this beloved Pañcaratnā, who is devoted to the scriptures, devoted to the guru, dedicated to Rudra, free from conceptual construction, intent on spiritual perfection, ever-sleeping, and endowed with the quality of sattva.
If such a woman is praised as being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpā*),
then even if she lacks all [auspicious] marks, O Goddess, she is considered most excellent;
she is the supreme one, produced from every caste, who should be employed by practitioners.
(188b) Furthermore, O Dear One, another [form] for the Vīrasiddhas should be made, wandering at a distance:
very emaciated, with a rough face, formidable, and with fierce eyes.
One with coarse hair, coarse conduct, red-black in complexion, and very terrifying;
free from hesitation and possessing a large nose—such an excellent female messenger (*dūtī*) should be employed.
Having placed her upon one's lap, one should kiss her and embrace her firmly.
One should effect the union of her face with one's own face, and the center should indeed be made formidable (bhairava).
As long as both remain in a state of bliss, then that which has arisen from the birch-bark (bhūrja) is produced.
Afterwards, the Vidyā is to be recited; O Goddess, listen to it exactly as it is.
Soma conjoined with Varuṇa, endowed with Vidhu and Kuśa,
the great path of wind (Mahānilapatha), joined with Māyā and the powder of fire (Vahnicūrṇa)—
this first *piṇḍa* should be given to the Sage, but it must be devoid of the *bindu*.
Having marked it with that [seed-syllable] adorned with three dots (the *bindu*),
one should restrain the *jihvīla*, the *vāyu*, the *trisūryāṅka*, and the *vāruṇa*;
[and likewise] the *cāpādya* mounted upon *vāyu* and joined with the head of *agnivāsa*.
That first [syllable] situated in Varuṇa, marked with three suns and fire;
the third first [syllable], the solitary one, condensed and preceded by the Yoni;
mounted on fire, marked with a triangle, and situated at the end of Varuṇa.
The arm, adorned with three dots (bindus) and beginning with the letter *ka*, is joined with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ).
Having raised the arm alone, it is struck by the goad (*aṅkuśa*) and belongs to Varuṇa.
An incomparable prohibition should be given; furthermore, that [arm] is joined with the fire-abode (*agni-veṣma*).

After that, one should place the *ḍaṃvara* (the seed-syllable ḌAṂ), and then give the Vidyā once more at the beginning. This Vidyā of terrible prowess, consisting of twenty-five syllables, which destroys even the greatest sins, should be placed three times before Bhīmaśaṅku.
O Supreme Goddess, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished through *haṭha* (forceful means),
whether it be this entire world or even that which is filled by those who know the Vedas.
By merely remembering her, one is not tainted by sin even after having committed [an offense].
This Ekavīrā is without attributes (*niraṅgā*) and bestows the fruits of all desires.
Merely through remembrance, she is perfected and brings about a tree of manifold enjoyments.
Endowed with great heroism, she is the Mother, the Leader of Mothers;
united with manifold purposes, she is a voracious devourer of the world;
delighting in great play, she is ever devoted to the abode of Śiva.
Having swallowed everything, she roars, longing for the festival;
she has three heads, is the destroyer of sins, and has arisen from the Three-headed One.
She is not surpassed by the Three-headed Goddess, the supreme Mistress of the three enemies.
The Heroine (Vīrā) consists of the union of the three abodes; she is the Terrible One (Ghorā), the bearer of the hand-drum (Karaṅkiṇī).
She is divided threefold within each of the three abodes, and within each of those three abodes, she is again threefold by three.
She possesses three forms, three paths, and resides in three places, delighting in the cavity of the triple-headed one.
The ground is the Mistress of the Wheel of Knowledge, the Queen of Gods, whose face is Bhairava.
She is the support, free from pearls, throbbing with nectar, and not to be traversed.
The Holy Goddess said:

Since the Goddess manifested herself as the one called Bhairavodyāna, she is the Mistress of the Three Heads and the Sovereign of the Three Powers. Just as she is the Mistress of the Wheel of the Earth, such is her meditation and such is her nature.
"O Bhairava, speak to me according to how I correctly understand it.
Having heard this, Hara, his body suddenly bristling with hair,
spoke these words to the Goddess of the lords of gods for the sake of dispelling her doubts.
Bhairava said:
"O Bhairavī, you ask about a great secret, incomparable and difficult to attain; although it is to be concealed, O Mistress of the Universe, I shall nevertheless declare it to you."
That supreme Śiva is pure, absolute existence alone;
he is the omniscient and omnipotent Supreme Lord who exists in three states. (189b)
The power of Him who possesses the luster of gold is the bearer of that dharma;
O virtuous one, it shines forth from the shoulders, abiding in the midst of the wheel of consciousness as will (icchā).
It is indeed both supreme (parā) and non-supreme (aparā), as well as manifest (santā) and intermediate (parāparā).
She consists of the three strands, resides in the three abodes, and is composed of will, knowledge, and action.
She is Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrā; she has three heads and arises from the three heads. She is Aghorā, Ghorarūpā, Ghorā, and Ghoratarātmikā.

The Goddess is peaceful, terrible, and likewise fierce; she is both existent and non-existent, as well as beyond existence. Indeed, that Sovereign of the Universe, whose nature consists of the individual soul (nara), power (śakti), and Śiva, has pervaded all things, consisting of substance, mantra, and ritual action.
Thus you have been explained in truth according to the nature of the Jewel.
O Goddess Mahasarāvinī, who brings to light the Kulakaula!
I bow to this Goddess, the ground proclaimed from the abyss.
Having become the root by drinking the pollen of the lotus of Śiva through the stalks of the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
she who bestows auspiciousness shines forth in the form of the bliss of the stages (*bhūmikā*), intoxicated by the drinking of the six-faced one.
Radiating with joy, she goes to the abode of the ancestors, her gaze directed upward from the land of birth.
Into its interior she enters a female serpent that has become empty, and she strikes it with her root-tendrils;
then, mounted effortlessly upon its stalk, the lotus spreads out as the seat of the throbbing wheel.
Abiding there, the consort of Brahmā, having indeed consumed the grains of poison in the lake of Guha, [attains her state].

There he experiences eight kinds of enjoyments; then, having worshipped the Kuṇḍala-kumbha, he experiences that kumbha as dripping with the radiance of the sun, a pure stream of touch. Having drunk the nectar there, Śiva and Śivā wander to the upper plane through their union.
Having perceived therein the intense [state] called contact, she who possesses reality enters the path of the earth of dust;
having known her to be of such a form there, she becomes the immortal nectar of the heart, that glory of Brahman.
Having released the loud laughter (*aṭṭahāsa*) there, he enters the digit of the moon (*śaśikalā*), the womb of the lotus of creation.
Having released the state (*bhāva*) upon contact, he then proceeds to the hundredfold crookedness and the emission of power (*śakti-visarga*).
Having formed an attachment to the virtuous women, he delights in the two—the resonance (*nāda*) and the point (*bindu*)—while under the sway of another.

Having performed her play, she who brings about all creation and dissolution ceases once she is fully satisfied; I bow to that Power whose head is perpetually saluted by those who possess bliss. The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of Kulakaula, filled with the sixteen supports,
Bhairava who has emerged from the stream, you whose head is threefold and who are the timeless leader—
by you has been declared the arrangement of the wheels of the stages, though it was scattered [in various places].

Now I wish to hear concerning the domain of Śiva beginning with Kūrma; tell me, O Blessed One, exactly as it was previously requested— that which is known through the sequence [of teachings], together with its means and the path.
By the mere knowledge of which one becomes the lord of all planes.
Śrī Bhairava said:
That which is supreme nirvāṇa, Bhairava, the sphere of existence—
Her will is the fullness of power; from it has emerged the Śakti known as Kulakaulinī. By her, all this—whether abiding in the Kula or situated within the womb of the earth—is pervaded.
She rests in one way, in two ways, in three places, and she takes recourse in four, five, and nine.
Having understood its coming and going through the sequential application of the three principles,
and having simultaneously blocked the two paths,
the wise one should unite [the mind] with the nature that is continuous like the scent of an elephant in rut.
Having immersed oneself again and again in the lake endowed with the experience of the six chakras filled with nectar, one becomes flooded in the waters of the void; there,
everything that was previously perceived as having parts returns in its entirety, purified by the fire of the partless.
Endowed with divine fragrance, one perceives everything as empty;
having performed the preliminary rite, one should cause [the disciple] to grasp the fundamental stage.
It takes away the activity of the five [senses] and brings about the excellence of divine yoga.
Śrī Devī said:
O Lord, what is the nature of that tortoise-like instrument by which it is attained?
O Lord of the Gods, tell me how the lord of yogis practices when he is thus engaged.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Having fixed the gaze at the end of the fifth [cakra], one should drink the nectar of the rays.
One should restrain the mental states within the *kanda* (the root-center), and apply them within the range of the *prastha*.
One should then restrain them again at the "birth-place" (*punarjanman*) and observe that which lies below it.
O beautiful one, this is proclaimed as the practice known by the name *Kacchapa* (the Tortoise).

Having restrained the movement of the *apāna*, one should exhale the elephant of vital energy (*śakti*). Having fixed the mind within the mind, one should perceive with the intellect the gateway of the infinite *cakras*, which is beautiful with the syllables *Ra* and *La*. One should observe this with the mind.
With its root of intrinsic nature firmly established, its trunk of activity moving and vast,
its excellent branches of radiant majesty, adorned with steady foliage,
it bears the incomparable fruit of the sky, overflowing with the sap of non-becoming.
Having ascended that tree of conceptualization— which has risen from the intoxication of supreme bliss and is centered in the mind— by means of the beautiful movement of the hands,
one who stands there trembles, shaken by the wind of the vital energy (*śakti*).
"Pervaded by Śiva and Śakti, one perceives everything as if it were empty. The Goddess said: "And what is that which is called compassion? It is that which makes known the state of bliss."
"O Bhairava, tell me truly how she is to be made known.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"By arresting the vibration of both, one should perform the retention of breath (kuṃbhaka) within the lotus of the sun."
One should release the *kuṃbhakī* breath through the *padmalaghu* movement of the *śakti*.
O Dear One, the *bījakī* technique consists of contracting the mouth below the point of contact;
one should exhale the wind residing in the channels by means of the *spṛṣṭigati*.
Having recited the mantra with attentive hearing, one should then cease from that [recitation];
having established the wealth within the consciousness, one should cause it to be free from [external] activity.
By the cessation of all vibration and speech, like the binding of the movement of a fish,
and by the restraint of hundreds of measures (mātrās), one should rely upon the innate nature (svabhāva).
When the gaze wavers, then it will become radiant.
Having stabilized that radiance, the cage of knots dissolves;
after remaining separated for a long time, it rises up at will and then enters into agitation,
characterized solely by one's own direct experience.
A thunderclap and lightning are seen as the indicators for the stage of the mountain peak.
The Goddess said:
"That which has been proclaimed as the instrument known as the thunderclap and lightning—"
"O God, O Wielder of the Trident, explain that which is known according to the prescribed rule.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Having first performed the dissolution of creation through the sequential differentiation of the three principles (tritatva),..."
The root-activity (mūlakarma) brings about the extraction [of the essence] from the apertures of the self, whose domain is the root.
Then, having performed the contraction, one should proceed to the state of water and fire;
O Dear One, this method for discharging lightning has been revealed.
Having brought together two hundred thousand [units] on one side, one should place them within three hundred thousand.
Then, having formed a trident, one should contemplate the triple void.
One should gaze upon the ground until the sun’s light appears; this is the "gazing for the sake of begging."
One should awaken the sun by means of the moon; one should awaken the state of being within the power [of consciousness].
Having established the state of being through its own nature, partlessness arises.
When the mind becomes one-pointed, the two-fold enumeration of the prior measures ceases.
When the female serpent of the great forest, sleeping within the cave of the body,
rises upward from exhaustion and does not retreat even a hundred thousand [leagues],
then the yogi, pierced by the agitation of the *śakti*, falls to the ground.
Having ascended to his birthplace by means of the Vāḍava application,
the venerable Goddess said:
"O Lord, please explain the knowledge of the birthplace and the means [for attaining it]."
(191b) "I do not know [it] in its ultimate sense; tell me, O Kaulika, the means thereto.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Just as rivers become empty and the face of the mouth is burned,
so too, having assumed that state, one is consumed by the tortoise-fire (*kūrmavahni*).
Therein, there is no cessation, no utterance, no form, and no discursive thought.
The Vāḍava [fire] has been proclaimed as the sole rule of contemplation.
Having bound the horse of the vital breath with the Mahāvartaka posture,
one should conquer it by means of the saddle of power in the great forest of the moon and sun.
The tortoise alone among these is the field of activity for karma at the end of action. O Lord, with the staff of play in his right and left hands, the practitioner,
having seized the bulbous root (kanda) and the stalk (gokala), is intent upon the rotation of the six chakras.
The wise know that the battle is the vast object of meditation and its grasping is the weapon.
By the service of the bulbous root (*kaṇḍa-golaka*), the sovereign practitioner attains [success].
The Śrī Devī said:

"O Blessed One, tell me in truth about the production of the Great Vortex (*mahāvarta*), which arises from the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), as well as the emergence of the fruit of the yoga of action (*karmayoga*).
The venerable Bhairava said:
When one has recited the extensive mantra that carries the three paths as a single stream,
and it becomes established in its own natural state, it is called the "Great Vortex.
Therein, the mantra and the essential nature of the self are firmly known by the most steadfast of minds.
Then, when poetry— which produces great whirlpools and bestows awakening—
is presided over by contemplation through its own essential nature, that which has arrived is declared to be "with bliss" (sānanda) and is called "vast" (vipula).
The object of meditation is the realization of one's own nature, the profound state belonging to the stages.
For one established therein, who perceives that which is agitated,
there arises the attainment of sovereignty through the very vision of the three times, O Beloved.
Through resting in the five stages and by abandoning upward and downward movement,
there occurs the attainment of the lotus, which is the union of the pervasive wheel.
Having performed the union with that which resides in the mantra, that which resides in its own form, and that which is situated in the movement between *namaḥ* and *anta*,
one becomes devoid of true being;
through the obstruction of the twenty-seven [tattvas], the upheaval of the body hairs arises.
Likewise, with a twofold [increase] there is vision; with a threefold [increase], heaviness of the body;
and with a fourfold [increase], the mother’s lineage becomes the illuminator of the command.
Upon seeing the assembly of mothers, however, weeping occurs first.
On the second day here, O Goddess, [one should practice] this; on the third, there is no doubt.
On the fourth, one should perform the leaping; on the fifth, it becomes sharpened.
On the sixth, there is the exposition of that which is to be known; on the seventh, one attains one's own state.
Established in his own state, Mahāpadma attains identity with the Mothers.
The Śrī Devī said:
[This occurs] through the abandonment of upward distraction.
"Tell me that yoga by which the instrument is made;
Śrī Bhairava said:
Having purified the instrument and equalized the channels of the vital breath,"
Abiding in the state of perfect peace, which is flooded by the rays of the sun and moon,
the enjoyer of emanation is situated within the center of the lotus-cup. Therein,
the lunar wheel is offered into the solar wheel, and the sun is offered into the mouth of the moon.
The yoga of withdrawal and absorption, the conjunction of both,
which penetrates the thousand-petaled lotus and brings about a dear union—
having uttered the mantra with a leap (*sapluta*) through the application of the palate and lips.
Having brought about cessation therein up to the limit of the reality of the Self,
and having bound the crest-lock directed upwards, with the ocean of the limbs restrained,
and having made the water end in its own radiance, one should not think of anything at all.
By the cessation of a hundred measures, one beholds the ocean of milk;
having seen the lotus situated in the midst of its waves, floating amidst the surging billows,
one should worship the Twilight Goddess (Sandhyā) stationed there until agitation arises.
(192b) To one who has fasted, there arises a divine vision that illuminates with knowledge.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O All-pervading Lord, we do not truly know that process called "internal water" (antarjala),
by which the lord of yogis effects the blackening of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Śrī Bhairava said:
One should apply the previously mentioned seat, distinct [from others], at the navel. One should gaze upon the three voids within the tortoise in the form of a staff.
When the state of haste is grasped, that which is diminished by the waning day is destroyed.
Having recited the sound as before, one should gradually fill the great vessel within the waters of the Gaṅgā up to the limit of the reality of the Vidyā; then,
having filled the aperture of Brahmā, one should perform the swallowing of the digits (kalās).

A conflict is created there until the twelfth digit of the moon appears; having seen its emergence, one should agitate the ocean of nectar. Then, sprinkled with the essence of nectar, one becomes a conqueror of death within six months.
In this state, there is no cause whatsoever, nor is there any binding by the vital air (māruta).
It is merely the resting of the movement [of breath] as it enters the abode of the serpent [Kuṇḍalinī].
Having uttered the resonance (nāda) as before, which obstructs the three functions (vṛtti), [one attains this].
Having fixed the feet in the three births, which destroys the two paths,
one should place the boat at the throat; with the gaze fixed on the drop entered into the cave,
and the heart filled by the resonance (nāda), one should deposit it within the triple-womb.
The power of the mind and the sun have entered the interior of the *bindu* and *nāda*.
Each is to be contemplated individually as they abide in the enjoyment and the seizing [of objects].
By blocking the twelve places, listen to the path of the gods through the eye.
When [the breath] is restrained for twice that duration, one experiences a cooling touch.
Then, being praised and honored, one experiences divine women together with bliss.
But when it is restrained for three times that duration, one perceives all things.
The supreme space is fourfold and flooded by the rays of the moon;
one who possesses a divine body may wander upon this earth without obstruction.
Thus, by the concealment of number, one becomes endowed with divine fragrance;
that [scent] brings the entire world under one's control like a servant.
One who possesses the six qualities becomes the enjoyer of all substances and an achiever of worldly success.
With seven [powers], he performs all actions without hesitation;
in the eighth, like Śiva himself, he perceives everything moving. Thus, the yogi who enjoys these modes of existence attains the stage of enjoyment.
Remaining there, one should exhale three times like a serpent with eight hoods;
established in its own function within the divisions, one should enter the state called Kokila.
Therein lies the sheath-vessel, sealed by Bindu and Nāda.
Having generated that which is born of birth, one should cause it to grasp the *kūrma* (tortoise) and *kandala*.
Having rendered them devoid of mental states (*bhāva*) through the realization of the hundredfold nature of oneness,
one should contemplate the trident (*śūla*) in the void, as if in deep sleep, with its two prongs clearly manifest.
Having understood the path through Brahmā at the confluence of the Dhārā and Sarit rivers,
one should behold the station of Viṣṇu, which is named "All" (Sarva) and is the source of all;
[beholding it] according to the sequence of short and long, and by the sequence of long and short.
He who always utters the prolonged resonance (*nāda*) heard as identical with his own self,
and drinks that nectar which is like milk drawn from the udders of a cow— he,
satisfied by that nectar, becomes free from both strength and weakness.
And he performs a most excellent song, endowed with the characteristics of the words;
on his back everything is told, and it is sung together with the Gandharvas.
With their hands raised, their bodies erect, and their eyes closed, they offer praise.
Through the practice of the restrained *pluta* [breath], speech regarding birth arises within the resonance.
When the tongue reaches the head of Viṣṇu at the junction of the void,
it is likewise devoid of even slight contact and enters the cavity of the palate.
O twice-born one, having formed a mouth resembling two hollowed cupped hands,
he should then lift it up until the tactile sensation has become firmly established according to its nature.
The yogi who has attained firm realization shall obtain his own natural state;
and by resting therein and discerning the two scents,
the nectar flows forth, struck by the tongue of the moon in the void.
Then, having tasted the nature of consciousness, it ascends fearlessly.
Indeed, this is the "uprooting of the krauñca-bird," the union of Śiva and Śakti.
It is the garden for the expansion of Śiva, characterized by the action of upward vision and the high-leaping utterance (pluta-uccāra).

One should join the *lalanā* at the palate and bestow it together with the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*). From the throat up to the cavity of the palate, extending as far as the twelve stages (*dvādaśa-bhūmika*), the fish are cooked by the fire; thus one attains the unstruck state (*anāhata-pada*).
One should bestow the eightfold name attained through the cultivation of that state.
Having perceived piercing, paralyzing, subduing, and attracting, one will accomplish everything.
By means of the upward-moving power (*ūrdhvaśakti*), one should forcibly lead [the breath] established in the plane of the Unstruck (*anāhata*).
Having caused the sound (nāda) to enter into touch (sparśa), and having brought touch into the state of sound,
one should place both of these within the wheel of the bindu like the frontal globes of an elephant.
Therein, one perceives everything situated within the frontal globe, including the door-panels, the lattice-work, and the large jar.
Piercing the thousand-spoked [lotus] and gradually moving through the flow of the waters,
having released the spheres of the upper secret [centers] which are endowed with garlands of light,
he reaches the sphere of the tortoise (kūrma) through the union of two moments.
One perceives all phenomena through the state of being, augmented by their intrinsic nature,
by means of the yoga of the three wheels and the revolution of the three lakṣas.
The equality of the three voids arises as the void within the expanse of space.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Lord of the Skull-Bearers, tell me how the foot of the practitioner rises upward according to its power, and by what means it may be understood.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Having withdrawn the state of the *samanā* and being established in the *unmanā*,
one becomes exceedingly emaciated by the fire of the Root Time (*mūlakālānala*) through the wind of meditative action.
There, having bound the elephant of the mind and brought it under control with the goad of power,
one should exhale the vital breath upward with a sound like the resonance of Śambhu.
Even while being pressed by the *argalā* (the bolt),
one should restrain the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within that limit until the upward step is attained;
this is the practice known as *helāgolapluta*, which has entered the consciousness of power (*śakti*).
Having performed the *sanmukha* gesture, [one should visualize] the Kaliṅgī river reaching the end of the triple path (*tripathāntaga*).
Having brought it onto one's own path, the gaze extends for eight finger-breadths (*dṛṣṭihyaṅgulamāriṇī*).
Struck by the thunderclap of the sky, it is struck by the rays of the two hunchbacks (*dvikubja*).
One should contemplate one's own nature, which culminates in the Lord, through the awakening of being.
Established therein, the wise person perceives [reality] by investigating what is desirable and undesirable.
Thus, one forcibly effects the union with the entire host of mothers.
Having recited the ninefold self (navātmā), which is presided over by the nine powers (navaśakti),
through the closing of the nine apertures (navaraṃdhra) according to the sequence ending with the nine principles (navatattva):
the letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, and the bindu itself.

The cessation of the half-moon and likewise the sound that has reached the end of sound; having fixed the mind near the forehead, one should ascend the lunar orb by means of the natural state of the name, and the sound resonates as *cini-cini*.
In the midst of that sound, the practitioner perceives the state devoid of both existence and non-existence;
at the beginning and end of the union of the moon and sun, he attains the Unborn.
It abides on the slope of the moon and is awakened by the rays of the sun.
It brings about the stability of the *piṇḍa* for one who discriminates the supreme reality.
Through the practice of yoga for six months, the lord of yogis becomes all-knowing.
Just as [the mantra] is recited, non-perception arises for the practitioner.
Then, abiding in the state of the stages (bhūmis), one perceives the form of the mind as a moon.
At the end of the twelfth stage, however, there is that which causes the delight of the three principles (tritatva);
pervaded by Vyāpinī, it stands in the center, nourished within the womb of Samanā.
Consciousness presided over by Śiva, having taken its seat through the power of Śiva,
shines forth in the midst of the Mothers within the sixteen-spoked wheel. (194b)
Having drunk the essence of the manifestation of silence, he perceives that equal state wherein the primordial Viśva,
standing upon the trident, sports with the six powers;
facing the true Bhairava of wine, he has partaken of what is called the great intoxicating drink.
White, red, yellow, black, or blue-black;
the first produces *stobha*, the second trembles violently,
the third wanders within the wheel, and the fourth floods it.
The fifth [vibration] floods the earth, and the sixth rises equally with its essence.
By that very power, there is great joy; when it is full, there is the sound of *phetkāra*. Where the upward resonance spreads, there are auspicious sounds of contentment.
The form [of the universe] is established by means of the exhalation (uccāra), wherein the sound (nāda) is dissolved.

O Lord of Yogis, having dissolved all sounds, one who moves through the upward and downward movements in a moment, contemplating with the intellect the mantra-nature that resides in Śiva and Śakti, becomes one whose state is characterized by melting away (drāva).
There, the Mothers stand in groups of four, swelling with power.
Having drunk there at Mahocchuṣma, one rejoices together with Ucchuṣma.
Within the mere interval of a night, one shall go to the seven worlds.
The bud of the supportless lotus-stalk rests upon the back;
that which is the supreme realm of enjoyment for the lap of Sadāśiva,
having seized it, one becomes intoxicated by the splendor of the great drinking-net.
It makes its movements up and down, cries out, and laughs repeatedly;
one should cause that quivering *haṃsa* to be caught in the cage of the *bhāva*.
Bound by the cord of the triple-void, the *haṃsa* shrieks like a wheel.
Having reached the stainless state,
he performs coming and going along the great path of the higher and the lower, together with those who possess insight into the three wheels.
There, the powers beginning with Pārā reside, fixed upon the trident of Śiva.
Having seen which, the child attains the triad by means of the three thrice-three;
beyond that is the world of emanation, the supreme state of Bhairava.
There, that power called Will, whose nature is Śiva, revolves;
by it everything originates, and from it everything ceases.
Therein one finds the eight-spoked wheel, which is saluted by the arrows of knowledge.
There the yogi, having fixed his station, becomes one who has mastered the five wheels (cakras).
There, all the Rudras and Bhairava-mothers have arisen;
they abide there in the Bindu and Nāda, performing creation and dissolution.
Stationed there, he perceives the wheels located in the ten spokes and six sections;
those who have passed [beyond them] are said in the world to be the eight Bhairava Mothers.
The Kaulika remains under the control of those [powers] belonging to that lord of men.
Having attained stability therein, one then perceives the three stages:
the tranquil, the entering, and the supreme Lord of the worlds. Through the union of the Nāda and Bindu, he effects the piercing that brings about perfect peace.
The emission (*visarga*) situated on the path of resonance (*nāda*) is that which enters the body of another;
it is the union of the supreme and the non-supreme within the wheel of living beings among the yoginīs.
Kissed by that which abides beyond time, the fettered soul (*paśu*) is released from its bonds.
One should unite the Joy of the Kula by means of the division of the six paths:
the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) resides in touch; the one called action (kriyā) moves along with the breath;
and the one called will (icchā), intent upon restraint and grace, is dissolved in the Supreme.
The practitioner whose mind is bound by these performs all rites;
with his staff-like arms, he should pierce the wheel of the wind-elephant.
Having leaped up, through the application of restraint, he enters the lotus of the nose.
Abiding in the essential nature of dharma and adharma, located at the ends of the three clenched fists,
know that which is devoid of its own form; abandon those two objects within the heart,
situated in the caves of the pores of the skin by means of the instrument called "emptiness."
Thus has been explained to you the knowledge pertaining to the stages, immersed in the nectar of the hundred streams,
together with its secret, and augmented by the words of the six chakras.
This Kaulika system of the secret method, joined with the means of practice, adorned with the three states, and flowing through the stream of Bhairava,
must not be given to wicked beings who lack discernment regarding the Mother Tantra.
It should be given to those who know the samaya and who long for the state of awakening—
that knowledge which has descended through the lineage of gurus, which is manifold yet once-deluded,
and which exists as the object of the fire of the instruments within the ninefold [body].
Thus has its essence been described to you; it is not without fruit, nor does it fail to issue forth.
Thus ends the "Rite of the Ground" (*bhūmikā-vidhi*) within the "Rite of Bhairavānanā" in the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses.
The Goddess said:
All of this supreme secret nectar has been understood by me.
Now I wish to know the determination regarding Bhairavodyāna;
that which was indicated by me, O Lord, has not yet been made manifest.
"How is it that she who arises from that [source] is the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśī) with the face of Bhairava?
How is she designated as having three heads? I wish to know this.
The Blessed Bhairava said:
Excellent! O you who are saluted by the lords of heroes, I shall explain it exactly as it is:
He is complete, tranquil in nature, all-pervasive, and free from the instruments of action.
He is existence, steadfastness, and the essence of light; he is the sprout of blissful, radiant expansion.
This god Udyānabhairava consists of five aspects and is nameless;
he is ninefold, yet not abiding within, possessing a ninefold body in nine ways.
He is the god who is the lord of the nine wheels, infinite, and filled with rays of light.
That [reality] is a dense thicket of the bliss of awakening and is the unrestrained Bhairava.
From it arises the Great Power (Mahāśakti), who has three heads and is garlanded with virility (vīrya). Abiding in the center of light and bliss, her form is the radiant mantra.
Waveless, supportless, nameless, and causeless;
formless, with its vigor destroyed, it is like a garland of lotuses within [the heart].
Abiding in the midst of light and bliss, she is Kādyā, Kaṅkālabhairavī;
from Ka and Kāla she is Kuṭilā, Kālī, who glides through the intervals of the digits (kalā);
she is the very nature of space, abiding in the center of space, moving through the sky, the skull-bearer, and the bird-like one.
Khaṭṭakī, whose form is like an elephant, Gandheśī, arisen from the sword;
Ghorā, merged within the terrible, she who assumes a body of sound;
Ghargharā, the adorned, Caṇḍā, the fierce one who adorns the left side of consciousness.
Carcarī, Kātarāntasthā, Caṇḍakālī, and Kārikā;
Chamanī, Chadmagamanī, Jayā, and Jambhanakārikā; Jihvilā, Jalajā, Jālyā, Jhāṅkāreśī, and Jharjharā.
Marked with the ṭaṃka, marked with the viṭaṃka, she whose form and station begin with the letter ṭa; ṭhamarī, with eyes like a well, ḍamarī, with a face like a ḍāmara;
ḍaṃbarā, ḍahalā, ḍāvyā, with ears like a ḍaṭṭa, and possessed of great splendor.
Taraṅgiṇī, Taraṅgā, Tanuśīlā, Tapaśvinī;
Svacirā, Manīṣāśī, Damanī, Dāmanī, Damā;
Dhenudhīrā, Dhīramātā, Dhūryā, Adhīrārthadāyinī.
Born from a lotus, with the essence of a lotus, she is Padmā, born from the face of Padmā;
she is the goddess who brings an end to the faces of the lotuses, Phakkarī, with quivering lips;
she is Phakkarī, Phekkārā, the fulfiller of sounds through the syllables Pha, Pha, E, and Pha.
She is of the nature of awakening, accessible through awakening, possessing powerful faces, and the destroyer of power.

She is remembered as Bhairavī, the pacifier of fear, and the one who brings about the end of worldly existence (bhava). By her own nature she is the devourer of the syllable *ḍāṭ* and ends with the syllable *mā*; she proclaims the fivefold meaning.
She who possesses five left hands and five goddesses, whose nature consists of five times five;
she who is risen as five and flows as five, intent upon the five times;
Yamaghaṇṭā, Yamā, Yāmyā, and she who is the most effective destroyer of Yama.
Raminī, Ratijā, Rambhā, Rathanī,
Retasaṃkāyā, Lambikā, Lalanā, Lālyā, Lālāntā, Lalani-parā. (196b)
The showerer, the vomiter, the one who has vomited, the one who carries the sacrificial grass, the Mistress of the Banyan;
she whose form is Śakti, who abides in tranquility, the pacifier, she who is devoted to the moon;
the Śavarī, the support of the six kalās, situated in the midst of the six kuśas and the remainder.
The Mistress of the six chakras, possessing six forms, with sixteen faces free from attachment;
she who dwells in the center of the station of the six drops, the ender of the Kula by means of the six-syllable mantra;
