she who is intent on devouring the six chakras and the complete shatterer of the six knots.
She who possesses all forms, who devours all, who is all-bliss, and the eternal;
she who is wrathful, the supreme, the piercing, and reclining upon the lotus-stalk of the heart;
she who is the lake, the essence, the source of prosperity, the peaceful radiance, and she whose form is infinite.
She whose abode is the food of swans, who holds a hand, who is smiling, and whose face is radiant with laughter;
she who delights in loud, boisterous laughter, and who resounds with cries of "Hā! Hā!
She is the destroyer of decay, the one who consumes all, the one who is eternally pure, and the sovereign of the temple of dissolution.
The wonderful, ageless Mother, the immortal one joined with the infinite;
she who is hope, composed of hope, like a wish-fulfilling gem, and whose form is that of the Lord;
the sovereign Goddess born from the *īru* [vagina], the destroyer, who has lifted up and sustains the sluggish.
Utpalā is also she who is swelling, whose hair stands erect, and who is terrifying;
she is one whose body is empty, red, and protectorless, whose form is the *liṅga*, and who is beyond the *ali* (the lineage).
She consists of the flame of flames, is knowledge itself, is called Ekarā, and possesses a triangular form.
The letter Ai is Aiśvarī, the sovereign, the shatterer of great delusion;
O is to be known as Ojasvinī, the goddess of the noble state of the Ṛ vowels;
Anta is Antakarī, the ender of the end; Aṃ is Ambā, the beauty of the immortals.
She whose form is the emission and the open vowel *ā*, beautiful with the nectar of emission;
she who is the support for contraction and expansion, whose body consists of the sixteen supports;
she is the Goddess Mahāmātreśvarī, whose very nature is the Garden.
Without her, there is no Lord of Gods; indeed, he likewise does not exist without her.
She is the Aparā, the Parā, and likewise another, the Parāparā.
The digit of consciousness (citkalā) is threefold, each being threefold again, abiding in three places and resting upon three paths.
It does not abide in the middle, nor does it abide among the animals, nor does it abide above; yet it is not contracted.
It is the support of all, consisting of all, and completely full with great splendor.

Such is the Blessed Lady, who reveals her own true nature; she is to be accomplished as the Great Mistress (Mahāmātrī), just as she is described by the Goddess. Having gone to the abode of Hara at night, one should remain stationed amidst a multitude of spirits (pretas).
Having taken up the hand-drum (ḍamaru), the practitioner, free from all affliction,
should sound it while forming the Bhairavī mudrā and meditating upon that goddess with the face of Bhairava.
By means of fifty recitations, the surface of the earth trembles.
All the directions blaze, and there is a wondrous falling of meteors;
then a terrible tumultuous roar arises.
Thereupon, Yoginīs of various forms and great ferocity arrive.
O slender-waisted one, when all the practitioners remain encircled [by you],
they shall grant whatever is desired to the high-souled practitioner; otherwise, O Goddess of gods, she would utter another hundredfold end.
To that king of heroes who sits [in meditation], Śivā herself—the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī), Bhairavī, and the others—comes of her own accord; of this there is no doubt.
Together with the lord of practitioners, she indeed leads him away; of this there is no doubt.
Alternatively, O Goddess, by means of the yoga of recitation— specifically by one hundred thousand or ten thousand recitations—
all the most excellent accomplishments (*siddhis*) that were previously proclaimed by me therein will undoubtedly be attained.
By means of the practice of reciting three hundred thousand [mantras], she will accomplish the Middle Path;
O Goddess, there is no doubt that these perfections belong to this lord of practitioners.
Alternatively, one should meditate on her of terrible prowess, ending with the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa).
She should meditate upon that fierce goddess who possesses the luster of a black crow, a raven,
a cloud, or a dark storm; she has three faces and is endowed with eighteen arms.
She was intensely ploughing, making a terrifying roar that shook all things,
and had assumed the form of a great *preta*. With various weapons raised,
her body bound by a garland of ploughs, with hair standing erect, she was fearsome.

Having thus meditated upon the Blessed Lady, the lord of practitioners, firm in his vows, should offer human lungs as the oblation in three sets of three, with the tenth state. At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, O Goddess, he shall accomplish whatever is desired in his mind.

That goddess comes forth of her own accord from the midst of the fire; of this there is no doubt. For the high-souled practitioner who has attained the status of the Lord of the Wheel, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished through the power of the God and Goddess.
As many sādhana practices as were previously mentioned from within this sovereign tantra, all of those I shall accomplish for you;
even common rites one may achieve through mere recollection.
In rites of subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, killing, and expulsion; likewise in paralyzing, stunning, causing hatred, deluding, or malevolent magic;
in the accomplishment of sorcery and vetāla-spirits, and in the wondrous suppression of clouds.
The entry into the city, the possession, the dream that accomplishes the goal,
the piercing possession, the cloth-possession, and that which is the pestle-possession;
the possession by the *kaṭorā* and so forth, as well as the work with minerals and ores in the mines.
The practitioner shall accomplish [the goal] with ease through mere recitation; of this there is no doubt.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method for preparing the *caru* (sacrificial porridge), which the lord of practitioners or a charming sister may perform.
By merely performing this quickly, the accomplishment of the *piṇḍa* arises;
having taken that from a great battle, as well as its head and flesh.
O Dear One, staying within the interior of the excellent chamber, one should accomplish that;
having taken recourse to the center of the altar, one should cook it there on wood.
O Mistress of the Gods, one should perform the stirring and other such actions there in another vessel.
O you of excellent vows, once it has been accomplished, one should then produce [the deity] from that;
having taken up the mantra situated in the vessel of flames, being unwearied, and having bound the Karaṅkiṇī mudrā, one should recite the mantra of the God of gods.
When a moment has passed, the goddesses arrive and search for the sacrificial oblation (caru), saying: "Give it, O lord of practitioners! Do not delay!
To them, the hero should say: "I shall bestow it upon you."
By her, that supreme sovereign Karaṅkiṇī was seen by me.
Indeed, for her sake, I have accomplished an excellent sacrificial oblation (*caru*).
Therefore, after you have seen her, that very [oblation] shall be given to you.
"O goddesses, listen to this: she will invoke the Goddess. There she comes, that terrible one, greedy for an offering of sacrificial rice (caru).
With both gentle and terrible forms, she bestows boons upon the practitioner."
Having prostrated before the Goddess, one should offer the *argha* from the left side;
thereafter, having formed the *karaṅkiṇī* mudrā, the *caru* should be presented.
Then the Goddess will be pleased and will cause the *caru* to be accepted.
Having grasped it, it becomes multiplied ten millionfold in a mere moment.
Then she herself consumes half of it; what remains is given to the goddesses.
Thereafter, Karaṅkeśī bestows [the remainder], and one should then take up the drink.
When that which is produced from the six flavors resides within the fire of the causal center,
the Mistress of the World dances by the mere act of drinking it with joy;
then the goddesses, their minds satisfied, [rejoice] likewise with various bound souls (paśus).
O fortunate one, those born from the lineages of Brahmā and Viṣṇu satisfy [the practitioner];
indeed, they bestow the divine drink upon the foremost of adepts.
O Goddess, he too, having become a physical body, shall attain the perfection of the *piṇḍa*;
becoming her equal, the man sports as he desires.
Thus has the supreme accomplishment of the *caruka* been fully described to you.
"What else shall I speak? Tell me, O Bhairavabhāminī!

Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the attainment of Bhairava, in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the fourth hexad, in the *Bhairavaśrotas* Vidyāpīṭha, concerning the Severing of the Head (*Śiraścheda*).
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear the definitive determination of the names of the phonemes (varṇas),
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes transcendent of all mantras."
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O beloved, as I shall tell you that essence which you ask about—
the all-pervading *oṃkāra* and the *pratoda*.
The Lord of All, the Praṇava, the illuminator of mantras;
the Self of all, consisting of three feet and three forms;
the essence of the abode, whose own nature is revealed through names.
The first [syllable] is the pervader of the letter *a*, the all-pervading Śiva, Nārāyaṇa, formless, the goad, and fierce-faced.
It is to be known by its name beginning with the long vowel; and the letter *i* is marked with three dots.
And the abode of Brahmā with three suns is proclaimed today as Māyā;
she is the Great Māyā of five dots, whose nature is to delude the power [of the senses].
O beautiful goddess, the fourth is declared to be Anumā, the letter *ī*.
Rudra, Pañcamabhānu, and likewise the fifth Śrītithi;
this is declared to be Krodhāsana, the great sound named with the letter *m*.
Then the sixth, Kālānala, Prāṇa, and the auspicious Jvala-tejas.
O slender-waisted one, the syllable *ū* is called "the upward and downward drawing.
The syllable *ṛ* is the first of the kalās of that deity; it is the seventh, the supreme Sun, renowned as the first of the neuter vowels, and its location is always the navel.
Longer than a *kalā* and situated above, its form is encircled by a *kalā*;
this is declared to be the gift (*dāna*), the letter *ṛ*, lovely and radiant.

Pragu, Guhāśaya, Bhṛṅga, Navama, Bhānu, Uttama, Trikata— these are the names by which the letter *sa* is always proclaimed. Kālānta, Daśama, Sūrya, Anta, and also Napuṃsaka [are the names for the letter *ha*].

Thus has the letter *E* been described; it is remembered as having its arms raised upward. It is the eleventh [vowel], the triangle, the abode of fire, that which resides in the womb (*yoni*), and the *śṛṅgāṭa*; it is celebrated by these names.
The bulb (kaṇḍa) is six-cornered, a hexagon, the great desire born of desire.
Vāgbhava is described as the Lord of the Bindu-face, known as the letter *e*.
Likewise, there is the Praṇava, Mārttaṇḍa, the state of *o*, and the goad (*aṅkuśa*).
The syllable *o*, which begins with three feet, is celebrated by various names.
O Goddess, that *o*— consisting of three feet, having an upraised hand, and being the Lord of the Lute (*tantrīśa*)— is likewise proclaimed as the fourteenth by its names.
The Lord of the lunar days (tithīśa) is declared to be the new moon (amāvāsyā) during an eclipse;
the anusvāra is the mark (lāñchana) and the ornament (bhūṣaṇa) in the manual of mantras (mantrapaddhati).
The Lord of the bindu (*bindveśa*) is called the *pa* [consonant] and the bindu itself, which is known as the letter *aṃ*.
That which ends in a vowel, the visarga, that which ends in *kalā*, and likewise *kṣaya*;
and the sixteenth, the Great Sun (*mahāsūrya*), the letter *a*—this is called emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
These Rudras who have been proclaimed, all of them, are the sixteen Suns.
Now listen to those thirty-four [syllables] born from the womb (*yoni*).
The cutting of the womb is proclaimed as the *kalaśa* (vase);
*brahmāṇa* and *śīrṣaka* are recited as the letter *ka*.
Chedakānta, Karpara, Khageśa, and likewise Naga—
these are renowned as the letter Ai, O best of sages, by these synonyms. (199b)

O lady of excellent complexion, the letter *ga* is declared to represent the elephant-headed Gaṇeśa, who has a single tusk, is a lord of the hosts (*mātaṅga*), and holds a skull-bowl; it also represents the *gharghara* sound,
the terrible roar, the trident, and the clanging of a heavy iron club.
The three-headed one with averted faces, the syllable *gha*, the jewel, the nose,
likewise the fangs, the syllable *ṛ*, the blood-red one, and likewise the blood-red belly;
having meditated upon the syllable *ka* as the seat of contemplation, it is designated by these names.
The first [syllable] of the third [group], as well as Caṇḍa, Granthivaktra, Karālina,
and the one named Caṇḍabhairava, are explained as the letter Ca. Padmāsana, Dvakūpa, Chamana, and likewise Chomaka.
The letter *cha* is proclaimed by these names: Ekanāla and Chakra.
The letter *ja* is proclaimed here as Jamadagni, Jayādya, Jihvila, Dvijihvika, Rasa, and Nāsāntara.
O Goddess, I have proclaimed to you these names: Bhairava, Bhīṣaṇa, Śūla, Ḍāmara, and Urdhvabāhuka;
likewise, Jhakāra, Adhobāhu, Saṃkaṭa, and Mahābhīmarava.
The letter *sa* has been fully explained to you; now the letter *ṭa* is being described.
Soma, Candra, and Amṛta are declared to be the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).
The letter *ṭha* is the well-mouth (*kūpavaktra*), and the full moon (*pūrṇacandra*) is circular (*vartula*).
I have proclaimed to you its form as an unbroken circle;
it is indeed the pestle and the crusher, beloved of the Yoginīs.
It should be known by its names, beginning with the syllable *ḍa*, as the support of the city of Ḍambara.
Bhairava, Dṛḍhakarṇa, Caṇḍogra, Haripiṅgala,
Granthīśa, and Ḍhakāra should always be known by these names. Aśva, Megha, and Avaktra are proclaimed as the letter Ṇa.
The downward-pointing goad, the ram, the boat, and likewise the crossing—these are declared to be the letter *ta*; now the letter *ṣa* is being described.
The letter *ca* is called the blue jay (*cāṣa*), the one with a central flow (*madhyasara*), the arrow (*śara*), and the abode of truth (*ṛtadhāman*).
It is remembered by the names knot (*granthika*), formidable (*dāruṇa*), self-controlled (*dānta*), and the letter *da*.
The letter *cha* is the bow (*cāpa*), the locus of the wielder of the bow (*dhanurdharādhāna*), the center of emptiness (*madhyaśūnya*), and the agent (*kāraka*).

O worshiper of the best of gods, I have described the letter *na*, known by its names as *niṣedha*, *ūrdhvaśaṅku*, and likewise *sa-granthi-malina*. The letter *pa* is a lotus with a turned-away face and two arms.
He is the one with earrings, the one of terrible roar, the one who causes resounding, the beloved of the Yoginīs,
the incomparable Lord of Kuṇḍalinī, the cruel one, the truly fearsome and formidable one,
and the abode of the splendor of the letter *pha*; he is thus proclaimed by these names.
The letter *ka* is Kumbha, the Lord of the Jar (*Kumbheśvara*), who is thoroughly cooked. The letter *bha* is Bhairava, the Terrible, declared to have downward-pointing shanks.
It is marked with the fifth vowel (*ū*) and is Time (*Kāla*) and the Supreme Person (*Puruṣa*).
The letter *ma* is declared to be Paśu, the innermost essence, and the lord of the common wind; the letter *ya* is Prāṇa. Furthermore, there is Bāhu, Ṭeṭibha, Devāsya, and Bhīmavigraha.
The syllable *phe* is declared to be wrathful, as well as blazing with splendor.
*Ja* is proclaimed as the lord of the earth, possessing sequential strength and stability.
The letter *la* is celebrated by its synonyms as the progenitor of fortune (*lakṣmī*).
The letter *va* is proclaimed as Vāruṇa, Candra, Dadhāsa, and Audha; the letter *śa* is declared to be Śiśireśa, Vara, Śambhu, and Samudāhṛta.
Likewise, *ḍa* is Dvigahvara, Ḍāvya, Śaṅkara, and Ḍāḍāraka.
It is proclaimed by these names: Soma, Amṛtanātha, Sudhāsāra, Sudhānidhi, Sakāra, Ṣadvasādhāra, Haṃsa, Śūnya, Prāṇa, Mahānāva, and Mahākalā.

The letter *ha* is known by its names as "Great Shadow" (*mahācchāyā*) and "Twice-Bent" (*dvikubja*). The letter *kṣa* is declared to be the Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśāna*), the Sun, and Destruction (*kṣaya*).

The sun-like abode that reaches the end of all things, the supreme essence of the Mātṛkās— thus, O Goddess, I have fully explained to you this supreme determination of the names of the collection of phonemes, the unsurpassed essence of everything.
All those devoid of this are proclaimed to be dull-witted.
O Mahālakṣmī, this has been declared as the essence in the path of mantra;
in this supreme tantra, I have explained this essence to you.

This should not be given to those of wicked intellect, nor to those who are devoted to other gods. This great knowledge, which has issued from the lotus-mouth of Śiva, should be given to one who is faithful, devoted to the guru, intent on the supreme good, and auspicious.
"Those great-souled ones who revere, worship, or even recite [this],
all of them should be known as Bhairavas— truly, truly, again and again. Thus,
this supreme rule for the letters has been given to you.
"Nothing else is so easily understood as that which has been correctly spoken here;
tell it clearly, O beloved of Parvata, O fair-browed one, for it resides within the lotus of your heart."

Thus ends the chapter on the Names of the Letters in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra (*Mahātantra*) of twenty-four thousand verses, within the fourth hexad of the *Śiraścheda* section of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavaśrotas*.
Having heard this from the Great Bhairava, whose feet are worshipped by the Lord of the Gods, the deities...
Again the Daughter of the Mountain King spoke to her beloved,
who was like another sun that has set, or like the radiant Vāḍava fire that completely dries up the ocean of worldly existence—
the eternal Krama, which is the teacher of the sequence of the Goddess of Liberation and transcends all things.
The Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord, I am satisfied by listening to this flood of knowledge;
today I have become one who has accomplished her purpose, as has this King Jayadratha."
Even now I have not understood that which was previously indicated by you:
how, at the conclusion of the tantra, there is the worship of the knowledge of the sequence.
"Why do I conceal that which ought to be told entirely and correctly? If you are pleased, O Blessed One, then please relate it out of your grace.
Having heard this, the Blessed One [spoke], like a mass of shimmering rays.
Having partaken of that which was produced from the first sacrifice, he spoke these nectar-like words.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent! Since I have been impelled by you, I shall indeed speak."
This incomparable great secret must be guarded with great effort.
I shall declare this most difficult-to-attain knowledge, which is divided into three parts:
that which has support and that which is without support, both established as a pair.
Between these two, there is another, wondrous dissolution of existence;
thus the three abodes have been described, and now I shall explain them to you.
The first is the Śākta [abode], throbbing with vitality and garlanded with radiant rays.
Resorting to that which is clearly manifest— the source of the radiance of consciousness, luminous, and the unification of all states—
one [attains] another as a dyad, then a triad, a tetrad,
another as a pentad, a sixfold state, and yet another as a sevenfold state.

O Gaurī, it is eightfold, ninefold, another which is tenfold, and consists of eleven; likewise, O auspicious one, it consists of twelve and thirteen varieties. O beautiful lady, that which consists of fourteen has become manifest with support.
Power (śakti) and vigor (vīrya) are inexpressible; the noble power of consciousness (cicchakti) is considered to be twofold.
Consciousness is supreme, and the power-consciousness (śakticaitanya) is declared to be the threefold division.
This triad, together with the mind (manas), is proclaimed as the fourfold group.
She is fivefold as Bhūti, Dhṛti, Mahānandā, Bhāsā, and Avyakti;
sixfold through the piercing of the six cakras; sevenfold by way of the internal divisions;
eightfold through the three divisions of the fallen constituents (dhātus); and ninefold by way of the absence of division (tv-abheda).
Through the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) on the elements and the sense faculties, [the *samādhi*] has been described to you as tenfold;
this is due to its reliance upon the intermediate functions of the mind (*manas*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and the intellect (*buddhi*).
That which is to be realized up to the fourteenth stage is indeed sequential and possesses an objective support.
Therein, the expansion of the power of undivided consciousness is radiant in its manifestation;
it is the observation of a vast and flourishing activity, throbbing with a multitude of rays.
O worshiper of the best of gods, in this manner it comes to have an object;
now hear the division of the collection of rays:
Siddhā is red, while another is called Suśuṣkā and Utpalā.
Kālī, Kālarātrī, Kāladhārā, Kāleśvarī; Siṃhavaktrā, Mārjārī, Uṣṭrā, and likewise Kāpālinī;
Khararūpā, Virūpā, Meṣarūpā, and Mahoragā.
Raktākṣī, Raktavāsā, and likewise Laṃbakarṇī; Pṛthodarī, Ekanetrā, Lokanāthā, and Bhayaṃkarī;
Ulūkavadanā, and another, Kālavaktrā, and Khiṅkiṇī.
Karaṅkā, Bhadrakālī, and likewise Mahābalā;
Bharuḍā, Aṭṭahāsā, Rākṣasī, and Āsurī—
these indeed are remembered as the rays, distinguished by the eightfold division of the gaze and the command.

Preceded by their family mantras (*kulavidyā*), with their own names placed in the middle, and followed by the word *padam*, they are to be worshipped; they grant the perfect accomplishment of the *prālamba*. Abiding within the sequence of the throbbing wheels (*cakras*), they expand from their own respective places.
"The multitude of their mental states is utterly destroyed; they consume all things and are intensely passionate.
Thus ends the section on the varieties of the Sālaṃba-krama ritual in the Jayadrathayāmala.
Hereafter, O Goddess worshipped by the lords of heroes, hear [the teaching] on the Nirālamba.
It is effortless, waveless, without path, and without a lord;
it is auspicious, all-pervading, and an all-encompassing expansion; it is devoid of the states of being and non-being;
it transcends the mind, its end is peace, and it is like a waveless ocean.
Appearing as everything yet unattached, the Lord Bhairava is described as being without support, free from limiting conditions, and infinite because he sustains all.
It is attainable through the accumulation of firm vigor, worthy of worship, and inherent in one's own nature;
it is described as the thirty-six principles and resides in the stages of the word-syllables such as the *piṇḍa*;
established in the nature of the states beginning with waking, it is declared to be without support.
O Bhairava,

that which was previously proclaimed as being present everywhere— even in the absence of external objects— is clearly that which resides within one's own part; it is beautiful, resting in its own essential nature, full, and non-dual.
That is declared to be without support, neither quiescent nor like the sky.
Listen now correctly, both of you, as I shall enter into the flood of rays:
Dhūmrā, Jvālā, Gāndhārī, Gahaneśī, and another.
Māyā is one, Mahāmāyā is another, and Nityā is indeed another, as is Anityatā.
Śāmbhavī, Gā, Pratiṣṭhā, and likewise Apratiṣṭhā—
these twelve alone are declared to be the rays of Vīramaṃtharā.
Among these, there is another group of eight known as Bhairava, located in the center:
Śrīvatsa, Śaṃvara, Śānta,
Jagadādhāra, Jagaddyuti, Viśveśa, Īśāna, and the one named Ajasa.

These eight have been fully described as they arise from the state of throbbing vigor. Among these, the supportless [reality] is established within the Īśas; it is joined at the end of the feet through the union with the syllables Hrīḥ and Śrīḥ.
In this procedure for the sequence of worship, all the mantras have been extracted.
Thus has the secret, which is without support, been declared, O Maheśvarī.
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the worship of the Supportless Sequence in the Jayadrathayāmala.
Now I shall proclaim another [teaching], the most secret and supreme,
which stands between these two, devoid of prior or posterior;
it is the incomparable withdrawal of existence, radiant with the dissolution of all things.
Regarding the two sequences that have been explained, therein is a great vibration which,
having become manifest through the differentiation of rays, is terrible and has entered upon a wrong path.
There stands the radiant Kālikā, whose terrible rays blaze and quiver;
she is the agent of dissolution, possessing a fearsome form, devouring all, with a terrifying countenance, and supremely the bringer of the end.
O slender-waisted one, I shall here describe the emission of rays exactly as it is.
First is proclaimed Saṃhāriṇī, the destroyer of Time;
another is Rakteśvareśvarī, and likewise Kṛtāntāntarī.
She is proclaimed as Kālarātri, as well as Caṇḍā and Caṇḍeśvarī;
likewise, O Goddess, another is celebrated as Vīrabhadrā.
She is the destroyer of Rudra’s destruction, ever intent on the time of the world's dissolution.
These have been proclaimed in the *Mahābhairavasaṃhārasaṃhāriṇī*:
thus, these eleven rays are of terrible appearance.
They are celebrated as being joined with the *Kulavidyā* at the beginning and ending with the feet [of the mantra].
O slender-waisted one, they should be worshipped precisely in reverse order,
whether in a linear arrangement or within a wheel consisting of a red triangular cloth;
thus is the excellent sequence, proclaimed as threefold, to be worshipped.
With every kind of heroic offering, such as wine, meat, and fermented liquors; with abundant "heroic drinks" consisting of great meat and spirits;
and with vast multitudes of large animals, through these forceful heroic practices (*vīrasādhana*).
One should worship the supreme Krama, the beloved of Mahābhairava.
Through the worship of this division of the Krama, the highest knowledge arises within the Saṃcara;
that which is the entire essence of the Krama is indeed threefold and fourfold.
O highly fortunate one, my word is fivefold and not false;
it is a most wonderful and supreme secret that one should guard as closely as a clenched fist.

O fortunate one, even at the cost of one's life, the supreme sequence must not be spoken; for by revealing it here to both [types of practitioners], even Bhairava himself would pass away prematurely. In this ritual procedure of the first sacrifice, the fourth division is the most excellent.
Having known that, O Bhairavī, perform the teaching for the three.
Thus ends the procedure for the dissolution of the states of the divisions of the *Krama* in the *Jayadrathayāmala*.
Having heard this, Girijā’s body was covered in horripilation.
He spoke this unsurpassed hymn, clear and profound:
"Salutations to You, whose nature is splendor, who move within the circle of rays;
to the God who is the form of creation, and likewise the ordainer of its maintenance."
Salutations to the one who abides in the sequence of dissolution and resides within the wheel of time;
salutations to the one whose form is the great withdrawal, whose nature is embodied. Salutations to the Teacher, who is fully satiated by the total eclipse of both the moon and the sun.
Salutations again and again to Bhairava, who is inflamed by the devouring of the lunar orb of consciousness;
salutations to Śambhu, intoxicated with the pride of having made the three fires his food; salutations to the one adorned with the digits (kalā), who feeds on rays of light, and who is Death itself.

Salutations to you who abide in the station of various words; salutations to the one of fierce and formidable form! Salutations to the twelve-fold dissolution; salutations to the sixteen-fold [consummation]!
O Lord of the burden of the three natures, likewise, O you who are filled with the eleven!
O you who delight in the manifold play of the five foods, salutations to you, the five jewels!
O you who are satiated by the bliss of the triangle, you who are intent upon the foundation of the triangle;
O sovereign of the burden of the three natures, whose form has arisen from the triple path!
Salutation to the enemy of Smara, who devours the three worlds as his meal of sandalwood, and who consumes the threefold aggregate through his threefold foundations.
Salutations, salutations, salutations to you, Bhairava, the severer of worldly existence.
I am completely filled and thoroughly satiated by partaking of the nectar of the secret.
O Blessed One, I desire to know the most supreme and ultimate secret.
"Since today you ought to explain the incomparable sacrifice exactly as it is.
When Bhairava, the bestower of abundant enjoyments, was thus praised by the Goddess,
he spoke of the supreme, primordial sacrifice according to its true meaning.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, you who are a vessel for pure knowledge!
I shall describe in brief the primordial sacrifice honored by the gods."
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva; Bhairava, Anāśrita, and likewise other liberated beings (muktapuruṣas);
Śakra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Ambhas, Vāyu, Soma, Artha, and Īśvara.
The Vasus, Aśvins, Ādityas, Grahas, Nāgas, Asuras, and others;
Mahākāla, Vighneśa, Nandirudra, and likewise Vṛṣa; Bhṛṅgin and all the Gaṇas, as well as Dakṣa and the rest.
All the yoginīs here are indeed goddesses and likewise powers (śaktis). Whatever other assembly of gods and assembly of siddhas there may be,
for them the primordial sacrifice is that which is called sexual union, the most excellent of all.
For them, sexual union itself is prescribed here as the act of recitation (*japa*).
Worship is situated within the *bhaga*; kissing is situated within the *bhaga*;
presence (*sānnidhya*) is situated within the *bhaga*; and the other yoga is established in the *bhaga*.
The means of accomplishment (sādhana) resides in the vulva-lotus; the mandala is born from the vulva-lotus.
The deities reside in the vulva-lotus, and the Sugata is situated in the center of the vulva.
The sacrificial pap (caru) is located in the vulva; for them, there is the extraction of the vulva and the interior of the vulva.
Therefore, O Goddess, sisters are to be worshipped for the sake of all accomplishments.
My vulva is the mark; my arm is the Śakti-mudrā; the vulva is remembered [as the means].
My arm is the divider; the God of gods is the supreme vulva.
The entire universe originates from the *bhaga* (the womb), and its dissolution is held to occur within the *bhaga*.
This entire world, both moving and unmoving, is marked by the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*.
Therefore, O one worshipped by the lords of heroes, hear now of that primordial (or most excellent) Great Sacrifice (*mahāyāga*).
Having attained which, practitioners who desire accomplishment do not grieve;
they are constantly devoted to practice and always remain free from delusion.
Having reached the sleeping chamber, which was well-spread and most beautiful,
adorned with various colorful designs, filled with the thick fragrance of fine incense,
sprinkled with sandalwood and aloe-wood, and languid with the weight of the scent of flowers.
Adorned with a garland of flowers made of precious gems, it was further beautified by a funeral pyre;
its eyes were made imposing by the addition of flames, and it was decorated with a network of tinkling bells.
It was filled with the cries of ruddy geese, Greek partridges, parrots, and pigeons.
There, having fashioned an auspicious bedstead, adorned with ivory, mother-of-pearl, and other ornaments;
fully endowed with various beauties, decorated with networks of small bells;
well-constructed with legs, and provided with elegant carved figures.
O beautiful woman, here the mattress should be made of wool, the bed-covering of grass, and the mountain for a pillow; a variegated cloth should be spread there as a sheet,
and it should be sprinkled with camphor or scented with the fragrance of love.
The practitioner of mantra should perform various acts there by which [the deity] becomes inflamed with passion.

Then he should lead the auspicious messenger (dūtī) there— her eyes rolling with intoxication, her lips like the bimba fruit, her teeth beautiful, and her face framed by a playful contraction of the eyebrows.
Her eyes have the luster of a young deer caught in a snare; she possesses a beautiful smile.
Her mass of hair resembles a shimmering swarm of bees.
Her glances, with their curved arches, are like the bow of the God of Love.
She has the color of molten gold, is of the same hue [as her ornaments], and is free from waves;
she is resplendent with hundreds of beautiful and variegated ear-ornaments;
she possesses a noble neck that is like the sky, adorned with the finest jewels.
She was bent low by the weight of her breasts, which were as massive and unrestrained as the frontal globes of an elephant;
she was adorned with plantain-tree-like arms that were well-rounded and thick;
and she was resplendent with fingers resembling the hoods of a serpent.
Her crest is adorned with shimmering jewels, and her fingers are decorated with variegated rings;
her face possesses the exquisite beauty of the full moon, captivating the mind.
O Great Lion of Hari’s weapon, she stands in the midst of the most excellent ants;
her hips possess three folds, her buttocks are like a thunderbolt, and her gait is languid;
her beautiful thighs and shanks have the form of plantain trees and elephant trunks.
Her feet, shod with beautiful golden sandals, were adorned with anklets; she was resplendent with long, hanging necklaces of gold coins and strings of pearls,
and her girdle tinkled with the sound of shimmering bells.
She was slow-moving due to the tinkling sound of her bracelets and bangles;
she possessed a gait like that of a rutting lordly elephant and a deep navel.
Her speech was as sweet and faltering as a swan’s, and she spoke with auspicious words.
Adorned with armlets, strings of thread, and garlands of flowers,
she whose mind has completely destroyed great delusion is meditated upon as the moon;
she whose sole nature consists in the relishing of the singular wonder of Bhairava.
Filled with the supreme bliss of tasting the nectar of supreme awakening,
her very nature is one of complete satisfaction from the fine wine of the essence of existence;
she is the enchanting *mohanī-mudrā* in this world of the moving and the unmoving.
One woman he captivates by his form, another by touch, and another by speaking;
another by his graceful movements, while others are won over by playful gestures and the like.
Some beloved women he wins by his restless glances, and others by a kiss.

In a firm embrace, no other woman of great strength could take him away. O deer-eyed one, she indeed must be born from the eight families; one should place that slender-waisted goddess upon the great couch.
Having covered [the area] with a pair of garments, one should commence the sacrifice there,
upon the vast lotus of the womb (bhaga-padma), which possesses the primary seat (pīṭha) and secondary seats (upapīṭha),
and is beautiful with circular doors marked by the footprints of Kurunāla.
(205a) It was moist at the edge, bearing the mark of the vulva, crowded with the footprints of the bannered one;
born from the mud of true passion, it possessed whirlpools of semen and swarms of bees.
By that [mantra], she was encircled by a triangle within the vessel of the mantra-weapon (maṃtrāstrakalaśa),
her face filled with lotuses, marked by arms and hair,
and rendered languid by the presence of the virtuous one, who was unrestrained by the weight of his mental passion.
One should utter the excellent mantra with the sound of "sītkāra" and the "kilikiñcita" gesture.
Therein, O Supreme Goddess, one should first worship the two Lords of Gods:
Nityaklinnā, Raktā, and Mohakoṭā who resides therein.

One should worship the Goddess, the beloved of Bhairava, who stands dried within the temple of Smara; she is the destroyer of [worldly] attachment through her leftward immersion (vāmāveśa). She is present both with support and without support, and she is that which brings about the dissolution of all states of being.
These very goddesses are to be worshipped here according to the sequence beginning with the daily rites (*nitya*).
One should worship them with an abundance of great offerings, according to one's means,
with various kinds of meat and liquors— both natural and artificial— and in diverse ways.

Having thus worshipped the Great Lord Krama situated there with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and various kinds of flowers, accompanied by the sounds of auspicious songs and the resonance of lutes and small drums; ||| 12 ||
Now listen to how and what one should subsequently offer as an oblation there:
having raised her up, with a radiant mind,
he should desire her with a sound of longing, his eyes agitated with joy.
From that triangular vulva-shaped sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should offer the *liṅga* and the *śruca* ladle;
one should then offer that first, incomparable semen for the purpose of libation (*tarpaṇa*). In this manner, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) until only a single morsel of food remains.
At that moment, the messenger enters, raising a great cry from her throat;
out of affection, she will surely speak to the Kaulika—of this there is no doubt.
At that very time, [the realization] arises through the complete sequence of transmission.
The goddesses come to the beloved union with the goddess for the sake of the practitioner;
he should then pray for the auspicious nectar.

One should drink from the mouth of the small bell (*ghaṇṭikā*) using the tip of a cotton swab (*picu*) according to the practice. One should draw [the substance] bit by bit through the process of extraction; as long as one kisses, drinks, and licks it, for that long one possesses all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
O Goddess, one who is free from the waves of conceptual thought and is permeated by the practice of non-duality shall indeed attain perfection; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
And the Yoginīs, together with the Bhairavas, always attend upon such a person.
The rays will follow him as he departs; of this there is no doubt.
O Bhairavī, as long as the practitioners have not performed such a great sacrifice, so long does the incomparable mouth of the Vāmācāra not flow forth.
This excellent sacrifice is perfected and protected by Mahābhairava;
it is renowned as bestowing accomplishment at once and bringing about great enjoyment.
That is the beloved object wherein one accomplishes [the goal] through force.
If the messenger (dūtī) should be devoid of the [proper] characteristics for the sake of the practitioner himself,
then she is praised in all rites as one whose heroic mind is unshakable;
such a one should be provided with food, or [invited] to the assembly of heroes (vīramelaka).
This primordial sacrifice, honored by the gods, has been fully explained to you.
What more shall I tell you? Speak that which resides in your heart.
Thus [ends] the fourth hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraścheda* division of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavaśrotas*.
The first chapter on the ritual procedure for sacrifice, concerning the worship of the Krama sequence.
Having heard this, the daughter of the mountain, her eyes wide with joy,
the Great Goddess Maheśvarī, prostrated before the Supreme Lord and spoke.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, whose crest is marked by the crescent moon, who are filled with the supreme nectar!
The ritual for the assembly of awakened heroes is the most supreme of all;
by merely performing it, one becomes a partaker of the meaning of the Krama-knowledge.
Having thus heard these words issuing from the lotus-face of the Daughter of the Mountain, [she was filled with joy].
The Blessed One spoke to the assembly of heroes with a profound voice.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, that you ask such a question!"
Although this secret has already been declared, I shall nevertheless explain it to you:
having taken refuge in the sleeping sanctuary, which is free from all afflictions,
beautiful, and filled with the fragrance of excellent incense and perfumes.
Having reached the Kulaparvan, one should perform the assembly of heroes (*vīramelāpa*). Then, all those who observe the Bhairava conduct should be invited—
those who know the *samaya*, O Goddess, who are devoted, contented, and intent upon the Krama.
The initiates (*samayin*), the spiritual sons (*putraka*), the practitioners (*sādhaka*), the teachers (*deśika*), and others,
as well as the awakened yoginīs and devotees from the netherworld—
bring them here and make them endure [the ritual], provided they are accompanied by their retinues.
Seats should be offered here according to their respective order;
they should be worshipped with the *praṇava* alone, using perfumes, incense, garlands, and so forth.
Then, one should cause them to sit properly according to the arrangement of the *cakras*.
The first wheel belongs to the gurus; the second to the sādhakas;
the third shall belong to the putrakas; then the fourth among the samayins;
and the fifth shall belong to the yoginīs. Thus one should perform [the worship] in due order.
In that union of all heroes, the mountain revolves;
there, Kālī, who is the power consisting of fifty [letters] and is entirely imperishable, manifests.
Yet, the union of heroes does not expand within her.
With that, the Supreme Goddess should worship that assembly of heroes with offerings of water,
flowers, incense, and [fragrances] smeared with sandalwood and agallochum.
One should worship each [deity] there according to the extent of one's means.
One should worship Madhyabhairava, who resides in the center of each wheel,
whose eyes are black, red, and crimson, and who is perfumed with supreme fragrance.
Having thus worshipped the central [deity], who brings about great bliss, is supreme, and causes the world to be intoxicated, one should fill the other vessels with them,
filled with great flowers and strewn with the five jewels.
Afterwards, O Goddess, various kinds of food should be given to them without weariness. Whatever is desired by each one, that should be provided for him once.
There should be various meats and diverse foods, both high and low.
With various foods to be licked, sucked, and drunk,
as well as those that are pungent, bitter, astringent, sweet, and sour—
and with many other such things— one should satisfy the five wheels.
At midday, having again fully gratified [the deities] until the churning of bliss,
one should then satisfy the five circles (cakrapañcaka) with offerings of water for honor (argha), songs, the sounds of lutes and flutes, and various wonderful acts that serve as water for the ears.
Then, from that wheel, intensely radiant rays burst forth;
they flash with great bliss, crowded with hundreds of playful movements.
They dance, laugh loudly, and blaze, intent on divine sport.
They all fall, run, and dwell there; they tremble, suffer, and become exhausted.
Others mutter mantras and speak of secrets.
Others spoke words endowed with the vital points (*marmas*) of truth;
and yet others, O Goddess, spoke various and wonderful things, addressing one another.
Some manifest the cooing of peacocks, some begin a series of ritual gestures (mudrās),
and others engage in the playful arts born of the Kaula scriptures.

They begin their dancing with various formations. Some, like heroic warriors, commence the tāṇḍava dance, while others, full of pride, engage in conversation with minds fixed on the contemplation of Bhairava, as if they were Time itself.
(207a) Some there raise their voices loudly, making the twelve directions tremble in many ways; some are intent on weeping, and what more can be said— some wander about in agitation.
Some, eager for it, enjoy the excellent juice of the five-fold play with their lovers; some display their garments with bold gestures;
and some suddenly support their own bodies with the [garland] emerging from the wheel.
Some vomit the essence [of the *bindu*] from their terrifying bodies;
some, with intense longing, perform the act of union; and others, filled with fervor, drink what has arisen therein.
Thus is the most excellent *melāpa*, wherein the feet of the Lord of Vīras are worshipped by the best of heroes.
From that, the one called Vīra arises intensely with a mass of widespread rays;
having seen which, those of excellent lineage prevail—how much more need be said?
O Beloved, these five [breaths], filled with the process of movement, likewise share a single intent.

Whatever has been set forth by me here as the sequence of the Maudra-empowerment, which serves as the powerful instruction for this [practice], that alone unfolds for him as the supreme, great truth; it is not merely nectar, but this heroic *tāṇḍava* dance of yours that has been fully described by me.
By merely performing this [rite] with a horse, one becomes worthy of all accomplishments;
indeed, the practitioner becomes uniquely skilled in the knowledge of the sequence.
There is no yoga superior to this within the interior of the world.

It pacifies all calamities and destroys all misfortunes. Within this very time, it is known in the Bhairava lineage that the perfection of the *piṇḍa* (the physical body) occurs after just one month; of this there is no doubt.
They all float through the sky as enjoyers, free from all feverish distress;
endowed with the attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, they are intensely eager for enjoyment.
O fortunate one, there is no object whatsoever that they cannot accomplish by their own power.
Now, what is the use of speaking at length? It is stated here in brief:
just as the sun is among the planets, and the moon among the host of stars;
He is like the blazing fire among luminous bodies, and the king of tridents among all weapons;
he is like Death among the hosts of powerful spells and mantras,
and like the supreme lord of waters on the banks of the river Gaṅgā.
In the same way, among all sacrifices, the Vīrayāga is praised;
likewise, the Ādiyāga should be known—this is the truth, the truth, again and again.
O Goddess, the majesty of these two sacrifices cannot be fully described even in ten thousand years.
It cannot be described even by those possessed of a thousand tongues, because it is inexpressible;
just as these two are the most excellent sacrifices, and just as the slender-waisted Goddess is [supreme],
so too, O Beloved, is this King of Kings in all the Tantras.
Worshipped according to the prescribed rite, it bestows the fruit of all desires.
Thus has been fully described the sequential practice of the *Tantra*, by which,
O fortunate one, one immediately attains the threefold manifestation of the Lord of the Jewel of True Yoga.
Furthermore, listen to another thing: surely that which resides in your mind, speak it out more clearly! I shall today tell you everything in its entirety within the *Uttara* of the *Tantrasāra*.
Thus [ends] the fourth hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, in the *Śiraścheda* section of the *Vidyāpīṭha* within the stream of Bhairava.
The chapter on the knowledge of the sequence of the procedure for the Hero’s Tāṇḍava dance.
Having thus heard [this] from the Lord of Heroes, whose commands are honored by the best of beings,
the Mistress of the Gods, having prostrated before him who is worshipped by the gods, spoke once again.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear the procedure for the King of Tantras;
how is this [text] to be installed, and how is it to be written in its most excellent form?
Or how is this [person] worthy of worship? Tell me, what might result from such worthiness?
Of what kind is his power, and how does it bring about excellence?
"I desire this explanation, O Blessed One, O best among the wise.
Having heard these excellent words of the goddess, the Lord of the Gods— whose intellect was noble, whose speech was profound and gracious, and who was the foremost of speakers— replied.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent! I shall explain that which I have been impelled by you to speak.
O highly fortunate one, this is the essence: namely, the worship of the boon-bestower therein."
There, first of all, having reached a place that is free from the pairs of opposites, very beautiful, liberated from all obstacles, and abounding in the finest flowers and fruits;
having constructed a splendid dwelling there, smeared with sandalwood and agallochum.

O lady of virtuous vows, having worshipped there according to the procedure that will be described— abounding in the fragrance of incense and adorned with canopies and other ornaments— the practitioner of mantra should then recite the mantra and, O beautiful one, the [image] should also be drawn.
Having consecrated the birch-bark leaves and performed the auspicious rites of protection (*kautuka*),
one should write the various letters— uniform, well-proportioned,
with excellent apertures, level-headed, beautiful, and free from any defects.
O observer of excellent vows,
one should write five, ten, or even thirty verses that are substantial, diverse, consisting of mere syllables, faultless, perfectly pure, equal, and supreme.
O Goddess, one should never write more than a hundred and fifty [verses].
The scribe here must be well-initiated and learned in the science of words, sentences, and logic.
A gold ring adorned with jewels should be given to him.
One should offer another pair of auspicious garments and ornaments such as bracelets;
one should burn incense continuously until the painting is completed, and during that time,
one should provide an uninterrupted supply of liquor and other offerings.
Afterwards, O fair-browed one, one should present the book that has been written;
then, one should gratify the scribe with sweet and delicious foods.
By this method, one should proceed until the tantra is completed;
however, at the conclusion of each group of six [chapters], one should perform the Hero’s Sacrifice (vīrayāga).
Having thus accomplished the Lord of Tantra, the Mountain [King] was filled with faith and devotion.
Listen now to how one should subsequently install the deity:
having offered the sacrificial materials such as wine, meat, and liquor,
and having worshipped with saffron, agallochum, camphor, musk, and sandalwood.
All things such as sesame seeds and the like, various mineral substances,
and such collections as these, including royal regalia and other implements—
one should consecrate the deity according to one's capacity, together with the manuscript.
Having placed the sovereign book upon an auspicious seat, one should worship it with flowers, incense, and other offerings, as well as with various precious substances, garlands, and ointments.
Mātṛkā is the mistress of all mantras; perform the worship and other rites by means of her.
Having brought offerings such as *naivedya* for the purpose of acceptance (*adhivāsa*), one should perform the ritual;
thereafter, one should worship Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, and the others. Then, [one should worship] the God and Goddess within the interior of the book, the slender-waisted one.
One should dissolve the Mātṛkā into its desired form.
One should bring down the supreme Vāgīśī, mounted upon Skanda, from the highest heaven;
one should meditate upon her as the abode of the Bindu, appearing in the form of rows of stars.
By means of the essential nature of one's own true form, through the act of manifesting that very nature,
one should properly deposit and cause the maṇḍala to descend upon a lotus.
Having worshipped there according to the ritual rule, one should then perform sacrifice upon the petals as well.
O Goddess of the Gods, by means of the eight groups [of letters], there is the separate eightfold Vāgeśvarī.
[The eight forms are: Haṃsā, Citrā, Bhairavā, another called Kadaṃbā, as well as Kamalā, Nityā, Subhagā, and Gaurī is the eighth.
All the goddesses are like the moon, all are seated upon thrones,
and all should be known as four-armed, holding nooses and goads in their hands.
O Bhairavī, one should meditate here upon her in the center, surrounded by goddesses intent on praise, adorned with all ornaments, and possessing their desired forms; she who,
having arisen from Akula as the unmanifest Rāviṇī, has now attained manifestation.

One should worship this supreme *kalā*, which resides in books and consists of the *mātṛkā* syllables and *skandhas*, by beholding its many wonders. One should worship it with various offerings of incense, as well as liquor, meat, fermented spirits, and the like.
One should worship [the deity] all around with various kinds of flowers,
having prepared an abundant collection of offerings while remaining free from stinginess regarding wealth. O lady of excellent complexion, one should offer guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter.
Then, having brought a beautiful celestial chariot, most splendid in every way,
variegated with various ornaments, adorned with diverse garlands and wreaths,
equipped with various small bells, and marked by bells and chowries;
With its body variegated by flags and banners, enveloped by many silken cloths,
endowed with great splendor, and adorned with hundreds of various artistic designs—
therein one should worship the supreme book, which is wrapped in a silk veil.

The carriers of the celestial chariot (vimāna), adorned with all ornaments, should all be made handsome and fortunate, and gratified with wine, meat, and other offerings. In front [of them], there should be various sounds of musical instruments, along with the blasts of conchs and kettledrums.
Then, O Maheśvarī, one should cause a fourfold canopy with a beautiful top to be fashioned at the front of the celestial chariot (vimāna). Furthermore,
courtesans, elegant women, and female ascetics should proceed in the lead.
They should be depicted dancing, their eyes rolling with intoxication,
standing directly before the Śiva-liṅga, with tridents held as supreme weapons in their hands. (209b)
Dancing, they cause the lead-bulls of the celestial chariot to turn;
these bulls should be covered with cloths, painted, adorned with flowers, and made to run ahead. Likewise, other figures such as dancers and wrestlers should also be depicted.

Various wandering performers (cāraṇas), adorned with all kinds of ornaments, should be employed. One should scatter gold, gems, pearls, and coral here and there; likewise, all items such as silver and copper, while remaining free from deceit regarding wealth.
In this manner, O beloved, one should cause [the disciple] to circumambulate the entire city in succession.
Speak, O God! My rays, arisen from Bhairava, are pleased with me.
This final birth is auspicious, for it is the most excellent of books.

"O God of gods, this has been attained through the grace of the accumulation of merit. Reciting thus before [the deity], the practitioner of yoga performs a dance to the excellent song proclaimed by Bhairava, which is based on the Madhyama-grāma scale.
Singing with a joyful soul, one who has accomplished his purpose should stand before [the Goddess]:
"O large-eyed daughter of the mountain, listen to the *Bhāṃbhagīti*!
O Sovereign of the supreme body and mechanism of all the lords of the Asuras, O All-pervading One!"
This stainless garland, consisting of the knowledge of all secret tantras, is fully capable of uplifting the world when properly applied;
therefore, always make my mind pure with this.
Thus, with a heart full of joy at having first gone forth into the religious life,
he wandered through the city and then returned home unwearied;
there, O fortunate lady, he set down the book after performing the auspicious rites.
Having placed [the deity] upon the maṇḍala, one should worship again, O Dear One,
with various offerings of flowers and all the services due to a hero.
And when one is devoid of wealth, one should wander about within the house itself.
A festival should be celebrated there according to one's means;
thereafter, one should place the image upon a level and auspicious throne.
He should honor the scribe with a seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood or else of *devadāru* wood;
thereafter, he should bestow cows, land, jewels, and gold.
Immediately after that, he should honor all those who are present there.
Then one should feed everyone with various meats, fermented liquors, and so forth.
Afterwards, the *tāṇḍava* dance should be performed just as it is in a gathering of heroes (*vīramelaka*).
In this manner, the rite should be performed for one day, or three, five, or seven days.
For ten or sixteen months, according to one's means and capacity,
by whomsoever a book has been thus consecrated, O slender-waisted lady,
by him the entire world, up to the realm of Brahmā, is established.
O Goddess, what need has he for numerous sacrifices, or for offerings made within mandalas,
or for recitations and vows that serve as the means for achieving yoga—
he who possesses such a book in his home is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
In that auspicious, excellent abode, Hara is eternally present,
as is the goddess Kālakaraṇī and other lords of the Bhairavas. Furthermore, there are seventy-seven crores of mantras of fearsome appearance.
Arising from the southern stream, they dwell there eternally:
those goddesses, powers (*śaktis*), yoginīs, and the terrible mothers (*mātṛs*);
likewise the *ḍāvis*, *ḍāmarikās*, *lāmās*, *svedyās*, and *kiṃkarikās*.
All [the goddesses] are eternally present there, satisfied and desiring the welfare of all;
they constantly produce the sound of chanting within that excellent house. They bestow wealth, grain, and the like, as well as long life, health, and prosperity.
Therefore, one should constantly worship [the book] according to the extent of one's wealth.
Just as bees resort to a honeycomb,
so do the goddesses resort to the great book within the ocean of mantras.
(210b) Through worship for six months, the tantra and the piṇḍa bestow accomplishment;
indeed, knowledge arises spontaneously for the practitioner within six months.
Indeed, for as far as a distance of one *yojana*, the sacred field (*kṣetra*) is ordained;
those who die there go to the world of Rudra.
O beautiful goddess, those who behold this book when it is being worshipped [attain the same].
O Goddess, these go to the world of Rudra; there is no doubt about this.
One should indeed utter the name preceded by "Śrī," and one should not pronounce "Śiraścheda.
O Ambikā, one should say "Jayadrathendra" and "Tantrarāja."
Indeed, at the time of yoga, one must certainly speak of the "severing of the head.
For as many syllables as there are contained within the king of books,
by uttering [the name] for tens of thousands of groups of years, [one attains the fruit].
In the world of Rudra, the Mātṛs are devoid of both knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*).
However, for one who is awakened and remembers [this] constantly, knowledge arises;
that which is established in the mouth of Kālī will manifest within six months—of this there is no doubt.
At that time, one should recognize that my powers have become clear;
at that time, this supreme tantra has been obtained through meritorious action.
Then, the best of practitioners should know that it is their final birth.
Alternatively, what is the use of speaking at length? Now listen to a summary:
from the constant worship, recitation, retention, hearing, meditation, and remembrance of this very supreme tantra, there arises a great fruit.
O Supreme Goddess, I do not have the power to describe this, even with tens of millions of tongues, each possessing a thousand million names, lasting for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
This supreme tantra is worthy of worship; it bestows the fruit of all desires.
When one causes [the disciple] to grasp the Praṇava, the god who is the supreme variety of emanation,
then causing him to hold a book in his hand shall be equal to wealth.
The equinox arises as the yoga; there is no need for deliberation here.
Having observed such a sign, one should always worship the book.
Once this excellent tantra has been properly obtained, one should discard everything else like straw.
This unsurpassed tantra must not be given to anyone;
the giver falls into hell and the loss of accomplishment occurs.
Therefore, the mantra-practitioner should not cause it to be given as long as one who acts according to the teaching has not appeared.
Thus, O Beloved, the worship of the book has been established and described; it is the most excellent of all, bringing welfare to the world, and bestowing true accomplishment and liberation.
It is a means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra—what more shall I tell you now?
He established that supreme yantra upon the face of each respective Lord of the Full Night.

Thus ends the chapter on the Authors of the Manuscripts in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra of the Severed Head (*Śiraścheda*) within the Seat of Knowledge (*Vidyāpīṭha*) of the Bhairava Current, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] collection, in the fourth hexad.
Having thus heard from the best of gods for the sake of severing the cycle of worldly existence,
the daughter of the mountain spoke once more to Hara, who is worshipped by the gods and has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel; she,
the beloved wife, was eager for the sequence of his exposition and was bowed low with the eight limbs of her body.
Having praised the Beloved with hymns again and again, [she praised] Bhairava at the very end.
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Supreme Lord adorned with the crescent moon, I am satisfied."
Having heard from you that which is thoroughly saturated with the nectar of knowledge,
I now desire to hear, O Lord of Mantras, the sequence of the exposition:
how should the exposition be performed by a Guru who knows the reality?
"Or how, O Lord of the gods of gods, tell me that, O Bhairava. Śrī Bhairava said:
"Excellent! O fortunate one, I shall speak that which I have been requested by you."
O Maheśvarī, just as accomplishment occurs within this teaching, so too,
having entered a well-concealed house perfumed with the fragrance of excellent incense, [one should practice]. (211b)
Scattered with heaps of flowers and anointed with sandalwood and agallochum, he—
surrounded there by his disciples— should worship the excellent book with various offerings of garlands, flowers, incense, and fragrances.
One should worship the entire lineage of gurus, together with their great majesty,
as well as oneself and the disciples, with flowers and incense. Then, O lady of excellent complexion, having caused the book to be recited without interruption, one should proceed.
Having worshipped [the deity], that which is to be recited should be explained with poetic embellishment,
using a voice accompanied by the offering of flowers and endowed with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and emotion (*bhāva*).
One who knows the words, the sentences, and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is declared to be a reciter (*vācaka*).
Immediately thereafter, O beloved, the teacher should provide the explanation once;
first by stating the division of words, then by means of that, the process of compound formation,
followed by the consideration of the meaning of the sentence through the correlation of what precedes and what follows.

One should begin the exposition by means of specific statements and through the manifestation of the great sayings (*mahāvākya*). Having presented the distinctions of the dust, one should cause the distinctions of the heart to be recited;
[one should employ] debate (*vāda*), wrangling (*jalpa*), and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), which possess positions, counter-positions, and opposing sides.

O Maheśvarī, the statements, injunctions, and ritual procedures— those that impel to action and those that prohibit, as well as those endowed with the meaning of valid means of knowledge— must be investigated here through the analysis of logical principles and their classification.

The twenty-one [topics] beginning with the "lion’s glance" (siṃhāvalokita) are not to be investigated elsewhere; they are presented here by way of summary rather than in detail. [Furthermore,] the connection, the subject matter, and the purpose [are explained] as follows.
Having thoroughly investigated that very purpose as well as other matters such as the verbal expression and so forth, the teacher who knows reality should speak.
[He should explain] the aphorism, the response to the aphorism, another [point], and furthermore, the concluding summary.
O radiant one, this chapter, which is to be explained in its various divisions,
contains those philosophical views that appear here as authoritative yet mutually contradictory.
One should first examine the objects of inference by means of the instruments of knowledge;
just as it was done in the previous hexad, so should it be performed by the wise man.
These are perception, inference, and likewise scripture.

This direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been analyzed as being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), and consisting of sensory perception and mental ascertainment (*indriyavyavasāya*).
Inference (*anumāna*) is preceded by that [perception] and is of three kinds in many ways.
The remainder is as previously stated, and the other is likewise; it is indeed the "inference based on general observation" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa).
In some cases it should be known as preceded by a sign (liṅgapūrva), in some cases as "prior" (pūrva), and in some cases it is recorded as such.
Thus, in this inference, there is that which is taught within the *Tantrarāja*.
The scriptures arising from the Supreme Lord and the rays of the sun of His words are truly great, serving as effective means for destroying the darkness of ignorance.
Because He is omniscient due to His being the creator of all, His speech is not contradicted.
Indeed, by some other means of valid cognition, one who is not omniscient has been postulated.
These very same means of valid cognition, which follow the nature of consciousness,
function through the internal experience of the speaker and not otherwise.
Perfected by the experience of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), it does not require another means of knowledge;
thus, its validity remains unimpaired.
Having thus reflected upon the words of the authority, one should explain [the matter] correctly.
The sixfold relationship is to be explained; it is analyzed by dividing [the categories]:

the Supreme (parā), the Great (mahatī), the Intermediate (anantarā), the Divine (divyā), the Non-divine (adivyā), and another called Mutual (itaretara); the sixth is proclaimed as the Other (parakīrtita).
Thus, this [reality] consists of twenty-six principles according to its pure and impure nature;
it is indeed declared as the subject matter through the exposition of the divisions of duality and non-duality.
It is called the "Shatterer of Saṃsāra," for it is the tearing asunder of impurity, karma, and the rest.
This purpose is to be known; that purpose is now stated:
the attainment of the fruits of accomplishment and liberation is thus demonstrated.
O Goddess, in the third hexad, the nomenclature has been examined.
In this sequence, the supreme *Tantrarāja* should be explained;
the true nature of the Goddess must be declared, for she is to be worshipped with special effort.
Having thus performed the exposition according to the intended method and having restrained the book,
one should first worship it according to the prescribed rite with offerings gathered from worldly existence;
thereafter, one should worship the Guru who has taken refuge in supreme non-duality.

Immediately thereafter, one who intends to perform the Vīrayāga must indeed burn incense continuously during the time of exposition. O beautiful one, one should not study on the first lunar day nor even on the fourth.
O beautiful one, it should never be explained on the eighth or ninth lunar day, nor on the fourteenth, nor on the new moon or the full moon. Furthermore,
it should not be taught during an earthquake, a conflagration, or during terrible national calamities.
Likewise, when the king has passed away, when one’s own mind is in distress,
or never at all during the death of one’s teachers, the [Tantra] should never be explained.
One should act in this same manner during the *saṃkrāntis*, the *vyatīpāta* yoga, and on festival days (*yātrās*).
O beautiful lady, the worship of the signs (nimitta-pūjā) should be performed with great distinction;
O Bhairavī, one should thoroughly examine the disciples through careful investigation—
those who are doubtful, those who are mistaken, and likewise those who lack proficiency.
Having investigated thoroughly in three ways, one should thereafter begin the exposition.
The "protector" (*pālaka*), the "grasper" (*grāhaka*), the other known as the "ataraṇṭaka," the "nameless" (*anāmaka*),
and the "caṅkapota"— these are proclaimed to be the defects of a disciple.
That which is not established anywhere, yet [one wonders] "What is this? or "What might this be?", is declared to be a state of doubt arising from the illumination of one's own reasoning.

One who speaks with hostility toward the investigation of the Guru’s words, one who is harsh, one who is clever at refuting the means of valid cognition of others, and one who does not investigate even when something is briefly stated—
such a person, being utterly perverted, is considered here to desire nothing at all.
Indeed, a fool who lacks proficiency may enter some [place];
yet one who is unlearned and speaks as if he were learned, or one who is more like a stone body than a human,
would become a scholar merely through the excessive pride of his own pedantry.
When the meaning of a sentence uttered by Niṣṭhākta was explained in secret in the presence of the Guru,
it indeed leaked from Gālakas;
that [meaning] did not remain within his body, for what was heard was exactly as it truly was.
The one named Vātareṭaka is proclaimed in the Sūtra as "the restless.
Wherever there may be an exposition, he is always indeed intent on the effort of beginning that exposition; he never at all performs a marriage ceremony anywhere.
O Goddess of the gods, that which is known as Vānareṭaka proceeds;
its name is indeed Nidrā (Sleep) always in the presence of the Guru.
O Goddess, it is considered to occur at the beginning of an exposition, and it is declared to be tāmasa.
O beloved, he who is indeed known as Kapota always says:
"From this [state], no illusion whatsoever has ever been heard;
O Goddess, they know nothing at all, whereas I know it according to reality."
Thus, having awakened the consciousness of the disciple who is like a pigeon,
he should constantly examine his various kinds of disciples. Having so examined them, the knower of the reality of the qualities should begin the exposition.

The principles of the Tantra must always be observed by practitioners, by spiritual sons, and especially by the highly fortunate gurus who know the commitments (samaya). One should initiate a special festival at each six-day period, as well as at the beginning, middle, and end.
Upon the completion of the King of Tantras, one should perform the Vīramelāpa;
endowed with pure devotion, this supreme tantra should be heard.
"Having heard much instruction, the wise should always act in secrecy.
Thus has been told the sequence of the commentary according to the *Tantravara*. Therefore, O Goddess, the conduct of the Guru and likewise the behavior of the disciple must be explained.

Thus ends the chapter on the Sequence of Exegesis in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra of the Severed Head (*Śiraścheda*) within the Seat of Knowledge (*Vidyāpīṭha*), in the Bhairava Current, consisting of twenty-four thousand verses, in the fourth hexad.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of the gods of gods, how indeed is one always fortunate through the Guru?
O God, what is his conduct, and what characteristics are considered his?
O Maheśvara, how should a disciple behave in the presence of the Guru?
O Supreme Lord, please explain the fruit of these two exactly as it is.
Śrī Bhairava said:
You have already described the characteristics of the Guru in the previous hexad.
O illustrious lady, although this has already been stated briefly for the disciple, I shall now describe it to you again according to its sequence as it pertains to you:
one who is devoted to the conduct of Bhairava, free from agitation, and devoid of greed.
A devotee of Śiva, tranquil in soul, possessed of courage, free from envy,
skilled in the meaning of all scriptures, following the lineage of gurus,
proficient in all arts and crafts, brave, steadfast, and indeed noble-minded.
Endowed with all limbs, truthful, firm in his vows,
devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, possessed of faith and devotion,
not given to drinking, possessing full knowledge, and free from greed and delusion.
Such is the teacher described in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the king of tantras. The disciple should be endowed with all virtues, possessed of courage, free from conceptual construction,
filled with faith and devotion, eloquent, a practitioner of the hero’s conduct (*vīrācāra*), and firm in his vows.
Sharing both happiness and suffering, and intent upon the means of accomplishment,
listen now to how one should conduct oneself in the presence of the guru.
He should remain silent, humble in spirit, truthful in speech, and with senses restrained. Pure in body and mind, likewise modest and with palms joined in reverence before him,
he should not transgress his shadow or his command even at the cost of his life.
One should avoid spitting, shedding tears, sneezing, yawning,
false speech, idle chatter, and censuring others. One should not laugh loudly in his presence, nor be angry, nor be filled with grief.
One should not show anything together with its tip before him; otherwise,
one is said to be scorched in the terrible world of the Kūṣmāṇḍas for more than a hundred years of Brahmā, if one steps over his shadow.
By disobeying his command there, one shall dwell for three times that duration;
by spitting in his presence, one shall dwell in the Raurava hell for a kalpa;
and by shedding tears of grief in his presence, one shall behold Avīci for a long time.
O Goddess, due to injury or yawning, one shall dwell for a long time in the Kumbha and Pāka hells;
together with him, he who goes to the Kūṭaśalmali hell shall suffer false torment for thirty manvantaras, O Supreme Goddess, even if he were a perfected being (siddha).
If one should engage in social discourse with him, either together with him or in his presence,
then for one year he shall dwell in the world of the Kūṣmāṇḍas.
Even a perfected one (siddha) shall go to hell by the act of censuring others.
If a person, out of anger or afflicted by grief, utters [the name] of this [deity] in its presence,
then for ten thousand years plus one, he shall become a *kūṣmāṇḍa* ghost in the realm of Brahmā.
This is indeed the same even if it occurs without cause, through ignorance, or from laughing.
O Goddess, entering into worldly affairs before that [realization] is extremely difficult;
therefore, one should remain humble, intent solely on the state of the Goddess.
If anything belonging to him should be lost or divided from us,
it must then be recovered by means of threats to his life or property;
however, one should not speak of this in his presence until he himself has first initiated the matter.
The Guru is proclaimed to be the god, the Guru the goddess, and the Guru the mantra.
The Guru is the scripture, the Guru is the mother, and the Guru alone is the grandfather.
O God, one is never born without a Guru.
When the entire universe is filled with elixirs and jewels and offered to him,
only then does one become free from debt;
for by that act, one is rescued from the terrible ocean of worldly existence, which is full of great delusion.
"O Goddess, tell me: what further debt does a man owe him?
Therefore, always perform devotion to the Guru through action and mind;
indeed, there is no such thing that cannot be accomplished through devotion."
One should strive with effort to avoid contact with him, for liberation is sought through such avoidance.
Thus, one who understands the true nature of his gestures should dwell in his presence for a very long time;
yet even then, one should not investigate his knowledge, his character, or his conduct.
One should not contemplate his various forms nor his activities.
O Goddess of the gods, when the teacher is intent on the destruction of [the disciple's] sins,
he must be restrained by the wise disciple who bows before him.
Thus, the conduct and creation of the six preceding [chapters] have been declared by me;
they have been stated here in brief for fear of overburdening the treatise with excessive weight. All this, which is the most essential essence of the Tantra, has been succinctly explained to you.
"Now, what shall I say? Speak, O you who are worshipped by the Lord of the Cakra!

Thus ends the chapter on the rules of conduct for the teacher and disciple in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, within the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the *Bhairavaśrotas*, in the twenty-four-thousand-verse [recension], in the fourth Ṣaṭka.
Having heard this, that goddess trembled, afflicted by fear.
And that [palace], whose foundations were struck by the wind, trembled violently;
yet, at the word of the God of gods, it shook even more with a faltering sound. (215a)
Having praised the Supreme Lord with clouds as flowers, the Goddess said:
"Alas! This most terrible thing is renowned, causing my heart to tremble."
O Kāru, what must be done by you today for this reason? By me, the various words spoken by Devananda have been set aside;
likewise, O Lord, all her movements have been restrained by me at all times.
Therefore, O Supreme Lord, what must I do here?
I shall now perform an expiation unto the end of my body,
so that I may not fall into the ocean of hell.
"Command me, O Destroyer of Tripura, what task must be done by me?
Save me, save me, O mighty-armed one! I have fallen into a deep abyss.
Having spoken thus to the Supreme Lord, Gaurī became agitated within her heart.
Falling to the ground with a bewildered mind, she lay there distressed;
then the Lord adorned with the moon raised her up.
Having consoled her, he wiped the beloved’s face with his palms.
The Lord of the Gods of gods spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"O dear one, do not be distressed; you are my beloved, always worthy of honor."

"Be fearless, O slender-limbed one; as I myself previously declared, so shall there surely be for you purity throughout all the worlds. O Goddess of beautiful limbs, remembering me, quickly become Bhairavī."
Whatever has been done by the command of the King of Varsa is indeed accomplished;
whatever boon is granted by him when pleased is the most excellent of boons. Or, even through hardship, a great curse that causes the fall from initiation [is likewise effective].
