It is renowned as the destroyer of all accomplishments; therefore, one should practice it accordingly. O Gaurī, by performing that, he shall [attain] the fruit of accomplishment.
Nevertheless, one should remain as if afraid, or even recall the presence of a protector.
Śrī Devī said:
O mighty-armed one, instruct me on that by which the destruction of faults may be achieved.
It arises for the foremost of practitioners through the grace of the one marked by the bull (Śiva).
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O beloved, I shall proclaim that which destroys all defects.
O Goddess, although this Vidyā— which destroys great sins, annihilates floods of misfortune,
and bestows the accomplishment of all goals— has indeed been spoken of before,
I shall nevertheless declare to you this Vidyā of terrible prowess.

O fortunate one, listen to that [mantra] which, by its mere remembrance, causes the entire universe to tremble violently; it dispels all sins. Having reached an auspicious place, with a chamber fragrant with excellent incense, [recite it].
There, in a place covered with heaps of flowers and perfumed with the fragrance of wine,
one should worship the Goddess Mātṛkā, the Mother of Mantras,
with all the offerings appropriate for a hero; thereafter, one should extract the Vidyā.

The first seed-syllable is declared to be *māyā* (the letter *i*), which is all-pervading, [joined with] the *haṃsa* (the letter *h*) and endowed with the fire-bindu (*ra*). Now hear from me the second:
it consists of the two-tongued one (*j*) and the man (*a*), enclosed within the jaws of the formidable bolt (*bhīmārgala*, the letter *ṣ*).

One should extract the Bindu and Māyā as the object of knowledge; the second seed-syllable is remembered as the Wind (Ya), pervaded by the Praṇava (Oṃ) and marked with the abode of Fire (Ra). One should then extract Varuṇa (Va) at the end of that, having combined them all into a single mass.
Likewise, the arm beginning with the Praṇava, situated in the wind;
then the night alone on the peak, and again time conjoined with creation.
[The descent] by the syllables of the Praṇava is the attainment of great fortune.
One destroys even the accumulation of great sins merely by remembering [this].
There is no sin here that it does not forcibly destroy.

I see no knowledge equal to this for dispelling the poison of evil. O beautiful daughter of the Asuras, on one side are all mantras and vidyās, and on the other side is this very vidyā; they are equal, O beloved, and equally dear.
She who, when remembered, burns away sin just as fire consumes a heap of cotton—
she has been described to you by me as the remover of the faults of one's commitments (samaya).
She is the primordial seed-syllable, the Kevalin, resplendent with the six long vowels.
Having pierced it with the Bindu, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Having extracted [the syllable] preceded by the Yoni and pierced by the Thunderbolt (*vidya*) and the Hook (*aṅkuśa*),
that which is called Mahākāla is situated at the southern door.
With grandeur, one should worship Śivādūtī at the left door,
remembering her as seated upon the shoulder of a great corpse or having the face of an Asura,
O lady with a vajra-like belly; one should worship her within the hexagonal world.
One should install in the center the Goddess Śivā, the source of Śiva, who has arrived for his sake;
she is radiant, established in the center, beautiful, sweet, and steadfast, adorned with hand-bells,
and whose daily observance is formed by the measurement of sixteen and twelve kalās.
She who is most capable of rending ten million Mahākālas,
whose nature is to seize and consume the collection of the wheels of the blazing fire,
who devours the six wheels, the sixteen supports, and the three wheels.
She whose nature is the fierce act of vomiting and swallowing the entire circle of the lords of all circles; she who arises from the center of the *vaṭa* tree as shimmering moonlight;
she who dwells within the bliss made manifest by the unobstructed great light.
The noble araṇi wood, which is like a flight of stairs upon the path to nirvāṇa,
and which brings about the auspicious blossoming of the cluster of the lotus of radiant consciousness.

She who is the sole moon raining down the nectar arising from her own essential nature; she whose splendor consists of the radiance of both the shimmering sun and the lunar nectar, yet who is like a collyrium-smoke [to those blinded by it]; she who has swallowed the three lights and is the supreme consciousness whose form is pure awakening.
She whose form is the throbbing vibration within the center of Śiva and Śakti;
she who causes the emission and the cause of re-emission through the swallowing of the six transformations;
she who, at the end of her own nature and the universal form, imitates the three worlds with their manifold variety.
Having restrained the supreme and the non-supreme through the mudrā and mantra,
one should rest in meditation upon one's own true nature, which is overflowing with the bliss of self-bliss;
[one should meditate on her] whose form is like a cloud raining down the nectar-essence of one's own essential nature.
She who terrifies the rows of gods with her fierce activity in a massive form;
she whose body is dark like the throat of Śiva, the slayer of Kāla; she who is terrifying;
she whose beautiful crest is resplendent with a multitude of severed heads.
The world-protectors are adorned with garlands of entrails hanging from their hands;
grasping them with both hands, she is intent on tasting human entrails.
By her, the great wheel of the universe, including children and cattle, is seized.
When one should remember her holding the vessel of Brahmā with her other hand—
six-armed, single-faced, adorned with a noose and a goad,
possessing blazing, terrible great eyes, and from which a fire issues forth like that of the dissolution of the two-fold world.
She whose fierce mandala was agitated by the tossing of her terrifyingly furrowed brows;
she who, with a sudden kick, cast down the foot that would shatter the cosmic egg;
she who wore excellent armlets and a supreme girdle fashioned from the serpents of the [primordial] lineage.
[She is] filled with the intense radiance of those whose splendor is intent upon striking the fierce mass of rays from the sun of the night;
agitated by hundreds of claps of the hands and teeth of the hosts of yoginīs;
and resounding with the cries of "Śiva! from the multitudes of trees that are the heroes and great lords of heroes.
At the forefront of the cremation ground of all that is imperishable, she is of terrifying appearance,
with blazing flames flickering from her hair, and she consumes the entire host of the Daityas with her fire.
She who shattered the shell of the universe with her terrible *huṃkāra* sound;
she who was terrifying with the knitting of her brows, which arose as the cause for the destruction of the world;
and from whose hips, due to exhaustion, fierce sparks of fire emerged like protruding flames.
Then one should meditate upon her, who has transcended the great vows, standing above the Daityas;
stationed at the gateway, her form is like ten thousand fires at the terrible end of an aeon,
and she resounds with a roar that devours hundreds of Mahākālas.

One should meditate upon Śivādūtī, who is more terrible than the most terrible, whose body possesses the splendor of ten thousand suns, who is adorned with a skull-topped staff, a trident, a noose, a sword, and a garland of skulls, who has deep-set eyes and a fearsome face, and who carries a gourd vessel. One should remember her.
She has the face of Śiva with a wide-open mouth, holding a noose and a goad raised aloft;
she carries a sword, a severed head, and a great skull-bowl, adorned with a khaṭvāṅga staff in her hand;
she is three-eyed, possesses fierce fangs, and is voracious in devouring the three worlds.
And one should remember her holding a bell and a hand-drum (ḍamaru), as well as Daṇḍa and Jvalā;
having remembered another [deity] intent on gazing at the Goddess within the maṇḍala,
and having thus meditated upon her who grants desired objects, one should thereafter perform the worship.

O Goddess, one should worship in various ways with diverse liquors, meats, and fermented spirits, as well as with perfumes, incense, garlands, and the like; with hundreds of great animals, both aquatic and terrestrial, and with other offerings originating from the atmosphere.

One should offer, according to one's ability, *śuṣkulīs*, *modakas*, *nopikās*, *khaṇḍas*, and *laḍḍukas*; as well as *mahāthakuṭa*, *māheśī*, rice with curd (*dadhyodana*), and rice with jaggery (*guḍodana*). One should always eat this, for it destroys all sin.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, for it would cut short one’s long life.

Afterwards, a fire-offering (homa) should be performed with mahāmāṃsa, liquor, and so forth. One should offer the three-eyed [deity] born of the Kṣatriya clan, which is the knowledge that brings satisfaction.
Then one should cause the disciple to enter— the hero, firm in his vows,
who has attained supreme non-duality and is adorned with manifold virtues.
With his eyes bound and his knees placed upon the ground,
O Goddess, he should be made to cast that very handful of flowers toward her.
Then, once it has been removed, one should reveal the God of gods.
One should indeed prostrate like a staff before him again and again with great joy.
Then, one should cause the disciple to worship the Goddess established within the mandala;
beginning from the east, one should worship the Heart-mantra and the others in the corners.

One should worship the two gatekeepers at the left and right doors. Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should then commence the initiation according to the previously stated procedure as enjoined in the Tantra.
Having thus initiated the disciple, one should likewise consecrate him.
O Goddess, one should bestow upon him the mantra of great power, accompanied by the mudrās.
O you who are worshipped by the lords of heroes, I shall now describe the binding of the mudrās.
By means of these very [mudrās], the lord of practitioners flies through the sky:
Daṃṣṭrā, Karāṅkā, Krodhā, Aparā, Bhairavī, Lelihānā, and Khecarī; by this group of six mudrās, one goes to heaven.
O Bhairavī, having turned [the hands] toward the face and joined the two hands together,
one should contract both the middle and ring fingers; thus the *puruṣāhatā* [mudrā] is formed by the index finger with the index finger and the little finger with the little finger.
O Goddess, one should tie it very firmly and insert the tongue in the middle.
Resorting to the power of the mudrā, with hollow eyes and a terrifying face,
O Dear One, the Mistress of Mudrās, who has protruding teeth, should bind [the senses] at the time of yoga.
Having bound this [mantra] in a cemetery, one should let out a roar for seven days;
then he floats in the sky and rejoices together with the sky-goers.
He attains the perfection of the *piṇḍa*—what is the use of saying more?
The hero-minded one should contract the left foot, lift up the head,
[and place] the eyes in the hollows; he should repeatedly lick the tongue with the teeth.
O Beloved, with the index fingers joined and the hands turned over,
with the face cast downward and the eyebrows contracted, and with the eyes fixed in a hollow gaze,
the wise practitioner should display the belly pressed against the back.
The mantra practitioner should utter the sound "phet"; within six months, he attains success.
This is the Karaṅkiṇī mudrā, which accomplishes all wonders.
O Goddess, when this vidyā is joined [with it] at the hour of spirits (bhūtāhna) from the abode of the ancestors (pitṛveśman), [it grants its fruits].
Then, by means of this continuous practice upon the corpse, one becomes the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara).
Contracting the eyebrows, one should cast a wrathful gaze.
Having placed the left cloth toward the southeast and the right toward the southwest, [one should direct it] to the west.
Having contracted the left hand, one should place it against the side of the waist;
at the root of the right ear, one should show the tips of the fingers.
The wise one should then extract the *savisarga* (*praśānta*) eightfold with grace.
Known as Krodhamudrā, she is Bhairavī, the beloved of Bhairava.
Through union with her, one attains perfection in just seven days;
by binding her alone for six months, a man becomes like Bhairava himself.
Indeed, always delighted by the fragrance of the qualities of all perfections,
one should prepare the mandala as the locus and extend both arms.
The wise one should turn the face away and utter the syllable *phuk*.
Having made the two hands contracted and positioned one above the other—
with the right hand situated above and the left arm situated below—
the knower of mantras, having smiled slightly, performs this mudrā known as Bhairavī.
O highly fortunate lady, as soon as he is bound, that best of men becomes filled with the bliss of his own true nature; within seven days he becomes as he was before,
and after six months, that most excellent of men truly becomes Bhairava himself.
Having bent the index finger of the left hand toward the thumb,
one should gaze at the face with a facial expression directed toward the interlocutor.
With eyes wide open, the practitioner of mantra should forcibly dry out his body;
he should occasionally contract half [his body] and constantly move his tongue here [in the mouth]. Then, by joining the index finger and thumb of the right hand—
O Mistress of Bhairava, by means of that [gesture], the conjunction of mudrās should be performed above the right ear,
relying on the power of the primordial vitality (*pūrvavīrya*).
This is known as the *lelihānā* mudrā, revealed by all the heroes.
As soon as this [mudrā] is bound, there occurs the state of forced union (haṭhamelāpa);
one possessing a body with the form of Bhairava floats through the expanse of the sky.
This has been revealed to you today in this most excellent king of tantras.
Therefore, listen indeed to another distinction regarding the khecarīmudrā:
having joined limb with limb, one should take refuge in the lotus of the mouth.
The yogi, situated within the womb of Śakti, should ascend upon the shadow of the Haṃsa.
O Mistress of Yoga, this mudrā is celebrated as Khecarī and is highly honored;
yet, O Goddess, it is extremely difficult for even the Bhairavas to obtain without the oral instructions of the Guru. By practicing it, a man becomes a traveler of the sky in that very instant.
Thus has the mudrā been fully described, which is worshipped by the virtuous yoginīs.
Endowed with the potency of the mudrā, one should recite [the mantra] of the Sovereign of the Lords of Yoga,
who resides within the temple of the kanda and flows through the central path.
There, the practitioner of mantra should recollect the Vidyā that emerges from the bolt of Kalaṅka—
the Yogīśvarī who is Yoga-māyā— having repeated it one hundred thousand times according to the count of syllables; then, having performed the ten-limbed rite, he should indeed offer oblations.
O Bhairavī, Mahākṣmā, through the repetition of mantras and other rites beginning with that and ending with the fire-oblation, one shall attain perfection;
O Vahnimadhyā, she appears in a gentle form as Yogeśvarī.
It arises without doubt, bestowing the fruit of all accomplishments.
Likewise, O Goddess of Gods, one floats through the courtyard of the sky together with it.
Thus has this most excellent accomplishment been described to you according to its true nature.
By reciting [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, she will accomplish the middling [attainment].
O highly fortunate one, success itself will surely bring it about; there is no doubt in this.
Or else, by reciting it one hundred thousand times, she will accomplish it; there is no doubt in this.
One may accomplish even ordinary tasks merely by reciting [this mantra];
it will destroy the faults of the great samaya through mere remembrance.
The Goddess, who bestows great good fortune, is attained through constant remembrance and worship.
There is no object here that this does not accomplish by its own power;
she, the auspicious Siddhayogeśvarī, should be known as the bestower of enjoyment and liberation.
Furthermore, this Supreme Goddess is likewise the mother of those who act according to their own will.
Thus has this incomparable ritual for you, O Goddess of gods, been proclaimed by me; it bestows the fruit of all spiritual accomplishments.
Furthermore, O Sovereign of the Suras, tell me what I shall speak to you now.
There is nothing else more profoundly secret than this, which is held within the heart.

Thus ends the chapter on the *Siddhayogeśvarī-vidhi* in the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraścheda* division of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairava-śrotas*.
Having heard this, the Goddess of the Gods, delighted by the choice of the Lord of the Suras,
bowed again to the Moon and the Sun and spoke according to the truth.
The Holy Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear this wonderful secret: tell me, O Maheśāna, by your grace, O Supreme Lord, who that primordial Śakti, the Great Goddess, is the mother of Svacchanda.
The glorious Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, you who are a vessel for the knowledge of secrets!"
O blessed lady, O mistress of the gods, although that which you ask regarding the determination of Mahārāviṇī should not be told, it is nevertheless set forth here;
for therein the entire essence and the most excellent core have been proclaimed.
From the radiant manifestation (*prollāsa*) of Śiva— who is perfect, all-pervasive, and non-dual—
there arises that digit (*kalā*) which draws forth time (*kālakarṣaṇī*), extending back to the very beginning.
[She manifests] the Lord Svacchandabhairava, whose form is that of radiant manifestation.
Then, that which is known as the "stream" (dhārā), spreading forth in the form of a serpent (kuṇḍalin),
is indeed the egg of the manifestation of that reality;
it appears as a mass of light, its own nature being exceedingly difficult to endure.
In the form of vomiting and devouring, that very [reality] has its door opened wide;
there, O Goddess, the *jayā*, *vārāhikā*, *khedvera*, and *aśmatā* manifest,
and the splendor of the *śāktayava* is revealed to you.
That which arises as the fruit beyond the supreme through the supreme power,
this great diversion— whether according to the arrangement of the gross or the subtle,
or that which has been explained as the sequential meaning— is indeed threefold and exceedingly fierce.
And there she was attained, shimmering with radiant points and blossoming like a blade of dūrvā grass;
having slightly approached the jar with the Ghorabhairava mudrā,
he was intent upon fulfilling the fourteen great paths.
Then, through the stabilization of the universal form, the Great arises.
Furthermore, by means of the bond of Khecarī, it now becomes even more gross;
it attains the Great Conjunction (mahāmelāpa) through the worship of Jayā-Vārāhī.
Listen, O slender-waisted one, to the description of its practice;
for although this mudrā has been taught in many ways in the supreme tantras, O beloved,
it is nonetheless the most excellent, possessing the power of primordial vigor by force.
She is recited by the *khecarīs* as "Mahārāvī" by name;
by the mere binding of whom, the multitude of throbbing powers (*śaktis*) [arises].

Upon merely seeing [this], one goes [to the desired state] suddenly within half a watch; of this there is no doubt. That entire circle of deities which is established in the three wheels—by the mere binding of him as a servant before one, he is established [in power].
All the Ḍākinīs, Ḍāmarikās, Lāmās, Ucchuṣmās, and Mothers appear within a moment through the power of the Rāva-mudrā.
Indeed, the authority over this belongs specifically to women; thus it is proclaimed.

When the practitioner stands upon the hero’s ground—which is waveless and free from conceptual construction—he should remain with his eyes bound; no one else [is qualified] for this, O slender-waisted one. Having taken hold of it by resorting to it, and having filled it, he should behold the digit of consciousness.
Koṭarākṣa has upward-facing eyes, a polished chest, and a deep throat;
the Goddess stands upon his left foot, or alternatively, she is born from the bliss at his root.
As he stands upright, his right heel is placed near her, while his [right] knee is slightly bent.
O fortunate one, by means of the application of the *upaveśa* posture, through the expansion of the *vīrāvalī*,
and also through contraction and the bending of both arms;
[one should join] the two middle and ring fingers of both hands.
By joining the contracted thumbs with the index fingers in the shape of an archway,
one should bind both little fingers together after turning them back; these two auspicious tips,
reaching toward the corners of the mouth, should extend as far as the region of the face.
One should place the ring finger and the middle finger in the middle of the bond and insert them into the tongue;
one should emit a terrible sound while performing the *mudrā* without laziness.
Thus, that *mudrā* is celebrated as *Rāviṇī*, also known as *Khecarī*.
O Goddess, by means of this, at that very moment one becomes a sky-walker;
O Goddess, the excellent hero partakes in the melāpa—of this there is no doubt.
O beautiful goddess, as many *mudrās* as there are who abide upon the *mudrā-pīṭha*, so many are these female practitioners (*sūnāyikā*), who produce immediate conviction.
Now, O slender-waisted one, I shall proclaim the supreme mantra of the Goddess.
The double-tongued Bhairava, whose jaws are clamped shut by the bolt of wrathful Māyā,
is the single-syllable mantra known as the Bindu, the immeasurable, studded with light;
it is the solitary hero, most terrifying, and the cause of wondrous marvels.
By the mere remembrance of this, the world is subdued;
the entire body trembles, and the abode of the *kanda* throbs.
It sows away the knot of the heart, and the *ādhāra-cakra* moves.
The auspicious sounds of the goddess’s presence arise;
the mass of sins and the transgressions of the *samaya* are reduced to ashes. Now, what is the use of much speaking? O Goddess, it is stated in brief:
O Goddess of the gods, as much vigor as is described in this supreme tantra under the name of *vidyā*, all that is established within every mantra in its condensed form.
Thus, this most terrible *vidyā* has been revealed to you today.
Bhairava, Dīrghasaṃbhinnam, Krodhārgalavibhedita,
and Bindubhinna— these six indeed are declared to be the six limbs (aṅga-ṣaṭka).
Haṃsa, situated upon Kālāgnirudra and struck by the head of Bindu and Nāda.
O Great Goddess, the *praṇava* of Kumbhīra is indeed proclaimed as "Namaḥ," which destroys birth and death.
The mantra of Jaya is said to be the double-tongued [letter] joined with the bindu.
O Goddess, having invoked [the deity] with this supreme mantra, which is merely a manifestation of majesty,
this foremost mantra has been revealed to you alone.
One should meditate upon her as possessing a radiance equal to ten million times ten thousand times ten million fires at the end of an aeon.
Resembling the throat of Śiva, which is dark like a raven, a cloud, or mist,
she is radiant with the power of thousands of flickering meteors;
she is beautified by hands holding a noose, a goad, a sword, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a skull-cup.
She has a great shaven head and a large lotus, her mouth filled with human entrails;
she is adorned with breasts radiant with the faces of lions and boars.
The god seated upon her lap is Svachanda, the leader of the universe;
he has five faces, ten arms, and bears all weapons—great and formidable. He drinks the sinew of the goddess’s left arm.
One should meditate upon Jayā, who stands upon the head of the Asura Kumbhīra, who is voracious in devouring the world, four-faced, adorned with eight arms,
the goddess bearing all weapons, and possessing the radiance of ten million moons.
Vārāhī has the luster of a Kaula cloud and is like the wind at the end of an eon;
she has the face of a boar, is terrifying, and is intent on swallowing the three worlds.
She bears a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and is adorned with a noose and a goad.
One should always remember the two goddesses at the left and right of the door.
One should worship the Goddess in the center of the lotus, with the six limbs upon its six petals.
She is to be worshipped with the previously mentioned offerings and entirely with the substances of the heroes.

One should worship the Mistress of the Gods according to one's ability with great quantities of flesh, liquor, meat, spirits, and so forth, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth. Having thus worshipped her, one should offer as an oblation the lungs of a human being.

Thereafter, one should cause the disciple—who follows the conduct of a hero and is firm in his vows—to enter. One should cause him to sleep upon excellent flowers and initiate him according to the previous [rite].
Having been initiated and consecrated, he should accomplish the supreme art (*kalā*).
Having gone to a mountain cave, one should recite ten million great mantras.
O slender-waisted goddess, one should perform the fire sacrifice as previously described for one-tenth that number;
at the conclusion of the sacrifice, O Goddess, one shall attain the presence of the Goddess.

Then, the accomplishment of the assembly (*melāpasādhana*) of the Heroic Mind should be performed by those who stand upon the ground of heroes, whose limbs are as if uninjured. Having brought that [hero] adorned [with ornaments], one standing behind him should recite the mantra of Śivā.
By the application of binding the mudrā, one shall fly up into the sky within half a watch;
or else, by means of the animal-sacrifice yoga, one should gratify the Supreme Goddess.
Now, a certain subtle procedure is being stated in brief:
having worshipped Kālasaṃhāra and established oneself in the eastern face,
and having worshipped the pair of small vessels with upward openings, one should worship the subtle *ucchū*.
O Bhairavī, by the hardness of the funeral pyre, even a minute hole will appear in it.
Then, having emerged from one's own house at a time when neither crows nor owls are present,
one should collect the dust of whatever person stands before one.
Distinguished by the division of female and male, or by the division of left and right—

the *mṛgī* should be bound with a smile and grasped with a mind free of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). Having grasped it in the form of a bowl, one should cast it into the slender-waisted [vessel].
Having performed [the preliminary rites], a person who is pure and composed should thereafter worship;
likewise, having anointed his limbs with unguents, he should perform the binding of the mudrās.
Otherwise, one should never bind the queen of mudrās at all.

And one should perform the binding in the back room, on the side, in the increasing [phase], from the cremation ground, at a crossroads, on a mountain, by a river, or in a hero’s [place]. Having uttered the eightfold *dhārāva*, and again the *haṃsa* joined with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
O Goddess of gods, by merely binding it in this manner, whatever clods of earth and other objects are there— twenty in number— they clearly burst apart and fall to pieces.
All the teeth blaze forth, and one’s own mouth becomes a flame.
Thus, by the power of the mudrā, one shall attract the lineage of the world;
there is no doubt about this within seven days, even if it were Bṛhaspati himself.
[One should perform this] with a skull-cup filled with the blood and nectar of the sun.
Having offered half [of the food] to the Goddess of Devas and having consumed the other half oneself,
one should thereafter wander through the formidable Great Cemetery (Mahāpitṛvana) while performing the binding of mudrās.
Then all those [goddesses], who are eager for food consisting of the six flavors, will arrive.
The Yoginīs possess divine bodies and bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. One should offer them an arghya, or else their favorite food, which is the most excellent caru.
Thus has the *melāpa* been explained by me to you through the yoga of the bound souls (*paśu*). O Goddess, by consuming the seven types of bound souls for the sake of the *melāpa*,
a mortal becomes omniscient, an all-doer, and a Great Lord (*maheśvara*).
There is nothing he does not do; there is nothing he cannot accomplish.
Then, having bound the *mudrā* alone according to the previously stated rule, the great hero, the leader whose mouth is the *khecarī*, indeed flies upward.
Or if a woman, O Goddess of gods, practices the mudrās with an undistracted mind,
then in merely seven days she will become a Yoginī.
Thus is the excellent sequence proclaimed for those who are difficult to discipline and have not refined their selves.
This secret essence of the entire sequence, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is like a hundred wish-fulfilling gems; it must not be given to those of wicked intellect.
O you who are fond of the lords of heroes, tell me, what else shall I say now?
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for the Mother of the *Svacchanda*, within the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala* in twenty-four thousand verses.
Having heard this, the Mistress of the Gods, overflowing with the nectar of satisfaction,
prostrated herself before the Lord of the Gods and spoke again in accordance with the truth.
The Goddess said:
Salutations to the one whose supreme abode is self-awareness fully blossomed;
to the one who is the singular form of all that is perceived; to the one who is the sole embodiment of Mahālakṣmī.

Having worshipped you, whose true nature is the single form of all existence, I am satisfied, I am fulfilled; I dance before you. Since that time, she has heard the entire *Yāmalendra* in its entirety.
Endowed with the potency of mantra and augmented by the potency of mudrā,
joined with the great sādhanas, and filled with many secrets; inlaid with manifold forms of knowledge and adorned with the union of conduct.
Now I wish to hear the auspicious Mahālakṣmīmata, complete with its origin, vows, specialized knowledge, conduct, and mantras.
The worship of the mudrās and the maṇḍala according to the karma of practitioners,
the fire-ritual (vahnikārya) as it stands, and the recitation (japa) which bestows the accomplishment of all aims—
O God, Lord of Gods, tell me that, as well as the means for achieving sovereignty and other goals.
Having thus heard the auspicious words spoken from the mouth of his beloved,
which were sent forth at the conclusion of the boon and were in accordance with the will of Mahālakṣmī, Bhairava said:
Bhairava said:
"O auspicious one, O Bhairavī, you ask about a most secret and painful matter.
Out of affection for you, I shall speak; listen with a one-pointed mind.
The peaceful Śivā-Śakti has arisen, her form invisible."
And she is established in twelve divisions according to the divisions of the wheels.
In the center resides Mahādeva Bhairava, whose face is distorted,
resembling pure crystal and possessing a luster like that of the snowy mountain.
Having the luster of the color of a white jasmine flower or the moon, as pale-white as a conch shell or cow’s milk;
with a face made terrifying by fangs, most fierce, and with a brow-browed countenance;
with hair standing erect, three-eyed, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with snakes and elephant-hide,
clothed in well-perfumed garments and covered by an elephant skin,
he has five faces, ten arms, and is endowed with fifteen eyes.
Holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, bearing a sword and a shield,
with hands busily grasping an arrow and a bow, and holding a trident and a paṭṭiśa;
with hands granting boons and fearlessness, he rejoices in the midst of the spear.
But the god consists of blood, established as the churning-stick;
resembling the pollen of safflower, honored by pomegranate blossoms,
and possessing most excellent hips that resemble natural vermilion.
Adorned with a girdle bound tightly and a magnificent row of tinkling bells,
it was likewise enriched by the splendor of jeweled ornaments on the head, feet, and other limbs.
Well-attired and endowed with exquisite beauty, anointed with divine fragrances,
possessed of great loveliness, and with a face slightly smiling—
the God who assumes any form at will, situated in the supreme Ocean of Milk.
Endowed with the true forms of the Goddess and accompanied by their respective vehicles and weapons,
listen now to the names of the Great Goddesses on the twelve-spoked wheel according to their actual significance:
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Lakṣmī, Dīptimālā, and Śivā.
Sumukhī, Cāmarī, Nandā, Harikeśī,
Hayānanā, Viśveśī, Yogeśvarī, and Mahābalā are thus proclaimed;
they abide within the center of the wheel according to the differentiation of the twelve vowels.
O illustrious one, as you were being churned, Mahālakṣmī arose, following the King who was established in the sequential order;
she resembled ten million moons and possessed a splendor equal to ten thousand suns.
She bears the face of a horse, is terrifying, adorned with twelve arms,
endowed with fifteen eyes, and possesses five faces; she is exceedingly fierce,
the devourer of all, wrathful, yet endowed with great beauty.
In the north she has the form of a Kaula; in the south she is Nārasiṃhikā.
In the zenith the goddess is Kharānanā, and in the west she is Kapicanatā.
The goddess is seated upon three skulls and is adorned with a dagger (kaṭṭāraka).
In her left hands she holds a skull-cup, a trident, a sword, an arrow,
a noose, a bow, a bell, and likewise a severed head and a hand-drum (ḍamaru). In her right hands she should hold a rosary, a wine-vessel, and a liṅga.
The Goddess, wearing a mass of matted hair, with the moon as her crest-ornament,
endowed with all ornaments, adorned with garlands of ploughs,
having a serpent as her sacred thread, and clothed in a tiger skin;
Possessing great good fortune and beauty, yet the abode of great suffering,
she dwells in the center of the lunar disc, encircled by three lotuses.
The supreme adept who meditates upon the Goddess, who assumes this form and destroys the suffering of those who bow before her,
shall indeed partake in the fruit of sovereignty.
Having visualized her emerging from another abode, he should contemplate her entering his own body.
By means of the flow through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), one should fill everything up to its root-maṇḍala—
extending from Śiva down to the realm of the earth—
with the stream of great nectar and the supreme current of the *ogha*.
Thus, from meditating every day, immortality is produced;
his fortune increases and misfortune perishes in an instant.
O Goddess, incomparable good fortune arises—of this there is no doubt.
Then Yami, who subdues death, old age, and disease, and who traverses the six paths, is attained. She is the terrible subduer of poverty and the auspicious generator of good fortune.
By her grace, O Goddess of Gods, even proud kings [attain their status].
I have described this other [power] in another tantra, which functions internally;
likewise, there is the supreme Saṃkarṣaṇī, who abides as the Great Messenger (Mahādūtī).
By her grace, men attain the status of lords of the earth.
With his mind supremely one-pointed, he should [recite] her mantra according to the prescribed method on a level, pure plot of ground smeared with cow dung,
situated in the back [of the house] within a delightful great garden or forest.
In a place that produces great joy, adorned on all sides, auspicious,
with well-constructed walls laid out by a skilled craftsman, well-refined,
rich with the sweet fragrance of incense, and decorated with heaps of flowers.
The preceptor, filled with the joy of wine, should sit facing the east;
he should be dressed in red garments, adorned with betel in his mouth, and his body,
from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head, should be thoroughly smeared with saffron.
With musk applied to his head and anointed with moon-fragrant sandalwood,
and holding chalk in his hand, he should draw a most beautiful lotus.
One should draw the pericarp and the collection of letters; Death (Mṛtyu) is situated above that.
One should write the six syllables in their sequential order and the Mātṛkā on the band.
One should worship the primordial Siddhas with an offering of *palāla* grass.
One should take the letter *bha* from below and join it with half of the letter *ca*.
O Goddess, one should join *ai* above; one should then place *ū* above in sequence.
O lady of excellent hips, this seed-syllable bestows great good fortune.
Having taken only the letter *ka* and then again the letter *ta*,
O Goddess of slender waist, one should join the first [letter] according to the sequence to be written;
one should write the final letter and likewise write the beginning of the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Below [the letter *m*], *ṛ* should be joined; three *yojanas* below that, *ī* should be joined.
Below that, *ṛ* should be joined; above [that], one should write *ū* alone.
Above that, O Goddess, *ga* alone; for the second [position], *ḍa* alone.
O Goddess worshipped by the best of gods and goddesses, one should apply [the vowel] below the letter *e*;
O Goddess, one should not join the letter *aṃ* below, but should write only the letter *ū* above.
Having taken the second [vowel] from below, it is adorned with a second [consonant].
The letter *gha* joined with the upper half of the second [letter], adorned with the second upper half of *ṇa*—
this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), O lady of excellent hips, which is the supreme heart of Rāhu.
Having taken the second lower half of *ḍa*, joined with the third lower half of *kha*.
Which third letter is to be joined to the [first] pada? It is marked by the upper half of the third [letter].

Having taken the lower half of that second [letter], it is situated below the upper half of the second [letter]. Conjoined with the upper half of the second [letter], this auspicious seed-syllable bestows liberation.
Having written [the letter] above the syllable *ṣa* and joined it with [the letter] below *gha*,
one should extract the fivefold [mantra] with the vowel *u* falling above.
This goddess of seven to twelve syllables is the cutter away of great suffering.
O beloved, even one who steals gold, a drinker of liquor, a killer of a Brahmin,
or one who violates the teacher’s bed is liberated by remembering this, even if they have committed many external transgressions.
A thousand horse-sacrifices as well as the destruction of a Brahmin—once uttered, the Goddess destroys these; of this there is no doubt.
Though bound by great fetters and rendered powerless by sense-objects, she remains.

Those who remember this Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) are liberated from all bonds. Having contemplated the imperishable within the imperishable, they enter their own radiant body; for them, birth, old age, disease, and death have gone to destruction.
O Goddess, within six months the yoginī shall attain equality with the immortals;
having quickly attained omniscience, she becomes Śiva or a knower of the yoga of Śiva.
O beautiful one, she shares the common status of the assembly of heroes and the host of siddhas.
O Goddess of the Gods, through the power of the salutation itself, all yogis become imperishable among the imperishable.
Furthermore, those great beings who are devoted messengers, possessing excellent devotion and auspicious marks,
should install the Great Vidyā in the three locations.
Within two months, that goddess is accomplished; there is no doubt in this matter.
Herein, man has the authority, for she bestows success upon them.
Where the sky is free from affliction, there she is established in the conduct of her state.
That infinite power of the All-pervading Lord is likewise united with the mantra;
O Goddess, it is always difficult to perceive by those lacking intelligence,
yet for one who perceives it, the three periods of time— consisting of the knowledge of what is to be remembered and what is to be known— remain as the means for attaining perfection.
Its rising is in the region of the heart; it is situated at midday between the eyebrows;
and for three periods of time, it remains in the wheel of the head until its setting occurs.
O Great Goddess, this Vidyā is established within all the gods.
It pacifies great sins and destroys epilepsy.
It bestows the sovereignty of the earth before long; of this there is no doubt.
It has been concealed in all tantras, but it is revealed here out of affection for you.
The Yoginī, born from the womb, is a portion of Rudra, free from impurity;
she is awakened by the descent of power and by my grace, O Bhairavī.
O Mistress of Yoga, having attained the unsurpassed ignorance (avidyā) through this glance,
therefore, O fawn-eyed one, it must be concealed with every effort.
It should be given from that place, O Bhairavī, only to one who is highly disciplined.
Thus ends the chapter on the Origin of the Goddess and the Extraction of Mantras within the Mahālakṣmīmata-cakra, in the fourth Ṣaṭka of the Jayadrathayāmala in twenty-four thousand verses.
Now, therefore, O fair-limbed one, O lovely-faced one, listen to its worship,
as well as the heart-mantras and other limbs, and how the messenger (dūtī) is integrated.
The mandala arising from three lotuses, which fulfills all desires, should be offered.
O Queen of the Gods, I shall explain it so that the practitioner may understand it:
having taken up the lower half of the third [line], one should place it upon the lower half of the third.
The letter *sa* (saṃhāra) joined with the letter *ka* (kāla), and the third vowel (*u*) below;
the letter *ga* joined with the lower half of the third vowel (*u*), and adorned with the lower half of the third vowel;
the letter *ṇa* with the third vowel (*ū*) above and below, and adorned with the upper half of the third vowel (*ū*).
Joined with the *praṇava* (OM) and adorned with the third letter [Ka],
this is the Self (*ātman*), O God of gods, residing within all beings.
Indeed, it is known as the "engine-driver" (*yantravāha*) among all three types of mantras.
This one, indeed, is the form of Bhairava, the bestower of grace upon all.
He is the vital breath of living beings; he is the supreme syllable. He is the sustainer of all, and he is the supreme Śiva.

That very [deity] is constantly accomplished through the eight divine flavors, by the hosts of Siddhas and Kinnaras, within the mandala of stringed instruments and the like, O Goddess. That same one, however, is the supreme form, according to the division of the supreme and the non-supreme.
O Great Goddess, even one who has killed a Brahmin or who delights in betraying his guru attains all accomplishments through the power of the Heart-mantra.
Having become all-pervading, one should wander everywhere with the khecarīs.
O Goddess, she who follows the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is eternally present.
O Goddess, one who is liberated from the four qualities is free from time.
At that very moment, the Supreme Brahman is characterized by supreme bliss;
therefore, one should always worship the Heart with every effort.
Having grasped the upper half of the letter *ha*, [one places it] upon the upper half of the letter *ya*.

The letter Kha is the fourth [vowel], mounted upon a chariot (Ra); it is adorned above by the second Dva (Dha). It is conjoined with the upper half of the second Na (Na), and its head is the supreme single-syllable [Oṃ]. Joined with Svāhā and the Praṇava (Oṃ), it causes the destruction of great sins.
One should take the third vowel *e*, join it with the third *ṛ* (i.e., *ṛ*),
pierce it with the head of the fourth letter (*ca*), and adorn it with the third *ṇa*. One should then apply this, preceded by the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and ending with *vauṣaṭ*, as the *śikhā* mantra.
Taking the third letter of *tha* and joining it with the third letter of *ṭa* below;
the third letter of *ḍa* should be joined above and below, and adorned with the third letter of *ṇa* above; this is the invincible armor (*kavaca*) named *chabja*, adorned at the beginning and end.
I shall now fully declare the "eye" (netra) by which one becomes a bestower of prosperity and desire.
One should first extract the Praṇava (Oṃ), then extract that which is equal to it (Hrīṃ), and thereafter join the Vaṣaṭkāra (Vaṣaṭ). This auspicious mantra grants enjoyment through Śrī.
I shall now fully declare the weapon-mantra by which liberation is attained for men:
having taken the three *da* sounds, the third *ṭa* joined with the vowel *ṛ*,
conjoined with the third *gha*, and united with the second *cha*.
Having written the exceedingly fierce word accompanied by *huṃ* and *phaṭ*,
and joined with the *praṇava* at its beginning, it is proclaimed as the Great Weapon (*mahāstra*).
It resembles a thousand rays and possesses a splendor equal to ten thousand suns.
One-footed, three-eyed, and auspicious with a thousand faces;
equipped with a thousand arms and adorned with serpent bracelets.
O Goddess, this is named the Brahmāstra-mantra, which causes the destruction of all sins.
It must not be given to wicked beings if one desires one's own welfare.
I shall now declare the faces; listen to the mantra as it truly stands.
That which has ascended to the time of withdrawal (saṃhāra), joined with the third vowel (u) below;
again, O Mistress of Gods, the sixth and eighth [letters] adorned with the second vowel (u);
endowed with its fourth head (the letter *m*), this is declared to be the eastern face.

Taking the fourth letter of the throat (kha), conjoined with the downward-pointing triangle (e) and joined with the letter *madhu* (u); below that, the fourth letter of the head (ra), conjoined with the downward-pointing triangle (e) and joined with the letter *mṛtyu* (ṛ); and [the letter] *ṛ* mounted upon the upward-pointing triangle (ū), adorned with a bindu at its crest.
This is proclaimed as the Great Lion (Mahāsiṃha), the right-facing mouth.
Taking the second [consonant] and the third joined with the vowel below (u),
then the third [consonant] joined with the upper half [vowel] (ī) and adorned with the second [consonant] (ṇa).
One should point out the northern great face as having the form of Kaula.
First, one should write the letter *bha* and so forth, joined with the letter *da* at the beginning;
this is the form of Death (*mṛtyumūrti*), which must always be protected, [and it is] the western face.
O Goddess, one should extract the letter *ū* from *ūrddhā*, place the letter *ṛ* joined with *dha*,
and make the fourth letter of the fourth group (*ḍa*) joined with the letter *śa*.
This fifth face, the donkey-faced one, bestows great liberation.
O Goddess, what need has he for many mantras, tantras, meditations, or dhāraṇīs?

O Goddess, for him who remembers [the mantra] with his mind, there shall be the destruction of great sins. O Beloved, I have described many varieties [of mantras], which are secured by a *kīlana* (pinning rite).
O beloved Queen of the Gods, she may be clever, or likewise cut off, burnt, or as if asleep;
she may be weak, or in the form of a child, or old, or young;
she may be whole, or divided, or knotted together.
This knowledge does not exist for others at all; it is always possessed by them.
If one desires the attainment of sovereignty, then those [gurus] should be propitiated with a serene mind. (226b)
One should worship according to the prescribed state; listen with a focused mind.
The preceptor must perform the ritual actions as previously described.
Then, one should draw a magnificent eight-petaled great lotus.
Having drawn that [mandala] outside, O beautiful one, draw the sixteenth; then, among the thirty-two [deities],
the leader of the Pramathas in the first [cell] has the luster of a white lotus, in the second she has a reddish glow,
and in the third the leader of the gods has a complexion like yellow orpiment.
Outside of that, however, is a line of space with a luster like blue collyrium.
One should fashion twenty-four filaments in the center of the lotus.
O Supreme Goddess, one should draw the collection of weapons, beginning with the vajra, on the exterior.
And having placed eight jars provided with all medicinal herbs,
adorned with white sandalwood and likewise decorated with cloths,
one should insert into the jar a three-leaved [leaf] by which [the desired result] arises.
Ear-ointment, the five gems,
a tail-feather, red chalk, a mark made with vermilion, and another [mark] smeared with saffron; as well as gorocanā, sauvīraka, tagara, and auspicious nāgakeśara.
O Lord of the Gods, agarwood, camphor, māṃsī, pūrikā,
as well as cloves, white sandalwood mixed with saffron,
and the excellent nutmeg should always be placed in the jar.
Having cast [the offerings] for the benefit of the practitioner,
the Lord of Teachers should indeed provide lamps filled with clarified butter following the sequence of the lotuses, O fair-eyed one;
likewise, O Goddess of the Suras, the heart-mantra and the limb-mantras should be performed mentally.
Thereafter, O beloved, the *karanyāsa* (hand-assignment) must be performed by the Guru.
Then, while meditating upon Mahālakṣmī, one should place [the mantra] on the thumb; the index finger is for the heart;
the middle finger is said to be for the head; and the ring finger shall be for the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
O fair-faced one, the little finger should be assigned as the armor;
likewise, the eye at the base of the joint, and one should project the weapon into the directions.
Likewise, the body, the face, and the limbs, as well as the meditation upon the Great Lord,
should be placed by the instructor in the center as the "all-devourer.
Then, after that, the group of eight beginning with Aruṇā should be placed in the beautiful [mandala].
Aruṇā, Ghoṣavatī, Caṇḍī, Sumukhī, Viṣvaksenā, Lakṣmī, Ānandā, and Bhadramangalā—
all this triple world, including all things moving and unmoving, is pervaded by these.

Listen, O slender-limbed one, regarding the second [day]: one should arrange Sunandā and the others. They are Sunandā, Viśvasaṃhārī, Subhagā, Kṣaudrabhojanī, Mahāraṇyā, Mahānādī, Mahānityā, and Suśobhanā.
The goddess Mahādhaneśvarī, Khaḍgajihvā, Mahābalā, Mantreśvarī, Anukhī, Gokarṇī,
Vijayā, Jayantī, Kālī, and the most excellent Ṣoḍaśī.
O Goddess, she who bestows the enjoyment of birth is situated in the middle wheel. Bhadrakarṇā, Vegavatī, Vikaṭā, Kaṭapūtanā, then Kālavaśā, and the Vidyā Cipiṭā is remembered as the seventh.
Kapotī, Vinatā, Bhadrā, Vidrāvaṇī, Mahojjvalā, Karṇāmoṭī, Ḍamarī, Jāninī, Mahābalā, Kekarā,
Rudrakālī, and another, Viḍālavadanā.
Cillā, Duṣṭacchāyā, Vārāhī, Vikarālikā,
Mohanī, Saiñjikā, Ghorā, Kumārī, Vāyasā, Vikaṭā, the excellent Vānarī, and likewise Hariṇī.

The Goddess of the lords of gods should install the thirty-two secret Mothers: Mudbandhinī, who bestows happiness and grants boons to practitioners; Raktākṣī, who is of terrible form; Khacarī, who is devoted to granting sovereignty.
Constantly residing in the sky-lotus, she bestows boons upon practitioners.
If not worshipped, she desires ruin and produces misfortune.

Therefore, O Goddess, she should always be worshipped by those who desire worldly enjoyment and liberation. At the time of his worship, O Sovereign of the Gods, the Yoginīs gaze upon him with very affectionate, pure, and bright looks, full of great grace.
If that goddess is recognized by someone through some auspicious deed,
due to the merits performed in previous births, she emerges from the womb of the Yoginī;
in an instant, by her own power alone, the sound "jhāṃkāra" arises.
They are joined with one another and extend for a yojana.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to their meditative absorption according to its state:
all have eyes wide open, and all have smiling faces.

She has two arms and one face, adorned with white garments; she is endowed with great beauty and wears ornaments of pearls. Her mouth is filled with betel, and she holds a jar of the nectar of the moon.
Residing within each petal, she moves along the inner path.
Listen, O beautiful one of single-minded focus, to their mantra according to its state:
having taken three *takāra*s, with the third *ṛ* situated below.
The third half of *gha* joined with the third half of *ṇa*, adorned with the third half of *ṇa*—
this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), O lady of excellent hips, the supreme heart of the Yoginīs.
Having written the fourth of *ḍa* joined below with the fourth of *kha*.
Endowed with the fourth head and adorned by the fourth [vowel],
this seed-syllable, O lady of excellent hips, is indeed all the Yoginīs.
O Goddess, it is embellished by one's own name and concludes with the utterance of "svāhā."
O Goddess, this is common to all; these [mantras] bestow the perfection of the sword (khaḍgasiddhi) and grant the sovereignty of a lord of the earth to the practitioner before long.
One should cause a magnificent and beautiful palace to be built for the great sovereign.
O Goddess, well-adorned with exquisite craftsmanship and beautifully perfumed with fine incense,
whatever kind of sacrificial ground one draws, the canopy should be of that same kind.
Accompanied by bards chanting auspicious sounds,
one should invoke the supreme form, O Dear One, namely Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī,
who is established by the preceptor while assuming her great form.
One should take a great conch-shell as an offering vessel filled with excellent liquor,
and having bound the supreme Mahāmudrā known by the auspicious name Kālāntakī,
one should place the two hands facing each other in a reversed order.
Having extended the index and ring fingers, one should rotate the two pupils once;
the *lalanā* should move swiftly, and one should utter the weapon-mantra *pheṭkāra*. When it swallows [the object] eight times perfectly, it is celebrated as the *Padmamudrā*.
Others [hold] a trident, a khaṭvāṅga, a vajra-staff, a mallet, and a skull-cup together with a lotus; this is described here as the group of mudrās.
They should be visualized at the time of worship; otherwise, one becomes a partaker of faults.
First, one should worship Gaṇanātha according to the prescribed rite:
five-faced, bearing a trident, three-eyed, and seated upon a mouse. "Come, come, O Gaṇanātha! Grant me the fruit of my worship."
O Goddess of the gods, by this mantra no obstacle shall afflict him.
O Sovereign of the Gods, one should worship Kṣetrapāla, who is to be highly honored;
O fawn-eyed one, the worship of the Guru should be performed until he is satisfied.
O Goddess, one should worship Indra and the others, and especially Dharma and the rest;
from Kālāgni up to Muṇḍa, O Sovereign of the Gods,
one should always worship them according to the three castes and the various divisions of conduct, seated upon their respective thrones.
Above that, one should worship Mahākṣmī according to the prescribed rite.
Having applied the limbs, beginning with the heart-mantra, extending to the end of the pericarp,
the deities on the exterior should then be worshipped in sequence, O leader of the gods.
The preceptor should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in the same manner as the worship.
He should likewise offer incense mixed with [fragrant substances] and ring the bell.
He should place various kinds of food offerings (*naivedya*) before the deity.
Then, with fragrant incense, garlands, and beautiful, sweet-smelling red flowers,
one should fill the foremost [vessel] with auspicious offerings such as fish, meat, and other meats.
One should offer three kinds of food offerings (naivedya): those with pieces of sugarcane and sugar, as well as milk-pudding (pāyasa), kṛsara, and other dishes mixed with curd, milk, and ghee.
These excellent mixed offerings, along with sweetmeats (laḍḍukas) and fried cakes (vaṭakas), should be presented.
One should offer *pūrikās* together with *ghārikās* as a food offering (*naivedya*) with devotion.
Then, O Goddess, one should satisfy [the deity] without hesitation by means of the nectar of the left (*vāmāmṛta*), mixed with grape juice, liquor (*āsava*), rum (*sīdhu*), and honey (*madhu*).

One should offer the beverage of *kavira* to the Goddess, which bestows great good fortune, as well as the divine *caru* produced from the forest of Mahālakṣmī. Then, having asked the Mistress of the Gods, the Sovereign of the Suras, for forgiveness with the eight-limbed prostration (*aṣṭāṅga*), [one should conclude].
One should begin the recitation (japa) before the Goddess with a large conch-shell rosary.
One should visualize [the deity] below the navel as having a terrifying countenance, blazing,
resembling a thousand rays, and possessing a splendor equal to twelve suns.
The glorious one, possessing five faces, is endowed with a clockwise curl;
one should contemplate the central face as a great, terrifying flame,
resembling pure crystal and possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns.
Then one should meditate on it as it goes out; this is called the "Garland of Syllables. It is led upward in sequence as far as the three auspicious fists.
O fair-eyed one, one should perform the recitation residing within the vital breath (*prāṇa*), slightly audible.
O Great Goddess, this recitation bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
any other syllables that may be mentioned grant neither accomplishment nor the means to it.
Therefore, O fawn-eyed one, it should be kept secret with every effort.
"From speaking [of this], O Goddess of the gods, a great loss ensues.
Thus ends the chapter on the sacrifice of Mahālakṣmī, in the fourth hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the twenty-four thousand [verse] compendium.

Henceforth, O Mistress of the Gods, listen with one-pointed attention to this most formidable secret, the Abode of the Mothers (Mātṛkālaya), which is prescribed to be remembered at the conclusion of the worship:
it is circular, measuring one cubit, and provided with eight lotus petals.
In a secluded and meditative place, one should have an excellent sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed.
Facing north and adorned with all ornaments,
one should [recite] "Nityasetu Mahālakṣmī Svāhā" conjoined with the Praṇava (Oṃ).
Having meditated upon the deities as before, one should cast each flower individually.
One should sequentially display the mudrās and address them with a most cordial welcome.
Just as the worship of the maṇḍala is performed, so indeed should it be arranged within the fire.
One of clear intellect should worship the seat of the womb in the heart. At the location of the tongue, one should contemplate the crest-lock (śikhā) and cast a flower for each.
One should protect with the armor-mantras in the directions starting from the southeast, and deploy the weapon-mantra.

One should place the eye in the center and join the head at the crown. O Dear One, those sixteen previously mentioned Mothers of Space (Ākāśamātṛs) should then be meditated upon as wandering there, O Ambikā, as the hosts of Sūryāvarta.
Furthermore, there are thirty-two secret Mothers (Guhyamātṛs) whose form is space;

they should be meditated upon as the "Moon-whirlpools" by one desiring to conquer worldly enjoyment and liberation. Having gone there, he should bring Mahālakṣmī, the forest, and the sacrificial animal.
Anointed with sandalwood and smeared with saffron from Kashmir,
adorned with garlands and strings of flowers, and consecrated by Mahālakṣmī—
one should utter three *phetkāra*s while recollecting Mahālakṣmī.
Taking up a sharp scissor and consecrating it with the Heart Mantra,
the one of great intelligence, having placed the corpse face upwards, should recite [the mantra].
When the form trembles and emits great roars, [success is attained].
Then, having seized that skull, the practitioner should mount the seat;
seated upon that seat, he should again [recite] the mantra...
Having reduced the body to pieces, the practitioner,
possessed by the *guḍuka* spirits and with a heroic mind, should perform the rite.
The mantrin should offer as a sacrifice the remains of the bones, as well as the *bali* offering, to the two leaders of the gods.
O Bhairavī, one should cause [the disciple] to swallow bone, marrow, and rice mixed with water;
then, with a great roar, one should utter the "pānuja" mantra, which accomplishes the divine mind and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O lady of virtuous vows, listen as I describe the signs that appear at the end of the roar:
a great rain, the gathering of great birds,
the falling of meteors, the burning of the quarters, and the terrible trembling of the earth and the destruction of animals.
Those who know the mantras must not break the [line] in the middle, like a web of semen.
Filled with the great nectar, one should offer the auspicious full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Then the Mistress of the Night, Vaiśvarināyikā, arrives from the presence of the Goddess.
Some had eyes wide open, some had smiling faces;
some had the faces of boars, and some auspicious ones had the faces of dogs.
Some had come from the netherworld (pātāla), accompanied by the daughters of Mura.
Some were the mistresses of Ṛkṣakarṇī, while others had the auspicious faces of lions;
one was seen weeping, another bore a *khaṭvāṅga* staff;
one stood naked, and another was tormented by the fire of passion.
Some held tridents in their hands, possessed three eyes, and were marked by the bull;
others were known as those holding mandāra flowers, having ascended the path to heaven;
still others were habituated to ringing bells and were proud of their beauty and charm.
Some had their hands raised with spears, while others stood with shaven heads;
numbering many hundreds of thousands, they approached by the will of another,
emitting a great roar and terrifying the ten directions.
One should not be afraid, O lady of excellent limbs; [this is] a favor comparable to a boon.
Placing his knees upon their joined eyebrows, he should cause the arghya offering to be presented to them.
O Goddess, one should offer the *caruka* and cause them to receive their share.
Thereby they grant sovereignty over the earth; at the end, there is the perfection of the *piṇḍa*.
Even by mere remembrance, the attainment of the qualities such as *aṇimā* arises.

O Goddess, by the mere remembrance of this, prosperity shall extend to seven generations. O Great Goddess, through a hundred thousand recitations (*japa*), and likewise through the supreme fire-oblation (*homa*),
or by offering oblations of lotuses, bilva fruits, and *śrīphala* fruits, Mahālakṣmī increases.
O Bhairavī, O highly fortunate one, she who is eternally established upon the chest of Viṣṇu, as well as that of Brahmā and Śakra, is Lakṣmī;
such indeed is this [goddess] for the practitioner, without a doubt.
The initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*abhiṣeka*) must be performed as previously described and determined;
O Dear One, in this *samaya*, the special initiation (*viśeṣadīkṣā*) must always be performed.
Although in this great tantra no distinction of caste (*jāti*) exists, [the rites must still be observed].

Nevertheless, O fair-eyed one, at the commencement of initiation (dīkṣā), it indeed occurs that for those who have been initiated, there is no [distinction of] caste; rather, there is but a single caste, which is that of the Lord (Īśvara). Therefore, in the case of a special initiation, one should perform what is about to be described.
O slender-waisted one, the Brāhmaṇas should be initiated with the falling of the *ali* [liquor], the Kṣatriyas with the water of the *śivā* [jackal],
the Vaiśyas with the drinking of sandalwood paste, and the Śūdras indeed with the ashes of Viśva;
and women should be initiated by the touch of the body of a hero.
Therefore, O lady worshipped by the lords of heroes, listen to the consecration ritual:
having brought eight virgins adorned with garments and ornaments,
their limbs smeared with sandalwood and aloe, and beautified with garlands and wreaths of flowers.
Anointed, honored, gratified, and composed,
they performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of those [mantras] upon their hearts and other limbs;
and with their own hands, their hair tied in braids, the young maidens performed the mutual placement for one another.
At the conclusion of the worship, O Dear One, one should worship nine jars,
having properly deposited the mantras extracted [from the root mantra] according to the ritual procedure.
One should assign the group beginning with Aruṇā there for the young maidens,
starting from the western direction and extending as far as the region of Nairṛta.
Having contemplated their names therein, one should perform the central sacrifice in the middle.
Then, one should visualize Mahālakṣmī upon the head and the surface of the earth.
O lady of excellent hips, the Guru should apply the mantras of those goddesses;
he should worship Lakṣmī with devotion and place the water-pot in her hand.

The ninth [finger] should be projected in sequence onto the hand of the disciple as before; by casting it and forming a circle, that which is nourished is established. O wise one, these nine joints exist according to this ritual procedure.
To whatever extent these tremblings gradually arise,
the practitioner becomes as if they were [the deity] held in their own hand.
Possessing the power to bestow both curses and grace, he shall become a giver of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
When authorized by the Guru, accomplishment is attained for the disciple. O Bhairavī, this supreme consecration of Mahālakṣmī, which bestows great good fortune,
should be kept secret from wicked beings and from atheists.
For the sake of those who merely desire knowledge, for the deceitful who live by hypocrisy and illusion,
and for those devoted to other systems, this radiant wisdom of Lakṣmī has been concealed everywhere; therefore, it is hidden from them.
O Bhairavī, it must be kept secret even from Guha, let alone anyone else.
A hero who has been consecrated and authorized, who has mastered wealth through Lakṣmī, may seek sovereignty over the earth; now hear of success in other sacred fields.
In which [lunar days] the practitioner of mantra attains perfection, by means of which one certainly obtains a kingdom—
whether it be the highest of the high, the middle, or likewise the high, O Dear One;
and in which ten [periods] success is achieved, whether it be the lowest of the high or the low.
O sinless one, the fivefold source of accomplishment consists of five types of mantras;
now listen, O Great Goddess, to that which is devoid of all nets of words.
The procedure for the complete accomplishment of kingship will be correctly explained [in the following].
[It concerns those born] on Mount Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śrīśaila, and the Vindhya mountain;
on the shores of the great ocean, on Mount Tugāra, and on the Himavat mountain.

O Great Goddess, these eight locations are for the accomplishment of sovereignty; they are known as the most excellent of the excellent, and I bow to them for the sake of prosperity. One should perform recitation (*japa*) in those places, for one will surely achieve success without doubt.
One sees Lakṣmī directly and shall certainly obtain consecration.
O Goddess of gods, I see all that upon the earth for such a man:
he is endowed with great good fortune and possesses great strength and prowess.

Now, what is the use of speaking at length? Listen to another [account] concerning the one called Uttama, who is like a second Śatakratu; it bestows the supreme kingdom. O Queen of the Gods, listen to the sacred sites themselves; I shall speak of another.
O Goddess praised by heroes, in Kaliṅga, Kāmarūpa, and Kuṅkaṇa;
in the land of Kaccha, at Pūrṇagiri, as well as in Magadha and Kāliñjara;
and in Devikoṭṭa, O Mahādevī, the highest attainments are likewise accomplished.
O beautiful one, the mantra-practitioner should recite a hundred thousand syllables in those places and perform oblations with the ten-fold ingredients combined with *mahāphalgu*.
There is no doubt that he will soon attain a lordship over men; of this there is no uncertainty.

By the power of the Earth, no obstructors arise for that sovereign of the mandala; she always stands at his gates. O Goddess of the gods, in the end he attains flight through the sky, and for him there is no destruction.
O Great Goddess, this Khecarī is supreme and bestows worldly enjoyment;
it is especially present at Prayāga, Varuṇa, Vārāṇasī,
Arvuda, Nepāla, and Ujjayinī, O Great Sovereign.
O Goddess of the gods, in the Aṭṭahāsa [cemetery], one attains middling accomplishment.
One should perform the recitation twice as much, adorned with mudrās and ornaments. (231b)
Devoted to sitting upon a human skull and consuming flesh at night, the hero who practices mantra attains success within six months and obtains [the desired fruit].
Then, the sound of "Victory! Victory! is heard, though the practitioner does not perceive it.
O Goddess, one shall obtain before [her] the stainless state of Śaṅkara.
In Jālandhara, in Kulūtā, and situated in the north at Urūśā,
she who resides in the Pīṭha that supports all bestows the command of authority.
One should perform the recitation threefold, endowed with the great vow;
as for the rite of oblation, it should be performed with meat mixed with guggulu.
After one year, there is the status of a lord of men, and at the end, the state of Śiva, free from all affliction.
O Goddess, praised by the ten [classes of] courtesans, [these places are] especially in Kāśmīra, Kanyakubja, Rājapurī, Mahātapa, Jayantī, as well as from the region of Lampāka, and in the forest.
And indeed, sovereignty is accomplished, which bestows great siddhi;
it is to be served by the host of Gocarīs and is presided over by Viṣṇu.
Adorned with the ornaments of Śrī, one should perform the recitation fourfold.
O Goddess, wearing a garland of skulls and always devoted to celibacy,
he constantly wanders through cremation grounds, smeared with great ashes.
There, without any hesitation, he worships the animal impaled upon the trident.
Wearing the garb of a madman and performing worship with the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*),
the lord of practitioners should, according to his desire, recite the mantra of Mahālakṣmī there in the terrible forest of Mahālakṣmī, which is fearsome with its four tusks.

The practitioner of mantra should offer meat combined with guggulu in ten parts; thus the practitioner attains the perfection of the *piṇḍa* and the certain state of liberation. However, one should avoid the auspicious *jaṃ* of Mahālakṣmī at the city gate.
O Goddess of gods, because all obstacles always arise there,
O fair-faced one, all the hosts of Śaktis become agitated there along with the Puṃs.

All [the forms], divine and non-divine, were immediately manifested by him whose mind was overcome with passion; they stood according to their actual state within the arrangement of the domestic crafts.
Beholding them, the eyes of the lord of practitioners rolled with power.
Their long eyes were darting and tossing with side-long glances;
their minds were agitated, and they moved slowly, reeling from intoxication.
Under the guise of the waves of their excellent hips, they caressed the pair of thighs.
Having abandoned shame, afflicted by the fire of passion and the sound of sighing,
and longing for the practitioner with very sweet words of affection, those women,
their faces deeply red with love, bestow the *Kaula* out of devotion upon him.
This has been concealed in all the scriptures by me in this *Pauruṣa-tantra*.
Therefore, one should not bestow this knowledge during the practice of the *Mahālakṣmī* sādhana;
O Goddess of the God of Gods, from such disclosure, a great disease arises.

Thus ends the chapter on the attainments of Mahālakṣmī and others, in the fourth Ṣaṭka of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the twenty-four thousand [verse] compendium. Now, O Goddess, I shall proclaim in due order and according to the truth that incomparable knowledge of Lakṣmī, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
O slender-limbed one, consciousness has been analyzed as being twofold in its division, which immediately produces conviction through its manifold distinctions;
O beloved, it is accompanied by the attainment of the yoga of consciousness and by rest.

O Goddess, consciousness, which arises from power, abides here in its own nature as the self through its own activity; its divisions are ordained by me. Abiding in manifold forms, it has attained both unity and multiplicity.
The [energies] are Kaivalyā, Vaindavī, Āmātvī, which consists of the *kalās*,
Sautikī, Cinmayī, Bhāvī, Jyotiḥ, and Apātmikī. (232b)
She who exists in various forms, the power that is the support of the universe, both supreme and non-supreme;
she is the Lakṣmī of consciousness, residing within the wheel of Lakṣmīs, for she is indeed the supreme Lakṣmī of light-rays.
She is the Lakṣmī of sound, the Lakṣmī of touch, the Lakṣmī of form, and the essence of taste.
The splendor of fragrance (*gandhalakṣmī*), the splendor of the mind (*manolakṣmī*), and the splendor of the ego of Brahmā (*brahmāhaṃkāralakṣmikā*)—
the formidable [Power] devours that object as it enters into its respective state of being.
Abiding within the rays of the Bhairava of Consciousness, she consists of intensely radiating beams of light.
Kaivalyā, Kevalā, and Śuddhā—these two are its attributes and its substrate.
Baindavī is of the nature of the *bindu* and bestows the union of the *kalās*.
That Goddess, traversing the path, is the sixfold Dārakī.
But having realized the path, O lady of excellent hips, she abides as the Self;
therefore, she should be known as the *tattva* when she possesses the nature of reality (*tattva-rūpiṇī*).
[She exists] through the relationship of support and supported, and by way of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper.

The supreme Śiva is the subject whose nature is the power of the object; like the object and the subject, he is consciousness consisting of pure awareness joined with the power of cognition. He alone, having grasped the stainless Lakṣmī who is established as everything, remains as such.
O Maheśvarī, she who is of the nature of the phonemes (varṇa) exists in fifty-three divisions.
From the phoneme comes Vāgīśvarī; therefore, O beloved, they know her then as the threefold [Vidyā].
When the circle of Kalās is consciousness (*caitanya*) within all things...

O highly fortunate one, listen as I shall tell you how a living being is liberated while still alive (*jīvanmukta*), O Maheśvarī: by means of the intellect and the latent impressions of the Self, one transcends the mass of passion (*rajas*) and the delusion of darkness (*tamas*) through truth and equanimity. Thus the creature is released.
Terrible, more terrible, and most terrible...
[is] the hundredfold enumeration of the *kalās*, which rests upon its own qualities.
Because it consists of elemental states, that *kalā* is peaceful yet joined with differentiation.
For all beings, [there is] equality...
[he] awakens them; of this there is no doubt.
From pure consciousness alone, that which is to be known and that which is yet to come must be understood; I shall now explain this.
That creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*) is it, and all existence is indeed that.
From that, all this [universe] proceeds for the sake of the Supreme.
Abiding in its own nature, free from appearance, it remains pervading the entire universe. Both [forms] are subtle and gross, possessing the form of shapes;
she is to be known as infinite and all-pervading, consisting of the reality of the substance.
O slender-limbed one, listen briefly to what is about to be said regarding the Light (*jyotis*).
Unobstructed by the multitude of sense organs and by tens of millions of mantras,
the supreme Light shines forth, illuminating everything on all sides.
The wise know that she is luminous, having withdrawn the senses from their objects; abiding in the midst of the lunar orb and remaining in a state of non-manifestation (amābhāva),
she is the primordial nourisher of the entire world, both mobile and immobile.
I shall fill the world with a supreme flood of nectar.
Then, the internal [nature] is to be known; what is its nature in terms of signs and knowledge?
The various distinctions have been explained as all-pervasive.
Just as oil resides in sesame seeds and clarified butter in milk,
so too does Mahālakṣmī abide within the sphere of the union of the principles (tattvasaṃdhāna). The supreme principle, the glory of the Self (ātmalakṣmī), and [Mahālakṣmī] do not leave one another.
This is remembered as the root of all that appears as both distinct and non-distinct.
One's own nature, which is sought through mental impressions, is to be understood through the dissolution of distinctions.
It brings about the offering of handfuls of flowers, the cleansing of the teeth, and the descent of the jar.

O Goddess, [the powers of] entering another's body, as well as the extraction of consciousness, the immobilization of form, likewise attraction, the removal of grey hair, the spreading [of healing], the moving of an image, and the possession of one's own self;
Satisfying, subjugation, causing enmity, paralyzing, and likewise killing; breaking spells, as well as bewildering, nourishing, satisfying, and pacifying.
Burning, parching, torment, paralysis, and the like constitute the continuous succession of fevers.
By means of the yoga of fixed meditation,
that which has been mastered by the practitioner becomes as pure and well-established as the meditation on crystal, arising from the most excellent object.
O Goddess of the gods, she enters that [body] and pervades it everywhere like the fiber of a lotus;
wherever she is directed, there she should be established.
O Maheśvarī, she is white, red, yellow, and black, yet by her radiance she is black.
It is like crystal and fire, yet it possesses the radiance of both snow and flame.
All this has been explained to you—the knowledge that fulfills all desires.
One who understands the investigation into the arising of prosperity is indeed liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O Goddess of the Gods, this should not be given to just anyone.
This doctrine of Mahālakṣmī was spoken by the one of divine form;
and from him, O Goddess of the Gods, it was received by the high-souled Śrīkaṇṭha.
Then Śukra obtained it from him;
from him, the self-controlled Vibhīṣaṇa received it, and he in turn offered it to Rāma.
Thereafter, I have related to you once more that which pertains to the other worlds.
Whether heard or recited, or being performed and experienced, they lead all beings to universal liberation; augmented by glory and splendor,
they bestow both perfection and liberation upon those subject to rebirth.
Thus, at the conclusion of the section on the bridegroom, Mahālakṣmī is proclaimed.
I do not see her equal anywhere within the Vidyāpīṭha.
In this supreme tantra, as many vidyās and mantras as have been cited [are contained therein].
To them, at that very moment, the Paramānandabhairava was spoken.
Thus, O fair-browed one, it has been declared by me at the conclusion of the Lakṣmīmata-maṇḍalatantra. What more shall I say now? Tell me, O Gaurī, what remains within your heart.
