(234a) Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of Mahālakṣmī in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the fourth hexad of the *Śiraścheda* section of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the stream of Bhairava.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Blessed One, we have a doubt; tell us that, O Destroyer of Tripura!
Regarding what has been proclaimed as the Bhairava named Paramānanda—
Since it has been proclaimed in this way that the goddesses are equal everywhere, O Blessed One, you should explain correctly what is indeed called "the beloved. Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O lady with a face like the full moon, to that which you have asked.
This is a supreme secret, most pure, and a destroyer of sins;
it has not been told to anyone, yet today I shall speak it.
At the conclusion of this most excellent king of tantras, there is the definitive teaching on the Joy of Bhairava.
Formerly, during the great festivals known as the Mahāyāga-vara-ḍambara, I was thoroughly satisfied by Bhairava; with a joyful soul, I am filled with the great family of supreme bliss.
Then, having projected the body of Śakti and expanded the Kula born of bliss,
he dances intensely at that time, situated in the midst of the bliss of light.
Meanwhile, from the wheel of Kula, there arises a great, resounding roar.
He arose, a form of great bliss, neither terrifying nor fearsome;
with rolling eyes, red and black in hue, with many feet and uplifted faces,
possessing many mouths and eyes, and slow with manifold wonders.
Endowed with many powers, filled with hundreds of various musical instruments,
absorbed in hundreds of diverse styles, adorned with many ritual vessels,
its ground illuminated by the feet of the trembling heroes, and gladdened by supreme bliss.
It destroys the great sins, brings about the exhaustion of the sin of killing a Brahmin,
generates great good fortune, bestows the great siddhis,
causes the rise of great prosperity, and grants auspicious success.
"Flow forth supreme bliss, the infinite essence from the very core!
O Goddess of Gods, having perceived this, I then became hungry.
O Maheśvarī, together with all the veils (*āvaraṇas*) and the powers (*śaktis*),
one should then satisfy the god Paramānandabhairava, O Goddess.
I shall explain that wonderful king of hymns (*stotrarāja*) accordingly.
Homage to you who assume the form of Bhairava;
homage to me, O embodiment of all the Ṛṣis!
Homage to you, who are supported by hundreds of powers (śaktis)!
Homage to you, who are eternally intoxicated with pride!
Homage to you, who have arisen from the station of Śakti! Homage to you, the Lord whose gait is that of a swan!
Homage to you, the one who transcends the family of the wheel; homage to you, who transcends the hundreds of channels.
Homage to you, the supreme of all families.
Homage be to you who dwell between the enemies of the left;
homage be to you who are adorned with all ornaments; homage be to you, O Lord Mātaṅga-gabhasti!
Homage to the one situated in the center of Maṇḍaleśvara;
homage to the one established upon all sacred seats (pīṭhas);
homage to the one situated in the center of Harṣeśvara.
Homage to the one who assumes the form of eternal festivity!
Homage to the great Kula of throbbing Great Bliss, the central wheel within the fire-drill of desire!
Be gracious to me quickly, O God, O Lord of the best of sages; grant me this body in the form of the king of mercury (rasarāja),
by which [I may master] the entire fierce circle of Bhairavas.
There exists that which is the most excellent even among the lords of yogis, by which the entire power of mantra is fully satisfied;
it stands as the very embodiment of the Yoginīs themselves.
"O Goddess, since I have thus performed this rite here,
which is the most excellent among all the six flavors;
having heard this, the Lord of Gods, Bhairava, was pleased with me."

O Goddess of the lords of gods, I have received that supreme nectar— the highest form of the essence of flowing fluids, whose nature is to liquefy one's own being— which consists of the state of the falling drop and resides within the portion of the *khādyaka* of the three sections.
The eighty-one throbbing vital points (*marmas*) were satisfied as the lords of the wheels; thereafter,
all the powers (*śaktis*), their forms now complete, burst forth.
Then Mahākālī was fully propitiated in her supreme form;
assuming the form of Bhairava, she became one with the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa).
Then that Bhairava-form became the most excellent of all circles (cakras).
The concealed state, which is the dissolution of the universe, is filled with stages such as Ānanda;
it is the multitude of tens of millions of ages, exalted by my own form.
Then, through the application of Kula and Akula, that tumultuous state becomes pacified.
Then, O Bhairavī, that Supreme Bliss-Bhairava was increased by the goddesses and Śaktis through thousands of austerities.
From that time forth, that Lord became the one who satisfies all mandalas.
It is the supreme nectar that illuminates all families of mantras.
O Maheśvarī, for one by whom it is smelled, heard, seen, drunk, or touched,
it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and sets in motion all spiritual accomplishments.
The entire great mantra family stands before him as a servant;
the hosts of yoginīs dwelling within the circle of all the Bhairavas praise him.
Intoxicated and exulting, he rejoices, sporting in the ocean of Bhairava.

O beautiful one, by merely taking it up, the excellent hero who possesses liberation shall become a partaker of enjoyment under the lord of wine. O passionate lady, there is nothing that would not be accomplished for the sovereign of practitioners.
By the power of the great liquor, one becomes manifest as Bhairava himself.
Whatever eighty-one wheels there are, and whatever their presiding goddesses may be— by satisfying them with the lord of liquor, one shall accomplish all goals, whether human or animal.
Now, what is the use of much speaking? It is explained in brief as follows:
Just as in the Bhairava-cakras, Śivabhairava is the leader.
Just as Kālāntakī is supreme among the multitude of divine assemblies (*devatācakra*),
so too is Rasendra the supreme leader among the lords of mercury (*rasendra*);
he should be known as the bestower of true prosperity and the granter of the fruits of all desires.
It should be known as the bestower of the accomplishment of the *piṇḍa* and the mastery of the great medicinal herbs;
everything proclaimed in the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyāga*) is accomplished by it with ease.
O Goddess, there is no purity of purpose without that Lord of Taste (*rasanāyaka*).
Therefore, for the purpose of neutralizing prohibited substances, one should perform this rite:
"In regions such as Himālaya and others, medicinal herbs have arisen;
may there be success regarding them for us, whether they be killed or consumed."
The mercury endowed with the "great seed" (mahābīja) attains a beautiful sound when bound.
Gold-mercury, silver-mercury, copper-mercury, and lead-mercury—
these are declared to be the "great seed," as well as khahaṃca and those consisting of uparasas.

O Goddess, when it has been processed and refined, it will possess the power of piercing a crore [of atoms]. Indeed, there are various kinds of *viṣṇukrāntā* and *kāñcanī* plants that are gathered by force;
others are yellow, red, or black, as well as the *padminī* that grows on dry land.
Mahāmedā, Somavallī, Nirguṇḍī, Lāṅgalī, Sarpākṣī, Kākajaṅghā, Rudatī, Mīnalocanā, Ekavīrā, Hanumatī, Kṣīrakākolikā, and likewise [others].
O illustrious one, such divine medicinal herbs as these have been described.
By the mere touch of them, the elemental spirits (bhūtas) will fall into bondage;
by means of which the practitioner, having colored his body with that power (bhūti), shall become a perfected master (sādhaka).
In the juice of *ghanāmbu* (Cassia fistula) and *khaṇḍā* (Piper chaba), along with the horn of a *bali* (buffalo) and *viṣā* (Aconitum heterophyllum),

one should place mercury (*sūtaka*) mixed with seeds into a woman’s menstrual flow. Having processed it with an eighth part of gold and other metals, it should be heated until it is thoroughly purified.
Place the impure [substance] into a lamp-mechanism together with very pure substances. When it is purified, apply it to the cooked molasses and the wick, while focusing the mind on the purification.

O Bhairava, one should perform fomentation (svedana) using whatever medicinal substances are available to eliminate the humors (doṣas). Thereafter, the procedures beginning with the seed-mantras (bīja) should be performed as prescribed.
Oil produced from Gandharva and other sources purifies the sacrificial offering (bali) at night.
Then, one should gradually join the pure [substance] with the number of sages (seven).
Immersed in pungent oil, that [substance] will always cause intoxication to blaze up.
O beloved, thereafter, for as many days as there are sages (seven days), one should kindle it with fire.
Taking [the substance] from the end of the *tedvajikā*-ball, perform it again in that same manner.
O highly fortunate one, when the sevenfold offering has been practiced for seven weeks and the mercury-king, hidden by the moon, has become digested;
Protected by thousands of great guardians,
he becomes as if born from a great fire;
place the cotton seeds and betel leaves there, having purified them in a crucible.
A mouth like a cloud [of smoke] shall arise; there, one should cast the *rāmī* powder.

Thus, by means of the three [substances], the application of the withered leaf is performed. When the piercing (*vedha*) has been accomplished, it is declared to be supreme; and when processed (*sārita*), it is [effective] thousands of times.

O Goddess, having traversed by the sequence of two and three through the middle of the *koṭi* at the junction of the four fires, the vital breath is drawn into the heart; this bestows the perfection of the *piṇḍa*.
The lord of practitioners becomes equal to Sadāśiva—of this there is no doubt.
Thus, these two excellent essences grant the accomplishment of happiness and good fortune;
for the complete attainment of the goals of human life and so forth, one should practice nothing else,
O slender-waisted lady, except for the eightfold discipline (yama) prescribed therein.
By performing this, the lord of practitioners attains perfection as one who is thoroughly accomplished.

Thus, I have explained to you in its entirety, according to the *Tantrarāja*, the whole of the secret essence—the stainless core, shining with lofty splendor, bearing the luster of a multitude of rays from great and radiant jewels. Now, O Kulāraṇi, contemplate this mantra.
It is proclaimed as the one that brings forth what has been ripened for me, bestowing all intended objects;
it is situated upon the earth of jewels, free from all barrenness, and is said to grant the accomplishment of the most excellent jewel of all states of being.
Having heard this, both that queen and King Jayadratha fell like a staff at the feet of Hara;
then the entire earth trembled, and the sky-dwellers clapped their hands.
All the kettledrums resounded and the world became filled with joy.
With various kinds of hymns, the Goddess gratified the Supreme Lord;
Jayadratha also gratified him in this way with piteous prayers.
Then the Goddess, exceedingly thrilled and deeply satisfied in mind,
danced with great joy the dance of the God of gods, which was radiant with its outstretched movements;
it was whirled about, brilliantly glowing, intensely blazing, and yet not sluggish.
The Queen of the Gods, accompanied by Lāsya, and King Jayadratha,
filled with the bliss of great joy, did not even look at the wielder of the Pināka bow;
instead, he spoke to them both regarding an excellent agreement for the sake of protecting the Tantra.
O King of Men, praised by the Lord of Devas,
this supreme Tantra— worthy of being protected like the garland of Hara— is exceedingly difficult to obtain and is the foremost of all lineages.
One should never even properly utter the name of this most excellent army of a hundred lords of Siddhas;
my Tantra is a secret, as are the hoards of cattle, land, and gold, as well as the mounts.

Having bestowed upon his disciple the Geya, Vidā, and a multitude of attendants, as well as the unsurpassed domestic ritual (*gṛhya*) and the supreme *Jayadratha-tantra*— which is honored by the lords of the thirty gods—
the two of them, their limbs thrilled with joy, heard this nectar-like speech from the lotus-face of the Supreme Lord.
By the command of the king of gods, the two then departed, and the king returned once more to his own abode.
He was being honored by hosts of gods and siddhas, as well as by yoginīs and heroes; he was being celebrated by throngs of excellent cāraṇas and likewise cherished by the hosts of Apsarases.
Then the Goddess, who is worshipped by all the lords of the gods, took hold of him and made him her own;
having embraced and pressed him again and again, Maheśa drank from her breasts and her lower lip.

Then the best of gods, who is worshipped by all the lords of the deities, being pleased with her and being the bestower of all perfections, placed the host of the crowns of the world upon the jewel mounted on his own crest.
Thus [ends] the fourth hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraścheda* of the Vidyāpīṭha in the stream of Bhairava.
This is the chapter on the accomplishment of the two rasas in the ritual of Mahālakṣmī.
This *Jayadrathāvatāra*, consisting of the sixfold mudrās, is completed.
It was [composed] in the year of the Naimisha era, in the ocean of one taste (1601), during the bright fortnight of Caitra, on the lunar day designated as the pair (the second).
On the day of Mars during the month of Turaṅgama (Aśvina), Kutu composed the Jayadrathatantra.
Śrī Kālidāsa, the preeminent among the twice-born, joined him in truth; and Kutu, endowed with effort, [composed it] for the sake of the fame of the son of Bhṛgu (Śukra).
In the year 792, on the second day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, under the Aśvinī nakṣatra, on a Tuesday, the astrologer Kutu completed this work.

This collection by the illustrious Kālidāsa was composed for the pleasure of the Lord Śiva, the consort of the illustrious Bhavānī. May this Tantra, compiled by Kālidāsa, lead to the joy of both [parents].
By the merit of this [work], may [the author’s] father attain liberation.
